Approved convention

This page is the canonical sample for lab code blocks. Terminal chrome (dark panel) versus file chrome (green filename bar) is the site-wide standard. Hard-refresh if styles look stale.

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text: Convention How it appears File to create Light panel + green filename bar (title="main.tf") Commands to run Dark terminal chrome (title="Terminal") — not the same as file blocks Expected output !!! example "Expected output" admonition Long files Optional linenums="1" (shown once below) Always tagged No bare fences

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Apply a tiny Docker Terraform stack and prove the container with CLI evidence — using the new code-block conventions.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Terraform CLI ≥ 1.5
  • Docker Engine running

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-labs/sample-code-blocks && cd ~/rebash-labs/sample-code-blocks

Runtime: local Docker Engine + kreuzwerker/docker provider.

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: A platform engineer is onboarding a disposable lab pattern: create config as files (not heredocs), run a short terminal session, and prove success with a clear expected-output panel — the same shape learners should see in production interview prep labs.

docs.title: Task 1 – Author provider and network
docs.text:
Create the provider pin and a bridge network.

versions.tf
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"
  required_providers {
    docker = {
      source  = "kreuzwerker/docker"
      version = "~> 3.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "docker" {}
main.tf
resource "docker_network" "lab" {
  name   = "rebash-sample-net"
  driver = "bridge"
}

resource "docker_image" "nginx" {
  name         = "nginx:1.25-alpine"
  keep_locally = true
}

resource "docker_container" "web" {
  name  = "rebash-sample-web"
  image = docker_image.nginx.image_id

  networks_advanced {
    name = docker_network.lab.name
  }

  ports {
    internal = 80
    external = 18080
  }

  labels {
    label = "rebash.sample"
    value = "code-blocks"
  }
}

output "container_name" {
  value = docker_container.web.name
}

Initialise and apply:

Terminal
cd ~/rebash-labs/sample-code-blocks
terraform init
terraform apply -auto-approve
docker ps --filter name=rebash-sample-web --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}' | tee docker-ps.txt
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:18080/ | tee http-code.txt
grep -q rebash-sample-web docker-ps.txt
grep -q 200 http-code.txt

Expected output

  • terraform apply creates the network and rebash-sample-web
  • docker-ps.txt lists rebash-sample-web as Up
  • http-code.txt contains 200

docs.title: Task 2 – Prove labels (interview-style evidence)
docs.text:
Inspect the container label set by Terraform:

Terminal
cd ~/rebash-labs/sample-code-blocks
docker inspect -f '{{index .Config.Labels "rebash.sample"}}' rebash-sample-web | tee label.txt
grep -q code-blocks label.txt
terraform output -raw container_name | tee output-name.txt
grep -q rebash-sample-web output-name.txt

Expected output

  • label.txt is code-blocks
  • output-name.txt is rebash-sample-web

docs.title: Task 3 – Optional: long file with line numbers
docs.text:
Use line numbers only when a file is long enough that reviewers discuss specific lines (example shape — do not require this file for the lab):

compose.example.yaml
# Example only — illustrates linenums on longer artefacts
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.25-alpine
    ports:
      - "18080:80"
    labels:
      rebash.sample: code-blocks
  # …
  # (truncated in real labs; linenums help when walking line 12 in review)

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• docker ps shows rebash-sample-web
  • HTTP check returns 200
  • Label and Terraform output match
  • Filename titles appear above file fences; Terminal title appears on command fences
  • Expected output uses green/example admonitions, not plain bold text alone

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Cannot connect to Docker Daemon not running Start Docker Desktop / dockerd Port 18080 in use Another local service Change external port in main.tf and re-apply Provider not found Skipped init Run terraform init again

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text: Add an output network_name and prove it with terraform output plus docker network ls.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• File fences carry title="filename" so copy targets are obvious
  • Terminal fences stay short and labelled
  • Success criteria sit in an Expected output admonition
  • Lab still does real apply / proof / cleanup

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-labs/sample-code-blocks
terraform destroy -auto-approve
rm -f docker-ps.txt http-code.txt label.txt output-name.txt

Expected output

Terraform reports destroy complete; docker ps -a --filter name=rebash-sample-web is empty.

docs.title: Authoring cheat sheet (for reviewers)
docs.text:
Create `main.tf`:

```hcl title="main.tf"
resource "docker_network" "lab" {
  name = "rebash-sample-net"
}
```

``` {.bash .ra-terminal title="Terminal"}
terraform apply -auto-approve
```

!!! example "Expected output"
    Apply succeeds; resource exists.

Do not use **Expected output:** as the only success signal once this convention is approved. Do not put multi-line files inside cat <<EOF heredocs.

docs.title: Lab Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: Write a package installer that is safe to re-run and works across apt/dnf family labs.

Scenario: Bastion images need curl, jq, and git pre-installed. Manual installs drift between Ubuntu and RHEL clones.

Expected outcome: A working script under ~/rebash-lab-shell with clear exit codes, stderr logging, and validation steps you can re-run.

This is a lab, not a tutorial

Apply Shell Scripting skills. Prefer small verified steps over rewriting everything at once.

docs.title: Business Scenario
docs.text: Platform wants a bootstrap script for lab VMs: detect the package manager, install a package list, and skip packages already present.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Detect apt vs dnf/yum
  • Install packages idempotently
  • Support --dry-run and a package list file
  • Fail clearly when the OS is unsupported

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
• Linux Admin Automation
  • Production Shell Scripting
  • Error Handling, Logging, and Debugging

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Tool Notes Bash required apt or dnf lab package manager sudo for real installs

Estimated cost: £0.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Ubuntu or Fedora/RHEL-like lab VM.

docs.title: Initial State

Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-shell/bootstrap
cd ~/rebash-lab-shell/bootstrap
printf '%s\n' curl jq git > packages.txt

docs.title: Task 1 — Detect package manager
docs.text:
detect_pm() {
  if command -v apt-get >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo apt
  elif command -v dnf >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo dnf
  elif command -v yum >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo yum
  else echo unsupported; return 1
  fi
}

docs.title: Task 2 — Build install-packages.sh
docs.text:
• Read packages from packages.txt or arguments
  • --dry-run prints planned actions
  • Skip packages already installed (dpkg -s / rpm -q)
  • Log to stderr

docs.title: Task 3 — Validate
docs.text:
./install-packages.sh --dry-run
# On a disposable VM only:
# sudo ./install-packages.sh
command -v curl
command -v jq || true

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Unsupported OS exits non-zero with a clear message
  • Dry-run never modifies the system
  • Second run skips already-installed packages
  • Package list file is supported

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Possible cause Resolution apt-get update slow/fails Mirror or network Retry; document offline labs Permission denied Not root Use sudo or dry-run jq not found after install Wrong package name on distro Map package names per PM

Terminal

docs.title: Stretch Goals
docs.text:
• Add a --dry-run mode that prints actions without changing the system
  • Emit a machine-readable RESULT status=... line on stdout for CI
  • Schedule the script with cron or a systemd timer

docs.title: Production Discussion
docs.text: In production, wrap scripts with lock files, structured logging, explicit PATH, and documented exit codes. Prefer configuration files over hard-coded hosts and thresholds. Never embed secrets in scripts — use environment variables or a secrets manager.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use #!/usr/bin/env bash and set -euo pipefail
  • Quote every expansion that may contain spaces
  • Log diagnostics to stderr; keep stdout for data
  • Prefer absolute paths in scheduled jobs
  • Validate inputs before destructive actions

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens Correct approach Unquoted paths Habit from interactive shell Always "$var" Missing pipefail Default Bash pipeline behaviour set -o pipefail Interactive-only PATH Cron/systemd minimal env Set PATH= at top Skipping dry-run Time pressure Default to dry-run for risky ops

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• Script runs under Bash with strict mode
  • Validation and failure paths are tested
  • Exit codes are documented
  • Cleanup leaves no lab artefacts (or documents what remains)

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Use SSH BatchMode and ConnectTimeout
  • Iterate hosts from a file
  • Capture per-host exit status
  • Never embed passwords; use keys

mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-shell/ssh
cd ~/rebash-lab-shell/ssh
printf '%s\n' '127.0.0.1' > hosts.txt

Use BatchMode=yes so missing keys fail fast instead of password prompts.

ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 127.0.0.1 'uptime' || true

Scenario: Nightly application data under /var/tmp (lab stand-in) must be archived with a 7-day retention policy.

docs.text: A small product team still runs pets. They need a boring backup script before object-storage backups land.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:

  • Create timestamped tar archives
  • Apply retention (delete older than N days)
  • Use mktemp, trap, and flock
  • Log success/failure with exit codes

docs.text:
• Linux Admin Automation

docs.text:
Tool Notes Bash required tar required flock util-linux find coreutils

mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-shell/backup/{data,backups,logs}
cd ~/rebash-lab-shell/backup

printf 'nested\n' > data/nested.cfg

docs.title: Task 1 — Backup script skeleton
docs.text: Create backup.sh that archives data/ into backups/data-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar.gz.

docs.title: Task 2 — Add trap and staging
docs.text: Stage files in mktemp -d, trap cleanup on EXIT INT TERM, then move the archive into backups/.

docs.title: Task 3 — Retention
docs.text: Delete archives older than --retain-days (default 7) using find ... -mtime.

docs.title: Task 4 — Locking
docs.text: Use flock on backup.lock so overlapping cron runs do not corrupt archives.

docs.title: Task 5 — Validate
docs.text:
./backup.sh
./backup.sh --retain-days 0   # optional aggressive cleanup after creating a sample
ls -la backups/

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Archive exists and extracts cleanly
  • Trap removes temp directories even on interrupt
  • Second concurrent run is blocked or exits cleanly via flock
  • Retention deletes old archives as configured

docs.text: Symptom Possible cause Resolution flock missing Non-Linux environment Use a Linux VM Permission denied writing backups Wrong directory Stay under ~/rebash-lab-shell Empty archive Source path wrong Verify data/ before tar

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:

  • Create an executable Bash script with a correct shebang
  • Print host facts and separate stdout from stderr logs
  • Use exit codes meaningfully (0 success, 2 usage)
  • Run the script via ./script and bash script

docs.text:

  • Shell Fundamentals — Bash vs sh and Execution

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Tool Notes Bash 4.2+ bash --version coreutils hostname, date, uname

Estimated cost: £0.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Any Linux host or WSL2. Work under ~/rebash-lab-shell.

docs.title: Initial State
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-shell
cd ~/rebash-lab-shell

docs.title: Task 1 — Create the script skeleton
docs.text:
Create first-script.sh:

first-script.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# first-script.sh — host snapshot for REBASH lab
# Usage: ./first-script.sh [name]

NAME="${1:-operator}"
echo "Hello, ${NAME}" 
echo "host=$(hostname)" 
echo "date=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" 
echo "kernel=$(uname -r)" 
exit 0

Run:

Terminal
chmod +x first-script.sh

docs.title: Task 2 — Run and inspect exit codes
docs.text:
./first-script.sh
echo "exit=$?"
./first-script.sh Ada
bash first-script.sh

docs.title: Task 3 — Add usage and stderr logging
docs.text:
Update the script so that -h/--help prints usage to stderr and exits 2. Log a one-line note to stderr: log: starting snapshot.

# After editing:
./first-script.sh --help; echo "exit=$?"
./first-script.sh 2> first-script.log
cat first-script.log

docs.title: Task 4 — Compare Bash vs sh invocation
docs.text:
bash first-script.sh
sh first-script.sh || true
head -1 first-script.sh

Confirm the shebang selects Bash when executed as ./first-script.sh.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Script is executable and starts with #!/usr/bin/env bash
  • --help exits with code 2 and writes usage to stderr
  • Normal run prints host, UTC date, and kernel on stdout
  • You can explain the difference between bash script and ./script

docs.text: Symptom Possible cause Resolution Permission denied Missing execute bit chmod +x first-script.sh Wrong interpreter Executed with sh and Bashisms present Use ./ or bash; keep POSIX if targeting sh Empty hostname Restricted container hostname Fall back to uname -n

docs.title: Lab Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: Write a disk usage monitor suitable for cron.

Scenario: On-call wants a simple alert when any filesystem crosses 80% before the full monitoring stack is ready.

Expected outcome: A working script under ~/rebash-lab-shell with clear exit codes, stderr logging, and validation steps you can re-run.

This is a lab, not a tutorial

Apply Shell Scripting skills. Prefer small verified steps over rewriting everything at once.

docs.title: Business Scenario
docs.text: A startup runs a few VMs. They need a disk check script that exits non-zero when thresholds are breached.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Parse df output safely
  • Compare usage against a threshold
  • Emit human logs on stderr and RESULT on stdout
  • Exclude tmpfs/devtmpfs noise

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
• Linux Admin Automation
  • Text Processing in Shell Scripts
  • Control Flow — Conditionals

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Tool Notes Bash required df/awk coreutils

Estimated cost: £0.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Any Linux host.

docs.title: Initial State
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-shell/monitor
cd ~/rebash-lab-shell/monitor

docs.title: Task 1 — Implement check-disk.sh
docs.text:
Create check-disk.sh:

check-disk.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
THRESH="${1:-80}"
alert=0
while read -r use mnt; do
  use="${use%\%}"
  if (( use >= THRESH )); then
    echo "ALERT disk ${use}% on ${mnt}" >&2
    alert=1
  else
    echo "OK disk ${use}% on ${mnt}" >&2
  fi
done < <(df -P -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs | awk 'NR>1 {print $5, $6}')
if (( alert )); then
  echo "RESULT status=alert metric=disk"
  exit 2
fi
echo "RESULT status=ok metric=disk"
exit 0

Run:

Terminal
chmod +x check-disk.sh
./check-disk.sh 80
./check-disk.sh 1 || true

docs.title: Task 2 — Document exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 All filesystems under threshold 2 One or more alerts 3 Usage / parse error

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Script exits 0 on a healthy host with a high threshold
  • Low threshold forces exit 2 and RESULT status=alert
  • tmpfs mounts are excluded

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Possible cause Resolution df columns differ BusyBox df Use df -P Arithmetic errors Percent sign not stripped Strip % before (( ))

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
rm -rf ~/rebash-lab-shell

docs.title: Stretch Goals
docs.text:
• Add a --dry-run mode that prints actions without changing the system
  • Emit a machine-readable RESULT status=... line on stdout for CI
  • Schedule the script with cron or a systemd timer

docs.title: Production Discussion
docs.text: In production, wrap scripts with lock files, structured logging, explicit PATH, and documented exit codes. Prefer configuration files over hard-coded hosts and thresholds. Never embed secrets in scripts — use environment variables or a secrets manager.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use #!/usr/bin/env bash and set -euo pipefail
  • Quote every expansion that may contain spaces
  • Log diagnostics to stderr; keep stdout for data
  • Prefer absolute paths in scheduled jobs
  • Validate inputs before destructive actions

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens Correct approach Unquoted paths Habit from interactive shell Always "$var" Missing pipefail Default Bash pipeline behaviour set -o pipefail Interactive-only PATH Cron/systemd minimal env Set PATH= at top Skipping dry-run Time pressure Default to dry-run for risky ops

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• Script runs under Bash with strict mode
  • Validation and failure paths are tested
  • Exit codes are documented
  • Cleanup leaves no lab artefacts (or documents what remains)

docs.title: Reflection Questions
docs.text:
1. What would break if this ran under /bin/sh (dash) instead of Bash?
  2. How would you make the script idempotent?
  3. How would you secure credentials and host inventories?
  4. How would you observe failures in production?

docs.title: Interview Connection
docs.text: Interviewers often ask about quoting, exit codes, cron environment differences, and how you prevent overlapping jobs. Be ready to walk through a small script and explain failure modes.

docs.title: Lab Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: Practise the Shell Scripting track under pressure — fix a deliberately unsafe ops script until it is schedulable.

Scenario: A nightly “cleanup” job has been emailing false successes, deleting the wrong paths when names contain spaces, and overlapping itself when cron drifts.

Expected outcome: A hardened script with set -euo pipefail, quoted paths, mktemp+trap, flock, stderr logging, and documented exit codes.

This is a lab, not a tutorial

Apply Shell Scripting skills. Prefer small verified steps over rewriting everything at once.

docs.title: Business Scenario
docs.text: On-call inherited cleanup.sh from a paste in Slack. It “works on my machine”, uses unquoted rm -rf $TARGET, ignores pipeline failures, and has no lock. You must ship a version safe for cron on a shared bastion.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Reproduce failures from unquoted expansions and missing pipefail
  • Add strict mode, logging helpers, and an exit taxonomy
  • Protect the job with flock and clean up with trap
  • Validate success and failure paths before scheduling

docs.text:
• Error Handling, Logging, and Debugging
  • Process Automation — Signals and Traps
  • Production Shell Scripting
  • Troubleshooting Shell Scripts

docs.text:
Tool Notes Bash 4.2+ bash --version flock util-linux (standard on Linux) mktemp coreutils

Estimated cost: £0.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Any Linux host or WSL2. Work under ~/rebash-lab-shell.

docs.title: Initial State
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-shell/{inbox,safe-target}
cd ~/rebash-lab-shell
printf 'x\n' > "inbox/my file.txt"
printf 'y\n' > inbox/keep.txt

docs.title: Broken script (starting point)
docs.text:
Create cleanup-broken.sh:

cleanup-broken.sh
#!/bin/bash
TARGET=$1
grep ERROR /var/log/syslog | wc -l
rm -rf $TARGET/*
echo SUCCESS

Run:

Terminal
chmod +x cleanup-broken.sh

docs.title: Step 1 – Reproduce the quoting bug
docs.text:
# DANGEROUS demo only inside the lab tree:
./cleanup-broken.sh ~/rebash-lab-shell/inbox || true
ls -la inbox || true

Recreate files if needed. Observe how spaces break the command.

docs.title: Step 2 – Rewrite with strict mode and quotes
docs.text:
Create cleanup.sh:

  • #!/usr/bin/env bash + set -euo pipefail
  • Require a target under $HOME/rebash-lab-shell
  • Refuse paths outside that prefix (realpath + prefix check)
  • Quote all expansions
  • Log to stderr; print RESULT status=... on stdout

docs.title: Step 3 – Add temp dir, trap, and flock
docs.text:
• mktemp -d for staging if needed
  • trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM
  • flock -n on ~/rebash-lab-shell/cleanup.lock (exit 0 if already running)

docs.title: Step 4 – Exit taxonomy
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 2 Usage / invalid path 3 Lock not acquired (optional alternate: 0) 4 Operational failure

docs.title: Step 5 – Validate
docs.text:
./cleanup.sh                           # expect usage -> 2
./cleanup.sh "$HOME/rebash-lab-shell/safe-target"
./cleanup.sh /tmp || echo "refused exit=$?"

Run two copies in parallel to confirm locking.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Broken behaviour understood (spaces / missing pipefail)
  • Hardened script uses strict mode and quoted paths
  • Prefix check blocks /tmp
  • Lock prevents overlap
  • Trap removes temp dirs

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix flock missing Install util-linux / use Linux VM realpath missing readlink -f on some distros trap not firing Ensure EXIT is included

docs.text:
Terminal
rm -rf ~/rebash-lab-shell

  • Compress rotated files with gzip
  • Enforce retention count
  • Avoid rotating an empty or missing file incorrectly

docs.text:

docs.text:
Tool Notes Bash required gzip required stat/find coreutils

Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-shell/rotate/logs
cd ~/rebash-lab-shell/rotate
# Grow a fake log
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('logs/app.log')
p.write_text('line\n' * 200000)
print(p.stat().st_size)
PY

docs.title: Task 1 — Write rotate-logs.sh
docs.text:
Arguments: --file, --max-bytes, --keep (default 5).

Behaviour:

  1. If file missing → exit 0 (nothing to do) or exit 2 if --strict
  2. If size < max → exit 0
  3. Else move to app.log.YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS and gzip
  4. Truncate/recreate original (or reopen-friendly rename pattern)
  5. Delete older compressed files beyond --keep

docs.title: Task 2 — Validate
docs.text:
./rotate-logs.sh --file logs/app.log --max-bytes 10000 --keep 3
ls -la logs/
./rotate-logs.sh --file logs/app.log --max-bytes 10000 --keep 3

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Large log is rotated and gzipped
  • Original log path exists after rotation
  • Only --keep compressed files remain
  • Small logs are left untouched

docs.text: Symptom Possible cause Resolution gzip: not found Minimal image Install gzip Race with writer App keeps FD open Document copytruncate vs rename; prefer proper logrotate in prod Too many files remain Glob/order bug Sort by mtime before deletion

docs.title: Lab — Build a User Management Script
Lab — Build a User Management Script
Lab Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: Build a small CLI that wraps safe user administration actions for a lab VM.

Scenario: Ops needs a scripted way to create service accounts with a consistent home layout — without pasting ad-hoc commands into Slack.

Expected outcome: A working script under ~/rebash-lab-shell with clear exit codes, stderr logging, and validation steps you can re-run.

This is a lab, not a tutorial

Apply Shell Scripting skills. Prefer small verified steps over rewriting everything at once.

docs.title: Business Scenario
docs.text: A SaaS team provisions short-lived lab users for contractors. Manual useradd steps drift. You automate create/list/disable with dry-run and audit logging.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Parse subcommands with case
  • Validate usernames before calling privileged tools
  • Log actions and refuse destructive ops without confirmation flags
  • Document an exit taxonomy for automation callers

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
• Linux Admin Automation
  • Functions, Parameters, and Locals

docs.text:

docs.title: Initial State
Task 1 — CLI skeleton
docs.text:
Create bin/usermgr.sh with subcommands: list, create, disable, and help:

Terminal
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
LOG_DIR="${LOG_DIR:-$HOME/rebash-lab-shell/users/logs}"
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"
log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" "$*" >>"$LOG_DIR/usermgr.log"; }

usage() {
  cat >&2 <<'USAGE'
Usage: usermgr.sh <list|create|disable|help> [options]
  create --user NAME [--dry-run]
  disable --user NAME [--dry-run]
USAGE
}

cmd="${1:-help}"; shift || true
case "$cmd" in
  help|-h|--help) usage; exit 2 ;;
  list|create|disable) ;;
  *) usage; exit 2 ;;
esac

Run:

Terminal
chmod +x bin/usermgr.sh

docs.title: Task 2 — Implement list
docs.text: Print local human users (UID >= 1000) using getent passwd and awk.

docs.title: Task 3 — Implement create (dry-run first)
docs.text: Accept --user and --dry-run. Validate ^[a-z_][a-z0-9_-]*$. In dry-run, print the useradd command; otherwise run sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash "$user" on a lab VM.

docs.title: Task 4 — Implement disable
docs.text: Lock the account with usermod -L / passwd -l (or print the command in dry-run). Log every action.

docs.title: Task 5 — Exit taxonomy
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 2 Usage / validation error 3 User already exists / not found 4 Privilege or system failure

docs.text:

docs.title: Lab Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: Practise the production Terraform loop used in pull requests: format, validate, save a plan, review it, apply that artefact, then destroy.

Scenario: Your platform team will not merge Infrastructure as Code (IaC) without a reviewed plan file. You must produce one for a small root module and prove apply matches the review.

Expected outcome: A lockfile committed locally, a binary tfplan you can show, successful apply of that plan, and a clean destroy.

This is a lab, not a tutorial

Concepts come from the Terraform track. Here you operate like CI: non-interactive flags and plan artefacts.

docs.title: Business Scenario
docs.text: A SaaS startup stores environment metadata as versioned files (feature flags, banner text, owners). They use Terraform with the hashicorp/local provider so engineers can rehearse plan review before touching AWS. Policy: no apply -auto-approve without a saved plan that passed review.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Author a pinned root module (required_version, required_providers, variables, outputs)
  • Run fmt, init, validate, and plan -out non-interactively
  • Read a plan and predict creates/updates before apply
  • Apply a saved plan file (not a live re-plan)
  • Destroy lab resources and leave no sensitive artefacts in Git

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
• Introduction to Terraform and IaC
  • Installing Terraform and the CLI Workflow
  • Variables, Locals, and Outputs
  • Terraform in CI/CD Pipelines

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Tool Notes Terraform CLI 1.9+ (1.15.x ideal) terraform version Git optional but recommended Network once to download hashicorp/local on first init

Estimated cost: £0 (local provider only). No cloud account required.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Any laptop or CI runner with Terraform installed. Work in an empty directory you can delete afterwards.

docs.title: Initial State
docs.text: Empty workspace. You will create the root module from scratch, then operate it as if a teammate must approve your plan.

docs.title: Task 1 — Scaffold the root module
docs.text:
Objective: Create a reviewable module layout.

Background: Production roots keep versions, variables, resources, and outputs in separate files for clearer pull request diffs.

Instructions:

Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-lab-tf-plan && cd ~/rebash-lab-tf-plan

cat > versions.tf <<'EOF'
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.9.0"

  required_providers {
    local = {
      source  = "hashicorp/local"
      version = "~> 2.9"
    }
  }
}
EOF

cat > variables.tf <<'EOF'
variable "project" {
  type        = string
  description = "Short project key used in filenames and tags"
  default     = "rebash"
}

variable "environment" {
  type        = string
  description = "Environment name"
  default     = "lab"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["lab", "dev", "staging"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be lab, dev, or staging for this exercise."
  }
}

variable "banner" {
  type        = string
  description = "Customer-facing banner text"
  default     = "Plan review before apply."
}
EOF

cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
locals {
  tags = {
    project     = var.project
    environment = var.environment
    managed_by  = "terraform"
  }
  artefact_path = "${path.module}/generated/${var.project}-${var.environment}-banner.txt"
}

resource "local_file" "banner" {
  filename        = local.artefact_path
  content         = <<-EOT
    project     = ${var.project}
    environment = ${var.environment}
    banner      = ${var.banner}
    tags        = ${jsonencode(local.tags)}
  EOT
  file_permission = "0644"
}

resource "terraform_data" "review_marker" {
  input = {
    lesson = "lab-terraform-plan-review-workflow"
    project = var.project
  }
}
EOF

cat > outputs.tf <<'EOF'
output "banner_path" {
  description = "Path of the managed banner file"
  value       = local_file.banner.filename
}

output "content_md5" {
  description = "MD5 of banner content"
  value       = local_file.banner.content_md5
}

output "review_marker" {
  description = "Lab marker stored in terraform_data"
  value       = terraform_data.review_marker.output
}
EOF

cat > terraform.tfvars <<'EOF'
project     = "rebash"
environment = "lab"
banner      = "Welcome to REBASH Academy labs."
EOF

cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
.terraform/
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
crash.log
tfplan
*.tfplan
EOF

Expected output

Files listed by ls include versions.tf, variables.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf, terraform.tfvars, .gitignore.

Validation:

Terminal
test -f versions.tf && test -f main.tf && echo "scaffold OK"

docs.title: Task 2 — Format, init, and validate (CI style)
docs.text:
Objective: Run the same checks a pipeline runs before planning.

Instructions:

Terminal
export TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1
terraform fmt
terraform init -input=false
terraform validate
terraform fmt -check

Expected output

Success! The configuration is valid. Lockfile .terraform.lock.hcl appears.

Validation:

Terminal
test -f .terraform.lock.hcl && terraform validate

docs.title: Task 3 — Create a saved plan artefact
docs.text:
Objective: Produce a binary plan for review — not an immediate apply.

Instructions:

Terminal
terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
terraform show -no-color tfplan | head -80

Expected output

Plan shows create for local_file.banner and terraform_data.review_marker. File tfplan exists.

Validation:

Terminal
test -f tfplan
terraform show -json tfplan >/dev/null && echo "plan readable"

Treat plan files as sensitive

Even local plans can embed variable values. Do not commit tfplan (already gitignored).

docs.title: Task 4 — Simulate pull request review
docs.text:
Objective: Practise reading the plan like a reviewer.

Background: Reviewers ask: unexpected destroys? wrong filenames? secrets in content?

Instructions: Answer these in your notes while reading terraform show tfplan:

  1. How many resources will be created?
  2. What filesystem path will Terraform write?
  3. What happens if you change banner after apply — update or replace?

Then introduce a deliberate surprise and re-plan:

Terminal
# Reviewer asks for a clearer filename — change local only after discussing
sed -i.bak 's/\${var.project}-\${var.environment}-banner.txt/\${var.project}-\${var.environment}-banner.v1.txt/' main.tf
# macOS/BSD sed used -i.bak; on GNU sed you may use sed -i

terraform fmt
terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
terraform show -no-color tfplan | head -60

Expected output

Plan still creates (fresh lab) or shows path change intent clearly.

Validation: You can explain whether the filename change is in-place update or replace for local_file.

Hint: local_file replaces when filename changes because the path is ForceNew-style behaviour for that argument.

docs.title: Task 5 — Apply the reviewed plan only
docs.text:
Objective: Apply the artefact, not a new live plan.

Instructions:

Terminal
terraform apply -input=false tfplan
cat generated/rebash-lab-banner.v1.txt 2>/dev/null || cat generated/rebash-lab-banner.txt
terraform output

If your sed path differs, ls generated/ and cat the file that exists.

Expected output

Apply completes; outputs print banner_path and checksums.

Validation:

Terminal
test -f "$(terraform output -raw banner_path)"
terraform output -raw content_md5 | grep -E '^[a-f0-9]{32}$'

docs.title: Task 6 — Drift awareness and destroy
docs.text:
Objective: See drift, then tear down cleanly.

Instructions:

# Simulate out-of-band edit
BANNER_FILE="$(terraform output -raw banner_path)"
echo "DRIFT" >> "$BANNER_FILE"
terraform plan -input=false

terraform destroy -input=false -auto-approve
rm -f tfplan

Expected output

Plan after drift proposes an update to restore content; destroy removes managed objects.

Validation:

Terminal
test ! -f "$BANNER_FILE"

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Check Pass criteria Pinning required_version and local ~> 2.9 present Lockfile .terraform.lock.hcl exists after init Plan artefact tfplan created before apply Apply Outputs resolve; banner file existed post-apply Hygiene .gitignore excludes state and plan files Cleanup Destroy removed managed files

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptoms Possible causes Resolution Verification Provider download fails Network/registry blocked Check access to registry.terraform.io terraform init validate fails before init Providers missing Run init first terraform validate Apply differs from review Re-planned instead of using -out Always apply tfplan Compare SHA of plan file in CI sed -i confusion GNU vs BSD sed Edit main.tf in your editor instead Re-run plan Permission denied under generated/ Directory not writable Ensure workspace is yours ls -ld .

docs.title: Challenge Extensions
docs.text:
• Split lab vs dev using terraform.tfvars files and -var-file
  • Add a terraform test file that asserts output paths
  • Encode the same workflow in GitHub Actions with plan artefact upload (see Terraform CI tutorial)
  • Move state to a remote backend once you leave local labs

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-lab-tf-plan
terraform destroy -input=false -auto-approve 2>/dev/null || true
cd ~
rm -rf ~/rebash-lab-tf-plan

No cloud spend — still delete state and plan files so secrets cannot leak from disk backups.

docs.title: Production Discussion
docs.text:
Production teams:

  • Store plans as CI artefacts with retention and access control
  • Separate plan and apply IAM roles (OIDC)
  • Require human approval on destroy and on unexpected replaces
  • Commit .terraform.lock.hcl; never commit *.tfstate*
  • Prefer remote state with locking and encryption before a second engineer joins

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1 and -input=false in every pipeline job
  • Reviewers read terraform show (or JSON plan) before approve
  • Keep modules small; this lab’s layout scales to cloud providers unchanged
  • Validation blocks catch bad environments early
  • Destroy labs completely — leftover state confuses the next exercise

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Why it happens Correct approach apply -auto-approve without -out Convenience Save and apply the reviewed plan Committing .terraform/ Large binaries Commit only the lockfile Putting secrets in banner / tfvars Demo haste Use placeholders; mark sensitive later Ignoring drift “It still works” Investigate every unexpected plan line

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
You can demonstrate:

  • A pinned root module with clear outputs
  • A saved plan you can explain line-by-line
  • Apply of that plan and proof via outputs
  • Full destroy and gitignore hygiene

docs.title: Reflection Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is applying a saved plan safer than re-running plan in the apply job?
  2. What belongs in Git for this root module on day one?
  3. How would remote state change your cleanup and locking story?
  4. How would you stop a plan that includes an unexpected destroy from reaching apply?

docs.title: Interview Connection
docs.text: Expect questions on plan vs apply, lockfiles, state sensitivity, and CI gates. Use this lab as a concrete walkthrough. Continue with interview prompts in the Terraform Interview Prep guide and Terraform in CI/CD Pipelines.

docs.title: REBASH Linux Mastery
docs.text:
Duration: 8–10 weeks · Lessons: ~145 · Labs / projects: 40+ planned · Capstones: 8

The most practical Linux course for Cloud, DevOps, Kubernetes, and Platform Engineers. Typical Linux courses stop at basic commands — this path trains production engineers.

How this course works

Modules build in order. Scaffolded lessons show structure and SEO; full tutorials (theory + lab + interview) publish as they are completed. Prefer Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 lab VMs.

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text: Beginners → Linux administrators → DevOps → Cloud → Platform / SRE engineers who need Linux that transfers to containers, CI/CD, and cloud operations.

docs.title: Learning roadmap
docs.text:
1. Fundamentals & shell — Modules 1–2
  2. Text, files, identity — Modules 3–5
  3. Runtime & packages — Modules 6–7
  4. Network & storage — Modules 8–9
  5. Automation & security — Modules 10–11
  6. Observability & DevOps — Modules 12–13
  7. Production & capstones — Modules 14–15

docs.title: Module 1 · Linux Fundamentals
docs.text:
Goal: Build a strong foundation for Cloud and DevOps Linux work.

Lab / project focus: Install Ubuntu Server and explore the filesystem.

# Lesson Level Status 1 Introduction to Linux Beginner Ready 2 Linux History and Open Source Beginner Ready 3 Linux Fundamentals — Distributions and Architecture Beginner Ready 4 Linux Kernel Explained Beginner Ready 5 Linux Desktop vs Server Editions Beginner Ready 6 Linux Installation (VirtualBox, VMware, WSL) Beginner Ready 7 Linux Boot Process Beginner Ready 8 First Login and Terminal Beginner Ready 9 Linux Directory Structure (FHS) Beginner Ready 10 Getting Help (man, info, --help) Beginner Ready — Module 1 Summary — Linux Fundamentals Beginner Ready

Module 1 complete

All ten Linux Fundamentals tutorials plus the Module 1 summary are published. Continue with Understanding the Shell (Module 2).

docs.title: Module 2 · Linux Command Line Essentials
docs.text:

docs.title: Access Control Lists (ACL) in Linux — Fine-Grained File Permissions
Access Control Lists (ACL) in Linux — Fine-Grained File Permissions
docs.text: Traditional Linux permissions allow access control for Owner, Group, and Others. However, in many real-world scenarios, you need to grant permissions to specific users or groups without changing ownership or creating new groups. Access Control Lists (ACLs) provide this fine-grained permission management and are widely used in enterprise Linux environments.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 4: File Management and Permissions → Lesson 7

Difficulty: Advanced

Reading Time: 55 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: File Management and Permissions

Lesson: 7 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Access Control Lists (ACLs)
  • Configure user-specific permissions
  • Configure group-specific permissions
  • Set default ACLs
  • View ACL entries
  • Remove ACLs
  • Troubleshoot ACL issues
  • Apply ACLs in production environments

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 Lessons 1–6

docs.title: Why Learn ACL?
docs.text:
Imagine a shared project directory.

project/

Owner:

alice

Group:

developers

Now you need to give Bob read-only access without:

  • Changing ownership
  • Changing the group
  • Giving everyone access

Traditional permissions cannot solve this.

ACLs can.

docs.title: What is ACL?
docs.text:
ACL stands for:

Access Control List

ACL extends standard Linux permissions by allowing:

  • Individual user permissions
  • Individual group permissions
  • Default permissions for new files

Think of ACL as an additional permission layer on top of the traditional Owner/Group/Others model.

docs.title: Traditional Permissions
docs.text:
Owner

Group

Others

docs.title: ACL Permissions
docs.text:
Owner

Group

Others

↓

Additional Users

Additional Groups

Default Permissions

docs.title: Verify ACL Support
docs.text:
Check filesystem mount options.

mount | grep acl

On most modern Linux distributions (such as Ubuntu, RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Debian, and SUSE), ACL support is enabled by default for common filesystems like ext4 and XFS.

You can also verify by creating a test ACL.

docs.title: Required Commands
docs.text:
ACL management uses:

getfacl

setfacl

Check availability.

which getfacl

which setfacl

If missing:

Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt install acl

RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux:

sudo dnf install acl

docs.title: View ACL
docs.text:
Create a file.

touch report.txt

View ACL.

getfacl report.txt

Output:

# file: report.txt

# owner: basha

# group: developers

user::rw-

group::r--

other::r--

Initially, ACL reflects the standard permissions.

docs.title: Grant Permission to a User
docs.text:
Give Bob read access.

setfacl -m u:bob:r report.txt

View:

getfacl report.txt

Output:

user::rw-

user:bob:r--

group::r--

mask::r--

other::r--

Bob now has read permission even though he is neither the owner nor necessarily in the owning group.

docs.title: Grant Read/Write Access
docs.text: setfacl -m u:bob:rw report.txt

docs.title: Grant Execute Permission
docs.text: setfacl -m u:bob:rwx script.sh

docs.title: Grant Permissions to a Group
docs.text: setfacl -m g:qa:r project.txt

docs.title: Remove an ACL Entry
docs.text:
Remove Bob's ACL.

setfacl -x u:bob report.txt

Verify:

getfacl report.txt

docs.title: Remove All ACL Entries
docs.text:
setfacl -b report.txt

This removes all extended ACL entries while leaving the standard permissions intact.

docs.title: Default ACLs
docs.text:
Suppose you have:

shared/

Every new file should automatically grant access to Bob.

Set a default ACL.

setfacl -d -m u:bob:rwx shared/

Verify:

getfacl shared/

Output:

default:user:bob:rwx

Now every new file created inside shared/ inherits this ACL.

docs.title: Recursive ACL
docs.text:
Apply ACL to an entire directory tree.

setfacl -R -m g:developers:rwx project/

docs.title: Copy ACL
docs.text:
Save ACLs.

getfacl project > acl-backup.txt

Restore ACLs.

setfacl --restore=acl-backup.txt

Useful during migrations and backups.

docs.title: Understanding the ACL Mask
docs.text:
Example:

mask::r--

The ACL mask defines the maximum effective permissions for:

  • Named users
  • Named groups
  • The owning group

Even if an ACL grants rwx, the effective permissions cannot exceed the mask.

View effective permissions:

getfacl report.txt

Look for entries marked with:

#effective:

docs.title: View ACL Indicator
docs.text:
Run:

ls -l

Example:

-rw-rw-r--+

Notice:

+

The plus sign indicates that extended ACL entries exist.

docs.title: Common ACL Commands
docs.text:
View ACL.

getfacl file.txt

Grant permission.

setfacl -m u:bob:rw file.txt

Remove user ACL.

setfacl -x u:bob file.txt

Remove all ACLs.

setfacl -b file.txt

Recursive ACL.

setfacl -R

Default ACL.

setfacl -d

docs.title: ACL vs Traditional Permissions
docs.text: Traditional Permissions ACL Owner, Group, Others Multiple users and groups One group only Multiple groups Simple Fine-grained Limited Flexible Default Linux permissions Enterprise environments

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Shared development directory.

setfacl -m g:developers:rwx project/

Grant QA read access.

setfacl -m g:qa:r reports/

Grant Jenkins access.

setfacl -m u:jenkins:rwx build/

Grant backup service access.

setfacl -m u:backup:r backups/

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
ACLs are widely used in:

  • Enterprise file servers
  • NFS shares
  • Samba shares
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Shared development environments
  • Application deployment directories
  • Backup systems

ACLs provide flexibility without changing ownership or reorganizing groups.

docs.text:
Create a file.

touch project.txt

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
View ACL.

getfacl project.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:

sudo setfacl -m u:bob:r project.txt

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:

getfacl project.txt

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:

sudo setfacl -x u:bob project.txt

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Create a shared directory.

mkdir shared

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Set a default ACL.

sudo setfacl -d -m u:bob:rwx shared

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Check the ACL.

getfacl shared

docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example getfacl View ACL Security audits setfacl -m Add/modify ACL Shared access setfacl -x Remove ACL entry Cleanup setfacl -b Remove all ACLs Reset permissions setfacl -R Recursive ACL Deployment directories setfacl -d Default ACL Shared workspaces

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A CI/CD pipeline fails because Jenkins cannot write to the deployment directory.

Investigation:

ls -l deploy/

getfacl deploy/

id jenkins

Permissions appear correct, but Jenkins is not the owner and is not in the owning group.

Solution:

sudo setfacl -m u:jenkins:rwx deploy/

The pipeline now has the required access without changing ownership or broadening permissions for other users.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use ACLs only when traditional permissions are insufficient.
  • Keep ACL configurations simple and well-documented.
  • Review ACLs regularly during security audits.
  • Use default ACLs for shared project directories.
  • Back up ACLs before large migrations.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting to verify the ACL mask.

✅ The mask may reduce effective permissions.

❌ Assuming chmod preserves ACL behavior.

✅ Changing standard permissions with chmod can modify the ACL mask and affect effective permissions.

❌ Using ACLs where normal groups are sufficient.

✅ Prefer the simplest permission model that meets your requirements.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • What ACLs are
  • Viewing ACLs
  • Adding and removing ACL entries
  • Default ACLs
  • Recursive ACLs
  • ACL masks
  • Enterprise use cases

ACLs extend Linux's traditional permission model by allowing fine-grained access control for individual users and groups. They are a powerful feature for enterprise environments where standard ownership and permission models are not flexible enough.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ACLs provide fine-grained permissions beyond Owner, Group, and Others.
  • Use getfacl to view ACL entries.
  • Use setfacl to add, modify, or remove ACLs.
  • Default ACLs are inherited by newly created files and directories.
  • The + in ls -l indicates extended ACLs.
  • Use ACLs when traditional permissions cannot meet your access control requirements.

docs.title: AppArmor — Application-Level Security in Linux
docs.text: AppArmor (Application Armor) is a Linux Security Module (LSM) that protects the system by restricting what applications are allowed to access. Instead of relying only on traditional Linux permissions, AppArmor uses security profiles to define which files, directories, capabilities, and network resources an application can use. If an application is compromised, AppArmor helps limit the damage by confining it to only the resources explicitly permitted by its profile. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand AppArmor to improve Linux system security.

docs.title: Why Learn AppArmor?
docs.text:
Imagine a web server is compromised.

Without AppArmor:

Web Server

↓

Compromised

↓

Access Entire System

With AppArmor:

Web Server

↓

Compromised

↓

Restricted by Profile

↓

Limited Damage

AppArmor helps contain attacks by limiting application access.

docs.title: What is AppArmor?
docs.text:
AppArmor is a Linux Security Module that enforces Mandatory Access Control (MAC) using application-specific security profiles.

It controls:

  • File access
  • Directory access
  • Network access
  • Linux capabilities
  • Process execution
  • Mount operations

Unlike traditional Linux permissions, AppArmor restricts what applications can do, even if they run with elevated privileges.

docs.title: How AppArmor Works
docs.text:
Application

↓

AppArmor Profile

↓

Allow or Deny Access

↓

System Resources

Every protected application follows its assigned security profile.

docs.title: AppArmor Profiles
docs.text:
A profile defines what an application is allowed to access.

Profiles typically include:

  • Allowed files
  • Allowed directories
  • Network permissions
  • Linux capabilities
  • Execution rules

Profiles are commonly stored in:

/etc/apparmor.d/

docs.title: Check AppArmor Status
docs.text:
Display status.

sudo aa-status

Example output:

AppArmor module is loaded.

Profiles are loaded.

docs.title: AppArmor Modes
docs.text:
Each profile operates in one of two primary modes.

Mode Description Enforce Blocks operations that violate the profile Complain Logs violations but allows the operation

docs.title: Enforce Mode
docs.text:
Applications must follow the profile.

Example:

Application

↓

Violation

↓

Access Denied

docs.title: Complain Mode
docs.text:
Useful for testing.

Example:

Application

↓

Violation

↓

Logged Only

↓

Application Continues

docs.title: View Loaded Profiles
docs.text:
sudo aa-status

Displays:

  • Loaded profiles
  • Enforced profiles
  • Profiles in complain mode
  • Unconfined processes

docs.title: Enable Enforce Mode
docs.text: sudo aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.man

docs.title: Enable Complain Mode
docs.text:
sudo aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.man

Useful when testing new applications.

docs.title: Disable a Profile
docs.text:
sudo ln -s /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.man \
/etc/apparmor.d/disable/

Reload AppArmor afterward.

docs.title: Reload Profiles
docs.text:
sudo systemctl reload apparmor

or

sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/profile_name

docs.title: Common AppArmor Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Solution Disabling AppArmor unnecessarily Keep it enabled whenever possible Leaving profiles in complain mode Return to enforce mode after testing Ignoring AppArmor logs Review logged violations Forgetting to reload profiles Reload after making changes Applying overly permissive profiles Follow the principle of least privilege

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A newly deployed application cannot read its configuration file.

Linux permissions:

Correct

Application still fails.

Investigation:

sudo aa-status

The application is confined by an AppArmor profile that does not permit access to the configuration directory.

Solution:

  1. Review AppArmor logs.
  2. Update the application's profile.
  3. Reload the profile.
sudo systemctl reload apparmor

The application now operates correctly while remaining confined by AppArmor.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep AppArmor enabled on supported systems.
  • Run production profiles in Enforce mode.
  • Use Complain mode only for testing and troubleshooting.
  • Review AppArmor logs regularly.
  • Reload profiles after making changes.
  • Follow the principle of least privilege.
  • Test profile changes before deploying them to production.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Disabling AppArmor to work around configuration problems.

✅ Avoid disabling AppArmor to work around configuration problems; fix the configuration instead.

❌ Leaving production profiles in complain mode.

✅ Do not leave production profiles in complain mode.

❌ Ignoring AppArmor log messages.

✅ Always review AppArmor log messages.

❌ Creating overly permissive profiles.

✅ Avoid this mistake: creating overly permissive profiles.

❌ Forgetting to reload profiles after modifications.

✅ Remember to to reload profiles after modifications.

AppArmor strengthens Linux security by confining applications to well-defined security profiles. Even if an application is compromised, AppArmor helps prevent it from accessing unauthorized system resources, reducing the impact of attacks and improving overall system security.

docs.title: Key Takeaways

docs.title: APT (Advanced Package Tool) — Package Management in Debian and Ubuntu
APT (Advanced Package Tool) — Package Management in Debian and Ubuntu
docs.text: APT (Advanced Package Tool) is the default package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and many Debian-based Linux distributions. It simplifies installing, updating, upgrading, removing, and managing software packages while automatically resolving dependencies. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) working with Ubuntu or Debian systems uses APT daily.

docs.title: Why Learn APT?
docs.text:
Imagine you need to install:

  • Docker
  • Git
  • NGINX
  • Kubernetes Tools
  • Python
  • Java

Instead of downloading software manually from websites,

Linux allows you to install trusted software using:

apt

APT automatically:

  • Downloads packages
  • Resolves dependencies
  • Installs required libraries
  • Verifies package integrity
  • Keeps software updated

docs.title: What is APT?
docs.text:
APT stands for:

Advanced Package Tool

It is a package management system that works with .deb packages.

APT communicates with online software repositories to install and manage applications.

docs.title: Package Management Workflow
docs.text:
APT Command
      │
      ▼
Package Repository
      │
      ▼
Download Package
      │
      ▼
Resolve Dependencies
      │
      ▼
Install Software
      │
      ▼
Ready to Use

docs.title: What is a Package?
docs.text:
A package is a compressed file that contains:

  • Application binaries
  • Libraries
  • Configuration files
  • Documentation
  • Metadata

Example:

nginx_1.24.0_amd64.deb

docs.title: Update Package Index
docs.text:
Before installing software, refresh the local package index.

sudo apt update

This downloads the latest package information from configured repositories.

Note

apt update updates the package index, not the installed software.

docs.title: Upgrade Installed Packages
docs.text:
Upgrade all installed packages.

sudo apt upgrade

Example:

25 packages upgraded

docs.title: Full System Upgrade
docs.text:
Upgrade packages and allow installation or removal of packages if required to satisfy dependencies.

sudo apt full-upgrade

Useful when upgrading to newer releases or handling complex dependency changes.

docs.title: Install a Package
docs.text:
Example:

sudo apt install nginx

Install multiple packages.

sudo apt install git curl vim

APT automatically installs required dependencies.

docs.title: Remove a Package
docs.text:
Remove application files.

sudo apt remove nginx

Configuration files remain on the system.

docs.title: Completely Remove a Package
docs.text:
Remove application and configuration files.

sudo apt purge nginx

docs.title: Remove Unused Dependencies
docs.text:
sudo apt autoremove

This removes packages that were automatically installed but are no longer required.

docs.title: Search for Packages
docs.text:
Search available packages.

apt search nginx

Example:

nginx

nginx-common

nginx-full

docs.title: View Package Information
docs.text:
apt show nginx

Displays:

  • Version
  • Dependencies
  • Description
  • Maintainer
  • Repository

docs.title: List Installed Packages
docs.text:
apt list --installed

List a specific package.

apt list --installed | grep nginx

docs.title: Check Package Version
docs.text:
apt policy nginx

Example:

Installed:

1.24.0

Candidate:

1.24.1

docs.title: Download Without Installing
docs.text:
apt download nginx

Downloads the .deb file without installing it.

docs.title: Clean Package Cache
docs.text:
Remove downloaded package files.

sudo apt clean

Remove obsolete cached packages.

sudo apt autoclean

docs.title: Package Cache Location
docs.text:
APT stores downloaded packages in:

/var/cache/apt/archives/

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Update package index.

sudo apt update

Upgrade packages.

sudo apt upgrade

Install package.

sudo apt install nginx

Remove package.

sudo apt remove nginx

Search packages.

apt search nginx

Show package information.

apt show nginx

sudo apt install ca-certificates curl gnupg

Update server.

docs.text:

Keeping packages updated is a critical part of system administration and security.

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example apt update Refresh package index Daily maintenance apt upgrade Upgrade installed packages Security updates apt full-upgrade Perform full system upgrade OS maintenance apt install Install packages Software deployment apt remove Remove software Cleanup apt purge Remove package and configuration Reinstallation apt search Search repositories Package discovery apt show Display package details Verification apt autoremove Remove unused dependencies System cleanup

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A DevOps engineer attempts to install Docker.

sudo apt install docker.io

Error:

Unable to locate package docker.io

Investigation:

The package index is outdated.

Solution:

sudo apt update

sudo apt install docker.io

The package installs successfully.

This demonstrates why refreshing the package index is usually the first troubleshooting step when installing software.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always run apt update before installing packages.
  • Regularly apply package updates and security fixes.
  • Remove unused dependencies with apt autoremove.
  • Use trusted repositories only.
  • Review packages before installing them on production systems.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Running apt install without updating the package index.

✅ Avoid running apt install without updating the package index.

❌ Confusing apt update with apt upgrade.

✅ apt update refreshes package information, while apt upgrade installs newer package versions.

❌ Using apt purge unintentionally when configuration files should be preserved.

✅ Avoid using apt purge unintentionally when configuration files should be preserved when a safer approach exists.

❌ Installing software from untrusted third-party repositories without validation.

✅ Avoid this mistake: installing software from untrusted third-party repositories without validation.

docs.title: Audit Logs — Monitoring Security Events in Linux
Audit Logs — Monitoring Security Events in Linux
docs.text: Audit Logs provide a detailed record of security-related events occurring on a Linux system. They help administrators track user activity, monitor system changes, investigate security incidents, detect unauthorized access, and meet compliance requirements. Linux provides several logging and auditing mechanisms, including system logs, systemd journal, and the Linux Audit Framework (auditd). Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand how to collect, analyze, and manage audit logs in production environments.

docs.title: Why Learn Audit Logs?
docs.text:
Imagine a critical configuration file changes unexpectedly.

Without auditing:

Configuration Changed

↓

Unknown User

↓

No Evidence

With auditing:

Configuration Changed

↓

Audit Log

↓

Username

↓

Time

↓

Action Recorded

Audit logs help identify who, what, when, and how an event occurred.

docs.title: What is Linux Auditing?
docs.text:
Linux auditing records security-related events, including:

  • User logins
  • Authentication failures
  • File access
  • File modifications
  • Command execution
  • Permission changes
  • System configuration changes

Audit logs support:

  • Security investigations
  • Compliance
  • Troubleshooting
  • Incident response

docs.title: Linux Logging Components
docs.text:
Linux systems commonly use:

Applications

↓

systemd-journald

↓

Syslog (optional)

↓

Log Files

For security auditing:

Linux Audit Framework

↓

auditd

↓

Audit Logs

docs.title: What is auditd?
docs.text:
auditd is the Linux Audit Daemon.

Responsibilities include:

  • Recording security events
  • Monitoring important files
  • Logging system calls
  • Detecting policy violations

docs.title: Install auditd
docs.text:
Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt install auditd

RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux:

sudo dnf install audit

docs.title: Start the Audit Service
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable auditd

sudo systemctl start auditd

Check status.

sudo systemctl status auditd

docs.title: Audit Log Location
docs.text:
Most Linux distributions store audit logs in:

/var/log/audit/audit.log

docs.title: View Audit Logs
docs.text:
Display the log.

sudo less /var/log/audit/audit.log

Monitor the log.

sudo tail -f /var/log/audit/audit.log

docs.title: Search Audit Logs
docs.text:
Use:

ausearch

Example:

sudo ausearch -m USER_LOGIN

Search authentication failures.

sudo ausearch -m USER_AUTH

docs.title: Generate Audit Reports
docs.text:
Use:

aureport

Summary report.

sudo aureport

Authentication report.

sudo aureport --auth

Login report.

sudo aureport --login

File report.

sudo aureport --file

docs.title: Add an Audit Rule
docs.text:
Monitor a file.

sudo auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa

Meaning:

  • -w → Watch file
  • -p w → Monitor writes
  • -p a → Monitor attribute changes

Combined:

wa

↓

Write + Attribute Changes

docs.title: Add a Rule with a Key
docs.text:
sudo auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes

Search by key.

sudo ausearch -k passwd_changes

docs.title: List Active Rules
docs.text: sudo auditctl -l

docs.title: Delete a Rule
docs.text: sudo auditctl -W /etc/passwd

docs.title: Persistent Rules
docs.text:
Temporary rules disappear after reboot.

Persistent rules are commonly stored in:

/etc/audit/rules.d/

After updating rules, restart the service.

sudo systemctl restart auditd

docs.title: Monitor Failed Logins
docs.text:
Search:

sudo ausearch -m USER_LOGIN

docs.title: Monitor File Changes
docs.text:
Example:

sudo ausearch -f /etc/passwd

docs.title: Monitor Command Execution
docs.text:
Example:

sudo ausearch -x passwd

docs.title: Using journalctl
docs.text:
View security-related journal entries.

journalctl -xe

View SSH logs.

journalctl -u ssh

or

journalctl -u sshd

(depending on the Linux distribution)

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
View audit log.

tail -f /var/log/audit/audit.log

Search events.

ausearch

Generate reports.

aureport

List rules.

auditctl -l

Add rule.

auditctl -w

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Monitor password database.

auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa

Search login events.

ausearch -m USER_LOGIN

Generate authentication report.

aureport --auth

Monitor SSH service logs.

journalctl -u ssh

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Audit logging is essential for:

  • Security investigations
  • Compliance (PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, SOC 2)
  • Incident response
  • Insider threat detection
  • Forensic analysis
  • Enterprise monitoring
  • Government environments
  • Financial institutions

Many compliance frameworks require security auditing and log retention.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Install auditd.

sudo apt install auditd

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Start the service.

sudo systemctl start auditd

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Check service status.

sudo systemctl status auditd

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
List current audit rules.

sudo auditctl -l

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Monitor /etc/passwd.

sudo auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Modify /etc/passwd (in a test environment) or inspect existing events, then search the audit log.

sudo ausearch -f /etc/passwd

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Generate an authentication report.

sudo aureport --auth

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Monitor the audit log in real time.

sudo tail -f /var/log/audit/audit.log

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example auditctl Manage audit rules Security monitoring ausearch Search audit logs Incident investigation aureport Generate audit reports Compliance reporting journalctl View system logs Troubleshooting tail -f Monitor logs live Security operations systemctl status auditd Verify audit service Health checks

docs.title: Common Audit Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Solution Not running auditd Enable and start the service Monitoring too few files Audit critical system files Creating only temporary rules Store persistent rules Never reviewing logs Schedule regular audits Ignoring audit storage Monitor disk usage and log retention

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

An administrator discovers that /etc/passwd was modified.

Without auditing:

Unknown User

↓

Unknown Time

↓

No Investigation Possible

With auditing:

sudo ausearch -f /etc/passwd

The audit log identifies:

  • User
  • Process
  • Timestamp
  • Command
  • Result

The security team can investigate the incident quickly and accurately.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Enable auditd on production systems.
  • Audit critical system files and directories.
  • Create persistent audit rules.
  • Review audit logs regularly.
  • Protect audit logs from unauthorized modification.
  • Synchronize system time using NTP or Chrony for accurate timestamps.
  • Archive and retain logs according to organizational policies.
  • Forward audit logs to a centralized logging or SIEM platform for long-term analysis.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Disabling auditing to save resources.

✅ Avoid disabling auditing to save resources; fix the configuration instead.

❌ Monitoring too few security events.

✅ Avoid this mistake: monitoring too few security events.

❌ Ignoring authentication failures.

✅ Always review authentication failures.

❌ Allowing audit logs to grow without retention planning.

✅ Do not allow audit logs to grow without retention planning.

❌ Never reviewing audit reports.

✅ Always reviewing audit reports.

docs.title: Backup Basics — Protecting Data in Linux
Backup Basics — Protecting Data in Linux
docs.text: Backups are one of the most important aspects of Linux system administration. A backup is a copy of data that can be restored if the original data is lost, corrupted, or accidentally deleted. Hardware failures, software bugs, ransomware, accidental deletions, and natural disasters can all result in data loss. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) must understand backup strategies to ensure business continuity and disaster recovery.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 85 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand backup fundamentals
  • Learn different backup types
  • Create backups using Linux tools
  • Design backup strategies
  • Verify backup integrity
  • Automate backups
  • Understand disaster recovery concepts

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 5 – Users and Groups

docs.title: Why Learn Backups?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • A hard disk suddenly fails.
  • A production database becomes corrupted.
  • A user accidentally deletes important files.
  • A ransomware attack encrypts company data.
  • A cloud virtual machine is permanently deleted.

Without backups:

Data Lost

↓

Business Downtime

↓

Financial Loss

With backups:

Failure

↓

Restore Backup

↓

Business Continues

docs.title: What is a Backup?
docs.text:
A backup is an additional copy of important data stored separately from the original.

Example:

Original Data

↓

Backup Copy

↓

Safe Storage

The backup can be restored whenever required.

docs.title: Why Are Backups Important?
docs.text:
Backups protect against:

  • Hardware failure
  • Human error
  • Accidental deletion
  • Malware
  • Ransomware
  • File corruption
  • Natural disasters

docs.title: Backup Types
docs.text:
The three primary backup types are:

  • Full Backup
  • Incremental Backup
  • Differential Backup

docs.title: Full Backup
docs.text:
A full backup copies all selected data.

Example:

Day 1

All Files

↓

Backup

Advantages:

  • Simple restoration
  • Complete copy of data

Disadvantages:

  • Takes more time
  • Requires more storage

docs.title: Incremental Backup
docs.text:
An incremental backup copies only data changed since the last backup (full or incremental).

Example:

Monday

Full Backup

↓

Tuesday

Changes Only

↓

Wednesday

New Changes Only

Advantages:

  • Fast backups
  • Smaller storage requirements

Disadvantages:

  • Restoration requires multiple backup sets

docs.title: Differential Backup
docs.text:
A differential backup copies changes since the last full backup.

Example:

Monday

Full Backup

↓

Tuesday

Changes Since Monday

↓

Wednesday

Changes Since Monday

Advantages:

  • Faster restoration than incremental backups
  • Less storage than repeated full backups

Disadvantages:

  • Larger backups over time until the next full backup

docs.title: Backup Comparison
docs.text: Backup Type Backup Speed Restore Speed Storage Required Full Slow Fast High Incremental Fast Slow Low Differential Medium Medium Medium

docs.title: Local Backup
docs.text:
Server

↓

External Disk

Advantages:

  • Fast
  • Simple

Disadvantage:

  • Vulnerable to hardware failure and disasters affecting the server location

docs.title: Remote Backup
docs.text:
Server

↓

Network

↓

Backup Server

Advantages:

  • Better disaster protection
  • Off-site storage

docs.title: Common Linux Backup Tools
docs.text:
Linux provides several backup utilities:

  • cp
  • tar
  • rsync
  • scp
  • dd

Enterprise backup software may also be used depending on organizational requirements.

docs.title: Backup Using cp
docs.text:
Copy files.

cp important.txt backup/

Suitable for small backups.

docs.title: Backup Using tar
docs.text:
Create an archive.

tar -czf backup.tar.gz /home/user

Options:

Option Meaning -c Create archive -z Compress using gzip -f Output file

docs.title: Backup Using rsync
docs.text:
Synchronize directories.

rsync -av /home/ backup/

Advantages:

  • Incremental transfers
  • Efficient synchronization
  • Preserves permissions

docs.title: Backup Using dd
docs.text:
Create a disk image.

sudo dd if=/dev/sda of=/backup/disk.img bs=4M

Commonly used for:

  • Disk cloning
  • Forensic imaging
  • Disaster recovery

docs.title: Automating Backups
docs.text:

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
“We have backups” sounds reassuring until someone asks: “When did you last restore?” This tutorial uses tar, rsync, and honest Recovery Point Objective (RPO) / Recovery Time Objective (RTO) thinking — not enterprise appliances.

Plain problem: A bad deploy deletes config. The team has a tarball somewhere — nobody tested restore. Hours lost. Capacity is the sibling problem: disks fill silently until everything stops.

This tutorial: create data, back up, destroy, restore, verify checksums, capture capacity signals — evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab25.

This is Tutorial 16b in Module 16: Production Linux of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ubuntu practice VM with free disk space (~500 MB for lab)
  • Production Hardening and Performance or comfort with df, du
  • sudo not required for most of this lab

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain backup vs Disaster Recovery (DR) in plain language
  • Define RPO and RTO with a simple example
  • Create and restore tar and rsync backups
  • Verify restore with checksums
  • Read basic capacity signals (df, du)
  • Answer fresher interview questions on backup and DR

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Backups copy data to secondary storage. DR is the plan and practise to restore service after larger failure. Capacity monitoring ensures you grow storage before backups themselves fail.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text: Intern deletes /etc/nginx trying to “clean up”. No tested restore. Team rebuilds manually from memory — wrong TLS cert, hours downtime. A 15-minute tested tar restore would have fixed it.

docs.title: Backup vs DR (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: Backup is photocopying important documents to a safe drawer. DR is the fire drill — who grabs the copies, how fast the office reopens, which copy is new enough.

Term Plain meaning Backup Copy of data at a point in time Restore Put data back from backup DR Process + infra to recover after major failure RPO Max acceptable data loss (time since last good backup) RTO Max acceptable downtime to restore service

Example: Nightly backup at midnight, incident at 09:00 → RPO ≈ 9 hours of changes lost unless incremental/hourly backups exist.

Interview line: “I test restores regularly; RPO/RTO drive backup frequency and architecture.”

docs.title: tar — archive one directory tree
docs.text:
Terminal
tar -czvf backup.tar.gz /path/to/data
tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz -C /restore/destination

-c create, -z gzip, -v verbose, -f file.

docs.title: rsync — efficient sync
docs.text:
Analogy: rsync is a smart copy — only changed blocks, great for large trees and remote hosts (user@host:/path).

Terminal
rsync -a --delete /source/ /backup/mirror/

-a archive mode (perms, times); trailing slashes matter.

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text:
Terminal
df -h
du -sh /var/log/*

Plan growth before 100% full — backups fail when destination has no space.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Backups on the same disk as source (single point of failure)
  • Never tested restore
  • Ignoring database consistency (apps need quiesce or native backup)
  • Confusing snapshot with backup without off-site copy

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Build sample app data, tar and rsync backups, delete source deliberately, restore, verify checksums, capture capacity — under ~/rebash-linux/lab25.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM Local disk space sha256sum Usually preinstalled

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab25/{data,backup-tar,backup-rsync,restore} && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab25
df -h . | tee df-before.txt

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Ticket: “Prove we can restore /opt/myapp/config after accidental deletion. Document RPO if we backup nightly.” You simulate with lab directories and checksum proof.

docs.title: Task 1 – Create sample data and checksum baseline
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab25
echo "version=1.0" > data/app.conf
echo "important=$(date -Is)" > data/state.txt
mkdir -p data/sub
echo "nested=ok" > data/sub/nested.txt
sha256sum data/* data/sub/* | tee checksums-before.txt
test -s checksums-before.txt

Expected output

Three files in data/; checksums listed in checksums-before.txt.

docs.title: Task 2 – tar and rsync backup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab25
tar -czvf backup-tar/app-data.tar.gz -C data . 2>&1 | tee tar-create.log
rsync -a data/ backup-rsync/data-mirror/
diff -qr data backup-rsync/data-mirror | tee rsync-diff.txt
test ! -s rsync-diff.txt
ls -la backup-tar backup-rsync/data-mirror | tee backup-listing.txt

Expected output

rsync-diff.txt empty (trees match). Tarball exists under backup-tar/.

docs.title: Task 3 – Destroy, restore, prove (break → fix → prove)
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab25
rm -rf data/*
ls data | tee data-after-delete.txt
test ! -s data-after-delete.txt
mkdir -p restore/data
tar -xzvf backup-tar/app-data.tar.gz -C restore/data 2>&1 | tee tar-restore.log
rsync -a backup-rsync/data-mirror/ restore/data/
sha256sum restore/data/* restore/data/sub/* | tee checksums-after-restore.txt
diff checksums-before.txt checksums-after-restore.txt | tee checksum-diff.txt
test ! -s checksum-diff.txt
du -sh data backup-tar backup-rsync | tee du-capacity.txt
df -h . | tee df-after.txt
echo "lab25 backup DR OK" | tee evidence.txt

Create rpo-rto-notes.md:

rpo-rto-notes.md
# RPO / RTO — lab25

- If we backup once per lab session, max data loss = changes since last tar/rsync.
- RTO here = time to extract tar + verify checksums (minutes on small data).
- Production would add off-site object storage and automated restore drills.

Expected output

checksum-diff.txt empty — restore matches original. Capacity files show disk use.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• Data deleted deliberately after backup
  • tar restore + rsync mirror both used
  • Checksums match before and after
  • RPO/RTO notes written in your words

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix tar: empty archive Wrong -C path Check directory contents before tar rsync copies wrong tree Trailing slash source/ vs source changes meaning Checksum mismatch Partial restore Re-run tar; verify paths No space for backup Disk full df -h; clean or expand volume

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text: Add a deliberate one-byte change to data/app.conf, re-rsync, show diff detects it — then restore from tar again.

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. sha256sum before backup — baseline for restore proof.
  2. tar -C data . — archive contents, not parent path confusion.
  3. rsync -a — fast incremental sync for large trees.
  4. Deliberate rm -rf data/* — simulates accidental deletion incident.
  5. diff checksums — objective restore success — better than “looks fine”.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Encrypt backups at rest and in transit for sensitive data.
  • Restrict backup directory permissions (chmod 700).
  • Off-site copies protect against site loss — local tarball alone is not DR.
  • Secrets should not live in plain tarballs in shared drives.
  • Test restore in isolated environment to avoid overwriting production.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Backup on same disk.

✅ Disk failure loses source and backup together — replicate off-host.

❌ Never tested restore.

✅ Backups are only as good as last successful restore test.

❌ Ignoring app consistency.

✅ Databases need coordinated backup (dump, snapshot, native tool) — not only file copy mid-write.

docs.title: Backup Strategy — Protecting Linux Systems and Data
Backup Strategy — Protecting Linux Systems and Data
docs.text: A Backup Strategy is a structured plan for protecting operating systems, applications, configurations, databases, and business-critical data against accidental deletion, hardware failures, cyberattacks, corruption, and disasters. An effective backup strategy ensures that data can be restored quickly and accurately when failures occur. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Infrastructure Engineer should understand how to design and implement reliable backup strategies for production environments.
