docs.title: Full Backup
docs.text:
Backs up everything.

Server

↓

Complete Copy

Advantages:

  • Simple restoration
  • Complete recovery

Disadvantages:

  • Large storage requirements
  • Longer backup time

docs.title: Incremental Backup
docs.text:
Backs up changes since the previous backup.

Sunday

↓

Full Backup

↓

Monday

↓

Changes Only

↓

Tuesday

↓

Changes Only

Advantages:

  • Fast backups
  • Minimal storage

Disadvantages:

  • Restore process is more complex

docs.title: Differential Backup
docs.text:
Backs up all changes since the last full backup.

Sunday

↓

Full Backup

↓

Monday

↓

Changes

↓

Tuesday

↓

Monday + Tuesday Changes

Advantages:

  • Faster restore than incremental backups

Disadvantages:

  • Backup size grows until the next full backup

docs.title: The 3-2-1 Backup Rule
docs.text:
A widely accepted backup strategy:

  • 3 copies of data
  • 2 different storage media
  • 1 copy stored offsite

Example:

Production Data

↓

Local Backup

↓

NAS Backup

↓

Cloud Backup

This strategy protects against hardware failures, site outages, and disasters.

docs.title: Backup Scheduling
docs.text:
Typical schedule:

Backup Type Frequency Full Weekly Incremental Daily Database Hourly or Daily (based on business needs) Configuration After significant changes or daily Snapshots Before major updates or deployments

Schedules should match business requirements and recovery objectives.

docs.title: Backup Retention Policy
docs.text:
Example retention:

  • Daily backups → 30 days
  • Weekly backups → 12 weeks
  • Monthly backups → 12 months
  • Yearly backups → 5–7 years (or organizational requirements)

Retention policies depend on compliance and business needs.

docs.title: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
docs.text:
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss.

Example:

RPO = 1 Hour

At most one hour of data can be lost.

docs.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
docs.text:
The maximum acceptable recovery time.

Example:

RTO = 30 Minutes

Systems must be restored within 30 minutes.

Never assume backups are valid.

  • Archive integrity
  • Restore process works

A backup that cannot be restored has little practical value.

Arrays — Managing Collections of Data in Bash Scripts
docs.text: Arrays allow Bash scripts to store multiple values under a single variable name. Instead of creating many individual variables, arrays organize related data into indexed collections, making scripts cleaner, easier to maintain, and more scalable. Arrays are commonly used in automation scripts, server management, cloud provisioning, deployment pipelines, and system administration to process lists of servers, files, users, packages, and other collections of data.

docs.title: Why Learn Arrays?
docs.text:
Imagine checking the status of multiple servers.

Without arrays:

SERVER1="web01"

SERVER2="web02"

SERVER3="db01"

Managing many variables becomes difficult.

Using an array:

SERVERS=("web01" "web02" "db01")

The script becomes much cleaner and easier to scale.

docs.title: What is an Array?
docs.text:
An array stores multiple values inside a single variable.

Example:

SERVERS

↓

[0] web01

[1] web02

[2] db01

Each item has an index.

docs.title: Creating an Array
docs.text:
Syntax:

ARRAY=(value1 value2 value3)

Example:

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A monitoring script checks multiple servers.

Without arrays:

ping web01

ping web02

ping db01

Improved:

SERVERS=("web01" "web02" "db01")

for SERVER in "${SERVERS[@]}"
do
    if ping -c1 "$SERVER" >/dev/null
    then
        echo "$SERVER is reachable"
    else
        echo "$SERVER is unreachable"
    fi
done

Adding a new server requires changing only one line in the array.

docs.title: What is Bash?
docs.text:
Bash stands for:

Bourne Again SHell

It is the default shell on most Linux distributions.

Bash acts as a command interpreter between the user and the Linux kernel.

User

↓

Bash

↓

Linux Kernel

↓

Hardware

Whenever you type a command:

Bash interprets the command and asks the Linux kernel to execute it.

docs.title: Conditions — Making Decisions in Bash Scripts
Conditions — Making Decisions in Bash Scripts
docs.text: Conditions allow Bash scripts to make decisions based on user input, command results, file existence, variable values, or system state. Instead of executing every command sequentially, a script can choose different execution paths depending on whether a condition is true or false. Conditional statements are one of the most important features of Bash scripting and are used extensively in automation, DevOps, cloud infrastructure, monitoring, deployment pipelines, and Linux system administration.

docs.title: Why Learn Conditions?
docs.text:
Imagine writing a backup script.

Without conditions:

cp /data/* /backup/

If /backup doesn't exist, the script fails.

With conditions:

if [ -d "/backup" ]; then
    cp /data/* /backup/
else
    echo "Backup directory not found."
fi

The script behaves intelligently.

docs.title: What is a Condition?
docs.text:
A condition evaluates whether something is:

  • True
  • False

Based on the result, Bash executes different code.

Example:

Is User Root?

↓

Yes

↓

Run Administrative Tasks

OR

No

↓

Display Error

docs.title: Basic if Statement
docs.text:
Syntax:

if [ condition ]
then
    commands
fi

Example:

AGE=20

if [ $AGE -ge 18 ]
then
    echo "Adult"
fi

Output:

Adult

docs.title: if...else
docs.text:
Syntax:

if [ condition ]
then
    commands
else
    commands
fi

Example:

AGE=16

if [ $AGE -ge 18 ]
then
    echo "Adult"
else
    echo "Minor"
fi

docs.title: if...elif...else
docs.text:
Useful for multiple decisions.

MARKS=75

if [ $MARKS -ge 90 ]
then
    echo "Grade A"

elif [ $MARKS -ge 75 ]
then
    echo "Grade B"

else
    echo "Grade C"
fi

docs.title: Numeric Comparison Operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning -eq Equal -ne Not Equal -gt Greater Than -ge Greater Than or Equal -lt Less Than -le Less Than or Equal

Example:

if [ $A -gt $B ]
then
    echo "A is larger"
fi

docs.title: String Comparison Operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning = Equal != Not Equal -z Empty String -n Not Empty

Example:

NAME="Linux"

if [ "$NAME" = "Linux" ]
then
    echo "Matched"
fi

docs.title: File Test Operators
docs.text:
Operator Description -f Regular file exists -d Directory exists -e File or directory exists -r Readable -w Writable -x Executable -s File is not empty

Example:

if [ -f "/etc/passwd" ]
then
    echo "File exists"
fi

fi

docs.text:
Using && inside [[ ]].

if [[ $AGE -ge 18 && $AGE -le 60 ]]
then
    echo "Working Age"
fi

docs.title: Logical OR
docs.text:

then
    echo "Administrator"
fi

docs.title: Logical NOT
docs.text:
if [ ! -f "/tmp/test.txt" ]
then
    echo "File not found"
fi

docs.title: Nested Conditions
docs.text:
if [ $AGE -ge 18 ]
then
    if [ "$COUNTRY" = "India" ]
    then
        echo "Eligible"
    fi
fi

docs.title: Checking Command Success
docs.text:
Every Linux command returns an exit code.

Example:

if [ $? -eq 0 ]
then
    echo "Directory created successfully"
fi

A better approach:

if mkdir test
then
    echo "Directory created"
else
    echo "Creation failed"
fi

docs.title: Error Handling — Building Reliable Bash Scripts
Error Handling — Building Reliable Bash Scripts
docs.text: Error Handling is the practice of detecting, reporting, and responding to errors during script execution. In production environments, failures such as missing files, invalid input, network issues, permission problems, or command failures are inevitable. A well-designed Bash script should detect these failures, provide meaningful error messages, clean up resources if necessary, and exit safely. Effective error handling is essential for Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, Platform Engineers, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs).

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand error handling
  • Detect runtime failures
  • Use set options effectively
  • Display meaningful error messages
  • Clean up resources using trap
  • Handle command failures
  • Write defensive Bash scripts

docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.title: Why Learn Error Handling?
docs.text:
Imagine a deployment script.

Without error handling:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

systemctl restart nginx

echo "Deployment Complete"

If deployment fails, the script still restarts the service and reports success.

With proper error handling:

if ! kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
then
    echo "Deployment failed."

    exit 1
fi

The script stops immediately and reports the failure.

docs.title: What is Error Handling?
docs.text:
Error handling is the process of:

  • Detecting errors
  • Reporting errors
  • Recovering when possible
  • Exiting safely when necessary

Example:

Command

↓

Success

↓

Continue

OR

Failure

↓

Handle Error

↓

Exit Safely

docs.title: Why Error Handling Matters
docs.text:
Proper error handling helps to:

  • Prevent data corruption
  • Avoid incomplete deployments
  • Reduce downtime
  • Improve troubleshooting
  • Increase script reliability

docs.title: Checking Exit Codes
docs.text:
Every command returns an exit code.

cp file1 file2

if [ $? -ne 0 ]
then
    echo "Copy failed."

    exit 1
fi

A cleaner approach:

if ! cp file1 file2
then
    echo "Copy failed."

    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Using set -e
docs.text:
Exit immediately when any command fails.

set -e

Example:

#!/bin/bash

set -e

mkdir project

cp missing.txt project/

echo "Completed"

The script exits when cp fails.

docs.title: Using set -u
docs.text:
Treat undefined variables as errors.

set -u

Example:

echo "$USERNAME"

If USERNAME is not defined, the script exits with an error.

docs.title: Using set -o pipefail
docs.text:
Normally, only the exit status of the last command in a pipeline is returned.

Example:

cat missing.txt | grep Linux

With:

set -o pipefail

The pipeline fails if any command in the pipeline fails.

docs.title: Recommended Script Header
docs.text:
Many production scripts begin with:

#!/bin/bash

set -euo pipefail

Meaning:

  • -e → Exit on errors
  • -u → Detect undefined variables
  • pipefail → Detect pipeline failures

docs.title: Displaying Error Messages
docs.text:
Write clear error messages.

echo "Error: Configuration file not found."

Better:

echo "Error: /etc/app/config.yaml not found."

Specific messages simplify troubleshooting.

docs.title: Using trap
docs.text:
The trap command executes cleanup actions before the script exits.

Example:

cleanup() {

    rm -f /tmp/tempfile
}

trap cleanup EXIT

The cleanup function runs automatically when the script exits.

docs.title: Handling Interrupt Signals
docs.text:
Handle Ctrl+C gracefully.

trap 'echo "Interrupted."; exit 1' INT

docs.title: Cleanup Example
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash

TEMP_FILE="/tmp/data.tmp"

touch "$TEMP_FILE"

cleanup() {

    rm -f "$TEMP_FILE"
}

trap cleanup EXIT

Temporary files are removed automatically.

docs.title: Defensive Scripting
docs.text:
Validate everything.

Example:

if [ ! -f "$1" ]
then
    echo "Input file missing."

    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Fail Fast
docs.text:
Stop immediately when a critical operation fails.

Example:

systemctl restart nginx || exit 1

docs.title: Error Logging
docs.text:
Display errors.

echo "Error: Backup failed."

Or write to a log file.

echo "Backup failed." >> backup.log

Dedicated logging is covered in the next lesson.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Exit on errors.

set -e

Undefined variables.

set -u

Pipeline failure detection.

Cleanup.

Validate configuration.

then
    exit 1
fi

systemctl restart nginx || exit 1

Create cleanup function.

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Error handling is essential in:

  • Deployment automation
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Kubernetes automation
  • Cloud provisioning
  • Backup scripts
  • Monitoring systems
  • Security automation
  • Infrastructure management

Reliable automation depends on proper error detection and recovery.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A deployment script creates temporary files and then fails during deployment.

Without cleanup:

Temporary Files

↓

Remain on Disk

Improved script:

cleanup() {

    rm -f /tmp/deploy.tmp
}

trap cleanup EXIT

Now, temporary files are removed automatically regardless of whether the script succeeds or fails.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use set -euo pipefail in production scripts.
  • Validate input before processing.
  • Handle failures immediately.
  • Write descriptive error messages.
  • Clean up temporary resources with trap.
  • Exit with meaningful status codes.
  • Test error scenarios as thoroughly as success scenarios.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Ignoring failed commands.

✅ Always review failed commands.

❌ Continuing execution after critical failures.

✅ Do not continue execution after critical failures.

❌ Forgetting to clean up temporary files.

✅ Remember to to clean up temporary files.

❌ Using vague error messages.

✅ Avoid using vague error messages when a safer approach exists.

❌ Not validating files, directories, or user input before use.

✅ Always validating files, directories, or user input before use.

docs.title: Exit Codes — Understanding Command Success and Failure in Bash
Exit Codes — Understanding Command Success and Failure in Bash
docs.text: Exit Codes are numeric values returned by commands, scripts, and functions to indicate whether an operation succeeded or failed. Every Linux command returns an exit code when it finishes execution. Bash scripts use these codes to detect failures, make decisions, trigger error handling, and integrate with automation tools such as Jenkins, GitLab CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes Jobs, and Ansible. Understanding exit codes is essential for writing reliable, production-ready Bash scripts.

After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

docs.title: Why Learn Exit Codes?
docs.text:
Imagine deploying an application.

Without checking the exit code:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

echo "Deployment Successful"

Even if the deployment fails, the script reports success.

Using exit codes:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

if [ $? -eq 0 ]
then
    echo "Deployment Successful"
else
    echo "Deployment Failed"
fi

The script accurately reports the outcome.

docs.title: What is an Exit Code?
docs.text:
An exit code is a numeric value returned by a command after execution.

Command

↓

Execution

↓

Exit Code

The shell stores the exit code of the most recently executed command.

docs.title: Standard Exit Codes
docs.text: Exit Code Meaning 0 Success Non-zero Failure 1 General error 2 Incorrect command usage 126 Command cannot execute 127 Command not found 130 Script terminated by Ctrl+C

docs.title: Viewing the Exit Code
docs.text:
Use the special variable:

$?

Example:

ls

echo $?

Output:

0

docs.title: Successful Command
docs.text:
mkdir demo

echo $?

Output:

0

docs.title: Failed Command
docs.text:
ls nonexistent

echo $?

Output:

2

docs.title: Using Exit Codes in Conditions
docs.text:
mkdir project

if [ $? -eq 0 ]
then
    echo "Directory Created"
else
    echo "Creation Failed"
fi

docs.title: Better Approach
docs.text:
Instead of checking $? separately:

if mkdir project
then
    echo "Directory Created"
else
    echo "Creation Failed"
fi

This is cleaner and more readable.

docs.title: Using the exit Command
docs.text:
Terminate a script with a specific exit code.

exit 0

Success.

exit 1

Failure.

docs.title: Example Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash

if [ ! -f "/etc/passwd" ]
then
    echo "File Missing"

    exit 1
fi

echo "File Found"

exit 0

docs.title: Custom Exit Codes
docs.text:
You may define custom exit codes for different situations.

Example:

exit 10

exit 20

exit 50

Document custom exit codes clearly so other users understand their meaning.

docs.title: Exit Codes in Functions
docs.text:
Functions return status codes.

check_file() {

    [ -f "$1" ]

    return $?
}

Call the function.

check_file file.txt

echo $?

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
View exit code.

echo $?

Exit successfully.

exit 0

Exit with failure.

exit 1

Return from function.

return 0

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Check deployment.

kubectl apply -f app.yaml

if [ $? -eq 0 ]
then
    echo "Deployment Successful"
else
    echo "Deployment Failed"
fi

Check backup.

tar -czf backup.tar.gz /data

if [ $? -ne 0 ]
then
    exit 1
fi

Restart service.

systemctl restart nginx

if systemctl is-active --quiet nginx
then
    echo "Service Running"
else
    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Exit codes are heavily used in:

  • Bash automation
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Kubernetes Jobs
  • Ansible playbooks
  • Jenkins pipelines
  • GitLab CI/CD
  • Monitoring scripts
  • Deployment automation

Most automation platforms rely on exit codes to determine whether a task succeeded or failed.

    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A CI/CD pipeline reports a successful deployment, but the application is unavailable.

Investigation:

The deployment command failed.

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

The script ignored the exit code and continued.

Solution:

if kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
then
    echo "Deployment Successful"
else
    echo "Deployment Failed"

    exit 1
fi

The pipeline now correctly reports failures and stops further execution.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Check the exit status of important commands.
  • Exit immediately when critical operations fail.
  • Use meaningful exit codes.
  • Return status codes from functions.
  • Prefer if command over checking $? separately.
  • Document custom exit codes.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Ignoring failed commands.

✅ Always review failed commands.

❌ Checking $? after executing another command.

✅ Avoid this mistake: checking $? after executing another command.

❌ Using return instead of exit in the main script.

✅ Prefer exit in the main script rather than using return.

❌ Returning text instead of numeric status codes.

✅ Prefer numeric status codes rather than returning text.

❌ Continuing execution after critical failures.

✅ Do not continue execution after critical failures.

Exit codes provide a standardized way for commands, functions, and scripts to communicate success or failure. Proper use of exit codes allows automation tools and other scripts to make informed decisions, improving the reliability and maintainability of production systems.

docs.title: Functions — Writing Reusable Code in Bash Scripts
Functions — Writing Reusable Code in Bash Scripts
docs.text: Functions are reusable blocks of code that perform a specific task. Instead of writing the same commands multiple times, you can place them inside a function and call it whenever needed. Functions make Bash scripts easier to read, maintain, debug, and extend. They are widely used in production automation, DevOps pipelines, cloud infrastructure, system administration, monitoring, and deployment scripts.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

docs.title: Why Learn Functions?
docs.text:
Imagine writing a backup script.

Without functions:

echo "Starting backup..."

tar -czf backup.tar.gz /data

echo "Backup completed."

echo "Starting backup..."

tar -czf backup2.tar.gz /logs

echo "Backup completed."

The same code is repeated.

Using functions:

backup() {
    echo "Starting backup..."

    tar -czf "$2" "$1"

    echo "Backup completed."
}

backup /data backup.tar.gz

backup /logs backup2.tar.gz

The script becomes cleaner and reusable.

docs.title: What is a Function?
docs.text:
A function is a named block of commands.

Function

↓

Perform Task

↓

Return Control

Functions execute only when they are called.

docs.title: Function Syntax
docs.text:
function_name() {

    commands

}

Example:

hello() {

    echo "Hello Linux"
}

Call the function.

hello

Output:

Hello Linux

docs.title: Function with Parameters
docs.text:
Parameters allow functions to work with different values.

Example:

greet() {

    echo "Hello $1"
}

greet Basha

Output:

Hello Basha

docs.title: Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
server_info() {

    echo "Server: $1"

    echo "IP: $2"
}

server_info web01 192.168.1.10

Output:

Server: web01

IP: 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Special Parameter Variables
Returning Status Codes
docs.text:
Functions typically return an exit status, not data.

check_user() {

    id "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1

    return $?
}

check_user root

echo $?

Return codes:

Code Meaning 0 Success Non-zero Failure

docs.title: Returning Values
docs.text:
A common approach is to print a value and capture it.

today() {

    date +%F
}

CURRENT_DATE=$(today)

echo "$CURRENT_DATE"

docs.title: Local Variables
docs.text:
Variables inside a function can be made local.

show_name() {

    local NAME="Linux"

    echo "$NAME"
}

Outside the function:

echo "$NAME"

No value is displayed because the variable exists only within the function.

docs.title: Global Variables
docs.text:
Variables declared outside functions are global.

NAME="Linux"

show() {

    echo "$NAME"
}

docs.title: Calling Functions Multiple Times
docs.text:
welcome() {

    echo "Welcome!"
}

welcome

welcome

welcome

docs.title: Function Execution Order
docs.text:
Functions should normally be defined before they are called.

Example:

backup() {

    echo "Backup Started"
}

backup

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Create function.

hello() {

    echo "Hello"
}

Call function.

hello

Access parameters.

$1

$2

Return status.

return 0

restart_service() {

    systemctl restart "$1"
}

restart_service nginx

Check disk usage.

check_disk() {

    df -h "$1"
}

check_disk /

Backup a directory.

backup_dir() {

    tar -czf "$2" "$1"
}

backup_dir /etc etc-backup.tar.gz

Large Bash scripts are typically divided into reusable functions for better readability and maintenance.

Scenario

A deployment script contains the same service restart commands in multiple places.

Before:

  • Use local variables whenever possible.

  • Avoid duplicating code across scripts.
  • Document complex functions with comments.

docs.title: Common Mistakes

❌ Writing one large function that performs multiple unrelated tasks.

✅ Avoid this mistake: writing one large function that performs multiple unrelated tasks.

❌ Using global variables for everything.

✅ Avoid using global variables for everything when a safer approach exists.

❌ Forgetting to validate function parameters.

✅ Remember to to validate function parameters.

❌ Returning strings using return.

✅ Avoid this mistake: returning strings using return.

❌ Repeating identical code instead of creating reusable functions.

✅ Prefer creating reusable functions rather than repeating identical code.

  • Use $1, $2, and $@ to access arguments.
  • Use local variables to avoid unintended side effects.
  • Return status codes to indicate success or failure.
  • Keep functions small, focused, and reusable.

docs.title: Input — Accepting User Input in Bash Scripts
Input — Accepting User Input in Bash Scripts
docs.text: Input allows Bash scripts to interact with users, accept command-line arguments, read data from files, and process information from standard input. Interactive scripts become more flexible because they can work with different values each time they are executed instead of relying on hardcoded data. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand how to safely collect and validate user input in production scripts.

docs.title: Logging — Recording Events in Bash Scripts
Logging — Recording Events in Bash Scripts
docs.text: Logging is the process of recording important events, actions, warnings, and errors while a script is running. Good logging helps administrators understand what happened during script execution, troubleshoot failures, monitor automation, and maintain production systems. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should implement proper logging in Bash scripts to improve observability and simplify troubleshooting.

docs.text:

With logging:

Every important event is recorded.

Logging is the process of recording events while a program executes.

Operations

Success / Failure

Log File

Logs provide valuable information for troubleshooting and auditing.

2026-08-18 10:30:15 Backup Started

docs.text:
Production scripts often classify log messages by severity.

Common levels:

  • INFO
  • WARNING
  • ERROR
  • DEBUG

Example:

INFO

Application Started

WARNING

Disk Usage High

ERROR

Backup Failed

docs.text: echo "$(date) [INFO] Backup Started" >> backup.log

Redirect command output.

ls -l >> backup.log

Capture errors.

ls missing-file 2>> backup.log

Capture both standard output and errors.

ls /tmp >> backup.log 2>&1

Display output and save it simultaneously.

echo "Backup Started" | tee -a backup.log

docs.title: Using the logger Command
docs.text:
Send messages to the system log.

logger "Backup Started"

Example:

logger "Deployment Completed Successfully"

Depending on the Linux distribution, these messages are stored in the system logging service (such as syslog or journald).

log() {

    echo "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') [INFO] $1" >> backup.log
}

Use it.

log "Backup Completed"

docs.title: Loops — Automating Repetitive Tasks in Bash Scripts
Loops — Automating Repetitive Tasks in Bash Scripts
docs.text: Loops allow Bash scripts to execute a block of code repeatedly until a specified condition is met or a collection of items has been processed. Instead of writing the same commands multiple times, loops enable automation with fewer lines of code, making scripts more efficient, scalable, and maintainable. Loops are extensively used in Linux administration, DevOps, cloud automation, infrastructure management, monitoring, and deployment pipelines.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand loops
  • Use for loops
  • Use while loops
  • Use until loops
  • Iterate through files and directories

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Modules 1–9

docs.title: Why Learn Loops?
docs.text:
Imagine backing up multiple directories.

Without loops:

tar -czf home.tar.gz /home

tar -czf etc.tar.gz /etc

tar -czf var.tar.gz /var

Using a loop:

for DIR in /home /etc /var
do
    tar -czf "$(basename $DIR).tar.gz" "$DIR"
done

The script becomes shorter, reusable, and easier to maintain.

docs.title: What is a Loop?
docs.text:
A loop repeatedly executes a block of commands.

Example:

Start

↓

Condition

↓

Execute Commands

↓

Repeat

↓

Exit

docs.title: Types of Loops
docs.text:
Bash supports:

  • for
  • while
  • until

Each is useful in different scenarios.

docs.title: for Loop
docs.text:
The for loop is used when iterating over a known list of items.

Syntax:

for VARIABLE in LIST
do
    commands
done

Example:

for NAME in Alice Bob Charlie
do
    echo "$NAME"
done

Output:

Alice

Bob

Charlie

docs.title: Numeric for Loop
docs.text:
Using brace expansion:

for i in {1..5}
do
    echo $i
done

Output:

1

2

3

4

5

docs.title: C-Style for Loop
docs.text:
for (( i=1; i<=5; i++ ))
do
    echo $i
done

docs.title: Loop Through Files
docs.text:
for FILE in *.txt
do
    echo "$FILE"
done

docs.title: Loop Through Directories
docs.text:
for DIR in /home/*/
do
    echo "$DIR"
done

docs.title: while Loop
docs.text:
A while loop runs as long as the condition is true.

Syntax:

while [ condition ]
do
    commands
done

Example:

COUNT=1

while [ $COUNT -le 5 ]
do
    echo $COUNT
    COUNT=$((COUNT+1))
done

docs.title: Reading a File Line by Line
docs.text:
while read LINE
do
    echo "$LINE"
done < users.txt

This technique is widely used for processing configuration files and logs.

docs.title: until Loop
docs.text:
An until loop executes until a condition becomes true.

Syntax:

until [ condition ]
do
    commands
done

Example:

COUNT=1

until [ $COUNT -gt 5 ]
do
    echo $COUNT
    COUNT=$((COUNT+1))
done

docs.title: break Statement
docs.text:
break exits a loop immediately.

Example:

for i in {1..10}
do
    if [ $i -eq 5 ]
    then
        break
    fi

    echo $i
done

Output:

1

2

3

4

docs.title: continue Statement
docs.text:
continue skips the current iteration.

Example:

for i in {1..5}
do
    if [ $i -eq 3 ]
    then
        continue
    fi

    echo $i
done

Output:

1

2

4

5

docs.title: Nested Loops
docs.text:
Loops can be placed inside other loops.

for i in {1..3}
do
    for j in {1..2}
    do
        echo "$i $j"
    done
done

docs.title: Infinite Loop
docs.text:
while true
do
    echo "Running..."
    sleep 5
done

Stop using:

Ctrl + C

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A monitoring script should check multiple servers.

Without loops:

ping server1

ping server2

ping server3

Using a loop:

for HOST in server1 server2 server3
do
    if ping -c1 "$HOST" >/dev/null
    then
        echo "$HOST is reachable"
    else
        echo "$HOST is down"
    fi
done

The script is easier to maintain and can scale to hundreds of servers.

docs.text:

  • Avoid unnecessary nested loops.
  • Quote filenames and variables.
  • Use break and continue to improve readability.
  • Test loops with small datasets before running them in production.

docs.title: Why Follow Best Practices?
docs.text:
Imagine two administrators maintaining the same script.

Poorly written script:

a=$1

b=$2

c=$((a+b))

echo $c

Improved script:

FIRST_NUMBER=$1

SECOND_NUMBER=$2

SUM=$((FIRST_NUMBER + SECOND_NUMBER))

echo "$SUM"

The second script is easier to understand, maintain, and debug.

docs.title: Write Readable Code
docs.text:
Use meaningful names.

Good:

BACKUP_DIR="/backup"

Poor:

b="/backup"

Readable scripts reduce maintenance effort.

docs.title: Use Comments
docs.text:
Explain complex logic.

# Create a compressed backup

tar -czf backup.tar.gz /data

Avoid comments that simply repeat the code.

Poor:

# Echo hello

echo "Hello"

docs.title: Use Consistent Naming

BACKUP_DIR

LOG_FILE

SERVER_NAME

Functions:

Choose one naming style and use it consistently.

docs.title: Use Strict Mode
docs.text:
Enable safer script execution.

#!/bin/bash

set -euo pipefail

Benefits:

  • Exit on command failures
  • Detect undefined variables
  • Detect pipeline failures

docs.title: Quote Variables
docs.text:
Always quote variables unless unquoted expansion is specifically required.

Good:

cp "$SOURCE" "$DESTINATION"

Poor:

cp $SOURCE $DESTINATION

Quoting prevents unexpected word splitting and filename expansion.

docs.title: Validate User Input
docs.text:
Check required values before using them.

if [ $# -lt 1 ]
then
    echo "Usage: ./backup.sh <directory>"

    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Check Command Success
docs.text:
Prefer:

if cp file1 file2
then
    echo "Success"
else
    echo "Failed"
fi

Instead of assuming every command succeeds.

docs.title: Use Functions
docs.text:
Organize scripts into reusable components.

backup() {

    tar -czf backup.tar.gz /data
}

Functions reduce duplicated code.

docs.title: Keep Functions Small
docs.text:
Each function should perform one task.

Good:

create_backup()

send_notification()

cleanup()

Avoid one function performing many unrelated operations.

docs.title: Handle Errors Properly
docs.text:
Display meaningful messages.

echo "Error: Backup directory not found."

exit 1

docs.title: Log Important Events
docs.text:
Record significant operations.

echo "$(date '+%F %T') Backup Started" >> backup.log

Logs simplify troubleshooting.

docs.title: Avoid Hardcoded Values
docs.text:
Poor:

cp file.txt /backup

Better:

BACKUP_DIR="/backup"

cp file.txt "$BACKUP_DIR"

docs.title: Use Constants
docs.text:
Values that should not change can be defined once.

readonly LOG_FILE="/var/log/app.log"

docs.title: Use Descriptive Exit Codes
docs.text:
exit 0

Success.

exit 1

General failure.

Document custom exit codes if they are used.

docs.title: Clean Up Temporary Files
docs.text:
Use trap.

cleanup() {

    rm -f "$TEMP_FILE"
}

trap cleanup EXIT

docs.title: Minimize Root Usage
docs.text:
Run scripts as a regular user whenever possible.

Use sudo only for operations requiring elevated privileges.

docs.title: Never Store Secrets in Scripts
docs.text:
Avoid:

PASSWORD="mypassword"

Instead:

  • Read from environment variables
  • Prompt securely using read -s
  • Use a secrets management solution when appropriate

docs.title: Use ShellCheck
docs.text:
Analyze scripts for common issues.

shellcheck script.sh

ShellCheck identifies syntax problems and recommends improvements.

docs.title: Test Scripts
docs.text:
Test:

  • Valid input

  • Missing files
  • Permission errors
  • Network failures
  • Edge cases

Testing helps identify problems before deployment.

Run script.

Enable debugging.

docs.text:
Scenario

A deployment script occasionally fails, but no one knows why.

Problems:

  • No logging
  • No error handling

Improved script:

#!/bin/bash

}

log "Deployment Started"

if [ $# -lt 1 ]
then
    log "Missing deployment file."

    exit 1
fi

kubectl apply -f "$1"

log "Deployment Completed"

The script is now safer, easier to troubleshoot, and suitable for production use.

docs.text: Variables are the foundation of every Bash script. A variable stores a value that can be reused throughout a script, making automation flexible, reusable, and easier to maintain. Instead of hardcoding values, scripts use variables to store filenames, user input, command output, configuration values, and system information. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should master variables to write efficient and production-ready Bash scripts.

docs.title: Why Learn Variables?
docs.text:
Imagine writing a backup script.

Without variables:

cp /home/basha/data.txt /backup/

tar -czf /backup/data.tar.gz /backup/

If the backup location changes, every occurrence must be updated.

Using variables:

BACKUP_DIR="/backup"

cp /home/basha/data.txt $BACKUP_DIR

tar -czf $BACKUP_DIR/data.tar.gz $BACKUP_DIR

echo "Backup stored in $BACKUP_DIR"

Only one value needs to change.

docs.title: What is a Variable?
docs.text:
A variable is a named container that stores data.

Example:

USERNAME

↓

basha

Whenever the script references USERNAME, Bash substitutes the stored value.

docs.title: Creating Variables
docs.text:
Syntax:

VARIABLE=value

Example:

NAME="Basha"

Display the value.

echo $NAME

Output:

Basha

docs.title: Important Syntax Rules
docs.text:
Correct:

CITY="Hyderabad"

Incorrect:

CITY = "Hyderabad"

Spaces around = are not allowed.

docs.title: Variable Naming Rules
docs.text:
Variable names:

  • May contain letters
  • May contain numbers
  • May contain underscores (_)
  • Cannot begin with a number
  • Cannot contain spaces

Valid:

USERNAME

server_ip

BACKUP_DIR

Invalid:

2user

server-ip

backup dir

docs.title: Using Variables
docs.text:
Reference a variable using $.

Example:

USER="linux"

echo $USER

Output:

linux

docs.title: Using Curly Braces
docs.text:
Curly braces improve readability.

FILE="backup"

echo "${FILE}.tar.gz"

Output:

backup.tar.gz

docs.title: String Variables
docs.text:
GREETING="Hello"

NAME="Basha"

echo "$GREETING $NAME"

Output:

Hello Basha

docs.title: Numeric Variables
docs.text:
COUNT=10

echo $COUNT

Output:

10

docs.title: Arithmetic Operations
docs.text:
Use arithmetic expansion.

A=20

B=10

echo $((A+B))

Output:

30

Other operations:

echo $((A-B))

echo $((A*B))

echo $((A/B))

docs.title: Command Substitution
docs.text:
Store command output.

DATE=$(date)

Display:

echo $DATE

Another example:

HOST=$(hostname)

echo $HOST

read NAME

echo "Hello $NAME"

Prompt the user.

read -p "Enter your name: " NAME

export APP_ENV=production

Double quotes allow variable expansion.

echo "Hello $NAME"

Single quotes prevent expansion.

echo 'Hello $NAME'

docs.text: Understand what happens from the moment you press the power button until the Linux login screen appears. Master the Linux boot process to troubleshoot boot failures, configure bootloaders, and understand how Linux starts in production environments.

docs.text:

  • Differentiate BIOS and UEFI
  • Understand the role of GRUB
  • Explain what the Linux Kernel does during boot

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, you should complete:

  • Introduction to Linux
  • Linux History and Open Source
  • Linux Fundamentals — Distributions and Architecture
  • Linux Kernel Explained
  • Linux Desktop vs Server Editions
  • Linux Installation

docs.title: Why Learn the Linux Boot Process?
docs.text:
Every Linux server follows the same sequence every time it starts.

Understanding this sequence helps you:

  • Troubleshoot boot failures
  • Recover broken systems
  • Repair GRUB
  • Debug kernel issues
  • Understand system initialization
  • Become a better Linux Administrator

In production environments, boot-related issues can prevent critical services from starting.

docs.title: Linux Boot Process Overview
docs.text:
The Linux boot process consists of several stages.

Power ON
    │
    ▼
BIOS / UEFI
    │
    ▼
Boot Loader (GRUB)
    │
    ▼
Linux Kernel
    │
    ▼
Initramfs
    │
    ▼
systemd (PID 1)
    │
    ▼
System Services
    │
    ▼
Login Prompt / GUI

Each stage hands control to the next. If one stage fails, the system may hang, drop to a recovery shell, or never reach a login prompt.

docs.title: Stage 1 — BIOS / UEFI
docs.text:
When you press the power button, firmware runs first.

Firmware Description BIOS Older firmware used on traditional systems UEFI Modern firmware used by most computers and cloud VMs

Firmware responsibilities:

  • Initialize hardware
  • Perform a Power-On Self-Test (POST)
  • Locate a bootable device
  • Hand control to the bootloader

On modern systems, UEFI is more common. Cloud virtual machines usually boot through UEFI or a hypervisor-managed boot path that behaves similarly.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Bootloader (GRUB)
docs.text:
The bootloader loads the Linux kernel into memory.

On most Linux distributions, the bootloader is GRUB (GRand Unified Bootloader).

GRUB typically:

  • Displays a boot menu (on some systems)
  • Loads the Linux kernel
  • Loads the Initramfs
  • Passes kernel parameters
  • Starts the kernel

Boot files are commonly stored under:

/boot

Example contents:

vmlinuz-*
initrd.img-* / initramfs-*
grub/

If GRUB is misconfigured or missing, the system may fail before Linux even starts.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Linux Kernel
docs.text:
Once loaded, the Linux kernel takes control of the system.

During boot, the kernel:

  • Initializes hardware drivers
  • Sets up memory management
  • Mounts early filesystems
  • Prepares the system for user space
  • Starts the first user-space process

The kernel is the bridge between hardware and the rest of the operating system.

docs.title: Stage 4 — Initramfs
docs.text:
Initramfs stands for Initial RAM Filesystem.

It is a temporary root filesystem loaded into memory during early boot.

Initramfs helps the kernel:

  • Load required storage drivers
  • Unlock encrypted disks (when configured)
  • Locate and mount the real root filesystem
  • Hand control to the real system

After the real root filesystem is ready, Initramfs is discarded and the system continues with the actual root (/).

docs.title: Stage 5 — systemd (PID 1)
docs.text:
Modern Linux distributions use systemd as the first user-space process.

systemd is PID 1 — the parent of all other processes.

systemd:

  • Mounts filesystems
  • Starts system services
  • Manages targets (runlevel-like states)
  • Brings the system to a usable state

Common targets:

Target Purpose multi-user.target Text-based multi-user system (typical servers) graphical.target Desktop / GUI environment rescue.target Minimal recovery environment

Most production servers boot into multi-user.target.

docs.title: Stage 6 — System Services
docs.text:
After systemd starts, it launches essential services such as:

  • Networking
  • Logging
  • SSH (Secure Shell)
  • Cron / timers
  • Application services

Service startup order and dependencies are managed by systemd unit files.

If a critical service fails during boot, the system may still reach a login prompt — or it may appear “up” while important workloads remain unavailable.

docs.title: Stage 7 — Login Prompt / GUI
docs.text:
Finally, the system presents a way for users to interact:

  • Text login prompt on servers
  • Graphical login on desktops
  • Remote SSH access for cloud servers

At this point, Linux is fully booted and ready for administration.

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
In production, engineers rarely watch a physical boot screen.

Typical scenarios:

Scenario Why boot knowledge matters Cloud VM won't accept SSH Boot may be stuck before networking/SSH starts Server hangs after kernel update Kernel or Initramfs issue Wrong default target Desktop target on a headless server Slow boot after change A service is delaying multi-user.target

Understanding each stage helps you answer:

  • Did firmware find a disk?
  • Did GRUB load a kernel?
  • Did the root filesystem mount?
  • Did systemd reach the expected target?
  • Did critical services start?

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Know your default systemd target.
  • Keep /boot healthy and monitored for space.
  • Test kernel updates in a lab before production.
  • Use systemd-analyze to investigate slow boots.
  • Document recovery steps for GRUB and Initramfs failures.
  • Prefer reversible changes when modifying boot configuration.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Thinking the login prompt means every service started successfully.

✅ Verify critical services with systemctl after boot.

❌ Ignoring /boot disk space.

✅ Full /boot partitions commonly break kernel updates.

❌ Changing GRUB or kernel parameters without a recovery plan.

✅ Always keep a working kernel entry and a rollback path.

❌ Confusing BIOS/UEFI differences during installation.

✅ Match boot mode (BIOS vs UEFI) with disk partitioning style.

docs.text:

  3. What is the Linux kernel's role during boot?
  4. What is Initramfs?

docs.text:

  4. How can you measure boot time on a Linux system?

  3. How do kernel updates introduce boot risk, and how would you reduce that risk?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Why the Linux boot process matters
  • The full boot sequence from power-on to login
  • The roles of BIOS/UEFI, GRUB, the kernel, Initramfs, and systemd
  • How system services start after boot
  • Practical commands to inspect boot state and performance

Mastering the boot process helps you recover systems faster and understand how Linux becomes ready for production workloads.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Boot is a staged handoff: firmware → bootloader → kernel → Initramfs → systemd → services → login.
  • GRUB loads the kernel and Initramfs.
  • Initramfs prepares the real root filesystem.
  • systemd (PID 1) brings the system to a target and starts services.
  • systemctl get-default, systemd-analyze, ls /boot, and journalctl -b are essential first checks.

docs.title: Capacity Planning — Preparing Linux Infrastructure for Future Growth
Capacity Planning — Preparing Linux Infrastructure for Future Growth
docs.text: Capacity Planning is the process of forecasting future infrastructure requirements based on current resource utilization, workload trends, business growth, and performance objectives. Rather than reacting to resource shortages after they occur, capacity planning enables organizations to proactively scale CPU, memory, storage, networking, and infrastructure to meet future demand. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Infrastructure Engineer should understand how to perform effective capacity planning.

docs.title: What is Capacity Planning?
docs.text:
Capacity planning ensures infrastructure can support:

  • Current workloads
  • Future business growth
  • Seasonal demand
  • Unexpected traffic spikes
  • Disaster recovery requirements

It combines monitoring, forecasting, and scaling strategies.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A production database server suddenly runs out of storage.

Investigation:

df -h

Filesystem usage:

100%

Further analysis:

du -sh /var/lib/*

Database files have grown steadily for several months, but no capacity review was performed.

The administrator:

  • Expands storage
  • Implements storage growth monitoring
  • Configures alerts at 80% utilization
  • Establishes monthly capacity reviews

The issue is resolved without future outages.

Root cause:

Lack of Capacity Planning

docs.text:

  • Forecast resource growth regularly.
  • Define capacity thresholds.
  • Review trends monthly.
  • Plan for seasonal demand.
  • Include disaster recovery requirements in capacity planning.
  • Document capacity forecasts and scaling decisions.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:

✅ Always review long-term growth trends.

❌ Monitoring only infrastructure and not applications.

✅ Avoid this mistake: monitoring only infrastructure and not applications.

❌ Forgetting storage growth.

✅ Remember to storage growth.

❌ Never reviewing or updating capacity plans.

✅ Always reviewing or updating capacity plans.

docs.title: CIS Benchmark Basics — Hardening Linux Systems Using Security Standards
CIS Benchmark Basics — Hardening Linux Systems Using Security Standards
docs.text: CIS Benchmarks are internationally recognized security configuration guidelines developed by the Center for Internet Security (CIS). They provide detailed recommendations for securely configuring operating systems, cloud platforms, databases, applications, and networking devices. Organizations around the world use CIS Benchmarks to reduce security risks, improve system hardening, and meet compliance requirements. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand the basics of CIS Benchmarks and how they improve Linux security.

docs.text:
Imagine deploying a new Linux server.

Without a security standard:

Server Installed

↓

Unknown Configuration

↓

Security Risks

With CIS Benchmarks:

Server Installed

↓

CIS Recommendations Applied

↓

Hardened Configuration

↓

A standardized security baseline improves consistency and reduces risk.

docs.title: What are CIS Benchmarks?
docs.text:
CIS Benchmarks are security best practices developed by the Center for Internet Security (CIS).

They provide recommendations for:

  • Linux operating systems
  • Windows
  • Kubernetes
  • Docker
  • Cloud platforms
  • Databases
  • Network devices
  • Applications

The goal is to establish a secure baseline configuration.

docs.title: Why CIS Benchmarks Matter
docs.text:
Benefits include:

  • Improve security
  • Reduce attack surface
  • Standardize configurations
  • Support compliance
  • Simplify security audits
  • Improve operational consistency

docs.title: CIS Benchmark Levels
docs.text: Most CIS Benchmarks organize recommendations into two implementation levels.

docs.title: Level 1
docs.text:
Suitable for most systems.

Focuses on:

  • Strong security
  • Minimal operational impact

Recommended for:

  • Production servers
  • General enterprise environments

docs.title: Level 2
docs.text:
Provides additional hardening.

Focuses on:

  • Higher security
  • More restrictive configurations

May affect application compatibility.

Often used for:

  • High-security environments
  • Government systems
  • Financial institutions

docs.title: Common Linux CIS Recommendations
docs.text:
Typical recommendations include:

  • Disable unused services
  • Secure SSH configuration
  • Configure firewalls
  • Enable auditing
  • Protect file permissions
  • Enable automatic security updates
  • Remove unnecessary software
  • Configure password policies
  • Secure bootloader settings
  • Enable Mandatory Access Control (SELinux or AppArmor)

docs.title: Example Hardening Checklist
docs.text:
✓ Firewall Enabled

✓ SSH Hardened

✓ Root Login Disabled

✓ Password Policy Configured

✓ Automatic Updates Enabled

✓ Audit Logging Enabled

✓ SELinux/AppArmor Enabled

docs.title: Password Policy
docs.text:
Example recommendations:

  • Strong passwords
  • Password aging
  • Password history
  • Minimum password length
  • Account lockout policies

docs.title: SSH Hardening
docs.text:
Typical recommendations:

PermitRootLogin no

PasswordAuthentication no

Use SSH keys whenever possible.

docs.title: File Permissions
docs.text:
Review:

  • World-writable files
  • SUID files
  • SGID files
  • Sensitive configuration files
  • SSH private keys

docs.title: Firewall Configuration
docs.text:
Allow only required ports.

Example:

SSH

HTTPS

Application Ports

Block everything else.

docs.title: Audit Logging
docs.text:
Enable:

auditd

Monitor:

  • Logins
  • File changes
  • Authentication
  • Privilege escalation
  • Administrative actions

docs.title: Security Updates
docs.text:
Recommendations include:

  • Apply updates promptly
  • Keep kernels updated
  • Remove vulnerable software
  • Review security advisories

docs.title: Compliance Assessment
docs.text:
Organizations regularly verify compliance by:

  • Reviewing configurations
  • Running security scans
  • Comparing settings with CIS recommendations
  • Generating compliance reports

docs.title: CIS-CAT
docs.text:
The CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT) helps assess systems against applicable CIS Benchmarks.

It can:

  • Detect non-compliant settings
  • Generate reports
  • Measure compliance
  • Identify remediation actions

docs.text:
Several tools help assess Linux security.

Examples:

These tools assist administrators in identifying security gaps.

docs.title: Common CIS Benchmark Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Solution Applying all recommendations without testing Test changes in staging first Ignoring application compatibility Validate workloads before deployment Never reviewing compliance Schedule regular audits Treating compliance as a one-time task Continuously assess and improve Ignoring documentation Record hardening changes and exceptions

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A security audit identifies several weaknesses.

Findings:

SSH Root Login Enabled

Firewall Disabled

Audit Service Stopped

Outdated Packages

Remediation:

  • Disable root SSH login.
  • Enable and configure the firewall.
  • Start and enable auditd.
  • Apply pending security updates.
  • Re-run the compliance assessment.

The system now aligns much more closely with recommended security baselines.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use CIS Benchmarks as a security baseline.
  • Apply Level 1 recommendations to most production systems.
  • Test Level 2 recommendations before deployment.
  • Regularly review system compliance.
  • Document security exceptions.
  • Combine CIS guidance with organizational security policies.
  • Continuously monitor and improve system hardening.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Treating CIS compliance as a one-time project.

✅ Avoid this mistake: treating CIS compliance as a one-time project.

❌ Applying recommendations without testing.

✅ Test before applying recommendations without testing.

❌ Ignoring application compatibility.

✅ Always review application compatibility.

❌ Leaving identified security issues unresolved.

✅ Do not leave identified security issues unresolved.

❌ Failing to document configuration changes.

✅ Avoid this mistake: failing to document configuration changes.

CIS Benchmarks provide a structured approach to securing Linux systems by defining standardized hardening recommendations. Following these guidelines helps reduce security risks, improve operational consistency, support compliance efforts, and strengthen the overall security posture of enterprise environments.

docs.title: Command History
docs.text: Every command you execute in the Linux shell is recorded in your command history. Learning how to view, search, reuse, and manage command history can dramatically improve your productivity and help you work faster on Linux systems.

After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals

docs.title: Why Learn Command History?
docs.text:
Imagine you previously executed a complex command like:

kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

Instead of typing it again, Linux allows you to retrieve it instantly.

Command history helps you:

  • Save time
  • Reduce typing errors
  • Repeat complex commands
  • Troubleshoot efficiently
  • Learn from previously executed commands

docs.title: What is Command History?
docs.text:
Bash automatically records the commands you execute during a session.

Example:

pwd

ls -la

cd /etc

cat hosts

history

Each command is assigned a unique history number.

docs.title: Display Command History
docs.text:
history

Example output:

1 pwd

2 ls -la

3 cd /etc

4 cat hosts

5 history

docs.title: Display Last Few Commands
docs.text:
Display the last five commands:

history 5

Example:

96 ls

97 pwd

98 whoami

99 date

100 history

docs.title: Execute Previous Commands
docs.text:
Run a command by its history number.

Example:

!98

Executes command number 98.

docs.title: Execute the Last Command
docs.text:
Run the previous command again.

!!

Example:

sudo !!

Scenario:

apt update

Permission denied.

Instead of typing again:

sudo !!

Bash automatically executes:

sudo apt update

This is one of the most useful Bash shortcuts.

docs.title: Execute Commands by Prefix
docs.text:
Run the most recent command starting with:

!git

If your previous command was:

git status

It runs automatically.

Other examples:

!kubectl

!docker

!terraform

docs.title: Search Command History
docs.text:
One of Bash's most powerful features.

Press:

Ctrl + R

Example:

Search:

docker

Output:

(reverse-i-search)`docker':
docker ps -a

Press:

  • Ctrl + R again for older matches
  • Enter to execute
  • Esc to edit before execution

docs.title: Search Using grep
docs.text:
Display commands containing a keyword.

history | grep docker

Example:

15 docker ps

18 docker images

20 docker logs

Another example:

history | grep kubectl

docs.title: History File
docs.text:
Bash stores history in:

~/.bash_history

View it:

cat ~/.bash_history

docs.title: History Variables
docs.text:
Display history size.

echo $HISTSIZE

Example:

1000

docs.title: Containers — Namespaces, cgroups, OverlayFS, and OCI
Containers — Namespaces, cgroups, OverlayFS, and OCI
Overview
docs.text:
When people say “we run it in Docker” or “Kubernetes pods”, beginners often think containers are tiny virtual machines (VMs). They are not. This tutorial shows what the Linux kernel actually does — namespaces, cgroups, and overlays — without requiring a Kubernetes cluster.

Plain problem: A container exits with Out Of Memory (OOM) killed, or disk fills with “image layers”. YAML and kubectl do not explain why — namespaces, cgroups, and OverlayFS on the host do.

A container is a normal Linux process (or tree of processes) with:

  1. Namespaces — isolated view (own process IDs, network, mount table, …)
  2. cgroups — CPU/memory/I/O limits
  3. Often OverlayFS — layered root filesystem
  4. OCI standards — portable image and runtime formats (runc, crun)

This is Tutorial 14 in Module 14: Containers & Cloud of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ubuntu practice VM with sudo
  • Docker Engine or docker.io package (lab installs if missing)
  • Basic process concepts from Process Management helpful

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain containers vs VMs in plain language
  • Name key namespaces and what each isolates
  • Explain cgroups memory/CPU limits simply
  • Inspect a running container from the host with ps, lsns, findmnt
  • Run a safe unshare demo without full Kubernetes
  • Answer fresher interview questions on container internals

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Container runtimes (Docker → containerd → runc) configure namespaces and cgroups, mount overlay rootfs, then exec your process. Kubernetes schedules pods on nodes that use the same kernel primitives.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text: Interview question: “What is a container?” Weak answer: “Docker.” Strong answer: “A process with isolated namespaces and cgroup limits, started by an OCI runtime on Linux.” That answer comes from this page.

docs.title: Containers vs VMs (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: A VM is a whole flat with its own kitchen (guest OS + kernel). A container is a roommate with labelled cupboards — same building kernel, separate labelled spaces (namespaces), and a lease on electricity (cgroups).

VM Container Kernel Guest + host Shared host kernel Boot Full OS Starts one app/process Isolation Hardware virtualisation Namespaces + cgroups Typical start time Minutes Seconds

Interview line: “Containers share the host kernel; isolation is OS-level, not hardware-level like VMs.”

docs.title: Namespaces (plain first)
docs.text:
Namespaces make a process think it has its own system slice:

Namespace Isolates pid Process IDs net Network interfaces, routes mnt Mount points uts Hostname ipc Inter-process communication user User/group IDs (user namespaces) Terminal
lsns
lsns -p 1

docs.title: cgroups (control groups)
docs.text:
Analogy: cgroups are utility caps — “this container may use 512 MB RAM and half a CPU.” Exceed memory → OOM kill inside the cgroup.

Modern Linux uses cgroups v2 unified hierarchy under /sys/fs/cgroup/.

Terminal
grep memory /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-*.scope/memory.max 2>/dev/null | head -3

(Docker path varies — lab inspects live container.)

docs.title: OverlayFS
docs.text:
OverlayFS stacks read-only lower layers + writable upper layer → container root filesystem. Many layers → disk use on the node.

Terminal
findmnt -t overlay

docs.title: OCI
docs.text:
Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines:

  • Image spec — filesystem bundle format
  • Runtime spec — how to run a container (config.json + rootfs)

Docker builds OCI-compatible images; runc is a common low-level runtime.

docs.title: Safe unshare demo (no Docker required)
docs.text:
Terminal
unshare --fork --pid --mount-proc /bin/bash
# inside: ps aux shows very few processes
exit

Requires user namespaces available; run on lab VM only.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Treating containers as VM substitutes for strong isolation boundaries
  • No memory limits → one container OOMs the node
  • Ignoring host disk from image/layer buildup
  • Debugging only inside container without checking node cgroups

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Run a Docker container with a memory limit, inspect namespaces and cgroups from the host, run unshare, and save proof under ~/rebash-linux/lab22.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM 2 GB+ RAM recommended Docker Lab installs docker.io if needed User in docker group OR use sudo docker

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab22 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab22
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y docker.io util-linux
sudo systemctl enable --now docker

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Platform ticket: “Pod OOMKilled — prove whether the cgroup memory limit caused it.” You reproduce a small limit, watch the container die, inspect cgroup files, and document host-side evidence.

docs.title: Task 1 – Run container with memory limit
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab22
sudo docker run -d --name lab22-mem --memory=64m nginx:alpine
sudo docker ps --filter name=lab22-mem | tee docker-ps.txt
CID=$(sudo docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' lab22-mem)
echo "$CID" | tee container-id.txt
test -n "$CID"

Expected output

Container lab22-mem running; container-id.txt holds full ID.

docs.title: Task 2 – Host inspection (namespaces, mounts, cgroups)
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab22
PID=$(sudo docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' lab22-mem)
echo "container pid=$PID" | tee container-pid.txt
sudo lsns -p "$PID" | tee lsns-container.txt
sudo findmnt -T /proc/"$PID"/root 2>/dev/null | tee findmnt-container.txt || sudo findmnt | grep overlay | head -5 | tee findmnt-container.txt
sudo cat /proc/"$PID"/cgroup | tee cgroup-proc.txt
test -s lsns-container.txt

Expected output

lsns-container.txt shows multiple namespace types (pid, net, mnt, …). Overlay mount appears in findmnt output.

docs.title: Task 3 – Break (OOM), fix (raise limit), prove
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab22
sudo docker update --memory=32m lab22-mem
sudo docker exec lab22-mem sh -c 'dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/shm/fill bs=1M count=64' 2>&1 | tee oom-attempt.txt || true
sleep 2
sudo docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' lab22-mem | tee oom-status.txt
sudo docker rm -f lab22-mem 2>/dev/null || true
sudo docker run -d --name lab22-mem-fixed --memory=256m nginx:alpine
sudo docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}}' lab22-mem-fixed | tee fixed-status.txt
unshare --fork --pid --mount-proc echo unshare-ok 2>&1 | tee unshare-proof.txt
echo "lab22 containers OK" | tee evidence.txt

Expected output

Low memory limit may show OOMKilled true or container restarted. After 256m limit, status running. unshare-proof.txt shows success or documents permission note.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• Docker container ran with --memory limit
  • lsns output saved for container PID
  • OOM or stress behaviour observed and documented
  • You can explain container vs VM in one minute

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Cannot connect to Docker Daemon down sudo systemctl start docker Permission denied Not in docker group Use sudo docker unshare fails User namespaces restricted Note in evidence; use Docker inspect path No overlay in findmnt Different storage driver docker info — graph driver

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text: Run sudo docker info | grep -E 'Storage Driver|Cgroup' and save to docker-info.txt.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• You saw containers as host processes with namespaces
  • You linked memory limits to OOM behaviour
  • You have host-side inspection commands for interviews

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
sudo docker rm -f lab22-mem lab22-mem-fixed 2>/dev/null || true
sudo docker system prune -f

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:

  • Can whiteboard namespaces + cgroups
  • Ready for troubleshooting methodology next

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. docker run --memory=64m — sets cgroup memory max; lab scales down to trigger OOM.
  2. docker inspect State.Pid — maps container to host process for lsns.
  3. lsns -p — proves namespaces without Kubernetes.
  4. /proc/PID/cgroup — shows cgroup membership path.
  5. unshare --fork --pid — minimal “container feel” without Docker.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Containers are not VMs — kernel escapes are critical CVE class; patch nodes.
  • Run as non-root inside containers; use user namespaces where supported.
  • Limit capabilities (--cap-drop); read-only rootfs when possible.
  • SELinux/AppArmor profiles apply to container processes on the host.
  • Scan images for CVEs; signed images from trusted registries.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ No resource limits.

✅ Always set memory/CPU requests and limits (Docker flags or Kubernetes resources).

❌ Debugging only inside container.

✅ OOM and disk are host cgroup/filesystem stories — inspect from the node.

❌ Root in Dockerfile.

✅ Use non-root USER; reduces risk if container boundary fails.

docs.title: CPU Monitoring — Monitoring Processor Performance in Linux
CPU Monitoring — Monitoring Processor Performance in Linux
docs.text: CPU Monitoring is the process of tracking processor utilization, system load, CPU wait times, process execution, and overall processor performance. High CPU utilization can lead to slow applications, increased response times, and poor system performance. By monitoring CPU usage, administrators can identify resource-intensive processes, detect bottlenecks, and optimize workloads before they impact production systems. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand how to monitor CPU performance in Linux.

docs.title: Crash Investigation — Diagnosing Linux System and Application Failures
Crash Investigation — Diagnosing Linux System and Application Failures
docs.text: Crash Investigation is the process of identifying, analyzing, and resolving unexpected failures in Linux systems, applications, services, or the Linux kernel. Crashes can result from software bugs, hardware failures, resource exhaustion, kernel panics, filesystem corruption, or configuration issues. A structured crash investigation helps minimize downtime, identify the root cause, and prevent similar incidents in the future. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should know how to investigate crashes in production environments.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A production Java application crashes repeatedly.

Investigation:

systemctl status application

Shows repeated failures.

Next:

journalctl -u application

Application logs show:

OutOfMemoryError

Further investigation:

free -h

Available memory is nearly exhausted.

Kernel logs:

journalctl -k | grep -i oom

Confirm the OOM Killer terminated the Java process.

Resolution:

  • Increase application heap size appropriately.
  • Optimize memory usage.
  • Add system memory if required.
  • Configure monitoring and alerts for memory pressure.

The application remains stable after remediation.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Preserve logs before restarting services.
  • Investigate both system and application logs.
  • Collect CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics.
  • Review previous boot logs after system crashes.
  • Enable core dumps for critical applications when appropriate.
  • Document investigation findings and corrective actions.
  • Perform post-incident reviews to prevent recurrence.
  • Automate monitoring and alerting for critical resources.

✅ Always checking kernel messages.

❌ Assuming every crash has the same cause.

✅ Verify every crash has the same cause instead of assuming it.

docs.title: curl — Transferring Data and Testing APIs from the Command Line
curl — Transferring Data and Testing APIs from the Command Line
docs.text: curl (Client URL) is one of the most powerful command-line tools for transferring data using URLs. It supports numerous protocols, including HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SFTP, and more. Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, API developers, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) use curl daily to test web servers, interact with REST APIs, download files, verify application health, and troubleshoot network services.

docs.text:

  • A website is unreachable.

The first command many engineers use is:

docs.title: What is curl?
docs.text:
curl stands for:

Client URL

It transfers data between a client and a server.

Supported protocols include:

  • HTTP
  • HTTPS
  • FTP
  • FTPS
  • SFTP
  • SCP
  • SMTP
  • LDAP
  • MQTT
  • File

docs.text:
Client
   │
   ▼
HTTP Request

Web Server

Client

docs.title: Basic Request
docs.text:
Request a web page.

curl https://example.com

The response body is displayed in the terminal.

docs.title: View Only HTTP Headers
docs.text:
curl -I https://example.com

Example:

HTTP/2 200

content-type: text/html

docs.text:

curl -L http://example.com

-L tells curl to follow redirects automatically.

docs.text:
Useful for troubleshooting.

curl -v https://example.com

Shows:

  • DNS lookup
  • TCP connection
  • TLS handshake
  • Request headers
  • Response headers

docs.title: Silent Mode
docs.text:
Suppress progress output.

Useful in shell scripts.

docs.text:

GET is the default HTTP method.

docs.title: Send a POST Request
docs.text: curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users

docs.title: Send JSON Data

curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"name":"Alice","role":"admin"}'

docs.title: Send Custom Headers
docs.text:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" \
https://api.example.com

https://example.com

-H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" \
https://api.example.com

docs.text:

https://example.com

200

To ignore certificate verification (testing only):

docs.text:
Feature curl wget API Requests ✅ Excellent Limited Download Files ✅ ✅ Excellent Upload Data ✅ Limited HTTP Methods Multiple Mostly GET Custom Headers ✅ ✅ Resume Downloads Basic Excellent

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A Kubernetes application fails its readiness probe.

Investigation:

Check the health endpoint.

curl -v http://localhost:8080/health

Response:

HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error

Check application logs.

journalctl -u myapp

The application cannot connect to its database.

After fixing the database connection:

curl http://localhost:8080/health

Response:

OK

The readiness probe now succeeds, and the application becomes available.

docs.text:

  • Use -s in automation scripts to suppress unnecessary output.
  • Verify HTTP status codes when testing APIs.
  • Protect authentication credentials and tokens.
  • Avoid using -k except in controlled testing environments.

docs.title: Disaster Recovery — Recovering Linux Systems from Major Failures
Disaster Recovery — Recovering Linux Systems from Major Failures
docs.text: Disaster Recovery (DR) is the process of restoring critical Linux systems, applications, infrastructure, and data after a major failure such as hardware failure, cyberattack, natural disaster, accidental deletion, or complete site outage. A well-designed Disaster Recovery plan minimizes downtime, protects business operations, and ensures services can be restored within acceptable recovery objectives. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Infrastructure Engineer should understand Disaster Recovery planning and execution.

docs.text:
Scenario

A ransomware attack encrypts a production Linux server.

Investigation confirms that the operating system and application data are compromised.

The Disaster Recovery plan is activated:

  • The compromised server is isolated.
  • A new Linux server is provisioned using Infrastructure as Code.
  • Clean backups are restored.
  • Applications are redeployed.
  • Network connectivity is validated.
  • Security patches are applied.
  • Monitoring confirms normal operation.

Business services resume within the organization's Recovery Time Objective (RTO).

Root cause:

Cybersecurity Incident Requiring Disaster Recovery

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Maintain a documented Disaster Recovery plan.
  • Define clear RPO and RTO objectives.
  • Test recovery procedures regularly.
  • Automate infrastructure recovery where possible.
  • Keep backups encrypted and protected.
  • Document recovery roles and responsibilities.
  • Monitor systems after recovery.
  • Review and improve the DR plan after every exercise or real incident.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Creating a Disaster Recovery plan without testing it.

✅ Avoid this mistake: creating a Disaster Recovery plan without testing it.

❌ Assuming backups alone guarantee recovery.

✅ Verify backups alone guarantee recovery instead of assuming it.

❌ Forgetting to validate applications after restoration.

✅ Remember to to validate applications after restoration.

❌ Keeping outdated recovery documentation.

✅ Avoid this mistake: keeping outdated recovery documentation.

❌ Ignoring communication during disaster events.

✅ Always review communication during disaster events.

docs.title: Disk Monitoring — Monitoring Storage Usage and Disk Health
Disk Monitoring — Monitoring Storage Usage and Disk Health
docs.text: Disk Monitoring is the process of tracking disk space, filesystem usage, inode consumption, disk I/O performance, and storage health to ensure Linux systems continue operating reliably. Running out of disk space or experiencing storage performance issues can cause application failures, database corruption, logging problems, and even system crashes. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should know how to monitor storage resources proactively in production environments.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A production application reports:

No Space Left on Device

Investigation:

df -h

Disk usage:

100%

Next:

du -sh /var/*

Findings:

/var/log

↓

Large Log Files

The administrator archives old logs, verifies logrotate is functioning correctly, and restores normal disk usage.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Monitor disk space continuously.
  • Configure alerts before disks become full (for example, at 80% usage).
  • Monitor inode usage in addition to disk capacity.
  • Rotate and archive logs regularly.
  • Review disk I/O performance.
  • Monitor SMART health for physical disks.
  • Plan storage expansion before capacity limits are reached.
  • Include storage monitoring in centralized monitoring platforms such as Prometheus and Grafana.
