docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Disk-full alerts look like this in real operations:

“Disk full — cannot write file.”

You need two answers fast:

  1. Which filesystem (mount) is full? → df
  2. Which folder tree grew? → du

Sometimes the error says “No space left” but df -h shows free megabytes — then you check inodes with df -i. Sometimes df and du disagree because a deleted log is still held open by a running process.

File attributes are metadata — permissions, owner, size, timestamps — that you read with ls -l and stat. “Permission denied” is often an attribute problem, not a disk problem.

This is Tutorial 5 in Module 3: Linux Filesystem of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series — practical Linux for Cloud and DevOps work.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Paths, Links, Mounts, and Inodes — you know mounts and inodes
  • A practice Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VM with write access under your home directory
  • Optional: sudo for system-wide lsof examples later in your career

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain the difference between df (per mount) and du (per directory tree)
  • Check block space and inode capacity with df -h and df -i
  • Find large directories with du and sort human-readable sizes
  • Read mode, owner, size, and timestamps with stat
  • Pack evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab05 for a capacity ticket

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Disk capacity is tracked per mount. File attributes live on the inode. df, du, and stat report different layers of the same storage story.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
On-call message: “App cannot write logs.” You SSH in and run df -h. Root / looks fine. You panic anyway and delete random files.

A senior engineer asks: “Which mount failed? Did you check /var? Inodes? du on the hot path?”

This section teaches the checklist before you delete anything.

docs.title: df — how full is each mount?
docs.text:
Analogy: df is the fuel gauge per petrol tank. Your car may have two tanks (OS disk and data disk). A full data tank does not help if the OS tank is empty.

Flag Plain meaning df -h Human-readable free space per mount df -hT Also show filesystem type (ext4, xfs, …) df -i Inode free count — how many new files you can still create

What you can say in an interview: “df answers whether the mount has free blocks or inodes. I always check both -h and -i on ‘no space left’ errors.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
df -hT
df -i
df -hT / /var

docs.title: du — which directory tree grew?
docs.text:
Analogy: du is weighing each room in the building to find who hoarded boxes.

Command Plain meaning du -sh path Total size of path (summary) du -h --max-depth=1 path Size of each immediate child du -ah path \| sort -h All files, sorted by size

What you can say in an interview: “df tells me the mount is full; du tells me which subdirectory to clean — on that mount, not always on / alone.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
du -sh ~
du -h --max-depth=1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail

docs.title: File attributes with stat
docs.text:
Analogy: stat is the ID card for one file: who owns it, how big, when touched, what permissions.

Field Plain meaning Mode Permissions (rwx for user/group/other) Uid/Gid Owner user and group Size Bytes Inode Number on this filesystem Access/Modify/Change times atime, mtime, ctime

What you can say in an interview: “Before blaming ‘disk full’, I run stat — permission errors are often mode/owner, not capacity.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
stat /etc/passwd
stat -c '%n %A %U %G %s inode=%i' /etc/passwd

docs.title: When df and du disagree
docs.text:
Situation What happened df full, du on / smaller Another mount is full, or deleted-but-open file still holds space Create fails, df -h OK Inode exhaustion — run df -i Permission denied on write Mode/owner — not a capacity issue

What you can say in an interview: “If I delete a huge log but space does not return, I look for processes still holding the file open — often with lsof +L1 under sudo.”

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Checking only / while /var or a data volume is full
  • Ignoring inodes — many tiny files exhaust them first
  • Deleting open log files without restarting the writer — space does not return
  • Running du / on a huge host without depth limits — very slow
  • Confusing “cannot write” (permissions) with “disk full”

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Build a controlled sample tree, measure it with du, compare mounts with df, inspect attributes with stat, and save ticket-ready evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab05.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu practice VM df, du, stat from coreutils Write access Under $HOME only

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab05 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab05
set -euo pipefail
whoami | tee lab-user.txt
df -hT . | tee df-workspace.txt

Expected output

lab-user.txt and df-workspace.txt exist; workspace is on a real mount.

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Ticket: “Disk almost full on practice VM — before expanding the volume, prove which mount is tight, which folder grew, and show normal file attributes on a sample config.”

docs.title: Task 1 – Build sample tree and measure with du
docs.text:
Create controlled “log” and “cache” sizes so du has something real to report.

Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab05
set -euo pipefail

rm -rf sample-tree
mkdir -p sample-tree/{logs,cache,data}

dd if=/dev/zero of=sample-tree/logs/app.log bs=1M count=8 status=none
dd if=/dev/zero of=sample-tree/cache/pkg.bin bs=1M count=4 status=none

printf 'config=ok\n' > sample-tree/data/app.conf
for i in $(seq 1 50); do
  printf 'x' > "sample-tree/cache/tiny-$i.dat"
done

du -sh sample-tree | tee du-total.txt
du -h --max-depth=1 sample-tree | sort -h | tee du-depth1.txt
du -ah sample-tree | sort -h | tail -n 8 | tee du-largest.txt

test "$(du -sb sample-tree/logs | awk '{print $1}')" -gt "$(du -sb sample-tree/data | awk '{print $1}')"

Expected output

du-total.txt shows roughly 12M+ for the tree. du-depth1.txt lists logs, cache, data; logs is largest.

docs.title: Task 2 – Mount capacity: blocks and inodes
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab05
set -euo pipefail

df -hT | tee df-hT.txt
df -i | tee df-i.txt
df -hT . / | tee df-here-and-root.txt
findmnt -T . | tee findmnt-here.txt || true

find sample-tree -printf '.' | wc -c | tee file-count-ish.txt
test -s df-hT.txt && test -s df-i.txt

Expected output

df-hT.txt shows filesystem type and free space. df-i.txt shows inode use percentage.

docs.title: Task 3 – Attributes with stat and evidence pack
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab05
set -euo pipefail

stat sample-tree/data/app.conf | tee stat-app.conf.txt
stat -c 'name=%n mode=%A owner=%U group=%G size=%s inode=%i' \
  sample-tree/data/app.conf sample-tree/logs/app.log | tee stat-summary.txt
ls -l sample-tree/data/app.conf | tee ls-app.conf.txt

stat -c '%s' sample-tree/logs/app.log | tee log-bytes.txt
test "$(cat log-bytes.txt)" -eq $((8 * 1024 * 1024))

tar -czf disk-usage-evidence.tgz \
  lab-user.txt df-workspace.txt \
  du-total.txt du-depth1.txt du-largest.txt \
  df-hT.txt df-i.txt df-here-and-root.txt findmnt-here.txt \
  stat-app.conf.txt stat-summary.txt ls-app.conf.txt log-bytes.txt
ls -l disk-usage-evidence.tgz | tee evidence-ls.txt
test -s disk-usage-evidence.tgz

Expected output

stat-summary.txt shows mode/owner/size. log-bytes.txt is 8388608. Archive is non-empty.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• du -sh sample-tree matches the sizes you created (~12M+)
  • Both df -hT and df -i output files exist
  • stat shows owner and mode for app.conf
  • disk-usage-evidence.tgz exists under ~/rebash-linux/lab05

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix du: cannot read directory Permission on system paths Stay under $HOME in this lab Create fails; df -h OK Inodes full or wrong mount df -i; findmnt -T . Space not returned after delete File still open Find process with lsof; restart writer

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text:
Create capacity-scan.sh:

capacity-scan.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
echo "=== df for workspace ==="
df -hT .
echo "=== top 3 under sample-tree ==="
du -ah sample-tree 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 3
AVAIL_K=$(df -P . | awk 'NR==2 {print $4}')
if [ "$AVAIL_K" -lt 102400 ]; then
  echo "FAIL: less than 100M free on ."
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: sufficient free space on ."
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab05
chmod +x capacity-scan.sh
./capacity-scan.sh | tee capacity-scan.out
grep -q '^OK:' capacity-scan.out

Expected output

Script prints df, top three du entries, and OK: sufficient free space.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Separated mount capacity (df) from tree usage (du)
  • Checked inode capacity with df -i
  • Inspected file attributes with stat
  • Saved ticket-ready evidence

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab05
rm -rf sample-tree
# Keep disk-usage-evidence.tgz for revision if you want.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Lab completed under ~/rebash-linux/lab05
  • Can explain when df and du disagree
  • Know to check df -i on “no space left” errors
  • Can read mode/owner/size from stat

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. df -hT + df -i on the failing path — blocks and inodes.
  2. findmnt -T path — confirm which mount you are on.
  3. du --max-depth=1 on that mount — find the hot directory.
  4. stat before delete — permission vs capacity.
  5. lsof +L1 when space does not return — deleted-but-open files.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Do not run destructive rm -rf on production paths from a capacity ticket without a second check
  • Restrict who can read log trees that may contain secrets
  • Treat sudo lsof output carefully — paths may expose credentials
  • Immutable flags (chattr +i) protect configs — document them
  • Prefer measuring under the app user’s directories when possible

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Checking only the root filesystem.

✅ /var or a data disk can be full while / looks fine. Fix: read the Mounted on column for the path that failed.

❌ Ignoring inodes.

✅ Creates fail with “No space left” even when df -h shows free megabytes. Fix: always run df -i.

❌ Deleting large files still held open.

✅ Space does not return until the process closes the file. Fix: find the process (lsof), restart or reopen logs, confirm with df.

❌ Using du / without depth limits.

✅ Very slow on large hosts. Fix: du the specific mount path with --max-depth=1 first.

Disk Usage in Linux — Monitoring Storage and Filesystem Space
docs.text: Disk space is one of the most critical resources on any Linux system. Running out of disk space can cause application failures, database crashes, Kubernetes pod failures, CI/CD pipeline errors, and even prevent a server from booting. Linux provides several powerful utilities to monitor and analyze disk usage effectively.

df

docs.title: Inode Usage
docs.text:
Filesystems have two limits:

  • Storage space
  • Inodes

Display inode usage.

df -i

Example:

Filesystem

Inodes

IUsed

IFree

docs.text:
Scenario

A Kubernetes node becomes NotReady.

Pods cannot start.

Investigation:

df -h

find /var/log -type f -size +500M

Findings:

  • Rotate or archive old logs.
  • Expand storage if required.
  • Configure log rotation and monitoring.

docs.title: dmesg — Viewing Linux Kernel Messages
docs.text: dmesg (display message) is a Linux command used to view messages generated by the Linux kernel. These messages include information about system startup, hardware detection, device drivers, memory initialization, storage devices, network interfaces, USB devices, kernel warnings, and errors. The dmesg command is one of the most valuable troubleshooting tools for diagnosing hardware issues, boot problems, and kernel-related errors. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand how to use dmesg in production environments.

DNF (Dandified YUM) — Package Management in RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux, and Fedora
docs.text: DNF (Dandified YUM) is the modern package manager used by Fedora, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, and other RPM-based distributions. It simplifies installing, updating, removing, and managing software packages while providing better dependency resolution, improved performance, and enhanced security compared to its predecessor, YUM.

DNS (Domain Name System) — Translating Domain Names into IP Addresses
docs.text: DNS (Domain Name System) is the Internet's distributed naming system that translates human-readable domain names (such as google.com) into IP addresses that computers use for communication. Without DNS, users would need to remember numerical IP addresses instead of simple domain names. Understanding DNS is essential for Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, Network Engineers, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs).

docs.title: Why Learn DNS?
docs.text:
Imagine you type:

https://www.google.com

Your browser does not know Google's IP address.

Instead,

it asks a DNS server:

"What is the IP address of www.google.com?"

Only after receiving the IP address can your browser connect to the website.

docs.title: What is DNS?
docs.text:
DNS stands for:

Domain Name System

Its primary job is:

Domain Name

↓

IP Address

Example:

www.google.com

↓

142.250.x.x

This process is called name resolution.

docs.title: Why DNS is Needed
docs.text:
Without DNS,

users would have to remember addresses like:

142.250.182.100

Instead of:

google.com

DNS makes networking user-friendly.

docs.text:
User
   │
   ▼
Browser
   │
   ▼
Local DNS Resolver

   ▼
Recursive DNS Server

   ▼

docs.title: DNS Components
docs.text:
The DNS infrastructure includes:

  • Client (Resolver)
  • Recursive DNS Server
  • Root DNS Server
  • Top-Level Domain (TLD) Server
  • Authoritative DNS Server

Each plays a role in locating the correct IP address.

docs.title: Common DNS Record Types
docs.text: Record Purpose A Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address AAAA Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address CNAME Creates an alias for another hostname MX Specifies mail servers NS Specifies authoritative name servers TXT Stores text information (SPF, DKIM, verification, etc.) PTR Reverse DNS (IP address to hostname) SRV Specifies the location of network services

docs.title: A Record
docs.text:
Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.

Example:

www.example.com

↓

192.168.1.100

docs.title: AAAA Record
docs.text:
Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address.

Example:

www.example.com

↓

2001:db8::10

docs.title: CNAME Record
docs.text:
Creates an alias.

Example:

www.example.com

↓

server.example.com

Useful when multiple hostnames should point to the same destination.

docs.title: MX Record
docs.text:
Specifies mail servers.

Example:

example.com

↓

mail.example.com

Email systems use MX records to determine where to deliver messages.

docs.title: NS Record
docs.text:
Identifies authoritative name servers.

Example:

ns1.example.com

ns2.example.com

docs.title: PTR Record
docs.text:
Performs reverse DNS lookup.

192.168.1.100

↓

server.example.com

Commonly used for:

  • Mail servers
  • Logging
  • Security

docs.title: DNS Port
docs.text:
DNS uses:

53

Protocols:

  • UDP 53 (most queries)
  • TCP 53 (zone transfers and larger responses)

docs.title: Configure DNS Servers
docs.text:
View configured DNS servers.

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Example:

nameserver 8.8.8.8

nameserver 1.1.1.1

On many modern Linux distributions, /etc/resolv.conf is automatically managed by services such as systemd-resolved or NetworkManager. Direct edits may not persist.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users report that a web application is unreachable.

Investigation:

Test network connectivity.

ping 8.8.8.8

The ping succeeds.

Test DNS resolution.

dig example.com

No response is returned.

Check DNS configuration.

cat /etc/resolv.conf

The configured DNS server is unreachable.

Update the DNS configuration using the system's network management tool, then verify:

dig example.com

The hostname now resolves successfully, and the application becomes accessible.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use reliable and redundant DNS servers.
  • Prefer managing DNS through the operating system's network configuration tools rather than editing /etc/resolv.conf directly.
  • Verify both forward and reverse DNS when troubleshooting.
  • Use dig for detailed DNS analysis.
  • Monitor DNS latency and availability.
  • Configure multiple DNS servers for redundancy.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming every connectivity issue is caused by DNS.

✅ Verify every connectivity issue is caused by DNS instead of assuming it.

❌ Editing /etc/resolv.conf directly on systems where it is automatically managed.

✅ Edit /etc/resolv.conf directly on systems where it is automatically managed only when appropriate and with a backup.

❌ Configuring only one DNS server.

✅ Avoid this mistake: configuring only one DNS server.

❌ Ignoring DNS caching during troubleshooting.

✅ Always review DNS caching during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You will see export API_URL=... in tutorials and wonder why it “disappears” tomorrow. Environment variables are how Linux passes configuration into programs for a session — and into services for their whole lifetime.

Plain problem: A script works in your SSH session but fails in cron with “command not found”. Same script — different environment. Cron did not load your .bashrc; PATH was shorter.

An environment variable is a named string every child process inherits: PATH (where to find commands), HOME, LANG, app settings. They live in three common places: interactive shell, startup files, and systemd units.

This is a Command Line tutorial in the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series — practical Linux for Cloud and DevOps work.

docs.text:
• Ubuntu practice VM or WSL2
  • Essential Linux Commands
  • Basic comfort typing commands in bash

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain environment variables in plain language
  • Inspect and set variables with export, env, and printenv
  • Add a lab-safe snippet under /etc/profile.d/
  • Understand why cron jobs miss SSH environment variables
  • Set Environment= in a systemd unit
  • Answer fresher interview questions on environment and shell config

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Login shell reads profile files → sets environment → starts processes that inherit copies. Non-interactive cron/systemd paths skip most of your personal .bashrc unless you configure them.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text: You add a tool to ~/bin and it works after export PATH=$PATH:~/bin in SSH. Night cron job still says mytool: not found. You did not persist PATH where cron looks.

docs.title: What is an environment variable? (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: Environment variables are sticky notes on your desk every helper (process) reads when they start — “find tools in these folders”, “use this language”, “API lives here”.

Variable Typical role PATH Directories searched for command names HOME Your home directory USER Username SHELL Default shell program LANG Locale / language

Interview line: “Processes inherit environment at fork time; cron and systemd need explicit PATH or env files.”

docs.title: View and set (session vs persistent)
docs.text:
Terminal
echo "$PATH"
export REBASH_LAB=hello
env | grep REBASH

Session-only export dies when you log out unless written to startup files.

docs.title: Startup files (Ubuntu bash — simplified)
docs.text:
File When /etc/profile Login shells /etc/profile.d/*.sh Modular login snippets (good for admins) ~/.bashrc Interactive non-login bash ~/.profile User login

Do not edit system files recklessly on production — use drop-ins under profile.d with clear names.

docs.title: systemd Environment=
docs.text:
Services do not read your .bashrc. Set env in the unit:

[Service]
Environment="APP_MODE=production"
EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env

docs.title: Cron vs SSH environment
docs.text: Cron runs with minimal env. Fix: absolute paths in scripts, or PATH= line at top of crontab, or wrap in systemd timer (prior scheduling tutorial).

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Putting secrets in world-readable env files
  • Expecting ~ expansion in systemd Environment= (use full paths)
  • Mixing login vs non-login shell behaviour
  • export in script without export keyword — child processes miss it

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Set lab variables, add a profile.d snippet, demonstrate cron missing PATH, fix with absolute path, add systemd Environment=, prove — under ~/rebash-linux/lab-env.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM bash default sudo For profile.d and systemd drop-in

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab-env/bin && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-env

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: App team adds ~/bin/deploy-helper. Works interactively; cron deploy fails. You document environment inheritance and fix cron path — ticket style.

docs.title: Task 1 – Custom tool and PATH
docs.text:
Create deploy-helper:

deploy-helper
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "deploy-helper ran OK at $(date -Is)"
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-env
chmod +x bin/deploy-helper
export PATH="$HOME/rebash-linux/lab-env/bin:$PATH"
deploy-helper | tee path-session-proof.txt
grep -q 'deploy-helper ran OK' path-session-proof.txt

Expected output

Helper runs when ~/rebash-linux/lab-env/bin is on PATH.

docs.title: Task 2 – profile.d persistence
docs.text:
Create rebash-lab-env.sh:

rebash-lab-env.sh
# REBASH lab-env — append lab bin to PATH for login shells
export PATH="$HOME/rebash-linux/lab-env/bin:$PATH"
export REBASH_APP_ENV=lab
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-env
sudo cp rebash-lab-env.sh /etc/profile.d/rebash-lab-env.sh
sudo chmod 644 /etc/profile.d/rebash-lab-env.sh
bash -lc 'echo PATH=$PATH; echo REBASH_APP_ENV=$REBASH_APP_ENV' | tee login-shell-env.txt
grep -q 'lab-env/bin' login-shell-env.txt

Expected output

Login shell simulation shows lab bin on PATH and REBASH_APP_ENV=lab.

docs.title: Task 3 – Break cron env, fix, systemd Environment=
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-env
( crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo '* * * * * deploy-helper >> '"$HOME"'/rebash-linux/lab-env/logs/cron-broken.log 2>&1' ) | crontab -
mkdir -p logs
sleep 65
tail -3 logs/cron-broken.log 2>/dev/null | tee cron-broken-tail.txt || true
grep -q 'not found' cron-broken-tail.txt && echo "cron missed PATH — expected break" | tee break-notes.txt
crontab -r
( crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo '* * * * * '"$HOME"'/rebash-linux/lab-env/bin/deploy-helper >> '"$HOME"'/rebash-linux/lab-env/logs/cron-fixed.log 2>&1' ) | crontab -
sleep 65
grep -q 'deploy-helper ran OK' logs/cron-fixed.log
echo "lab-env OK" | tee evidence.txt

Create rebash-env-demo.service:

rebash-env-demo.service
[Unit]
Description=REBASH lab env demo oneshot

[Service]
Type=oneshot
Environment="REBASH_APP_ENV=systemd-demo"
ExecStart=/usr/bin/env bash -c 'echo REBASH_APP_ENV=$REBASH_APP_ENV >> /tmp/rebash-systemd-env.log'
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-env
sed "s|/tmp/rebash-systemd-env.log|$HOME/rebash-linux/lab-env/logs/systemd-env.log|" rebash-env-demo.service | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/rebash-env-demo.service >/dev/null
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start rebash-env-demo.service
grep systemd-demo logs/systemd-env.log
crontab -r 2>/dev/null || true

Expected output

Cron fails without full path; succeeds with absolute path. systemd log shows systemd-demo.

docs.text:

  • profile.d affects login shell simulation
  • Cron break/fix documented
  • systemd Environment= proven in log file

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix command not found in cron PATH Absolute path or PATH= in crontab Variable empty in systemd Not in unit Environment= or EnvironmentFile= profile.d not loaded Non-login shell Use bash -l or correct file Permission denied profile.d Bad perms 644, root-owned

sudo systemctl daemon-reload

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. export PATH=... — session only until profile.d or unit file persists.
  2. /etc/profile.d/ — modular admin-friendly login snippets.
  3. Cron without PATH — deliberate break; mirrors production incidents.
  4. Absolute path fix — simplest reliable cron fix.
  5. systemd Environment= — services ignore .bashrc by design.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Never put passwords or API keys in world-readable profile.d or unit files in Git.
  • Use secret managers or restricted EnvironmentFile (0600, root-only).
  • Audit /etc/environment and profile.d for stale exports.
  • Limit who can edit systemd unit drop-ins.
  • Scrub env snapshots before sharing in tickets.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Secrets in export lines.

✅ Environment leaks via ps, logs, and core dumps — use proper secret storage.

❌ Assuming cron loads .bashrc.

✅ It does not — configure env explicitly.

❌ Tilde in systemd paths.

✅ Use full paths like /home/user/bin/app.

docs.title: Environment Variables in Linux — Configuring the Linux Environment
Environment Variables in Linux — Configuring the Linux Environment
docs.text: Environment variables are dynamic values maintained by the operating system that influence how programs, shells, and scripts behave. They store information such as user details, executable paths, language settings, application configurations, and runtime parameters. Environment variables are fundamental to Linux administration, shell scripting, DevOps, Docker, Kubernetes, and cloud computing.

docs.text:
Imagine you install Java.

Instead of running:

/usr/lib/jvm/java-21/bin/java

every time,

you simply run:

java

How does Linux know where Java is installed?

The answer is:

Environment Variables, especially the PATH variable.

docs.title: What is an Environment Variable?
docs.text:
An environment variable is a name-value pair stored by the shell.

Example:

USER=basha

HOME=/home/basha

SHELL=/bin/bash

Applications use these values to determine how they should run.

docs.title: Shell Variables vs Environment Variables
docs.text: Shell Variable Environment Variable Available only in the current shell Available to child processes Not inherited Inherited by child processes Created with VAR=value Exported using export

docs.title: Viewing Environment Variables
docs.text:
Display all environment variables.

env

or

printenv

Example:

HOME=/home/basha

USER=basha

PATH=/usr/bin:/bin

SHELL=/bin/bash

docs.title: Display a Specific Variable
docs.text:
Syntax:

echo $VARIABLE

Examples:

echo $USER

echo $HOME

echo $PATH

echo $SHELL

docs.title: Common Environment Variables
docs.text: Variable Description USER Current username HOME User's home directory PATH Executable search path PWD Current directory OLDPWD Previous directory SHELL Current shell HOSTNAME System hostname LANG System language TERM Terminal type LOGNAME Login username

docs.title: Creating a Shell Variable
docs.text:
CITY=Hyderabad

Verify:

echo $CITY

Output:

Hyderabad

This variable exists only in the current shell.

docs.title: Exporting an Environment Variable
docs.text:
export CITY=Hyderabad

Verify:

printenv CITY

Output:

Hyderabad

Now child processes can access it.

docs.title: Difference Between Shell and Environment Variables
docs.text:
Create a shell variable.

PROJECT=REBASH

Open a new shell.

bash

Check:

echo $PROJECT

Output:

The variable is not available.

Now export it.

export PROJECT=REBASH

Open another shell.

bash

Check again.

echo $PROJECT

Output:

REBASH

docs.title: Removing Variables
docs.text:
unset PROJECT

Verify.

echo $PROJECT

Output:

docs.title: Understanding PATH
docs.text:
Display:

echo $PATH

Example:

/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin

When you run:

python

Linux searches each directory in PATH until it finds the executable.

docs.title: Adding a Directory to PATH
docs.text:
Temporarily:

export PATH=$PATH:/opt/tools/bin

Verify:

echo $PATH

Now executables inside /opt/tools/bin can be run without specifying the full path.

docs.title: Environment Variables in Scripts
docs.text:
Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "User: $USER"

echo "Home: $HOME"

echo "Shell: $SHELL"

Run:

bash info.sh

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A Java application fails to start.

Error:

JAVA_HOME is not set

Investigation:

echo $JAVA_HOME

printenv JAVA_HOME

The variable is missing.

Solution:

export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21

export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH

Verify:

The application now starts successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use uppercase names for environment variables.
  • Keep variable names descriptive.
  • Avoid storing sensitive information (such as passwords or API keys) directly in environment variables on shared systems unless required and properly protected.
  • Use export only for variables that child processes need.
  • Configure permanent variables in profile files rather than setting them manually every session.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:

❌ Overwriting the PATH variable.

✅ Incorrect:

export PATH=/opt/tools

Correct:

export PATH=$PATH:/opt/tools

❌ Hardcoding application paths in scripts instead of using environment variables.

✅ Prefer using environment variables rather than hardcoding application paths in scripts.

  • Move and rename files
  • Delete files safely
  • Understand file overwrite behavior
  • Work efficiently with multiple files
  • Apply file management best practices

docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

docs.title: Why Learn File Management?
docs.text:
Everything in Linux is stored as a file.

Examples include:

  • Configuration files
  • Application code
  • Log files
  • Shell scripts
  • Databases
  • Docker Compose files
  • Kubernetes YAML manifests

As a Linux administrator, you'll manage thousands of files every day.

docs.title: Creating Directories
docs.text:
Create a new directory.

mkdir projects

Verify:

ls

Output:

projects

docs.title: Create Multiple Directories
docs.text: mkdir dev test production

docs.title: Create Nested Directories
docs.text:
Use the -p option.

mkdir -p projects/dev/app

Without -p, Linux reports an error if parent directories don't exist.

docs.title: Creating Files
docs.text:
Create an empty file.

touch notes.txt

Verify:

ls

Output:

notes.txt

docs.title: Create Multiple Files
docs.text: touch app.py config.yaml README.md

docs.title: Display File Details
docs.text:
ls -l

Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 basha users 0 Jul 12 notes.txt

docs.title: Copy Files
docs.text:
Syntax:

cp source destination

Example:

cp notes.txt backup.txt

Verify:

ls

docs.title: Copy Files to Another Directory
docs.text: cp notes.txt /tmp

docs.title: Copy Multiple Files
docs.text: cp file1 file2 file3 backup/

docs.title: Copy Directories
docs.text:
Use:

cp -r projects backup

The -r option copies directories recursively.

docs.title: Move Files
docs.text:
Syntax:

mv source destination

Example:

mv notes.txt Documents/

docs.title: Rename Files
docs.text:
Moving and renaming use the same command.

mv notes.txt linux-notes.txt

docs.title: Rename Directories
docs.text: mv projects dev-projects

docs.title: Delete Files
docs.text:
Use:

rm notes.txt

The file is permanently deleted.

docs.title: Delete Multiple Files
docs.text: rm file1 file2 file3

docs.title: Delete Directories
docs.text:
Empty directory:

rmdir test

docs.title: Delete Non-Empty Directories
docs.text: rm -r projects

docs.title: Force Delete
docs.text:
rm -rf projects

Warning

rm -rf permanently deletes files and directories without asking for confirmation.

Never use it unless you understand its impact.

docs.title: Interactive Delete
docs.text:
Prompt before deleting.

rm -i notes.txt

Output:

remove regular file 'notes.txt'?

docs.title: Confirm Before Overwriting
docs.text:
cp -i file1 file2

If the destination exists:

overwrite file2?

docs.title: Verbose Output
docs.text:
Display each operation.

Copy:

cp -v notes.txt backup.txt

Move:

mv -v backup.txt archive.txt

Delete:

rm -v archive.txt

docs.title: Wildcards
docs.text:
Delete all text files.

rm *.txt

Copy all YAML files.

cp *.yaml backup/

Move all log files.

mv *.log logs/

docs.text: Command Purpose mkdir Create directory mkdir -p Create nested directories touch Create empty file cp Copy files cp -r Copy directories mv Move or rename rm Delete file rm -r Delete directory rm -rf Force delete rmdir Delete empty directory

docs.title: Real Production Example
docs.text:
Imagine you're deploying an NGINX configuration.

Create backup:

cp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak

Edit configuration.

Verify.

Restart service.

If something goes wrong:

mv /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

Restart NGINX.

This simple backup strategy prevents downtime.

docs.text:
Linux engineers constantly perform file operations.

Examples:

Copy configuration:

cp config.yaml config.yaml.bak

Move application:

mv app /opt/

Delete old logs:

rm old.log

Archive data:

cp -r project project-backup

These commands are used daily by:

  • Linux Administrators
  • Cloud Engineers
  • DevOps Engineers
  • Platform Engineers
  • SREs

docs.text:
Create a lab directory.

mkdir linux-lab

docs.title: Task 2

cd linux-lab

├── app

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Create backups before modifying important files.
  • Use cp -i to prevent accidental overwrites.
  • Verify your current directory before deleting files.
  • Avoid using rm -rf unless absolutely necessary.
  • Use descriptive file names.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Running:

✅ Use:

rm -rf /

This is one of the most dangerous commands in Linux.

Never execute commands you don't fully understand.

❌ Forgetting -r while copying directories.

✅ Use:

cp project backup

Produces an error.

Correct:

cp -r project backup

❌ Using rmdir on non-empty directories.

✅ Use:

rm -r directory

instead.

docs.title: Fail2Ban — Protecting Linux Servers from Brute-Force Attacks
Fail2Ban — Protecting Linux Servers from Brute-Force Attacks
docs.text: Fail2Ban is an intrusion prevention tool that monitors log files for suspicious activity, such as repeated failed login attempts, and automatically blocks offending IP addresses using the system firewall. It helps protect Linux servers against brute-force attacks targeting services like SSH, FTP, web servers, and mail servers. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should know how to deploy and manage Fail2Ban in production environments.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 11: Linux Security → Lesson 6

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 90 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Linux Security

Lesson: 6 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Fail2Ban fundamentals
  • Learn how Fail2Ban works
  • Configure jails
  • Protect SSH from brute-force attacks
  • Monitor banned IP addresses
  • Customize Fail2Ban settings
  • Troubleshoot Fail2Ban
  • Apply production security best practices

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Modules 1–10
  • Module 11 Lessons 1–5

docs.title: Why Learn Fail2Ban?
docs.text:
Imagine a public Linux server.

Without Fail2Ban:

Internet

↓

Thousands of Login Attempts

↓

Possible Password Guessing

With Fail2Ban:

Repeated Failed Logins

↓

Fail2Ban Detects Attack

↓

Firewall Blocks IP

↓

Server Protected

Fail2Ban automatically reduces the risk of brute-force attacks.

docs.title: What is Fail2Ban?
docs.text:
Fail2Ban is a security tool that:

  • Monitors log files
  • Detects repeated authentication failures
  • Temporarily or permanently bans malicious IP addresses
  • Integrates with the system firewall

docs.title: How Fail2Ban Works
docs.text:
Failed Login Attempts

↓

Log File

↓

Fail2Ban Filter

↓

Jail Rules

↓

Firewall

↓

IP Address Blocked

docs.title: Commonly Protected Services
docs.text:
Fail2Ban supports many services, including:

  • SSH
  • FTP
  • Apache HTTP Server
  • Nginx
  • Postfix
  • Dovecot
  • OpenVPN
  • Custom applications

docs.title: Install Fail2Ban
docs.text:
Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt install fail2ban

RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux:

sudo dnf install fail2ban

docs.title: Start the Service
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable fail2ban

sudo systemctl start fail2ban

Check status.

sudo systemctl status fail2ban

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Main configuration:

/etc/fail2ban/jail.conf

Recommended practice:

/etc/fail2ban/jail.local

Never modify jail.conf directly because updates may overwrite your changes.

docs.title: What is a Jail?
docs.text:
A jail defines:

  • Service to protect
  • Log file to monitor
  • Detection rules
  • Ban duration
  • Retry limits

Example:

SSH Jail

↓

Monitor SSH Logs

↓

Block Attackers

docs.title: Basic SSH Jail
docs.text:
Example:

[sshd]

enabled = true

maxretry = 5

findtime = 10m

bantime = 1h

Meaning:

  • Monitor SSH
  • Ban after 5 failed attempts
  • Count failures within 10 minutes
  • Ban for 1 hour

docs.title: Important Jail Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description enabled Enable or disable the jail maxretry Failed attempts before banning findtime Time window for counting failures bantime Duration of the ban port Protected service port logpath Log file to monitor

docs.title: Restart Fail2Ban
docs.text:
After making configuration changes:

sudo systemctl restart fail2ban

docs.title: Check Fail2Ban Status
docs.text:
Overall status.

sudo fail2ban-client status

Example:

Jail list:

sshd

docs.title: View Jail Status
docs.text:
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

Example:

Currently failed: 0

Currently banned: 2

docs.title: Unban an IP Address
docs.text: sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 192.168.1.100

docs.title: Ban an IP Manually
docs.text:
sudo fail2ban-client set sshd banip 192.168.1.100

Useful for testing or emergency blocking.

docs.title: Ignore Trusted IP Addresses
docs.text:
Example:

ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 192.168.1.0/24

These addresses are never banned.

docs.title: View Logs
docs.text:
Systemd systems:

journalctl -u fail2ban

Or monitor logs.

tail -f /var/log/fail2ban.log

(depending on the Linux distribution and logging configuration)

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Check service.

systemctl status fail2ban

View jails.

fail2ban-client status

View SSH jail.

fail2ban-client status sshd

Restart service.

systemctl restart fail2ban

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Enable SSH protection.

[sshd]

enabled = true

View banned IPs.

fail2ban-client status sshd

Restart after configuration changes.

systemctl restart fail2ban

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Fail2Ban is widely used on:

  • Internet-facing Linux servers
  • Cloud virtual machines
  • Bastion hosts
  • Web servers
  • Mail servers
  • Database servers
  • VPN gateways
  • Enterprise infrastructure

It provides an automated response to repeated authentication failures.

sudo systemctl start fail2ban

sudo fail2ban-client status

docs.title: Common Fail2Ban Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Solution Editing jail.conf directly Use jail.local Forgetting to restart Fail2Ban Restart after configuration changes Setting an extremely short bantime Choose an appropriate duration Not protecting SSH Enable the SSH jail Ignoring Fail2Ban logs Review logs regularly

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A production server experiences thousands of SSH login attempts every hour.

Without Fail2Ban:

Attack Continues

↓

Repeated Password Attempts

↓

High Risk

With Fail2Ban:

Five Failed Attempts

↓

Fail2Ban Detects Attack

↓

Firewall Blocks Source IP

↓

Further Attempts Prevented

The server automatically blocks repeated attacks without administrator intervention.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use jail.local for custom configuration.
  • Enable protection for SSH on all Internet-facing servers.
  • Choose reasonable values for maxretry, findtime, and bantime.
  • Whitelist trusted management networks with ignoreip.
  • Monitor Fail2Ban logs regularly.
  • Keep Fail2Ban updated with security patches.
  • Combine Fail2Ban with SSH keys and firewall rules for layered security.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Editing jail.conf instead of jail.local.

✅ Prefer jail.local rather than editing jail.conf.

❌ Forgetting to restart the service after configuration changes.

✅ Remember to to restart the service after configuration changes.

❌ Setting overly aggressive ban policies that block legitimate users.

✅ Avoid this mistake: setting overly aggressive ban policies that block legitimate users.

❌ Not protecting Internet-facing SSH services.

✅ Always protecting Internet-facing SSH services.

❌ Assuming Fail2Ban replaces strong passwords, SSH keys, or firewalls.

✅ Verify Fail2Ban replaces strong passwords, SSH keys, or firewalls instead of assuming it.

Fail2Ban provides automated protection against brute-force attacks by monitoring authentication logs and temporarily blocking malicious IP addresses. When combined with SSH hardening, firewalls, strong authentication, and regular security updates, it becomes an effective component of a layered Linux security strategy.

docs.title: I am a college graduate with no Linux experience. Can I follow this?
docs.text: Yes — that is the primary audience. Tutorials start with a real problem and a simple analogy before jargon. You need basic computer skills and a practice Ubuntu (or similar) VM. You do not need prior sysadmin jobs.

docs.title: Which Linux should I install for labs?

docs.title: Do I need to buy anything?

docs.title: Linux File Attributes — Protecting Files Beyond Permissions
Linux File Attributes — Protecting Files Beyond Permissions
docs.text: Linux file permissions control who can access a file, but file attributes provide an additional layer of protection by controlling how a file can be modified, even by the root user in some cases. File attributes are commonly used to protect configuration files, logs, system files, and critical application data.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 4: File Management and Permissions → Lesson 8

Difficulty: Advanced

Reading Time: 50 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: File Management and Permissions

Lesson: 8 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Linux file attributes
  • View file attributes
  • Modify file attributes
  • Protect files from deletion
  • Create append-only files
  • Secure log files
  • Troubleshoot attribute-related issues
  • Apply file attributes in production

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 Lessons 1–7

docs.title: Why Learn File Attributes?
docs.text:
Imagine this situation.

A critical configuration file:

/etc/ssh/sshd_config

has the correct permissions.

Yet someone accidentally deletes it.

Permissions cannot prevent deletion if the user has write access to the directory.

Linux file attributes can.

docs.title: What are File Attributes?
docs.text:
File attributes are special flags stored by the filesystem.

Unlike permissions, attributes control behaviors such as:

  • Prevent deletion
  • Prevent modification
  • Allow append-only writes
  • Disable updates
  • Enable compression (filesystem dependent)

Attributes provide protection beyond standard Linux permissions.

docs.title: File Permissions vs File Attributes
docs.text: Permissions File Attributes Control who can access Control how files behave Owner / Group / Others Additional filesystem flags Managed with chmod Managed with chattr Viewed using ls -l Viewed using lsattr

docs.title: Supported Filesystems
docs.text:
File attributes are commonly supported on:

  • ext2
  • ext3
  • ext4

Some attributes are also supported by XFS, Btrfs, and others, but support varies.

docs.title: View File Attributes
docs.text:
Create a file.

touch report.txt

Display attributes.

lsattr report.txt

Example:

---------------------- report.txt

No attributes are currently set.

docs.title: The chattr Command
docs.text:
Syntax:

sudo chattr [+|-|=] ATTRIBUTE FILE

Examples:

+

Add attribute

-

Remove attribute

=

Set attributes exactly

docs.title: Immutable Attribute (i)
docs.text:
One of the most important attributes.

Set:

sudo chattr +i report.txt

View:

lsattr report.txt

Output:

----i--------------- report.txt

docs.title: Immutable File Behavior
docs.text:
Try:

echo "Linux" >> report.txt

Output:

Operation not permitted

Delete:

rm report.txt

Output:

Operation not permitted

Rename:

mv report.txt new.txt

Fails.

Even root cannot modify or delete the file unless the immutable attribute is removed.

docs.title: Remove Immutable Attribute
docs.text:
sudo chattr -i report.txt

Now:

rm report.txt

Works normally.

docs.title: Append-Only Attribute (a)
docs.text:
Enable:

sudo chattr +a application.log

Now:

Allowed:

echo "Started" >> application.log

Not allowed:

nano application.log

truncate application.log

rm application.log

Append-only is ideal for log files.

docs.title: Remove Append-Only
docs.text: sudo chattr -a application.log

docs.title: View Attributes
docs.text:
lsattr

Example:

----i--------------- config.yaml

-----a-------------- app.log

docs.title: Common File Attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Meaning i Immutable a Append Only A Do not update access time d Exclude from dump backups (where supported) S Synchronous updates u Attempt to preserve deleted data (filesystem dependent)

Note

Not every filesystem supports every attribute.

docs.title: Immutable Example
docs.text:
Protect SSH configuration.

sudo chattr +i /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Verify.

lsattr /etc/ssh/sshd_config

docs.title: Append-Only Example
docs.text:
Protect audit logs.

sudo chattr +a /var/log/application.log

Applications can append log entries but cannot overwrite or delete the file.

docs.title: Remove All Attributes
docs.text: sudo chattr -ia file.txt

docs.title: Recursive Attributes
docs.text:
Protect an entire directory.

sudo chattr -R +i configs/

Remove recursively.

sudo chattr -R -i configs/

Use recursive immutable settings carefully, especially on system directories.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
View attributes.

lsattr

Immutable.

sudo chattr +i file.txt

Remove immutable.

sudo chattr -i file.txt

Append only.

sudo chattr +a file.log

Remove append.

sudo chattr -a file.log

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Protect SSH configuration.

sudo chattr +i /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Protect /etc/passwd (for demonstration only—avoid doing this on production without understanding the impact).

sudo chattr +i /etc/passwd

Protect application logs.

sudo chattr +a app.log

Protect deployment configuration.

sudo chattr +i deployment.yaml

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
File attributes are commonly used for:

  • Security hardening
  • Critical configuration files
  • Log protection
  • Compliance
  • Digital forensics
  • Immutable infrastructure
  • Security audits

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create a file.

touch secure.txt

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
View attributes.

lsattr secure.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Set immutable.

sudo chattr +i secure.txt

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Try deleting it.

rm secure.txt

Observe the error.

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Remove immutable.

sudo chattr -i secure.txt

Delete the file.

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Create a log file.

touch app.log

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Set append-only.

sudo chattr +a app.log

Append a log entry.

echo "Application started" >> app.log

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
View attributes.

lsattr app.log

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example lsattr View attributes Security audits chattr +i Immutable Protect configuration chattr -i Remove immutable Maintenance chattr +a Append-only Log protection chattr -R Recursive changes Large deployments

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A system administrator cannot edit a configuration file even though they are root.

Investigation:

lsattr /etc/myapp/config.yaml

Output:

----i---------------

The immutable attribute is set.

Solution:

sudo chattr -i /etc/myapp/config.yaml

Make the required changes.

Re-enable protection.

sudo chattr +i /etc/myapp/config.yaml

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use the immutable attribute for critical configuration files.
  • Use append-only for application and audit logs.
  • Remove attributes only when maintenance is required.
  • Document attribute usage in production environments.
  • Verify attributes after system migrations or restores.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting that an immutable file cannot be modified, renamed, or deleted.

✅ Always check with:

lsattr

❌ Applying immutable attributes recursively to system directories without testing.

✅ This can prevent package updates and system maintenance.

❌ Assuming permissions override file attributes.

✅ Attributes are enforced independently and can block operations even for privileged users.

docs.title: Beginner

docs.title: File Permissions Review — Securing Files and Directories in Linux
File Permissions Review — Securing Files and Directories in Linux
docs.text: File Permissions are one of the most important security mechanisms in Linux. They determine who can read, write, or execute files and directories, preventing unauthorized access and protecting sensitive system resources. Incorrect permissions can expose confidential data, allow unauthorized modifications, or even lead to privilege escalation. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) must understand how to review, audit, and manage Linux file permissions effectively.

Incorrect permissions:

Anyone can read or modify the file.

Secure permissions:

Only the owner has access.

Proper permissions protect systems from unauthorized access and accidental changes.

1

Example:

Users can delete only their own files within the directory.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A web application stores database credentials in a configuration file.

Permissions:

-rw-rw-rw-

Any user can modify or read the file.

Secure configuration:

sudo chown appuser:appgroup app.conf

  • Group members can read it if necessary.
  • Other users have no access.

docs.text:

  • Assign correct file ownership.
  • Protect SSH keys with 600 permissions.
  • Audit SUID and SGID files regularly.
  • Remove unnecessary execute permissions.
  • Review file permissions during security audits.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assigning 777 permissions to application files.

✅ Avoid this mistake: assigning 777 permissions to application files.

❌ Leaving SSH private keys publicly readable.

✅ Do not leave SSH private keys publicly readable.

❌ Ignoring file ownership.

✅ Always review file ownership.

❌ Giving execute permission to non-executable files.

✅ Avoid this mistake: giving execute permission to non-executable files.

❌ Never reviewing permission changes.

✅ Always reviewing permission changes.

docs.title: File Types in Linux — Understanding Every Type of File
File Types in Linux — Understanding Every Type of File
docs.text: Everything in Linux is treated as a file. Regular files, directories, devices, sockets, pipes, symbolic links, and even hardware are represented as files. Understanding Linux file types is fundamental for Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, SREs, and Security professionals.

Course Progress

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Linux file types
  • Identify different file types
  • Use ls -l to determine file types
  • Understand device files
  • Differentiate hard links and symbolic links
  • Recognize sockets and named pipes
  • Understand the "Everything is a File" philosophy

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing

docs.title: Why Learn File Types?
docs.text:
Imagine you're troubleshooting a production server.

You see:

-rwxr-xr-x

drwxr-xr-x

lrwxrwxrwx

crw-rw----

srwxrwxrwx

Questions:

  • Which one is a directory?
  • Which one is a symbolic link?
  • Which one is a device?
  • Which one is a socket?

Understanding file types allows you to confidently manage Linux systems.

docs.title: Linux Philosophy
docs.text:
One of the most famous Linux principles is:

Everything is a File

Examples include:

  • Text files
  • Directories
  • Hard disks
  • SSDs
  • USB devices
  • Printers
  • Network sockets
  • Pipes
  • Processes (through /proc)
  • System information (through /sys)

This unified design simplifies system administration and programming.

docs.title: Viewing File Types
docs.text:
Use:

ls -l

Example output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 basha users 1200 Jan 10 notes.txt

drwxr-xr-x 2 basha users 4096 Jan 10 Documents

lrwxrwxrwx 1 basha users   12 Jan 10 latest -> release-v2

The first character indicates the file type.

docs.title: Linux File Type Indicators
docs.text: Symbol File Type - Regular File d Directory l Symbolic Link c Character Device b Block Device p Named Pipe (FIFO) s Socket

docs.title: 1. Regular File (-)
docs.text:
Example:

-rw-r--r--

Regular files store:

  • Documents
  • Source code
  • Images
  • Videos
  • Shell scripts
  • Configuration files

Examples:

notes.txt

script.sh

photo.jpg

config.yaml

Create:

touch notes.txt

Verify:

ls -l notes.txt

docs.title: 2. Directory (d)
docs.text:
Example:

drwxr-xr-x

Directories organize files.

Create:

mkdir projects

View:

ls -ld projects

Examples:

/home

/etc

/var

/opt

/usr

docs.title: 3. Symbolic Link (l)
docs.text:
Example:

lrwxrwxrwx

A symbolic link (soft link) points to another file or directory.

Create:

ln -s notes.txt latest-notes

View:

ls -l latest-notes

Output:

latest-notes -> notes.txt

Common use cases:

  • Current application version
  • Shared configuration
  • Simplified paths

docs.title: 4. Character Device ©
docs.text:
Example:

crw-rw-rw-

Character devices transfer data one character at a time.

Examples:

/dev/tty

/dev/random

/dev/null

/dev/zero

View:

ls -l /dev/null

Output:

crw-rw-rw-

docs.title: 5. Block Device (b)
docs.text:
Example:

brw-rw----

Block devices transfer data in blocks.

Examples:

/dev/sda

/dev/sdb

/dev/nvme0n1

View:

ls -l /dev/sd*

Typical block devices include:

  • HDDs
  • SSDs
  • USB drives
  • Virtual disks

docs.title: 6. Named Pipe (FIFO) (p)
docs.text:
Example:

prw-r--r--

Named pipes enable communication between processes.

Create:

mkfifo mypipe

View:

ls -l mypipe

Example output:

prw-r--r--

Named pipes are commonly used in:

  • Shell scripts
  • Inter-process communication
  • Streaming data

docs.title: 7. Socket (s)
docs.text:
Example:

srwxrwxrwx

Sockets allow communication between processes.

Examples:

Docker

MySQL

PostgreSQL

Nginx

systemd

View socket files:

find /run -type s

Or:

find /var/run -type s

docs.title: The file Command
docs.text:
Determine a file's actual type:

file notes.txt

Output:

ASCII text

Executable:

file /bin/ls

Output:

ELF 64-bit executable

Image:

file photo.jpg

Output:

JPEG image data

Unlike ls, the file command examines the file contents rather than relying on the filename.

find /dev -type b

docs.text:

  • Configuration files

  • Kubernetes volume mounts
  • Named pipes
  • Storage devices

Understanding file types is essential for troubleshooting permissions, storage, and process communication.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A web application suddenly stops responding.

Investigation:

  1. Check if the Nginx socket exists.
  2. Verify the symbolic link to the latest release.
  3. Confirm mounted storage devices.
  4. Inspect configuration file types.

Commands:

find /run -type s

ls -l /var/www/current

lsblk

file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

These checks quickly identify missing sockets, broken symbolic links, storage issues, or incorrect file types.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always verify file types before modifying or deleting files.
  • Use symbolic links for application version management.
  • Use file when the extension is misleading or missing.
  • Avoid manually creating device files unless necessary.
  • Understand the difference between block and character devices.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming file extensions determine file type.

✅ Linux determines file types by metadata and content, not by filename extensions.

❌ Confusing symbolic links with hard links.

✅ A symbolic link points to a pathname, while a hard link references the same inode. (Hard links are covered in a later lesson.)

❌ Deleting a symbolic link's target instead of the link.

✅ Always verify with:

ls -l

before removing files.

docs.title: Filesystem Paths, Links, Mounts, and Inodes
Filesystem Paths, Links, Mounts, and Inodes
Overview
docs.text:
Sooner or later every Linux learner hits these problems:

  • A deploy “worked” but the site still serves the old version — broken symbolic link
  • “Disk full” but df -h shows free space — inode exhaustion
  • A cron job fails while the same command works in SSH — relative path vs working directory

Linux presents storage as one tree starting at /. A path names a place in that tree. An inode holds the real file metadata. Hard links and symbolic links (symlinks) create extra names. Mounts attach other filesystems onto directories.

This tutorial answers, in order:

  1. What is the difference between absolute and relative paths?
  2. What is an inode, and how do hard links differ from symlinks?
  3. What is a mount point, and why can mounts “hide” files?
  4. How do teams use a current → releases/v1 symlink pattern in deploys?

This is Tutorial 4 in Module 3: Linux Filesystem of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series — practical Linux for Cloud and DevOps work.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Essential Linux Commands — you can mkdir, ln, ls, and cat
  • A practice Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VM with write access under your home directory
  • findmnt available (util-linux, default on Ubuntu)

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain absolute vs relative paths and why cron prefers absolute paths
  • Show inode numbers with ls -i and relate them to hard links
  • Create and resolve symlinks with ln -s and readlink -f
  • List mounts with findmnt and check inode capacity with df -i
  • Build a versioned release layout with a current symlink and prove it

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Directory entries map names to inode numbers. Hard links share one inode. Symlinks store a path string. Mounts graft other filesystems into the tree so disks and pseudo-filesystems appear as ordinary paths.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
Your team deploys by unpacking releases/2026-08-04/ and pointing current at it. After a cleanup script deletes the old release folder, the site breaks — but files still exist somewhere. The current symlink now points at a missing target (dangling link).

Or: a script uses logs/app.log (relative path). It works in your SSH session but fails in cron because cron’s working directory is not your home folder.

This section gives you the model behind those tickets.

docs.title: Paths — absolute vs relative
docs.text:
Analogy: An absolute path is a full postal address starting from the country (/). A relative path is “turn left at the next corridor” — it only works if everyone agrees where you are standing.

Style Starts with Example Breaks when Absolute / /home/ubuntu/app/logs/app.log Home moves (rare) Relative No leading / logs/app.log Working directory changes

What you can say in an interview: “Cron and systemd units should use absolute paths, or set WorkingDirectory= deliberately — relative paths depend on cwd.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
pwd
cat /etc/hostname          # absolute
cat etc/hostname             # relative — fails unless cwd is /

docs.title: Inodes and hard links
docs.text:
Analogy: An inode is the warehouse slot number. The filename is the label on the shelf pointing at that slot. A hard link is a second label on the same slot — same data, two names.

Term Plain meaning Inode Metadata + pointers to data blocks; identified by number on one filesystem Hard link Another directory entry for the same inode (same filesystem only) Link count How many names point at the inode; data deleted when count hits 0 and no process holds the file open

What you can say in an interview: “Hard links share an inode; you cannot hard-link across filesystems. Deleting one name does not delete data until the last link is gone.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
echo hello > a.txt
ln a.txt b.txt
ls -li a.txt b.txt

docs.title: Symbolic links (symlinks)
docs.text:
Analogy: A symlink is a signpost with directions written on it — not the warehouse slot itself. If you move the building the sign points at, the sign is wrong (dangling).

Type Same inode? Cross filesystem? Typical use Hard link Yes No Extra name for one file Symlink No (stores path) Yes current → releases/v1

What you can say in an interview: “Deploys use symlinks for a stable current name. Flip with ln -sfn new current and verify with readlink -f.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
ln -s /etc/hosts myhosts.link
readlink myhosts.link
readlink -f myhosts.link

docs.title: Mounts
docs.text:
Analogy: A mount is grafting a separate storage disk onto a doorway in the building. Walk through that door and you see the disk’s contents — which may hide whatever was behind the door before.

Term Plain meaning Mount point Directory where another filesystem is attached Bind mount Mount an existing directory at another path Persistence /etc/fstab or systemd .mount units (prefer UUID)

What you can say in an interview: “Mounting over a directory hides previous contents until unmount. Always findmnt before assuming files are gone.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
findmnt /
findmnt -T "$HOME"
df -i .

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Symlinks with relative targets that break when the link file moves
  • Hard links across disks (Invalid cross-device link)
  • Assuming df -h is enough — check df -i for inode exhaustion
  • Cron scripts with relative paths that worked only in SSH
  • Deleting a symlink target and leaving a dangling current link

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Prove paths, inodes, hard links, symlinks, and mounts with a deploy-style release layout under ~/rebash-linux/lab04, and pack evidence.

pwd-pathlab.txt ends with pathlab/releases/v1 or similar after cd.

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Your team deploys by unpacking release directories and flipping a current symlink. You practise that pattern, prove inode behaviour with a hard link, and document mounts for the lab filesystem.

docs.title: Task 1 – Absolute vs relative paths (prove cwd matters)
docs.text:
Create pathlab/releases/v1/app.txt:

pathlab/releases/v1/app.txt
v1 app
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab04/pathlab
set -euo pipefail

printf 'v1 app\n' > releases/v1/app.txt
cat releases/v1/app.txt | tee ../read-relative.txt

ABS="$(pwd)/releases/v1/app.txt"
echo "$ABS" | tee ../abs-path.txt
cat "$ABS" | tee ../read-absolute.txt

cd /tmp
if cat releases/v1/app.txt 2>../relative-fail.txt; then
  echo 'ERROR: relative path should fail from /tmp' >&2
  exit 1
fi
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab04/pathlab
grep -Ei 'No such file|cannot' ../relative-fail.txt

Expected output

Reads succeed from pathlab; relative read from /tmp fails and is recorded in relative-fail.txt.

docs.title: Task 2 – Inodes, hard links, and deploy symlink
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab04/pathlab
set -euo pipefail

echo 'payload' > releases/v1/data.bin
ln releases/v1/data.bin releases/v1/data-hard.bin
ln -s data.bin releases/v1/data.sym
ln -s "$(pwd)/releases/v1" current-release

ls -li releases/v1/data.bin releases/v1/data-hard.bin | tee ../inode-hardlinks.txt
INO1=$(stat -c '%i' releases/v1/data.bin)
INO2=$(stat -c '%i' releases/v1/data-hard.bin)
test "$INO1" = "$INO2"

stat -c 'links=%h inode=%i name=%n' releases/v1/data.bin | tee ../stat-hard.txt
readlink releases/v1/data.sym | tee ../symlink-target.txt
readlink -f current-release | tee ../current-resolved.txt
ls -l current-release | tee ../current-ls.txt

Expected output

Same inode for both hard links; link count ≥ 2. current-resolved.txt points at …/releases/v1.

docs.title: Task 3 – Mounts, inodes, dangling link, evidence pack
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab04
set -euo pipefail

findmnt -T "$HOME" | tee findmnt-home.txt
findmnt -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS / | tee findmnt-root.txt
df -hT . | tee df-pathlab.txt
df -i . | tee dfi-pathlab.txt

ln -sf /no/such/target pathlab/dangling.sym
readlink pathlab/dangling.sym | tee dangling-target.txt
ls -l pathlab/dangling.sym | tee dangling-ls.txt
test ! -e /no/such/target

tar -czf paths-links-evidence.tgz \
  pwd-pathlab.txt read-relative.txt abs-path.txt read-absolute.txt relative-fail.txt \
  inode-hardlinks.txt stat-hard.txt symlink-target.txt current-resolved.txt current-ls.txt \
  findmnt-home.txt findmnt-root.txt df-pathlab.txt dfi-pathlab.txt \
  dangling-target.txt dangling-ls.txt pathlab
ls -l paths-links-evidence.tgz | tee evidence-ls.txt
test -s paths-links-evidence.tgz

Expected output

findmnt-home.txt shows the mount holding your home. dfi-pathlab.txt shows inode use. Archive is non-empty.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• Relative read from /tmp fails; absolute read succeeds
  • Hard links share one inode
  • current-release resolves with readlink -f
  • findmnt and df -i outputs exist
  • paths-links-evidence.tgz exists under ~/rebash-linux/lab04

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Invalid cross-device link Hard link across mounts Use symlink Symlink wrong after move Relative target + moved link Prefer absolute targets for system links findmnt: command not found Minimal image Install util-linux

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text:
Create pathlab/releases/v2/app.txt:

pathlab/releases/v2/app.txt
v2 app
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab04/pathlab
mkdir -p releases/v2
printf 'v2 app\n' > releases/v2/app.txt
ln -sfn "$(pwd)/releases/v2" current-release
readlink -f current-release | tee ../current-v2.txt
grep -q 'v2' releases/v2/app.txt

Expected output

current-v2.txt ends with releases/v2. Both v1 and v2 directories remain for rollback practice.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Proved why absolute paths matter when cwd changes
  • Created hard links and symlinks; inspected inodes
  • Listed mounts and inode capacity
  • Practised deploy-style current → release layout

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab04
# rm -rf pathlab *.txt paths-links-evidence.tgz

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Lab completed under ~/rebash-linux/lab04
  • Can explain inode vs filename vs symlink in plain English
  • Know hard link vs symlink trade-offs
  • Know mounts can hide directory contents and that df -i matters

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Absolute paths in automation — cron/systemd do not share your SSH cwd.
  2. readlink -f before deploy checks — confirm current points where you think.
  3. ls -i for hard links — same inode = same data.
  4. findmnt -T path — which filesystem am I on?
  5. df -i in capacity incidents — inodes exhaust before bytes sometimes.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Symlinks in world-writable directories can be abused (symlink races) — be careful in /tmp
  • Do not follow untrusted symlinks in privileged scripts without checks
  • Mount options (nosuid, nodev, noexec) matter on user-writable volumes
  • Document bind mounts — they confuse audits and backups
  • Restrict who can edit fstab or mount filesystems

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Relative paths in cron or systemd.

✅ Working directory is not your SSH home. Fix: absolute paths or explicit WorkingDirectory=.

❌ Dangling current symlink after cleanup.

✅ Site down though files exist elsewhere. Fix: flip symlink before deleting old release; verify with readlink -f.

❌ Only checking df -h.

✅ Inodes can be exhausted first. Fix: always run df -i in capacity tickets.

❌ Hard links across filesystems.

✅ Kernel rejects them. Fix: use symlinks for cross-mount references.

docs.title: Filesystems — Organizing and Managing Data on Linux Storage
Filesystems — Organizing and Managing Data on Linux Storage
docs.text: A filesystem is the method Linux uses to organize, store, retrieve, and manage data on a storage device. Without a filesystem, a partition is simply raw storage that cannot hold files or directories. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) must understand filesystems because they form the foundation of data storage in Linux.

docs.title: Why Learn Filesystems?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • Installing Linux on a new server.
  • Formatting a newly created partition.
  • Creating storage for databases.
  • Mounting a new SSD.
  • Recovering from filesystem corruption.

Before storing data, every partition must contain a filesystem.

docs.title: What is a Filesystem?
docs.text:
A filesystem defines how data is stored and organized on a storage device.

Without a filesystem:

Disk

↓

Raw Storage

↓

Cannot Store Files

With a filesystem:

Disk

↓

Filesystem

↓

Files

Directories

Permissions

Metadata

docs.title: Filesystem Components
docs.text:
A filesystem manages:

  • Files
  • Directories
  • Metadata
  • Permissions
  • Ownership
  • Timestamps
  • Free space
  • Inodes

docs.title: Common Linux Filesystems
docs.text:
Linux supports many filesystem types.

Common examples:

  • ext4
  • XFS
  • Btrfs
  • FAT32
  • exFAT
  • NTFS
  • Swap

docs.title: ext4
docs.text:
The default filesystem for many Linux distributions.

Advantages:

  • Stable
  • Reliable
  • Excellent performance
  • Journaling support
  • Large file support

Commonly used for:

  • Root filesystem
  • Home directories
  • General-purpose servers

docs.title: XFS
docs.text:
Enterprise filesystem developed for high-performance workloads.

Advantages:

  • Excellent scalability
  • High performance
  • Online filesystem expansion
  • Efficient handling of large files

Commonly used for:

  • Database servers
  • Enterprise storage
  • Red Hat Enterprise Linux

docs.title: Btrfs
docs.text:
Modern Linux filesystem.

Features:

  • Snapshots
  • Compression
  • Checksums
  • RAID support
  • Subvolumes

Commonly used for:

  • Advanced storage
  • Snapshot management
  • Development environments

docs.title: FAT32
docs.text:
Supported by almost every operating system.

Limitations:

  • Maximum file size: 4 GB
  • No Linux permissions
  • No journaling

Commonly used for:

  • USB drives
  • Memory cards

docs.title: exFAT
docs.text:
Designed for flash storage.

Advantages:

  • Supports large files
  • Cross-platform compatibility
  • Better than FAT32 for modern USB devices

docs.title: NTFS
docs.text:
Microsoft Windows filesystem.

Linux can read and write NTFS using appropriate drivers.

Commonly used for:

  • Dual-boot systems
  • External drives

docs.title: Journaling Filesystems
docs.text:
A journal records pending filesystem changes before they are written.

Advantages:

  • Faster recovery after crashes
  • Reduced filesystem corruption
  • Better reliability

Examples:

  • ext4
  • XFS
  • Btrfs

docs.title: View Filesystems
docs.text:
Display mounted filesystems.

df -Th

Example:

Filesystem

Type

Size

Mounted on

docs.title: View Block Devices
docs.text:

Shows:

docs.title: View Filesystem UUIDs

Example:

TYPE="ext4"

docs.title: Create an ext4 Filesystem
docs.text: sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1

Choosing the correct filesystem is critical for performance and reliability.

docs.title: ext4 vs XFS vs Btrfs
docs.text: Feature ext4 XFS Btrfs Stability Excellent Excellent Good Journaling Yes Yes Yes Snapshots No No Yes Compression No No Yes Online Expansion Yes Yes Yes Enterprise Adoption High Very High Growing

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A new storage volume has been attached to a Linux server.

The administrator creates a partition but cannot mount it.

Investigation:

Check the filesystem.

lsblk -f

Output:

FSTYPE

(blank)

The partition has no filesystem.

Create an ext4 filesystem.

sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1

Verify.

blkid

The partition now has a valid filesystem and can be mounted successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use ext4 for general-purpose Linux servers.
  • Use XFS for enterprise workloads requiring high scalability.
  • Use Btrfs when snapshot and advanced storage features are required.
  • Always verify the target partition before formatting.
  • Use filesystem labels and UUIDs for easier administration.
  • Back up important data before creating or reformatting filesystems.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Formatting the wrong partition.

✅ Avoid this mistake: formatting the wrong partition.

❌ Forgetting that formatting erases existing data.

✅ Remember to that formatting erases existing data.

❌ Choosing an inappropriate filesystem for the workload.

✅ Choose carefully: avoid an inappropriate filesystem for the workload when inappropriate.

❌ Ignoring filesystem labels and UUIDs.

✅ Always review filesystem labels and UUIDs.

❌ Attempting to mount an unformatted partition.

✅ Avoid this mistake: attempting to mount an unformatted partition.

docs.title: Firewall (UFW) — Securing Linux Network Access
docs.text: A Firewall controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predefined security rules. It acts as the first line of defense by allowing legitimate connections while blocking unauthorized access. UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a user-friendly firewall management tool for Linux that simplifies configuring iptables or nftables (depending on the distribution). Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should know how to configure UFW to protect production systems.

Course Progress

docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand firewall fundamentals

  • Open and close ports

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Modules 1–10
  • Module 11 Lessons 1–2

docs.title: Why Learn Firewalls?
docs.text:
Imagine a Linux server connected directly to the Internet.

Without a firewall:

Internet

↓

All Ports Open

↓

Attack Surface Increases

With a firewall:

Internet

↓

Firewall

↓

Only Approved Ports

↓

Secure Server

A firewall significantly reduces the attack surface.

docs.title: What is UFW?
docs.text:
UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a command-line utility that simplifies Linux firewall management.

UFW allows administrators to:

  • Allow traffic
  • Deny traffic
  • Restrict traffic
  • Manage ports
  • Control protocols
  • Configure default security policies

docs.title: Install UFW
docs.text:
Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt install ufw

Verify installation.

ufw version

docs.title: Check Firewall Status
docs.text:
sudo ufw status

Example:

Status: inactive

docs.title: Enable the Firewall
docs.text:
sudo ufw enable

Example:

Firewall is active and enabled on system startup.

docs.title: Disable the Firewall
docs.text:
sudo ufw disable

Use only when necessary.

docs.title: Default Firewall Policies
docs.text:
A secure starting point is:

sudo ufw default deny incoming

sudo ufw default allow outgoing

Meaning:

  • Block unsolicited incoming connections.
  • Allow outbound connections initiated by the server.

docs.title: Allow SSH
docs.text:
Before enabling the firewall on a remote server, allow SSH access.

sudo ufw allow ssh

Or specify the port.

sudo ufw allow 22/tcp

Important

Always allow SSH before enabling UFW on a remote system to avoid locking yourself out.

docs.title: Allow Specific Ports
docs.text:
Allow HTTP.

sudo ufw allow 80/tcp

Allow HTTPS.

sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

Allow a custom application.

sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp

docs.title: Deny Traffic
docs.text:
Block a port.

sudo ufw deny 21/tcp

docs.title: Reject Connections
docs.text:
sudo ufw reject 23/tcp

Unlike deny, reject informs the client that the connection was refused.

docs.title: Allow UDP Traffic
docs.text:
Example:

sudo ufw allow 53/udp

Useful for DNS services.

docs.title: Delete a Rule
docs.text:
Delete by rule.

sudo ufw delete allow 8080/tcp

docs.title: Numbered Rules
docs.text:
Display numbered rules.

sudo ufw status numbered

Example:

[1] 22/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere

[2] 80/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere

Delete by number.

sudo ufw delete 2

docs.title: Application Profiles
docs.text:
View available profiles.

sudo ufw app list

Example:

Apache

OpenSSH

Nginx Full

Allow an application profile.

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH

docs.title: View Firewall Rules
docs.text:
sudo ufw status verbose

Shows:

  • Rules
  • Default policies
  • Logging status

docs.title: Enable Firewall Logging
docs.text:
sudo ufw logging on

Logging helps monitor blocked and allowed traffic.

docs.title: Reload Firewall
docs.text:
After making changes:

sudo ufw reload

docs.title: Reset UFW
docs.text:
Restore default settings.

sudo ufw reset

Use with caution because all custom rules are removed.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Enable firewall.

sudo ufw enable

View status.

sudo ufw status

Allow SSH.

sudo ufw allow ssh

Allow HTTPS.

sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

Reload rules.

sudo ufw reload

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Secure web server.

sudo ufw default deny incoming

sudo ufw default allow outgoing

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH

sudo ufw allow 80/tcp

sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

Allow Kubernetes API (example).

sudo ufw allow 6443/tcp

Allow application port.

sudo ufw allow 3000/tcp

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Firewalls are essential for:

  • Cloud virtual machines
  • Web servers
  • Database servers
  • Bastion hosts
  • Kubernetes nodes
  • CI/CD servers
  • Monitoring systems
  • Enterprise infrastructure

A properly configured firewall blocks unnecessary services while allowing only authorized network traffic.
