docs.title: Why Learn Filesystem Navigation?
docs.text:
Every Linux task begins with navigation.

Whether you're:

  • Editing configuration files
  • Viewing logs
  • Deploying applications
  • Running scripts
  • Managing Docker
  • Configuring Kubernetes

you'll constantly move between directories.

Professional Linux administrators spend hundreds of times each day navigating the filesystem.

docs.title: Understanding the Linux Filesystem
docs.text:
Unlike Windows:

C:\Users\John

Linux has only one filesystem.

Everything begins from:

/

Example:

/

├── home
│   └── basha
│       └── projects
│
├── etc
├── var
├── usr
└── tmp

docs.title: Current Working Directory
docs.text:
Every terminal session has a Current Working Directory (CWD).

Display it:

pwd

Example:

/home/basha

Whenever you execute a command, Linux assumes you're referring to the current directory unless you specify another location.

docs.title: Listing Files
docs.text:
Display files:

ls

Example:

Documents
Downloads
Pictures
projects

docs.title: Detailed Listing
docs.text:
ls -l

Displays:

  • Permissions
  • Owner
  • Group
  • Size
  • Date
  • File Name

docs.title: Display Hidden Files
docs.text:
ls -a

Example:

.bashrc

.profile

.gitconfig

Hidden files begin with a dot (.).

docs.title: Most Common Option
docs.text:
ls -la

Displays:

  • Hidden files
  • Detailed information

This is the most commonly used ls command.

docs.title: Changing Directories
docs.text:
Move into a directory:

cd Documents

Display location:

pwd

Output:

/home/basha/Documents

docs.title: Return to Home Directory
docs.text:
Simply type:

cd

or

cd ~

Both commands take you to your home directory.

docs.title: Move to Parent Directory
docs.text:
cd ..

Example:

/home/basha/projects

↓

cd ..

↓

/home/basha

docs.title: Move Up Multiple Levels
docs.text:
cd ../..

Example:

/home/basha/projects/demo

↓

cd ../..

↓

/home

docs.title: Previous Directory
docs.text:
Switch back to the previous directory:

cd -

Example:

/home/basha

↓

cd /etc

↓

cd -

↓

/home/basha

Very useful during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Root Directory
docs.text:
Navigate directly to the root:

cd /

Display location:

pwd

Output:

/

docs.title: Absolute Paths
docs.text:
Absolute paths begin from the root directory.

Example:

cd /home/basha/projects

No matter where you currently are, Linux navigates to the exact location.

docs.title: Relative Paths
docs.text:
Relative paths begin from the current directory.

Example:

Current:

/home/basha

Navigate:

cd Documents

Linux interprets:

/home/basha/Documents

docs.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths
docs.text: Absolute Path Relative Path Starts with / Starts from current directory Independent of location Depends on current directory Always reaches the same location Changes based on where you are

docs.title: Special Directory Symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning . Current Directory .. Parent Directory ~ Home Directory / Root Directory

Examples:

Current directory:

cd .

Parent:

cd ..

Home:

cd ~

Root:

cd /

docs.title: Tab Completion
docs.text:
Instead of typing:

cd Documen

Press:

Tab

Linux automatically completes:

cd Documents

Benefits:

  • Faster
  • Fewer typing mistakes
  • Increased productivity

Professional Linux administrators use Tab completion constantly.

docs.title: Viewing Directory Contents
docs.text:
Display files:

ls

Display hidden files:

ls -a

Display detailed information:

ls -l

Human-readable sizes:

ls -lh

Most common combination:

ls -lah

docs.title: Tree View
docs.text:
Some Linux systems include:

tree

Example:

projects

├── app.py

├── Dockerfile

├── README.md

└── src

If not installed:

Ubuntu:

sudo apt install tree

docs.title: Real Production Example
docs.text:
Suppose you're troubleshooting NGINX.

Navigate:

cd /etc/nginx

View files:

ls -la

Open configuration:

cat nginx.conf

Move to logs:

cd /var/log/nginx

View log files:

ls

Every production troubleshooting session involves filesystem navigation.

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Cloud Engineers frequently navigate directories such as:

/etc

Configuration

/var/log

Logs

/home

Scripts

/opt

Applications

/usr/local/bin

Custom Commands

Efficient navigation saves valuable time during incidents.

docs.title: netstat — Viewing Network Statistics and Connections in Linux
netstat — Viewing Network Statistics and Connections in Linux
docs.text: netstat (Network Statistics) is a classic Linux networking utility used to display active network connections, listening ports, routing tables, interface statistics, and protocol information. Although ss has replaced netstat on most modern Linux distributions due to better performance, netstat is still widely used on legacy systems, older documentation, and enterprise environments.

docs.title: Why Learn netstat?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • You're working on an older RHEL server.
  • A troubleshooting guide instructs you to use netstat.
  • You need to verify if a service is listening on a specific port.

Understanding netstat allows you to work confidently with legacy Linux systems.

docs.title: What is netstat?
docs.text:
netstat stands for:

Network Statistics

It displays:

  • Active TCP connections
  • UDP connections
  • Listening ports
  • Routing tables
  • Network interface statistics
  • Protocol statistics

docs.title: Install netstat
docs.text:
On most modern Linux systems, netstat is provided by the net-tools package.

Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt install net-tools

RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux:

sudo dnf install net-tools

docs.title: View Interface Statistics

Shows statistics for:

Useful when diagnosing protocol-level problems.

docs.title: netstat vs ss
docs.text:
Feature netstat ss Performance Slower Faster Default on Modern Linux ❌ ✅ Socket Statistics Basic Advanced Shows Active Connections ✅ ✅ Shows Listening Ports ✅ ✅ Displays Processes ✅ ✅ Recommended Tool Legacy systems Modern Linux

ss is the preferred tool for modern Linux systems because it provides faster and more detailed information.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users cannot connect to a web application.

Investigation:

Check listening ports.

sudo netstat -tulpn | grep :80

No output.

Check service status.

systemctl status nginx

NGINX is not running.

Start the service.

sudo systemctl start nginx

Verify again.

sudo netstat -tulpn | grep :80

Output:

tcp

0

0

0.0.0.0:80

LISTEN

The web server is now accepting connections.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Prefer ss for modern Linux systems.
  • Learn netstat for compatibility with legacy environments.
  • Verify that services are listening before troubleshooting firewalls.
  • Use numeric output (-n) for faster results.
  • Combine netstat with ping, traceroute, and curl during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming netstat is installed on every Linux distribution.

✅ Verify netstat is installed on every Linux distribution instead of assuming it.

❌ Ignoring the LISTEN state.

✅ Always review the LISTEN state.

❌ Forgetting to use sudo when viewing process information.

✅ Remember to to use sudo when viewing process information.

❌ Using netstat when ss provides better performance.

✅ Avoid using netstat when ss provides better performance when a safer approach exists.

docs.title: nice and renice — Managing Process Priorities in Linux
nice and renice — Managing Process Priorities in Linux
docs.text: Linux allows multiple processes to compete for CPU time. The nice and renice commands help control process scheduling priority, allowing administrators to favor important workloads while reducing the impact of less critical tasks. Proper use of process priorities improves system responsiveness and overall performance in production environments.

docs.title: Why Learn nice?
docs.text:
Imagine a production server running:

  • Database
  • Web Server
  • Backup Job
  • Log Compression
  • File Synchronization

The backup job suddenly consumes all available CPU.

Users begin experiencing slow application performance.

Should the backup receive the same CPU priority as the database?

No.

Linux allows us to assign different priorities.

docs.title: What is Process Priority?
docs.text:
Linux schedules CPU time based on process priority.

Higher-priority processes generally receive CPU time before lower-priority processes when CPU resources are limited.

Priority can be adjusted using:

  • nice
  • renice

docs.title: What is a Nice Value?
docs.text:
A nice value tells the Linux scheduler how "nice" a process should be to other processes.

A higher nice value means the process is more willing to yield CPU time.

A lower nice value means the process receives higher scheduling priority.

docs.title: Nice Value Range
docs.text:
-20  -------------------->  19

Highest Priority          Lowest Priority
Nice Value Meaning -20 Highest priority 0 Default priority 19 Lowest priority

Note

Regular users can usually increase the nice value (lower priority) for their own processes. Lowering the nice value (raising priority) generally requires administrative privileges.

docs.title: View Nice Values
docs.text:
Display running processes.

ps -el

Example:

PID PRI NI CMD

245 20 0 bash

600 20 5 backup.sh

Observe:

NI

This represents the nice value.

docs.title: Start a Process with a Nice Value
docs.text:
Default:

python app.py

Lower priority:

nice -n 10 python app.py

Verify:

ps -el

docs.title: Highest User Priority
docs.text:
Administrator only.

sudo nice -n -10 python app.py

This gives the process a higher scheduling priority.

docs.title: Change Priority of a Running Process
docs.text:
Use:

renice

Example:

sudo renice 5 -p 1234

Meaning:

PID

1234

↓

Nice Value

5

docs.title: Increase Priority
docs.text:
Example:

sudo renice -10 -p 1234

Requires administrative privileges.

docs.title: Decrease Priority
docs.text:
Example:

renice 15 -p 1234

Regular users can generally lower the priority of their own processes by increasing the nice value.

docs.title: View Process Priority
docs.text:
ps -o pid,ni,comm

Example:

PID NI COMMAND

1200 0 nginx

2400 10 backup

docs.title: CPU Scheduling Example
docs.text:
Database

NI = -5

↓

Web Server

NI = 0

↓

Backup Job

NI = 15

The scheduler generally favors higher-priority processes when CPU resources are constrained.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Start with default priority.

command

Start with custom priority.

nice -n 10 command

Change priority.

renice 10 -p PID

View priority.

ps -el

Display nice values.

ps -o pid,ni,comm

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Low-priority backup.

nice -n 15 tar -czf backup.tar.gz /data

Database maintenance.

nice -n 5 vacuumdb

Log compression.

nice -n 19 gzip large.log

Long-running reports.

nice -n 10 python report.py

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Process priorities are useful for:

  • Database maintenance
  • Backup jobs
  • Log processing
  • File synchronization
  • Batch processing
  • CI/CD runners
  • Data analytics
  • Large file compression

They help ensure background workloads don't unnecessarily impact interactive users or critical services.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Start a low-priority process.

nice -n 10 sleep 300

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Find its PID.

ps -ef | grep sleep

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Display nice values.

ps -o pid,ni,comm

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Change the priority.

renice 15 -p PID

Replace PID with the process ID from the previous task.

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Verify the change.

ps -o pid,ni,comm

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Display detailed process information.

ps -el

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Start another process with the default priority.

sleep 300

Compare the nice values.

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Terminate the test processes.

kill PID

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example nice Start a process with a custom priority Batch jobs renice Change a running process priority Performance tuning ps -el Display priorities Monitoring ps -o pid,ni,comm Display nice values Troubleshooting

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A nightly backup begins at midnight.

Users report:

  • Slow application response
  • High CPU utilization

Investigation:

top

ps -el

Findings:

The backup process is running with the default priority.

Solution:

Lower its scheduling priority.

sudo renice 15 -p 3456

Result:

  • Backup continues running.
  • Business applications receive CPU time more quickly.
  • Overall system responsiveness improves.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Run non-critical batch jobs with higher nice values (lower priority).
  • Keep critical services at the default priority unless tuning is necessary.
  • Increase process priority only when justified.
  • Monitor CPU utilization before changing priorities.
  • Test priority changes in non-production environments.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assigning the highest priority to every application.

✅ This defeats the purpose of process prioritization.

❌ Using negative nice values without understanding their impact.

✅ High-priority processes can reduce CPU availability for other workloads.

❌ Assuming nice changes process memory usage.

✅ It only influences CPU scheduling priority.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Process priorities
  • Nice values
  • The nice command
  • The renice command
  • CPU scheduling
  • Priority management
  • Production best practices

Linux process priorities help administrators balance competing workloads by controlling CPU scheduling. Proper use of nice and renice improves system responsiveness and ensures critical applications receive appropriate CPU resources.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Nice values range from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest priority).
  • The default nice value is 0.
  • Use nice to start a process with a custom priority.
  • Use renice to modify the priority of a running process.
  • Lower-priority background jobs should typically have higher nice values.
  • Use process priorities carefully to maintain system performance.

docs.title: Linux File Ownership — Understanding Users, Groups, and File Ownership
Linux File Ownership — Understanding Users, Groups, and File Ownership
docs.text: Every file and directory in Linux belongs to a User (Owner) and a Group. File ownership is a fundamental security mechanism that controls who can access, modify, and manage files. Understanding ownership is essential for Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, SREs, and Security professionals.

docs.title: Why Learn File Ownership?
docs.text:
Imagine your application suddenly stops working.

The error log shows:

Permission denied

The file permissions look correct:

-rw-r--r--

But the owner is:

root

while the application runs as:

www-data

Even with correct permissions, incorrect ownership can prevent applications from accessing files.

docs.title: Understanding Ownership
docs.text:
Every file has:

  • Owner (User)
  • Group

Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 basha developers 1024 Jan 10 config.yaml

Breakdown:

-rw-r--r--

Permissions

1

Link Count

basha

Owner

developers

Group

1024

Size

docs.title: Viewing Ownership
docs.text:
Display files.

ls -l

Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 basha developers 1200 report.txt

Owner:

basha

Group:

developers

docs.title: Viewing Numeric IDs
docs.text:
ls -ln

Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 1000 1000 1200 report.txt

Here:

  • UID = 1000
  • GID = 1000

docs.title: Understanding Users
docs.text:
Each Linux user has:

  • Username
  • User ID (UID)
  • Home directory
  • Login shell
  • Primary group

Display current user.

whoami

Example:

basha

Display user information.

id

Output:

uid=1000(basha)

gid=1000(developers)

groups=1000(developers),27(sudo)

docs.title: Understanding Groups
docs.text:
Groups simplify permission management.

Example:

Developers

Administrators

QA

DevOps

Instead of assigning permissions to every individual user, permissions can be granted to a group.

Display current groups.

groups

docs.title: Root Ownership
docs.text:
Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 root root

Owner:

root

Group:

root

The root user has unrestricted access to most files and directories.

docs.title: Ownership vs Permissions
docs.text:
Ownership determines who permissions apply to.

Permissions determine what actions are allowed.

Example:

-rwxr-x---

Owner:

alice

Group:

developers

If Bob belongs to developers, he receives the group permissions (r-x).

docs.title: View Detailed Information
docs.text:
stat report.txt

Example:

Uid: (1000/basha)

Gid: (1000/developers)

docs.title: Changing File Owner
docs.text:
Syntax:

sudo chown USER FILE

Example:

sudo chown basha report.txt

Verify:

ls -l report.txt

docs.title: Changing Group Ownership
docs.text:
Syntax:

sudo chgrp GROUP FILE

Example:

sudo chgrp developers report.txt

docs.title: Change Owner and Group Together
docs.text: sudo chown basha:developers report.txt

docs.title: Recursive Ownership
docs.text:
Change ownership of an entire directory.

sudo chown -R basha:developers project/

Useful for:

  • Web applications
  • Shared directories
  • Deployment folders

Group:

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Ownership is critical for:

  • Web servers
  • Kubernetes
  • Docker
  • Databases
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Shared storage
  • Application deployments
  • SSH authentication

Incorrect ownership is one of the most common causes of application failures.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A web application cannot upload files.

Error:

Permission denied

Investigation:

ls -l /var/www/uploads

stat /var/www/uploads

id www-data

Output:

Owner:

root

Group:

root

The web server runs as:

www-data

Solution:

sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/uploads

The application can now create and modify files successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Assign ownership to the application user.
  • Avoid running applications as root.
  • Use groups for collaborative access.
  • Verify ownership after deployments.
  • Audit ownership regularly on production systems.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Running applications as root.

✅ Create dedicated service accounts instead.

❌ Changing ownership recursively without verification.

✅ Always double-check the target directory before using:

sudo chown -R

❌ Confusing ownership with permissions.

✅ Ownership determines which permissions apply.

Permissions determine what actions are allowed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Installing and updating software is weekly work on Linux servers. This tutorial teaches the package manager workflow and how to read the errors when a dependency fails.

Plain problem: Your teammate says “run apt install nginx”. On another server the same command fails because that host uses dnf (Red Hat family) or apk (Alpine). Installing the wrong way wastes time and can break production images.

A package manager is the distro’s official shop for software: it downloads signed packages, tracks versions, and removes files cleanly. Unpatched packages are security debt — attackers exploit known bugs in old versions.

This tutorial answers, in order:

  1. What is a package and a package manager?
  2. How does apt work on Ubuntu?
  3. What are dnf, yum, and apk?
  4. How do you install, query, hold, and remove a package safely?
  5. How do you prove package state for a ticket or interview?

This is Tutorial 10 in Module 10: Package Management of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series — practical Linux for Cloud and DevOps work.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A practice Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VM, cloud Free Tier VM, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2) Ubuntu
  • SSH or local terminal access
  • A normal user account with sudo when the lab asks for it
  • Completed SSH and Remote Access or equivalent comfort in a terminal

You do not need to have built software from source before.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain what a package manager does in plain language
  • Refresh metadata, install, query, and remove packages with apt on Ubuntu
  • Map apt commands to dnf/yum/apk equivalents on other distros
  • Place an apt hold so a package does not upgrade by accident
  • Save a package evidence pack for tickets or interviews
  • Answer common fresher interview questions on package management

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Your shell talks to the package manager (apt), which reads package lists from repositories on the internet (or a mirror), verifies signatures, and installs files into standard paths (/usr/bin, /lib, …). Lower-level tools (dpkg on Debian family, rpm on RHEL family) track what is installed on disk.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
You join a team and need tree (a small directory-listing tool) on a build server. You Google “install tree linux” and see five different command sets. You pick one at random. Half work; half fail with “command not found” for the package manager itself.

The fix is always the same: identify the distro family first (cat /etc/os-release), then use that family’s package manager.

docs.title: What is a package? (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: A package is a pre-packed box from a trusted warehouse — the program, its libraries, and a manifest saying which files go where. The package manager is the shop clerk: finds the box, checks the seal (signature), unpacks it, and records what you own so uninstall is clean.

Term Plain meaning Package Archive of software + metadata (name, version, dependencies) Repository (repo) Server listing available packages for your distro Package manager Tool that installs, updates, and removes packages (apt, dnf, …) Dependency Another package this one needs to run Hold / pin Mark a package so it does not auto-upgrade

What you can say in an interview: “On Ubuntu I use apt to install from signed repositories; I always refresh metadata with update before upgrade, and I query installed version before blaming the app.”

docs.title: apt on Ubuntu and Debian
docs.text:
Goal Command Refresh package lists sudo apt update Upgrade installed packages sudo apt upgrade Install a package sudo apt install <name> Show installed version apt list --installed <name> Show files from a package dpkg -L <name> Remove package sudo apt remove <name> Prevent upgrade sudo apt-mark hold <name>

Tiny example — check if curl is installed:

Terminal
apt list --installed curl 2>/dev/null | head -5
dpkg -l curl 2>/dev/null | tail -1

docs.title: Other families (you will meet these at work)
docs.text:
Family Tool Install example Query example Debian / Ubuntu apt / dpkg sudo apt install tree dpkg -l tree RHEL / Rocky / Amazon Linux dnf / rpm sudo dnf install tree rpm -q tree Alpine (containers) apk apk add tree apk info tree SUSE zypper sudo zypper install tree rpm -q tree

Interview line: “I never assume apt; I read /etc/os-release and use the matching tool.”

docs.title: update vs upgrade vs dist-upgrade
docs.text:
• apt update — downloads new package lists (catalogues). Does not change installed software.
  • apt upgrade — installs newer versions of packages already installed (safe default).
  • apt full-upgrade — may remove/replace packages to resolve dependency conflicts (use with care on production; test first).

docs.title: Holds, snapshots, and production habits
docs.text: Golden images and Configuration Management (Ansible, cloud-init) assume a known package set. An accidental kernel or OpenSSL upgrade during an incident window can break apps. apt-mark hold pins one package. Teams also snapshot disks or bake new images instead of upgrading live servers blindly.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Running apt install without sudo update first (stale lists → “package not found”)
  • Using Ubuntu tutorials on Rocky Linux (dnf not apt)
  • Confusing “remove package” with “delete my data in /home” (config files may remain — use purge when appropriate)
  • Installing random .deb files from the internet without checking signatures

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Install and query tree, place a hold, remove it cleanly, and save a package evidence pack under ~/rebash-linux/lab16.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu practice host 22.04 or 24.04 Network Outbound HTTPS to Ubuntu mirrors sudo Required for install/remove

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab16 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab16
cat /etc/os-release | grep -E '^(NAME|VERSION_ID)='

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Your mentor asks: “Install tree on the build agent, confirm the version, pin it so tonight’s auto-upgrade does not change it, then show me how you would remove it after the test.” This lab is that ticket with proof files.

docs.title: Task 1 – Refresh metadata and install tree
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab16
sudo apt update 2>&1 | tee apt-update.log
sudo apt install -y tree 2>&1 | tee apt-install-tree.log
command -v tree
tree --version | tee tree-version.txt
test -s tree-version.txt

Expected output

command -v tree prints a path such as /usr/bin/tree. tree-version.txt shows a version line.

docs.title: Task 2 – Query files and place a hold
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab16
dpkg -L tree | head -20 | tee tree-files-head.txt
apt list --installed tree 2>/dev/null | tee tree-installed.txt
sudo apt-mark hold tree
apt-mark showhold | tee hold-list.txt
grep -q tree hold-list.txt

Expected output

hold-list.txt contains tree. tree-installed.txt shows installed status.

docs.title: Task 3 – Break, fix, and prove (simulate stale install attempt)
docs.text:
Create bad-install-notes.md:

bad-install-notes.md
# Wrong-family mistake (lab note)

If you run `dnf install tree` on Ubuntu, you get "command not found" for dnf.
Fix: use `apt` after confirming NAME=Ubuntu in /etc/os-release.
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab16
! command -v dnf && echo "dnf absent on Ubuntu — expected" | tee dnf-check.txt
sudo apt-mark unhold tree
sudo apt remove -y tree
! command -v tree && echo "tree removed OK" | tee remove-proof.txt
sudo apt install -y tree
tree --version | tee tree-version-after-reinstall.txt
echo "lab16 package evidence OK" | tee evidence.txt
ls -la

Expected output

remove-proof.txt confirms tree was absent after remove. Reinstall succeeds; evidence.txt marks completion.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• apt update and apt install tree completed without errors
  • You demonstrated hold and unhold with apt-mark
  • Evidence files exist under ~/rebash-linux/lab16
  • You can explain apt vs dnf without notes

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix E: Unable to locate package tree Stale lists or wrong distro Run sudo apt update; confirm Ubuntu with /etc/os-release E: Could not get lock Another apt process running Wait or identify process: ps aux \| grep apt dpkg: error processing Interrupted install sudo dpkg --configure -a then retry hold ignored in upgrade Used unattended-upgrades override Check /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/; document exception

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text:
Create family-cheatsheet.md with one install and one query command each for apt, dnf, and apk in your own words.

Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab16
test -s family-cheatsheet.md
echo "challenge OK" | tee challenge.txt

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• You installed and removed a real package on Ubuntu
  • You used hold/unhold like a cautious operator
  • You have interview-ready evidence of package state

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab16
sudo apt-mark unhold tree 2>/dev/null || true
# Optional: sudo apt remove -y tree
# Keep evidence files for revision

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Lab completed under ~/rebash-linux/lab16
  • Can map three package managers to three distro families
  • Ready for scheduling and automation next

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. apt update before install — refreshes catalogues; prevents “not found” on valid packages.
  2. dpkg -L — shows which files a package owns; useful when config paths confuse you.
  3. apt-mark hold — production pin for one package; document why in tickets.
  4. Remove then reinstall — proves you understand lifecycle, not only install.
  5. Log with tee — attaches command output to evidence files for mentors.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Install only from your distro’s signed repositories unless security team approves exceptions.
  • Patch regularly; unpatched OpenSSH, OpenSSL, and glibc CVEs are common breach paths.
  • Do not curl | bash random install scripts on production hosts.
  • Review what a package installs (dpkg -L) before adding to golden images.
  • Use sudo for package changes; do not run daily work as root.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Skipping apt update.

✅ Always refresh lists before install or upgrade on Ubuntu. Stale metadata causes false “package not found” errors.

❌ Mixing distro tutorials.

✅ Rocky Linux needs dnf. Alpine containers need apk. Ubuntu needs apt. Check /etc/os-release first.

❌ Removing without checking dependents.

✅ Removing a library package can break other apps. Use apt remove and read proposed changes; test on non-production first.

docs.title: Package Troubleshooting — Diagnosing and Resolving Package Management Issues
Package Troubleshooting — Diagnosing and Resolving Package Management Issues
docs.text: Package installation and updates don't always go as planned. Dependency conflicts, broken repositories, corrupted package databases, network failures, and version mismatches are common issues encountered by Linux administrators. Understanding how to troubleshoot package-related problems is an essential skill for Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs).

docs.title: Why Learn Package Troubleshooting?
docs.text:
Imagine a production deployment fails because:

  • Docker cannot be installed.
  • Package dependencies are broken.
  • A repository is unavailable.
  • A package database is corrupted.
  • Security updates fail.

Knowing how to troubleshoot these issues minimizes downtime and keeps systems operational.

docs.title: Common Package Problems
docs.text:
Typical issues include:

  • Package not found
  • Broken dependencies
  • Repository unavailable
  • GPG key errors
  • Corrupted package database
  • Disk space issues
  • Network connectivity problems
  • Package version conflicts

docs.title: Troubleshooting Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Error
      │
      ▼
Read Error Message
      │
      ▼
Check Repository
      │
      ▼
Verify Network
      │
      ▼
Repair Dependencies
      │
      ▼
Retry Installation

docs.title: Problem 1: Package Not Found
docs.text:
Example:

sudo apt install docker

Error:

Unable to locate package docker

Possible causes:

  • Package index is outdated
  • Repository is missing
  • Package name is incorrect

Solution:

sudo apt update

Search again:

apt search docker

docs.title: Problem 2: Broken Dependencies
docs.text:
Ubuntu:

sudo apt --fix-broken install

Repair package configuration.

sudo dpkg --configure -a

docs.title: Problem 3: Repository Errors
docs.text:
Example:

404 Not Found

Check repository configuration.

Ubuntu:

cat /etc/apt/sources.list

DNF:

dnf repolist

Refresh metadata.

sudo apt update

or

sudo dnf makecache

docs.title: Problem 4: GPG Key Errors
docs.text:
Example:

NO_PUBKEY

Import the required signing key from the software vendor following the repository's installation instructions.

Then refresh package metadata.

sudo apt update

RPM-based systems:

sudo rpm --import <GPG_KEY_URL>

docs.title: Problem 5: Corrupted Package Cache
docs.text:
Ubuntu:

sudo apt clean

sudo apt autoclean

DNF:

sudo dnf clean all

Rebuild cache.

sudo dnf makecache

docs.title: Problem 6: Package Database Locked
docs.text:
Ubuntu:

Could not get lock

Another package management process is already running.

Check running processes.

ps -ef | grep apt

Wait for the other process to complete or stop it only if it is safe to do so.

docs.title: Problem 7: Disk Space Full
docs.text:
Check disk usage.

df -h

Remove unnecessary packages.

Ubuntu:

sudo apt autoremove

Clean package cache.

sudo apt clean

docs.title: Problem 8: Network Connectivity
docs.text:
Test Internet access.

ping google.com

Check DNS.

nslookup google.com

Verify repository access.

curl https://archive.ubuntu.com

docs.title: RPM Database Issues
docs.text:
Rebuild the RPM database if necessary.

sudo rpm --rebuilddb

Use only when the RPM database is suspected to be corrupted.

docs.title: Verify Installed Package
docs.text:
Ubuntu:

apt policy nginx

DNF:

dnf info nginx

RPM:

rpm -qi nginx

docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example apt --fix-broken install Repair dependencies Recovery dpkg --configure -a Configure interrupted packages Recovery apt clean Clear package cache Maintenance dnf clean all Clear repository cache Maintenance rpm --rebuilddb Rebuild RPM database Database repair df -h Check disk space Troubleshooting ping Test connectivity Network diagnosis curl Verify repository access Repository validation

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A deployment pipeline fails while installing Docker.

sudo apt install docker.io

Error:

Unable to locate package docker.io

Investigation:

sudo apt update

Still failing.

Check repository:

cat /etc/apt/sources.list

The required repository is missing.

After adding the correct repository and refreshing package metadata:

sudo apt update

sudo apt install docker.io

The installation completes successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Read the complete error message before troubleshooting.
  • Refresh package metadata regularly.
  • Use trusted repositories.
  • Verify network connectivity before investigating package issues.
  • Monitor available disk space.
  • Back up systems before major package upgrades.
  • Test changes in non-production environments.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Ignoring dependency errors.

✅ Always review dependency errors.

❌ Deleting package manager lock files while another package operation is active.

✅ Do not delete package manager lock files while another package operation is active until it is safe to do so.

❌ Mixing repositories from different Linux versions.

✅ Avoid mixing repositories from different Linux versions.

❌ Installing packages from untrusted repositories.

✅ Avoid this mistake: installing packages from untrusted repositories.

❌ Ignoring GPG signature warnings.

✅ Always review GPG signature warnings.

docs.title: System Updates — Keeping Linux Systems Secure and Up to Date
System Updates — Keeping Linux Systems Secure and Up to Date
docs.text: Regular system updates are one of the most important responsibilities of a Linux administrator. Updates provide security patches, bug fixes, performance improvements, hardware support, and new features. Proper update management helps maintain system stability, protects against vulnerabilities, and ensures production environments remain reliable.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Linux system updates
  • Update installed packages
  • Upgrade operating systems safely
  • Apply security updates
  • Plan production maintenance
  • Verify successful updates
  • Roll back when necessary
  • Follow update best practices

docs.title: Why Are System Updates Important?
docs.text:
Imagine a production web server running for two years without updates.

Potential risks include:

  • Security vulnerabilities
  • Software bugs
  • Unsupported packages
  • Compatibility issues
  • Performance degradation

Regular updates help reduce these risks.

docs.title: What is a System Update?
docs.text:
A system update installs newer versions of:

  • Installed applications
  • System libraries
  • Security patches
  • Kernel packages
  • Device drivers
  • Utilities

Updates generally do not remove user data.

docs.title: Update Workflow
docs.text:
Refresh Package Metadata
          │
          ▼
Check Available Updates
          │
          ▼
Download Packages
          │
          ▼
Install Updates
          │
          ▼
Restart Services (if required)
          │
          ▼
Reboot (if required)

docs.title: Update on Ubuntu/Debian
docs.text:
Refresh package information.

sudo apt update

Install available updates.

sudo apt upgrade

Perform a complete upgrade.

sudo apt full-upgrade

Remove unused packages.

sudo apt autoremove

docs.title: Update on RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux/Fedora
docs.text:
Check available updates.

sudo dnf check-update

Install updates.

sudo dnf upgrade

Older systems using YUM:

sudo yum update

docs.title: Check Installed Updates
docs.text:
Ubuntu/Debian:

apt list --upgradable

DNF:

dnf check-update

YUM:

docs.title: Update a Specific Package
docs.text:
Ubuntu:

sudo apt install nginx

If a newer version is available, APT upgrades the package.

DNF:

sudo dnf upgrade nginx

YUM:

sudo yum update nginx

docs.title: Kernel Updates
docs.text:
Kernel updates improve:

  • Security
  • Hardware support
  • Performance
  • Stability

After installing a new kernel:

sudo reboot

Verify the running kernel.

uname -r

docs.title: Distribution Upgrade
docs.text:
Upgrade to a newer operating system release.

Ubuntu:

sudo do-release-upgrade

RHEL:

Use supported upgrade tools such as Leapp for major version upgrades.

Major operating system upgrades should always be planned and tested.

docs.title: Automatic Updates
docs.text:
Ubuntu:

Install unattended upgrades.

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades

Configure automatic updates.

sudo dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades

RHEL-based systems:

Automatic updates can be configured using services such as dnf-automatic.

docs.title: Verify System Health After Updates
docs.text:
Check failed services.

systemctl --failed

Verify system logs.

journalctl -p err -b

Check service status.

systemctl status nginx

Kernel version:

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A production server receives scheduled monthly updates.

Maintenance steps:

sudo apt update

sudo apt upgrade

After the update:

systemctl --failed

Output:

nginx.service failed

Investigation:

journalctl -u nginx

The configuration file contains a syntax error introduced before the update.

After correcting the configuration:

sudo systemctl restart nginx

The service starts successfully and the maintenance window is completed.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Apply updates regularly.
  • Test updates in non-production environments first.
  • Schedule maintenance windows for production servers.
  • Back up critical systems before major upgrades.
  • Verify application and service health after updates.
  • Reboot when required, especially after kernel updates.

docs.text:

❌ Ignoring reboot requirements after kernel updates.

✅ Always review reboot requirements after kernel updates.

❌ Skipping backups before major upgrades.

✅ Avoid this mistake: skipping backups before major upgrades.

❌ Forgetting to verify services after updates.

✅ Remember to to verify services after updates.

docs.title: PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) — Understanding Linux Authentication
PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) — Understanding Linux Authentication
docs.text: PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) is the authentication framework used by Linux to control how users are authenticated and authorized. Instead of every application implementing its own authentication mechanism, applications such as SSH, sudo, login, and passwd rely on PAM to provide a centralized, flexible, and secure authentication system.

docs.title: Why Learn PAM?
docs.text:
Imagine a company with:

  • SSH logins
  • sudo authentication
  • Console logins
  • FTP access
  • Database authentication
  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

Should every application implement its own password verification?

No.

Linux uses PAM to provide one centralized authentication framework.

docs.title: What is PAM?
docs.text:
PAM stands for:

Pluggable Authentication Modules

PAM provides a common authentication interface between:

Applications

↓

PAM

↓

Authentication Modules

Applications simply ask PAM to authenticate users.

PAM decides how authentication should happen.

docs.title: PAM Authentication Flow
docs.text:
User Login
      │
      ▼
Application
(ssh, sudo, login)
      │
      ▼
PAM
      │
      ▼
Authentication Module
      │
      ▼
Password / LDAP / MFA / Kerberos
      │
      ▼
Access Granted or Denied

docs.title: Why PAM?
docs.text:
Benefits:

  • Centralized authentication
  • Consistent security
  • Flexible configuration
  • Easy integration
  • Enterprise authentication support

Without PAM, every application would require its own authentication implementation.

docs.title: PAM Configuration Directory
docs.text:
Configuration files are stored in:

/etc/pam.d/

View:

ls /etc/pam.d

Example:

login

sshd

sudo

passwd

su

Each application has its own PAM configuration.

docs.title: Example PAM File
docs.text:
Display:

cat /etc/pam.d/sshd

Example:

auth required pam_unix.so

account required pam_unix.so

password required pam_unix.so

session required pam_unix.so

Each line defines how authentication is processed.

docs.title: PAM Components
docs.text:
Every PAM rule has four parts:

Type

Control Flag

Module

Arguments

Example:

auth required pam_unix.so

Breakdown:

Part Meaning auth Authentication step required Control flag pam_unix.so Authentication module (optional) Module arguments

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Verifies identity.

auth

Examples:

  • Password verification
  • SSH authentication
  • MFA

docs.title: Account
docs.text:
Checks account status.

account

Examples:

  • Account expiration
  • Login restrictions
  • Time-based access

docs.title: Password
docs.text:
Handles password changes.

password

Examples:

  • Password updates
  • Complexity rules
  • Password history

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
Manages user sessions.

session

Examples:

  • Login
  • Logout
  • Resource limits
  • Session logging

docs.title: required
docs.text:
Authentication must succeed.

Failure is remembered, but PAM continues processing the remaining modules.

docs.title: requisite
docs.text:
Authentication must succeed.

Failure immediately stops authentication.

docs.title: sufficient
docs.text: If successful, authentication succeeds immediately (provided no earlier required module has failed).

docs.title: optional
docs.text: Used when the module's result is not essential unless no other modules are configured for that type.

docs.title: Common PAM Modules
docs.text:
Module Purpose pam_unix.so Local password authentication pam_env.so Load environment variables pam_limits.so Resource limits pam_access.so Access control pam_pwquality.so Password complexity (commonly used on many distributions) pam_faillock.so Account lockout after failed logins (common on RHEL-based systems)

Note

The available modules vary depending on the Linux distribution.

docs.title: Password Complexity
docs.text:
Many Linux systems use:

pam_pwquality.so

to enforce:

  • Minimum length
  • Uppercase letters
  • Lowercase letters
  • Numbers
  • Special characters

Example configuration:

password requisite pam_pwquality.so retry=3

docs.title: Account Lockout
docs.text:
Some distributions use:

pam_faillock.so

to lock accounts after repeated failed login attempts.

This helps mitigate brute-force attacks.

docs.title: PAM and sudo
docs.text:
Display:

cat /etc/pam.d/sudo

Every time you execute:

sudo

PAM authenticates the user according to the configured policy.

docs.title: PAM and SSH
docs.text:
Display:

cat /etc/pam.d/sshd

When a user connects through SSH:

SSH

↓

PAM

↓

Authentication

docs.title: Enterprise Authentication
docs.text:
PAM supports:

  • LDAP
  • Active Directory
  • Kerberos
  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
  • Smart Cards
  • Biometric authentication (where supported)

Applications don't need to change—only the PAM configuration does.

View sudo configuration.

cat /etc/pam.d/sudo

View login configuration.

cat /etc/pam.d/login

PAM

LDAP

↓

PAM

Password Policy

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
PAM is used extensively for:

  • Linux servers
  • Enterprise authentication
  • Active Directory integration
  • LDAP authentication
  • SSH security
  • sudo authentication
  • Password policies
  • Multi-factor authentication (MFA)

Almost every Linux login passes through PAM.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users suddenly cannot log in through SSH.

Investigation:

sudo cat /etc/pam.d/sshd

sudo journalctl -u ssh

The PAM configuration was modified incorrectly.

Solution:

Restore the correct PAM configuration from backup or reinstall the appropriate PAM package according to your distribution.

After restarting the SSH service (if required), authentication works again.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Avoid manually editing PAM configuration unless you understand the authentication flow.
  • Always back up PAM configuration files before making changes.
  • Test configuration changes in a non-production environment first.
  • Use PAM modules provided by your Linux distribution.
  • Document custom authentication policies.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Editing PAM configuration on production systems without testing.

✅ Edit PAM configuration on production systems without testing only when appropriate and with a backup.

❌ Removing required authentication modules.

✅ This can prevent users—including administrators—from logging in.

❌ Assuming PAM configuration is identical across all Linux distributions.

✅ Module names and configuration files may differ.

docs.title: Linux Password Policies — Securing User Authentication
Linux Password Policies — Securing User Authentication
docs.text: Passwords are the first line of defense in Linux security. Weak passwords or poorly configured password policies can lead to unauthorized access, privilege escalation, and security breaches. Linux provides built-in mechanisms to enforce password complexity, expiration, aging, and account locking to protect systems from misuse.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Linux password policies
  • Manage user passwords
  • Configure password aging
  • Set password expiration
  • Lock and unlock user accounts
  • Understand the /etc/shadow file
  • Apply password security best practices
  • Enforce enterprise password policies

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials

docs.title: Why Learn Password Policies?
docs.text:
Imagine a production Linux server.

A user account has:

  • Password: admin123
  • Never expires
  • Shared by multiple administrators

This creates a serious security risk.

Linux password policies help enforce:

  • Strong passwords
  • Password expiration
  • Password history
  • Account security
  • Compliance requirements

docs.title: What is a Password Policy?
docs.text:
A password policy defines rules such as:

  • Minimum password length
  • Password complexity
  • Password expiration
  • Password aging
  • Password reuse restrictions
  • Account locking

These policies reduce the risk of unauthorized access.

docs.title: The Password Lifecycle
docs.text:
Create Password
       │
       ▼
Password Active
       │
       ▼
Password Expires
       │
       ▼
User Changes Password
       │
       ▼
New Password Active

docs.title: Changing a Password
docs.text:
Change your own password.

passwd

Example:

Changing password for basha.

Current password:

New password:

Retype new password:

docs.title: Change Another User's Password
docs.text:
Administrator only.

sudo passwd developer

docs.title: Password Information
docs.text:
Display password aging information.

chage -l basha

Example:

Last password change

Password expires

Password inactive

Account expires

docs.title: Password Aging
docs.text:
Linux supports:

  • Minimum password age
  • Maximum password age
  • Warning period
  • Inactive period

These settings help enforce regular password updates.

docs.title: Configure Password Expiration
docs.text:
Example:

sudo chage -M 90 basha

Meaning:

Maximum password age

90 Days

docs.title: Minimum Password Age
docs.text:
Prevent immediate password changes.

sudo chage -m 7 basha

Meaning:

Minimum age

7 Days

docs.title: Warning Before Expiration
docs.text:
Warn users before expiration.

sudo chage -W 14 basha

Meaning:

Warn user

14 Days

docs.title: Account Expiration
docs.text:
Set account expiration.

sudo chage -E 2027-12-31 basha

Disable expiration.

sudo chage -E -1 basha

docs.title: Lock a User Account
docs.text:
Temporarily disable password authentication.

sudo passwd -l basha

Check status.

sudo passwd -S basha

docs.title: Unlock a User Account
docs.text: sudo passwd -u basha

docs.title: Force Password Change
docs.text:
Require the user to change their password at the next login.

sudo passwd -e basha

docs.title: Understanding /etc/shadow
docs.text:
Linux stores password information in:

/etc/shadow

View (requires elevated privileges).

sudo cat /etc/shadow

Example:

basha:$y$j9T$...

:20240:7:90:14:::

Fields include:

  • Username
  • Password hash
  • Last password change
  • Minimum age
  • Maximum age
  • Warning period
  • Inactive period
  • Account expiration

Passwords are stored as hashed values, not plain text.

docs.title: Difference Between /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
docs.text: File Purpose /etc/passwd User account information /etc/shadow Password hashes and aging information

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Change password.

passwd

Display aging.

chage -l basha

Set maximum age.

sudo chage -M 90 basha

Set minimum age.

sudo chage -m 7 basha

Set warning days.

sudo chage -W 14 basha

Lock account.

sudo passwd -l basha

Unlock account.

sudo passwd -u basha

Force password reset.

sudo passwd -e basha

docs.title: Password Complexity
docs.text:
Many Linux systems enforce password complexity using PAM modules.

Common requirements include:

  • Minimum length
  • Uppercase letters
  • Lowercase letters
  • Numbers
  • Special characters
  • Password history

We'll learn how Linux enforces these policies in the PAM Overview lesson later in this module.

docs.text:
Force password reset after onboarding.

sudo passwd -e developer

Lock a terminated employee's account.

sudo passwd -l employee1

Set a 90-day password expiration policy.

sudo chage -M 90 developer

Review password aging.

sudo chage -l developer

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Password policies are essential for:

  • Enterprise Linux servers
  • Cloud virtual machines
  • SSH access
  • Compliance standards (CIS, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS)
  • Financial systems
  • Healthcare systems
  • Government environments

Strong password policies reduce the risk of credential compromise.

docs.text:
Scenario

A user cannot log in.

Error:

Your password has expired.

Investigation:

sudo chage -l developer

sudo passwd -S developer

The password has exceeded the maximum age.

Solution:

Reset the password.

sudo passwd developer

or require a password change on the next login.

sudo passwd -e developer

The user successfully regains access after updating the password.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Enforce strong password complexity.
  • Set password expiration policies for enterprise accounts.
  • Lock accounts that are no longer in use.
  • Force password changes for newly created users.
  • Protect the /etc/shadow file.
  • Regularly audit password policies.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using weak or predictable passwords.

✅ Avoid using weak or predictable passwords when a safer approach exists.

❌ Sharing user accounts and passwords.

✅ Avoid this mistake: sharing user accounts and passwords.

❌ Allowing passwords to never expire in enterprise environments without a justified exception.

✅ Do not allow passwords to never expire in enterprise environments without a justified exception.

❌ Granting unnecessary access to the /etc/shadow file.

✅ Avoid this mistake: granting unnecessary access to the /etc/shadow file.

docs.title: Performance Troubleshooting — Diagnosing and Resolving Linux Performance Issues
Performance Troubleshooting — Diagnosing and Resolving Linux Performance Issues
docs.text: Performance Troubleshooting is the systematic process of identifying, analyzing, and resolving bottlenecks that affect the responsiveness, throughput, and stability of Linux systems. Performance issues may originate from CPU, memory, storage, networking, applications, or operating system configuration. A structured troubleshooting approach helps administrators identify the root cause quickly and minimize downtime. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should master performance troubleshooting for production environments.

Users Report Slow Response

Random Guessing

Apply Fix

A systematic process reduces troubleshooting time and improves system reliability.

docs.title: What is Performance Troubleshooting?
docs.text:
Performance troubleshooting involves identifying problems affecting:

  • CPU utilization
  • Memory usage
  • Storage performance
  • Network performance
  • Application behavior
  • System configuration
  • Resource contention

The goal is to determine the root cause, not just the visible symptoms.

docs.title: Common Performance Symptoms
docs.text:
Examples include:

  • Slow applications
  • High response times
  • Timeouts
  • High CPU usage
  • Memory exhaustion
  • Excessive disk I/O
  • Slow database queries
  • Network latency

docs.title: Performance Troubleshooting Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Problem

↓

Collect Metrics

↓

Analyze Resources

↓

Identify Bottleneck

↓

Find Root Cause

↓

Implement Fix

↓

Validate Improvement

docs.title: Step 1: Verify System Uptime
docs.text:
uptime

Example:

load average:

8.5

7.8

7.2

High load may indicate CPU contention or processes waiting on resources.

docs.title: Step 2: Check CPU Utilization
docs.text:
top

or

htop

Look for:

  • High CPU utilization
  • CPU-intensive processes
  • High I/O wait
  • Load average

docs.title: Step 3: Check Memory Usage
docs.text:
free -h

Look for:

  • Low available memory
  • High swap usage
  • Memory pressure

docs.title: Step 4: Check Disk Usage
docs.text:
df -h

Verify:

  • Available space
  • Filesystem utilization

A full filesystem can cause applications to fail.

docs.title: Step 5: Check Disk I/O
docs.text:
iostat -x

Important metrics:

  • Utilization
  • Read/write latency
  • Await time

High values may indicate storage bottlenecks.

docs.title: Step 6: Check Network Connectivity
docs.text:
Test connectivity.

ping

Trace network path.

traceroute

Test application connectivity.

curl

System logs:

journalctl

dmesg

Authentication logs:

less /var/log/auth.log

or

less /var/log/secure

docs.text:
systemctl status service-name

Example:

systemctl status nginx

docs.title: Step 10: Check Network Connections
docs.text:
ss -tuln

Verify:

  • Listening ports
  • Established connections

docs.text:
Avoid fixing only the symptom.

Example:

High CPU

↓

Why?

↓

Database Query

↓

Missing Index

↓

Root Cause

The real issue is the inefficient query, not the CPU usage itself.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users report slow response times from a production API.

Investigation:

uptime

Shows:

Load Average

↓

High

Next:

top

CPU usage appears normal, but:

I/O Wait

↓

Very High

Further investigation:

iostat -x

Shows high storage latency.

Finally:

df -h

The disk is nearly full because application logs have grown excessively.

The administrator:

  • Cleans unnecessary logs
  • Verifies logrotate
  • Frees disk space
  • Restarts the affected service

Performance returns to normal.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Follow a structured troubleshooting methodology.
  • Collect metrics before making changes.
  • Correlate CPU, memory, disk, network, and application metrics.
  • Review logs during every investigation.
  • Document findings and remediation steps.
  • Monitor systems continuously using centralized monitoring platforms.
  • Validate improvements after applying fixes.
  • Conduct post-incident reviews to prevent recurrence.

docs.title: Performance Tuning — Optimizing Linux Systems for Production
Performance Tuning — Optimizing Linux Systems for Production
docs.text: Performance Tuning is the process of analyzing, optimizing, and maintaining Linux systems to achieve maximum efficiency, stability, and scalability under production workloads. A well-tuned Linux system delivers better application performance, lower latency, improved resource utilization, and greater reliability. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Performance Engineer should understand how to monitor and optimize Linux systems.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A production web application becomes significantly slower during peak traffic.

Investigation:

top

CPU utilization remains moderate.

Next:

free -h

Memory usage is healthy.

Further analysis:

iostat

Disk utilization is consistently near 100%.

Large application log files are generating excessive disk writes.

The administrator:

  • Configures log rotation
  • Moves logs to faster storage
  • Reduces unnecessary logging
  • Monitors disk I/O after the changes

Application response times improve substantially.

Root cause:

Disk I/O Bottleneck

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This error shows up constantly in Linux work:

Permission denied

Most of the time it is not a mysterious kernel bug. It is mode (read/write/execute bits), ownership, umask, or an Access Control List (ACL) — plus occasionally special bits (sticky, SUID, SGID).

Linux file access starts with three classes: user (owner), group, and other. Each can have read (4), write (2), and execute (1). Directories need the execute bit to traverse (enter) the path. ACLs add named users or groups beyond those three classes. The sticky bit on /tmp-style folders stops users deleting each other’s files.

This is Tutorial 7 in Module 4: Users & Permissions of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series — practical Linux for Cloud and DevOps work.

Lab safety

Create lab users only on a practice VM. Requires sudo and the acl package.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Users, Groups, and sudo — you understand users, groups, and id
  • A practice Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VM with sudo
  • Install ACL tools: sudo apt-get install -y acl

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Set and verify POSIX modes with chmod and ownership with chown/chgrp
  • Explain umask and check the current umask
  • Grant a named user read access with setfacl and prove it with getfacl
  • Apply the sticky bit on a shared drop directory and explain why it matters
  • Pack allow/deny evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab07

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Permissions sit between identity (UID/GID from the previous tutorial) and the filesystem. Mode bits, ACLs, and special bits decide whether a process may read, write, traverse, or delete.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
Your team shares a deploy folder. A junior runs chmod 777 shared so “everyone can write”. Security rejects the change ticket. Auditors flag world-writable paths. Meanwhile a contractor needs read-only access but is not in the deploy group.

POSIX owner/group/other is not enough. You need groups, ACLs, and sometimes the sticky bit — not 777.

docs.title: POSIX permissions — simple words
docs.text:
Analogy: A file is a room. Owner holds the main key. Group members share a team key. Other is everyone else in the building.

Class Letter in ls -l Meaning User (u) First rwx triplet Owner Group (g) Second triplet Members of file’s group Other (o) Third triplet Everyone else Bit Value On a file On a directory r 4 Read content List names w 2 Change content Create/delete names x 1 Run as program Traverse (enter/search)

What you can say in an interview: “Without execute on every directory in the path, you get Permission denied even if the file mode looks open.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
ls -l /etc/passwd
chmod 640 secret.conf
stat -c '%A %U %G %n' secret.conf

docs.title: umask — default mask for new files
docs.text:
umask subtracts bits from the default when you create files. Common 0022 yields 644 files and 755 directories.

What you can say in an interview: “Loose umask on CI can create world-readable artefacts; tight umask can break the next job — set it deliberately and verify with stat.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
umask
touch newfile.txt
stat -c '%A %n' newfile.txt

docs.title: ACLs — named users beyond owner/group/other
docs.text:
Analogy: ACLs are guest badges with their own rules — “contractor may read, not write” — without opening the building to other.

Command Plain meaning getfacl path Show ACL + POSIX mode setfacl -m u:alice:r-- path Give alice read setfacl -d -m … Default ACL for new children

What you can say in an interview: “I use ACLs when two users need different access but should not share a primary group — and I prove with getfacl plus login-as tests.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
getfacl /etc/passwd

docs.title: Special bits — sticky, SUID, SGID
docs.text:
Bit On directories On executables Sticky (+t) Only owner/root can delete others’ files (/tmp) Rare SGID (+s on dir) New files inherit directory’s group Runs with file’s group SUID (+s on file) N/A Runs with file owner’s UID — audit carefully

What you can say in an interview: “Sticky on shared drop dirs; SGID on team project trees; SUID on random binaries is a security finding.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
ls -ld /tmp

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Fixing access with chmod 777 instead of group or ACL
  • Forgetting directory execute — path lookup fails
  • Leaving test SUID binaries on a server
  • ACLs on filesystems mounted without ACL support
  • Changing ownership of SSH keys and locking yourself out (~/.ssh should be 700/600)

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Create a shared project directory with correct group modes, grant a contractor read-only ACL, demonstrate sticky-bit delete protection, and save evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab07.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu with sudo chmod, chown, acl package Lab users Created in Task 1

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab07 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab07
set -euo pipefail
sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y acl
umask | tee umask-default.txt
whoami | tee lab-admin.txt

Expected output

acl tools available. umask-default.txt shows a value such as 0022.

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Security ticket: shared deploy folder on a practice VM — group-writable for deployers, read-only ACL for a contractor, sticky bit so users cannot delete each other’s drop files. Prove allow and deny before closing the ticket.

docs.title: Task 1 – Group, users, and POSIX modes (SGID directory)
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab07
set -euo pipefail

sudo groupadd rebash-perm || true
if ! id rebash-dev >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G rebash-perm rebash-dev
fi
if ! id rebash-contractor >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash rebash-contractor
fi
sudo usermod -aG rebash-perm rebash-dev

sudo mkdir -p /opt/rebash-perm/shared
sudo chown root:rebash-perm /opt/rebash-perm/shared
sudo chmod 2770 /opt/rebash-perm/shared

sudo -u rebash-dev bash -c 'echo deploy-artefact > /opt/rebash-perm/shared/app.txt'
sudo -u rebash-dev bash -c 'ls -l /opt/rebash-perm/shared/app.txt' | tee ls-shared-file.txt
stat -c '%A %U %G %n' /opt/rebash-perm/shared /opt/rebash-perm/shared/app.txt | tee stat-shared.txt
getent group rebash-perm | tee group-rebash-perm.txt
grep 's' stat-shared.txt

Expected output

Directory mode shows SGID (s in group execute). app.txt group is rebash-perm. rebash-dev could create the file.

docs.title: Task 2 – ACL for contractor (read allow, write deny)
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab07
set -euo pipefail

sudo setfacl -m u:rebash-contractor:rx /opt/rebash-perm/shared
sudo setfacl -m u:rebash-contractor:r /opt/rebash-perm/shared/app.txt
sudo getfacl /opt/rebash-perm/shared /opt/rebash-perm/shared/app.txt | tee getfacl-shared.txt

sudo -u rebash-contractor cat /opt/rebash-perm/shared/app.txt | tee contractor-read.txt
if sudo -u rebash-contractor bash -c 'echo hack > /opt/rebash-perm/shared/app.txt' 2>contractor-write-deny.txt; then
  echo "ERROR: contractor could write" >&2
  exit 1
fi
grep -Ei 'Permission denied|denied' contractor-write-deny.txt
grep -F 'user:rebash-contractor:r' getfacl-shared.txt

Expected output

Contractor read succeeds. Write fails with Permission denied. getfacl shows contractor entries.

docs.title: Task 3 – Sticky drop box and evidence pack
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab07
set -euo pipefail

sudo mkdir -p /opt/rebash-perm/drop
sudo chown root:rebash-perm /opt/rebash-perm/drop
sudo chmod 1770 /opt/rebash-perm/drop

sudo -u rebash-dev bash -c 'echo from-dev > /opt/rebash-perm/drop/dev.txt'
if ! id rebash-dev2 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G rebash-perm rebash-dev2
fi
sudo -u rebash-dev2 bash -c 'echo from-dev2 > /opt/rebash-perm/drop/dev2.txt'

if sudo -u rebash-dev2 rm -f /opt/rebash-perm/drop/dev.txt 2>sticky-deny.txt; then
  echo "ERROR: sticky bit did not block delete" >&2
  exit 1
fi
grep -Ei 'Permission denied|denied|Operation not permitted' sticky-deny.txt
ls -ld /opt/rebash-perm/drop | tee ls-drop.txt
grep -E 't|T' ls-drop.txt

tar -czf permissions-evidence.tgz \
  lab-admin.txt umask-default.txt \
  ls-shared-file.txt stat-shared.txt group-rebash-perm.txt \
  getfacl-shared.txt contractor-read.txt contractor-write-deny.txt \
  sticky-deny.txt ls-drop.txt
ls -l permissions-evidence.tgz | tee evidence-ls.txt
test -s permissions-evidence.tgz

Expected output

Sticky delete of another user’s file is denied. ls-drop.txt shows t in mode. Archive exists.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• /opt/rebash-perm/shared is mode 2770 (or drwxrws---)
  • getfacl shows contractor read on the file
  • Contractor write fails; sticky delete fails
  • permissions-evidence.tgz exists under ~/rebash-linux/lab07

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix setfacl: command not found acl package missing sudo apt-get install -y acl Operation not supported FS without ACL Use ext4/xfs; check mount options Contractor cannot enter dir Missing x on directory ACL setfacl -m u:user:rx on directory Sticky test succeeds Mode not sticky chmod 1770 / chmod +t; re-check

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text:
Add a default ACL so new files grant contractor read automatically:

Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab07
sudo setfacl -d -m u:rebash-contractor:r /opt/rebash-perm/shared
sudo -u rebash-dev bash -c 'echo new-file > /opt/rebash-perm/shared/new.txt'
sudo getfacl /opt/rebash-perm/shared/new.txt | tee default-acl-proof.txt
grep 'user:rebash-contractor:r' default-acl-proof.txt

Expected output

New file inherits contractor read ACL without manual setfacl on each file.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Applied SGID group-shared directory modes
  • Used ACLs for a named user without widening “other”
  • Proved sticky-bit delete protection
  • Saved permission evidence for a change ticket

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab07
set -euo pipefail
sudo rm -rf /opt/rebash-perm
sudo userdel -r rebash-dev 2>/dev/null || true
sudo userdel -r rebash-dev2 2>/dev/null || true
sudo userdel -r rebash-contractor 2>/dev/null || true
sudo groupdel rebash-perm 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Lab completed under ~/rebash-linux/lab07
  • Can explain POSIX mode vs ACL vs sticky bit
  • Know why chmod 777 fails security review
  • Can list when SUID on files is a finding

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. ls -l + stat + id — who is trying what?
  2. namei -l path — which directory denies traverse?
  3. Prefer group (2770) or ACL over chmod o+rwx
  4. getfacl after every ACL change — prove named entries
  5. Allow + deny tests as the real user — not only as root

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Never make secrets world-readable (o+r on keys)
  • Keep ~/.ssh at 700 and private keys at 600
  • Audit unexpected SUID/SGID binaries on hardened images
  • ACLs can hide access — include getfacl in reviews
  • Sticky bit reduces cross-user deletion in shared directories

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Fixing access with chmod 777

✅ World-writable paths fail audits. Fix: group (2770) or named ACL.

❌ Forgetting directory execute.

✅ Path lookup fails even when file mode looks open. Fix: x on every directory in the path.

❌ Assuming ACL works on every mount.

✅ Some network mounts ignore ACLs. Fix: verify with getfacl after mount.

❌ Casual SUID binaries.

✅ Bugs become privilege escalation. Fix: capabilities, sudo allow-lists, or narrow root helpers.

docs.title: ping — Testing Network Connectivity in Linux
ping — Testing Network Connectivity in Linux
docs.text: The ping command is one of the most commonly used network troubleshooting tools in Linux. It uses the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) to test connectivity between devices, measure network latency, and detect packet loss. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Network Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should know how to use ping effectively.

docs.title: Why Learn ping?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • A server cannot access the Internet.
  • SSH is not working.
  • A web application cannot reach its database.
  • Kubernetes nodes cannot communicate.

The first troubleshooting tool most administrators use is:

ping

docs.title: What is ping?
docs.text:
ping is a command-line utility that checks whether a remote host is reachable over an IP network.

It works by sending ICMP Echo Request packets to a destination and waiting for ICMP Echo Reply packets.

docs.title: How ping Works
docs.text:
Source Computer
       │
       ▼
ICMP Echo Request
       │
       ▼
Destination Host
       │
       ▼
ICMP Echo Reply
       │
       ▼
Source Computer

If replies are received, the destination is reachable.

docs.title: What is ICMP?
docs.text:
ICMP stands for:

Internet Control Message Protocol

It is used for:

  • Connectivity testing
  • Error reporting
  • Network diagnostics
  • Route discovery

Unlike TCP and UDP, ICMP does not use port numbers.

docs.title: Basic ping Command
docs.text:
Ping a hostname.

ping google.com

Ping an IP address.

ping 8.8.8.8

Example output:

64 bytes from 8.8.8.8:
icmp_seq=1
ttl=117
time=18.5 ms

docs.title: Understanding the Output
docs.text:
Example:

64 bytes from 8.8.8.8:
icmp_seq=1 ttl=117 time=18.5 ms

Meaning:

Field Description 64 bytes Size of the reply icmp_seq Sequence number ttl Time To Live value time Round-trip latency

docs.title: Stop ping
docs.text:
By default, Linux continues sending packets until interrupted.

Stop the command using:

Ctrl + C

Summary example:

4 packets transmitted

4 received

0% packet loss

docs.title: Send a Specific Number of Packets
docs.text:
Send four requests.

ping -c 4 google.com

docs.title: Set Time Interval
docs.text:
Send one request every two seconds.

ping -i 2 google.com

docs.title: Set Packet Size
docs.text:
Send a 1000-byte packet.

ping -s 1000 google.com

docs.title: Continuous Monitoring
docs.text:
Run continuously until stopped.

ping google.com

Press:

Ctrl + C

to stop.

docs.title: Ping IPv6
docs.text:
ping6 ipv6.google.com

or

ping -6 ipv6.google.com

docs.title: Ping Localhost
docs.text:
ping 127.0.0.1

or

ping localhost

Tests the local TCP/IP stack without using the physical network.

docs.text:
Successful connection.

25% packet loss

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
ping is commonly used for:

  • Network troubleshooting
  • Cloud infrastructure
  • Kubernetes clusters
  • Virtual machines
  • VPN testing
  • Load balancer verification
  • Firewall testing
  • Monitoring network latency

Some production systems intentionally block ICMP traffic for security reasons, so a failed ping does not always mean the service is unavailable.

docs.text:

docs.title: Task 2

Replace <gateway-ip> with your gateway address.

docs.text:

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Test IPv6 connectivity (if available).

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:

Review:

  • Packet loss
  • Minimum latency
  • Average latency
  • Maximum latency

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A Linux web server cannot connect to a database.

Investigation:

Test the local network stack.

ping -c 4 localhost

Test the gateway.

ping -c 4 192.168.1.1

Test the database server.

ping -c 4 192.168.1.50

The database server does not respond.

Check:

  • Routing
  • Firewall rules
  • Database server status
  • Security groups (cloud environments)

After correcting the network configuration, the server responds successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Test connectivity step by step (localhost → gateway → remote host).
  • Use -c when scripting or automating tests.
  • Verify both IP address and hostname connectivity.
  • Remember that some servers intentionally block ICMP.
  • Combine ping with other tools such as traceroute, ss, and curl for complete network troubleshooting.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming a failed ping always means the server is offline.

✅ Verify a failed ping always means the server is offline instead of assuming it.

❌ Forgetting that firewalls may block ICMP traffic.

✅ Remember to that firewalls may block ICMP traffic.

❌ Testing only hostnames without verifying DNS.

✅ Avoid this mistake: testing only hostnames without verifying DNS.

❌ Ignoring packet loss and latency values.

✅ Always review packet loss and latency values.

ping is one of the simplest yet most powerful Linux networking tools. It provides a quick way to verify connectivity, measure latency, and identify basic network issues. Combined with other networking utilities, it forms the foundation of effective network troubleshooting.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• ping uses ICMP Echo Request and Echo Reply messages.
  • It helps verify whether a host is reachable.
  • Packet loss indicates communication problems.
  • Latency measures the time required for packets to travel to the destination and back.
  • A failed ping does not always mean the destination service is unavailable.
  • Use ping together with other networking tools for comprehensive troubleshooting.

docs.title: Pipes (|) in Linux
docs.text: Pipes are one of the most powerful features of Linux. They allow you to connect multiple commands together, where the output of one command becomes the input of another. Instead of creating temporary files, you can build efficient command pipelines for filtering, searching, analyzing, and processing data.

docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 Lessons 1–9

docs.title: Why Learn Pipes?
docs.text:
Suppose you have 5,000 running processes.

You don't want to see all of them.

Instead, you only want to find:

  • Docker
  • Kubernetes
  • NGINX
  • SSH

Without pipes, this becomes difficult.

With pipes:

ps -ef | grep nginx

One command.

Instant results.

docs.title: What is a Pipe?
docs.text:
A pipe (|) sends the Standard Output (stdout) of one command directly to the Standard Input (stdin) of another command.

Instead of displaying output on the screen, Linux transfers it directly between commands.

docs.title: How Pipes Work
docs.text:
Command 1

↓

Standard Output

↓

Pipe (|)

↓

Standard Input

↓

Command 2

↓

Output

Example:

ls | wc -l

Workflow:

List Files

↓

Pipe

↓

Count Files

↓

Display Count

docs.title: Basic Pipe Example
docs.text:
Without pipe:

ls

Displays:

Documents

Downloads

Pictures

Videos

With pipe:

ls | wc -l

Output:

4

docs.title: Pipe with grep
docs.text:
Find running SSH processes.

ps -ef | grep ssh

Pipeline:

ps -ef

↓

grep ssh

↓

Matching Processes

docs.title: Pipe with head
docs.text:
Display only the first five files.

ls -l | head -5

docs.title: Pipe with tail
docs.text:
Display the last five files.

docs.title: Multiple Pipes
docs.text:
Linux allows unlimited pipelines.

Example:

cat users.txt | sort | uniq

Workflow:

Read File

↓

Sort

↓

Remove Duplicates

↓

Display Result

docs.title: Count Matching Results
docs.text:
Example:

cat users.txt | grep admin | wc -l

Pipeline:

Read File

↓

Find "admin"

↓

Count Matches

↓

Display Total

docs.title: Sort Output
docs.text:
Example:

Output:

Bob

Charlie

David

docs.title: Remove Duplicate Entries
docs.text:

Example:

docs.title: Pipe with tee

Display output while saving it.

Output:

Documents

Downloads

Pictures

The same output is saved to:

docs.title: Pipe with less

Benefits:

  • Scroll
  • Search

Ideal for production logs.

docs.text:
Suppose you have:

file1.txt

file2.txt

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

An NGINX server is experiencing intermittent failures.

Tasks:

  1. Find the NGINX process.
  2. Display only error logs.
  3. Count the number of error entries.
  4. Save filtered errors to a file.
  5. Display and save the output simultaneously.

Solutions:

ps -ef | grep nginx

journalctl | grep ERROR

journalctl | grep ERROR | wc -l

journalctl | grep ERROR > errors.log

journalctl | grep ERROR | tee errors.log

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use pipes instead of temporary files whenever possible.
  • Keep pipelines readable.
  • Test each command individually before combining them.
  • Use tee when you need to both save and view output.
  • Filter data early to improve performance.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Creating unnecessary temporary files.

✅ Instead of:

cat files.txt

Use:

ls | less

❌ Building very long pipelines without testing.

✅ Test each stage before combining them.

❌ Forgetting that pipes transfer only stdout.

✅ If you also need stderr, redirect it appropriately.
