docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When a service “hangs” or a host runs hot, you need to see which processes are running, what they use, and how to stop them safely.

Every command you run — ls, nginx, a Python script — becomes a process: a running programme with an ID number, a parent, and resource use (CPU, memory). On a busy cloud virtual machine (VM), knowing how to see, stop, and prioritise processes is basic hygiene before you touch systemd services.

Plain problem: A deploy script hangs. CPU hits 100%. Your mentor asks “what is eating the CPU, and can you stop it cleanly?” This tutorial teaches you to answer with ps, signals, and job control — not by rebooting the server first.

This is Tutorial 9 in Module 6: Process Management of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series — practical Linux for Cloud and DevOps work.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Text Processing with grep, sed, and awk — comfortable with pipes and basic commands
  • A practice Linux host: Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VM with a normal user account
  • Optional: htop (sudo apt install htop) — not required

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain PID, parent process, signals, and niceness in plain words
  • Inspect processes with ps and read useful columns
  • Start background work, use job control, and stop processes cleanly
  • Send TERM before KILL and explain why that matters
  • Complete the lab under ~/rebash-linux/lab09 with evidence files
  • Answer common fresher interview questions on process management

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: User commands and long-running services become processes scheduled by the kernel. Operators observe them, send signals, adjust priority, or hand durable work to systemd (next tutorial).

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
You SSH into a build agent. The load average is high. Something is spinning. If you kill -9 everything, you may corrupt a half-written file or leave a lock. If you do nothing, the whole VM becomes unusable and costs money.

You need to identify the process, ask it politely to stop, and only force if it ignores you.

docs.title: What a process is (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: A process is a worker in a factory. Each worker has a badge number (PID — Process ID), a manager (PPID — parent PID), a desk full of open files, and a CPU time sheet.

Term Plain meaning PID Unique ID for this running instance PPID PID of the process that started this one State Running (R), sleeping (S), zombie (Z), stopped (T) Signal A short message to a process (stop, continue, terminate) Niceness CPU priority hint (−20 highest to +19 lowest; default 0)

What you can say in an interview: “A process is a running programme instance with a PID; I inspect with ps, stop with signals, and use systemd for supervised services in production.”

docs.title: Inspecting processes
docs.text:
Tiny example:

Terminal
ps -p $$ -o pid,ppid,user,stat,cmd    # your current shell
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,pcpu,pmem,cmd --sort=-pcpu | head
pgrep -a bash
Tool Role ps Snapshot of processes top / htop Live updating view pgrep / pidof Find PID by name

Interview line: “I sort ps by %CPU or %MEM to find runaway processes before I kill anything.”

docs.title: Signals — polite stop vs force
docs.text:
Analogy: TERM (15) is tapping someone on the shoulder — “please finish up and leave.” KILL (9) is pulling the fire alarm — the process cannot ignore it and may leave a mess.

Signal Number Meaning Use when TERM 15 Polite terminate First choice KILL 9 Force kill Process ignored TERM HUP 1 Hangup (reload configs in some daemons) After config change STOP / CONT 19 / 18 Pause / resume Debugging (careful) Terminal
kill -TERM 1234          # same as kill 1234
kill -KILL 1234          # force — last resort
pkill -TERM nginx

Interview line: “I always try SIGTERM before SIGKILL so the app can flush buffers and release locks.”

docs.title: Job control — foreground and background
docs.text:
When you start a command in your terminal, it is usually foreground (you wait for it). Append & to run in background. Ctrl-Z suspends; bg resumes in background; fg brings back to foreground.

Terminal
sleep 300 &
jobs
fg %1

Interview line: “Job control is for my shell session; production services belong in systemd, not nohup in tmux forever.”

docs.title: nice and renice — CPU priority
docs.text:
Analogy: Niceness is letting others go first in a queue. Higher niceness (+19) means “I am not urgent.” Lower (−20) means “I am important” — usually needs root.

Terminal
nice -n 10 stress-ng --cpu 1 --timeout 30s
renice -n 5 -p 1234

docs.title: nohup vs systemd
docs.text: nohup keeps a command running after you log out — fine for ad-hoc lab work. Production long-running apps should be systemd services with restart policy, logging, and boot persistence (next tutorial).

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Jumping to kill -9 immediately — can corrupt data
  • Killing PID 1 or random systemd children — breaks the system
  • Confusing %CPU on top (can exceed 100% on multi-core) with “number of cores used”
  • Leaving zombie processes — usually fix the parent that is not reaping children

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Start lab processes, inspect them with ps, adjust niceness, stop them with TERM, and prove each step with evidence files.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Linux practice host Ubuntu preferred stress-ng optional sudo apt install stress-ng — lab works without it using sleep Normal user Most tasks need no sudo

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab09 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab09

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: A CI job left a sleep process running on a shared agent. It is not harmful, but it holds a job slot. You must find its PID, confirm it is yours, stop it cleanly, and attach command output to the ticket.

docs.title: Task 1 – Start background work and capture PID
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab09
sleep 600 &
echo $! | tee sleeper.pid
ps -p "$(cat sleeper.pid)" -o pid,ppid,user,stat,cmd | tee sleeper-ps.txt
test -s sleeper.pid && test -s sleeper-ps.txt

Expected output

sleeper.pid contains one number. sleeper-ps.txt shows the sleep 600 line with state S (sleeping).

docs.title: Task 2 – Job control and second process
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab09
( while true; do echo tick >> ticker.log; sleep 2; done ) &
echo $! | tee ticker.pid
jobs > jobs.txt
sleep 3
wc -l ticker.log | tee ticker-lines.txt
test -s ticker.pid

Expected output

jobs.txt lists at least one running job. ticker.log grows (line count ≥ 1 after a few seconds).

docs.title: Task 3 – Inspect and renice
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab09
ps -eo pid,nice,cmd | grep -E 'sleep 600|ticker' | grep -v grep | tee nice-before.txt
renice -n 10 -p "$(cat sleeper.pid)" 2>/dev/null | tee renice-out.txt || echo "renice may need same user — OK on lab VM"
ps -p "$(cat sleeper.pid)" -o pid,nice,cmd | tee nice-after.txt
grep -q 'sleep 600' nice-after.txt

Expected output

nice-after.txt shows the sleeper with niceness 10 (or renice message if policy blocks it).

docs.title: Task 4 – Stop cleanly with TERM, then verify
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab09
kill -TERM "$(cat ticker.pid)"
sleep 1
ps -p "$(cat ticker.pid)" >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "still running" || echo "ticker stopped" | tee ticker-stop.txt
kill -TERM "$(cat sleeper.pid)"
sleep 1
ps -p "$(cat sleeper.pid)" >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "still running" || echo "sleeper stopped" | tee sleeper-stop.txt
grep -q 'stopped' ticker-stop.txt sleeper-stop.txt
echo "lab09 process lifecycle OK" | tee evidence.txt

Expected output

Both ticker-stop.txt and sleeper-stop.txt report stopped. evidence.txt confirms completion.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• You captured PIDs before killing processes
  • You used TERM, not KILL, first
  • Evidence files exist under ~/rebash-linux/lab09
  • You can explain zombie vs stopped vs sleeping

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix kill: (1234) - No such process Already exited Re-run start step; check ps immediately Operation not permitted on renice Not owner / policy Normal on shared systems; note in ticket Job not in jobs Started outside current shell Use ps and PID file instead ticker.log empty Loop not started Check ticker.pid; ps -p $(cat ticker.pid)

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text:
Create stop-if-running.sh that reads a PID file and sends TERM, waiting up to 5 seconds before reporting status.

Create stop-if-running.sh:

stop-if-running.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
pidfile="${1:?usage: stop-if-running.sh pidfile}"
pid="$(cat "$pidfile")"
if ps -p "$pid" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  kill -TERM "$pid"
  for _ in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    ps -p "$pid" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "stopped $pid"; exit 0; }
    sleep 1
  done
  echo "still running after 5s: $pid"
  exit 1
else
  echo "not running: $pid"
fi
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab09
chmod +x stop-if-running.sh
sleep 120 & echo $! > challenge.pid
./stop-if-running.sh challenge.pid | tee challenge-out.txt
grep -q 'stopped' challenge-out.txt

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• You started and tracked background processes with PIDs
  • You stopped processes with SIGTERM and verified exit
  • You have interview-ready evidence of process hygiene

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab09
pkill -TERM -f 'sleep 600' 2>/dev/null || true
pkill -TERM -f 'ticker.log' 2>/dev/null || true
rm -f challenge.pid
# Keep evidence files for revision

docs.text:

  • Can explain TERM vs KILL to a classmate
  • Ready for systemd services next

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. echo $! — PID of last background job; save it immediately.
  2. ps -p PID -o … — narrow view of one process; safer than grepping all of ps.
  3. kill -TERM first — production habit before -9.
  4. jobs vs ps — jobs are shell-local; ps is system-wide.
  5. Move long-running work to systemd — next tutorial; do not rely on nohup in prod.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Do not kill processes you do not own on shared servers without approval.
  • Runaway processes as root can be symptoms of compromise — investigate before killing blindly.
  • pkill -f matches full command line — double-check pattern to avoid collateral kills.
  • Limit who can renice negative values — usually root-only.
  • Document process stops in change tickets on production hosts.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ kill -9 as first move.

✅ Forces immediate death; databases and queues may corrupt. Fix: kill -TERM, wait, then -KILL if needed.

❌ Killing the wrong PID.

✅ Numbers are reused. Fix: always ps -p PID -o cmd= immediately before kill.

❌ Zombie hoard.

✅ Zombies (Z) are dead children waiting for parent to reap. Fix: restart or fix the parent process, not the zombie.

❌ nohup for production services.

✅ No restart policy, no structured logging. Fix: systemd unit with Restart= and journalctl.

Experienced Linux administrators follow consistent best practices to minimize operational risks, simplify troubleshooting, and ensure production environments remain stable over time. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Infrastructure Engineer should adopt these practices as part of daily operations.

Production Checklist — Preparing Linux Systems for Production
docs.text: A Production Checklist is a structured verification process that ensures a Linux system is secure, reliable, performant, maintainable, and ready to run critical workloads. Before deploying applications into production, administrators should verify system configuration, security, networking, storage, monitoring, backups, and operational readiness. Following a standardized checklist minimizes risks, prevents outages, and improves system stability. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should use a production checklist before deploying or handing over a Linux server.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Moving from “it works on my VM” to production raises two questions: Is it safe? and Will it stay fast under load? You need sensible baselines for hardening and performance — not kernel-developer depth on day one.

Plain problem: A server accepts connections from everywhere, time drifts breaking TLS, one runaway process consumes all file descriptors, and nobody measured normal CPU before launch day.

This tutorial covers lab-scoped hardening (sysctl, limits) and performance baselines (time sync, listening ports audit) with proof under ~/rebash-linux/lab24.

This is Tutorial 16a in Module 16: Production Linux of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain hardening vs performance baselines in plain language
  • Apply a sysctl drop-in safely and verify values
  • Set limits for open files in a lab drop-in
  • Verify time sync with chrony/timedatectl
  • Audit listening ports and failed units
  • Answer fresher interview questions on production Linux baselines

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Hardening reduces attack surface and resource exhaustion risk. Performance baselines measure normal behaviour so alerts mean something. Both use drop-in config files and verification commands — not one-off magic tweaks.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text: Launch day: API TLS fails because clock was five minutes wrong. Separate incident: legacy service opens thousands of sockets — hits default nofile limit — partial outage. Baselines prevent both classes of surprise.

docs.title: Hardening (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: Hardening is locking side doors, not just the front — fewer ways in, fewer ways one guest can wreck the building.

Common areas:

Area Tool Example Kernel network knobs sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward, SYN cookies Process limits limits.conf / systemd Max open files, processes Time chrony Accurate clock for TLS/logs Exposure audit ss, systemctl What listens; what failed

Interview line: “I apply sysctl via drop-ins, verify with sysctl, sync time with chrony, and audit listening ports after deploy.”

docs.title: sysctl
docs.text:
Live values in /proc/sys/. Persistent drop-ins under /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf.

Terminal
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies

Lab example (syncookies help under SYN flood — teach concept, do not over-tune on laptop):

net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1

Always: sudo sysctl --system after adding drop-in.

docs.title: limits (ulimit / PAM / systemd)
docs.text:
Analogy: limits cap how many files or processes one user may have — stops one leak from eating the host.

/etc/security/limits.d/ drop-ins for login sessions; systemd units can set LimitNOFILE=.

docs.title: Performance baselines
docs.text:
Not the same as hardening — you measure normal:

  • vmstat / iostat idle and util (prior tutorial)
  • Peak connection counts
  • Application latency under expected load

Without baseline, alerts are guesses.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Copying random sysctl lists from blogs without understanding
  • Setting limits so low legitimate apps fail
  • Disabling NTP “because VM clock looks fine”
  • Hardening without monitoring — brittle unknown state

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Add lab sysctl and limits drop-ins, verify time sync, audit listeners, break sysctl with a typo, fix, prove — evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab24.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM chrony or systemd-timesyncd sudo For /etc/sysctl.d, limits.d

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab24 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab24
timedatectl status | tee time-before.txt

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Platform ticket: “Baseline new app server — syncookies on, nofile raised for app user, time synced, document listeners.” You implement lab-scoped drop-ins and an audit snapshot.

docs.title: Task 1 – sysctl drop-in and verify
docs.text:
Create 99-rebash-lab24.conf:

99-rebash-lab24.conf
# REBASH lab24 — teaching drop-in only
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab24
sudo cp 99-rebash-lab24.conf /etc/sysctl.d/99-rebash-lab24.conf
sudo sysctl --system 2>&1 | tee sysctl-apply.txt
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies | tee syncookies-value.txt
grep -q '= 1' syncookies-value.txt

Expected output

syncookies-value.txt shows net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1.

docs.title: Task 2 – limits drop-in and port audit
docs.text:
Create 99-rebash-lab24.conf (limits):

99-rebash-lab24-limits.conf
# REBASH lab24 — raised open files for lab user
* soft nofile 8192
* hard nofile 8192
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab24
sudo cp 99-rebash-lab24-limits.conf /etc/security/limits.d/99-rebash-lab24.conf
ulimit -n | tee ulimit-before-login.txt
ss -tlnp | tee listening-ports.txt
systemctl --failed --no-pager | tee failed-units.txt
timedatectl status | tee time-after.txt
grep -q 'synchronized: yes' time-after.txt || grep -q 'System clock synchronized: yes' time-after.txt

Expected output

Listening ports listed; time sync shows synchronized (may need systemd-timesyncd/chrony active).

docs.title: Task 3 – Break sysctl syntax, fix, prove
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab24
echo 'not.a.real.key = banana' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-rebash-broken.conf >/dev/null
sudo sysctl --system 2>&1 | tee sysctl-broken.txt || true
grep -qi 'error\|unknown\|invalid' sysctl-broken.txt || echo "sysctl reported bad key" | tee sysctl-broken.txt
sudo rm -f /etc/sysctl.d/99-rebash-broken.conf
sudo sysctl --system 2>&1 | tee sysctl-fixed.txt
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies | tee syncookies-after-fix.txt
echo "lab24 production baseline OK" | tee evidence.txt

Expected output

Bad key produces sysctl warning/error; after removal, apply succeeds and syncookies still 1.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• sysctl drop-in applied and verified
  • limits drop-in installed (new login may be needed for full effect)
  • Time sync and listening port audit saved
  • Break/fix sysctl demonstrated

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix sysctl not applied Typo in path Files must end .conf in /etc/sysctl.d/ ulimit unchanged Existing session Log out/in or su - user Time not synced NTP disabled sudo systemctl enable --now systemd-timesyncd ss permission denied Needs root for process names Use sudo ss -tlnp

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text: Save vmstat 1 3 baseline to vmstat-baseline.txt for future comparison (links to monitoring tutorial).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• You applied kernel and limits drop-ins safely
  • You audited exposure and time sync
  • You validated config before assuming success

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
sudo rm -f /etc/sysctl.d/99-rebash-lab24.conf /etc/security/limits.d/99-rebash-lab24.conf
sudo sysctl --system

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab24
  • Can explain one sysctl and one limit knob
  • Ready for backup and DR next

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. /etc/sysctl.d/ drop-ins — modular kernel tuning; easier rollback than one giant file.
  2. sysctl --system — load all drop-ins; shows errors on bad keys.
  3. limits.d — PAM applies on new sessions; document for app users.
  4. ss -tlnp — production exposure audit after every deploy.
  5. timedatectl — TLS and distributed logs need correct time.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• sysctl changes affect whole host — test on staging; document rollback.
  • Raising limits increases DoS surface if one user compromised — scope per service user.
  • Remove unused listeners; firewall complements ss audit.
  • Automate baseline checks in CI for golden images.
  • Combine with SSH and MAC layers from prior security tutorials.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Random sysctl paste.

✅ Understand each knob; wrong TCP settings hurt latency and debuggability.

❌ Ignoring time sync.

✅ Certificate validation and log correlation break with clock skew.

❌ No baseline before tuning.

✅ Measure first; tune second; measure again.

docs.title: The ps Command — Viewing and Analyzing Processes in Linux
The ps Command — Viewing and Analyzing Processes in Linux
docs.text: The ps (Process Status) command is one of the most important Linux utilities for viewing running processes. It provides detailed information about process IDs (PIDs), users, CPU usage, memory consumption, parent-child relationships, process states, and running commands. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, SRE, and Cloud Architect uses ps daily for troubleshooting and system monitoring.

docs.title: Why Learn the ps Command?
docs.text:
Imagine a production application stops responding.

Questions:

  • Is the application running?
  • What is its PID?
  • Who owns the process?
  • How much CPU is it using?
  • Is it stuck?

The first command most Linux administrators use is:

ps

docs.title: What is ps?
docs.text:
ps stands for:

Process Status

It displays information about running processes.

Unlike top, ps shows a snapshot of the processes at the moment you execute the command.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
ps

Example:

PID TTY          TIME CMD

3241 pts/0 00:00:00 bash

3410 pts/0 00:00:00 ps

By default, it displays processes associated with the current terminal.

docs.title: Display All Processes
docs.text:
ps -e

or

ps -A

Example:

PID TTY TIME CMD

1 ? 00:00:03 systemd

645 ? 00:00:01 sshd

1200 ? 00:00:04 nginx

docs.title: Full Process List
docs.text:
ps -ef

Example:

UID PID PPID C STIME TTY TIME CMD

root 1 0 0 systemd

root 642 1 0 sshd

basha 2501 642 0 bash

docs.title: BSD Style Output
docs.text:
Linux also supports BSD-style options.

ps aux

Example:

USER PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND

Unlike ps -ef, BSD-style options omit the leading hyphen.

docs.title: Understanding ps -ef Output
docs.text: Column Description UID Process owner PID Process ID PPID Parent Process ID C CPU scheduling value STIME Start time TTY Terminal TIME CPU time used CMD Command

docs.title: Display Process Tree
docs.text:
ps -ejH

or

pstree

Example:

systemd

└── sshd

     └── bash

          └── python

docs.title: Display Process State
docs.text:
ps -eo pid,state,comm

Example:

PID S COMMAND

1 S systemd

245 R bash

300 S sshd

docs.title: Display Specific Process
docs.text:
Using a PID.

ps -p 1

Example:

PID COMMAND

1 systemd

Multiple PIDs.

ps -p 1,100,500

docs.title: Display Processes by User
docs.text:
ps -u basha

Example:

PID CMD

321 bash

550 python

Display all processes owned by root.

ps -U root

docs.title: Filter Using grep
docs.text:
Example:

ps -ef | grep nginx

Find Docker.

ps -ef | grep docker

Find Java.

ps -ef | grep java

docs.title: Custom Output
docs.text:
Show PID, user, and command.

ps -eo pid,user,comm

Show CPU and memory usage.

ps -eo pid,%cpu,%mem,comm

Show elapsed running time.

ps -eo pid,etime,comm

docs.title: Sort Processes
docs.text:
Sort by CPU.

ps -eo pid,%cpu,comm --sort=-%cpu

Sort by memory.

ps -eo pid,%mem,comm --sort=-%mem

Display the top 10 CPU consumers.

ps -eo pid,%cpu,comm --sort=-%cpu | head

docs.title: View Parent-Child Relationship
docs.text:
ps -f

Observe:

PID

PPID

This helps identify process hierarchies.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Basic process list.

ps

All processes.

ps -e

Detailed view.

ps -ef

BSD format.

ps aux

Single process.

ps -p PID

By user.

ps -u username

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:

Check Kubernetes.

ps -ef | grep kubelet

Check Docker.

ps -ef | grep docker

Check PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
The ps command is used extensively for:

  • Troubleshooting applications
  • Identifying running services
  • Monitoring process ownership
  • Finding PIDs
  • Preparing to terminate processes
  • Capacity planning
  • Performance analysis

It is one of the first commands used during production incident investigations.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users report that the company web application is unavailable.

Investigation:

ps -ef | grep nginx

ps -ef | grep java

ps -ef | grep node

Findings:

  • NGINX is running.
  • The backend Java application is missing.

Next steps:

  • Review application logs.
  • Restart the backend service if appropriate.
  • Investigate why the process terminated unexpectedly.

The ps command quickly confirms whether critical services are running before deeper troubleshooting begins.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use ps -ef for detailed process information.
  • Use grep to locate specific processes.
  • Verify the process owner before taking action.
  • Use custom output (ps -eo) when creating reports.
  • Combine ps with other monitoring tools such as top and systemctl for comprehensive diagnostics.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming a service is running without verifying it.

✅ Verify a service is running without verifying it instead of assuming it.

❌ Killing the wrong process because the PID was not checked carefully.

✅ Avoid this mistake: killing the wrong process because the PID was not checked carefully.

❌ Forgetting that ps displays a snapshot, not a live view.

✅ Use top or htop for real-time monitoring.

docs.title: Disk Quotas — Controlling Storage Usage in Linux
Disk Quotas — Controlling Storage Usage in Linux
docs.text: Disk Quotas allow Linux administrators to control and limit the amount of disk space and the number of files (inodes) that users or groups can consume on a filesystem. Quotas help prevent a single user or application from exhausting available storage, ensuring fair resource allocation and maintaining system stability. Disk quotas are widely used on multi-user systems, universities, enterprise servers, shared hosting platforms, and cloud environments.

docs.title: Why Learn Disk Quotas?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • One user fills an entire shared server with log files.
  • A developer accidentally uploads hundreds of gigabytes of data.
  • A web hosting customer consumes all available storage.
  • A backup application generates excessive files.

Without quotas:

One User

↓

Consumes All Disk Space

↓

Other Applications Fail

With quotas:

User Reaches Limit

↓

Write Operation Denied

↓

System Continues Operating

docs.title: What are Disk Quotas?
docs.text:
Disk quotas allow administrators to limit:

  • Disk space usage
  • Number of files (inodes)

Quotas can be applied to:

  • Individual users
  • Groups

docs.title: Why Use Quotas?
docs.text:
Quotas help:

  • Prevent storage exhaustion
  • Ensure fair resource allocation
  • Protect shared servers
  • Improve storage management
  • Reduce operational risks

docs.title: Types of Quotas
docs.text:
Linux supports:

  • User Quotas
  • Group Quotas

Example:

Filesystem

↓

User Quotas

↓

Group Quotas

docs.title: Soft Limit
docs.text:
A soft limit is a warning threshold.

Example:

Limit

100 GB

Current Usage

102 GB

The user can temporarily exceed the limit during the configured grace period.

docs.title: Hard Limit
docs.text:
A hard limit is an absolute maximum.

Example:

Hard Limit

110 GB

Once reached:

Write Operation

↓

Denied

docs.title: Grace Period
docs.text:
The grace period allows users to temporarily exceed the soft limit.

Example:

Soft Limit

100 GB

↓

Grace Period

7 Days

↓

Hard Enforcement

After the grace period expires, the soft limit is enforced as if it were a hard limit until usage is reduced.

docs.title: Quota Workflow
docs.text:
User Writes File

↓

Quota Check

↓

Below Limit

↓

File Created

OR

Hard Limit Reached

↓

Operation Denied

docs.title: Enable Quotas
docs.text:
Edit:

/etc/fstab

Example:

UUID=abcd-1234

/home

ext4

defaults,usrquota,grpquota

0

2

Options:

  • usrquota
  • grpquota

docs.title: Remount the Filesystem
docs.text: sudo mount -o remount /home

docs.title: Create Quota Database
docs.text:

Options:

Option Meaning -c Create quota files -u User quotas -g Group quotas

docs.text:

Verify:

sudo quotaon -p /home

docs.title: Configure User Quota
docs.text:

Example:

Soft

100000

Hard

120000

docs.text:
Copy quota settings from one user to another.

sudo edquota -p user1 user2

RAID Concepts — Improving Storage Performance and Reliability
docs.text: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) is a storage technology that combines multiple physical disks into a single logical storage unit to improve performance, availability, or fault tolerance. RAID is widely used in enterprise servers, databases, virtualization platforms, storage appliances, and cloud infrastructure to protect data against disk failures while increasing storage performance.

Imagine:

  • A production database server loses a disk.
  • A web server handles thousands of requests every second.
  • A storage server requires maximum uptime.
  • A backup server needs protection against hardware failure.

Without RAID:

Single Disk Failure

↓

Complete Data Loss

With RAID:

Disk Failure

↓

System Continues Running

docs.title: What is RAID?
docs.text:
RAID stands for:

Redundant Array of Independent Disks

RAID combines multiple disks into a single logical storage device.

Benefits include:

  • Improved performance
  • Higher availability
  • Fault tolerance
  • Increased storage capacity (depending on RAID level)

docs.title: Why Use RAID?
docs.text:
RAID helps to:

  • Protect against disk failures
  • Improve read performance
  • Improve write performance (certain RAID levels)
  • Increase storage capacity
  • Minimize downtime

docs.title: How RAID Works
docs.text:
Instead of storing data on one disk:

Application

↓

Disk

RAID distributes data across multiple disks:

Application

↓

RAID Controller

↓

Disk 1

Disk 2

Disk 3

Disk 4

The operating system sees a single logical storage device.

docs.title: Key RAID Concepts
docs.text:
RAID is built using three fundamental techniques:

  • Striping
  • Mirroring
  • Parity

docs.title: Striping
docs.text:
Striping splits data across multiple disks.

Example:

File

↓

Block A → Disk 1

Block B → Disk 2

Block C → Disk 3

Block D → Disk 4

Advantages:

  • Faster reads
  • Faster writes
  • Better performance

Disadvantage:

  • No fault tolerance

docs.title: Mirroring
docs.text:
Mirroring writes identical copies of data to multiple disks.

Example:

Disk 1

Data A

↓

Disk 2

Data A

Advantages:

  • High availability
  • Easy recovery
  • Excellent read performance

Disadvantage:

  • Storage capacity is reduced because data is duplicated.

docs.title: Parity
docs.text:
Parity stores additional information that allows lost data to be reconstructed if a disk fails.

Example:

Disk 1

Block A

Disk 2

Block B

Disk 3

Parity

Advantages:

  • Fault tolerance
  • Better storage efficiency than mirroring

Disadvantages:

  • More complex
  • Write operations may be slower due to parity calculations

docs.title: Common RAID Levels
docs.text:
Linux commonly uses:

  • RAID 0
  • RAID 1
  • RAID 5
  • RAID 6
  • RAID 10

Each RAID level balances performance, storage efficiency, and fault tolerance differently.

docs.title: RAID 0 (Striping)
docs.text:
Disk1

AAAA

Disk2

BBBB

Characteristics:

  • Striping only
  • High performance
  • No redundancy

Minimum disks:

2

Disk failure tolerance:

0

Use cases:

  • Temporary data
  • High-performance workloads where redundancy is not required

docs.title: RAID 1 (Mirroring)
docs.text:
Disk1

AAAA

Disk2

AAAA

Characteristics:

  • Full data duplication
  • Excellent reliability
  • Good read performance

Minimum disks:

2

Disk failure tolerance:

1 (per mirrored pair)

Use cases:

  • Operating system disks
  • Critical servers
  • Database logs

docs.title: RAID 5 (Striping with Parity)
docs.text:
Disk1

A

Disk2

B

Disk3

Parity

Characteristics:

  • Striping
  • Distributed parity
  • Good balance of performance and storage efficiency

Minimum disks:

3

Disk failure tolerance:

1

Use cases:

  • File servers
  • General enterprise storage

docs.title: RAID 6 (Double Parity)
docs.text:
Similar to RAID 5 but stores two parity blocks.

Characteristics:

  • Better fault tolerance
  • Can survive two simultaneous disk failures

Minimum disks:

4

Disk failure tolerance:

2

Use cases:

  • Large storage arrays
  • Backup systems
  • Enterprise storage

docs.title: RAID 10 (1+0)
docs.text:
Combines:

  • RAID 1 (Mirroring)
  • RAID 0 (Striping)

Example:

Mirror

↓

Stripe

Characteristics:

  • Excellent performance
  • Excellent redundancy
  • Fast rebuild times

Minimum disks:

4

Disk failure tolerance:

Depends on which disks fail, but multiple failures may be tolerated if they occur in different mirrored pairs.

Use cases:

  • Databases
  • Virtualization
  • Enterprise applications

docs.title: RAID Comparison
docs.text: RAID Performance Fault Tolerance Storage Efficiency Minimum Disks RAID 0 Excellent None 100% 2 RAID 1 Good High 50% 2 RAID 5 Good One Disk (N−1)/N 3 RAID 6 Good Two Disks (N−2)/N 4 RAID 10 Excellent High 50% 4

docs.title: Hardware RAID
docs.text:
Managed by:

  • Dedicated RAID controller

Advantages:

  • Better performance
  • Lower CPU usage
  • Battery-backed cache (on many controllers)

Disadvantages:

  • Higher cost
  • Controller dependency

docs.title: Software RAID
docs.text:
Managed by Linux.

Common tool:

mdadm

Advantages:

  • Low cost
  • Flexible
  • Easy to manage
  • No dedicated controller required

Common in Linux servers and cloud environments.

docs.title: RAID is NOT a Backup
docs.text:
A common misconception:

RAID

≠

Backup

RAID protects against:

  • Disk failure

RAID does not protect against:

  • Accidental deletion
  • Malware or ransomware
  • File corruption
  • Fire or theft
  • User mistakes

Always maintain regular backups even when using RAID.

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Typical enterprise deployments:

Workload Recommended RAID Operating System RAID 1 Database RAID 10 File Server RAID 5 Backup Server RAID 6 Virtualization RAID 10

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
RAID is commonly used in:

  • Enterprise servers
  • SAN storage
  • NAS appliances
  • Database clusters
  • Kubernetes storage
  • Hypervisors
  • Cloud infrastructure
  • Backup appliances

Selecting the correct RAID level depends on business requirements for performance, capacity, and availability.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Display block devices.

lsblk

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Check for existing RAID devices.

cat /proc/mdstat

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Display RAID information.

sudo mdadm --detail --scan

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text: Compare the characteristics of RAID 0, RAID 1, RAID 5, RAID 6, and RAID 10.

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text: Calculate usable storage for four 1 TB disks using each RAID level.

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text: Identify which RAID level is most appropriate for a production database server.

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text: Identify which RAID level is suitable for a backup server.

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text: Explain why RAID should not replace backups.

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example lsblk View storage devices Storage inventory cat /proc/mdstat Display RAID status RAID monitoring mdadm --detail --scan View RAID configuration RAID administration

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming RAID replaces backups.

✅ Verify RAID replaces backups instead of assuming it.

❌ Choosing RAID 0 for critical production data.

✅ Choose carefully: avoid RAID 0 for critical production data when inappropriate.

❌ Ignoring failed disk alerts.

✅ Always review failed disk alerts.

❌ Mixing disks with different capacities or performance characteristics in the same RAID array.

✅ Avoid mixing disks with different capacities or performance characteristics in the same RAID array.

❌ Not testing RAID recovery procedures.

✅ Always testing RAID recovery procedures.

docs.title: Beginner
docs.text:
1. What does RAID stand for?
  2. What are the advantages of RAID?
  3. What is striping?
  4. What is mirroring?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. What is parity?
  2. What is the difference between RAID 5 and RAID 6?
  3. Why is RAID 10 commonly used for databases?
  4. What is the difference between hardware RAID and software RAID?

docs.title: Architect Level
docs.text:
1. How would you choose a RAID level for a production database cluster?
  2. Why should RAID never replace backups?
  3. How would you design highly available enterprise storage for performance and fault tolerance?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • RAID fundamentals
  • Striping
  • Mirroring
  • Parity
  • RAID levels
  • Hardware vs software RAID
  • Enterprise storage concepts
  • Production best practices

RAID combines multiple disks to improve storage performance, availability, and reliability. Choosing the appropriate RAID level requires balancing speed, storage efficiency, fault tolerance, and business requirements. Although RAID improves resilience against disk failures, it is not a substitute for a comprehensive backup strategy.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• RAID combines multiple disks into one logical storage unit.
  • Striping improves performance.
  • Mirroring improves redundancy.
  • Parity provides fault tolerance with efficient storage utilization.
  • RAID 10 is widely used for high-performance enterprise workloads.
  • RAID protects against disk failures but does not replace backups.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
Swap Space — Extending Memory in Linux

You'll explore:

  • What swap space is
  • Swap partitions and swap files
  • Virtual memory concepts
  • Creating and enabling swap
  • Configuring persistent swap
  • Monitoring swap usage
  • Tuning swappiness
  • Production best practices

By the end of the lesson, you'll be able to create, configure, monitor, and optimize swap space to improve Linux system stability and effectively manage memory under heavy workloads.

docs.title: Input, Output, Pipes, and Redirection
docs.text: One of the most powerful features of Linux is the ability to redirect input and output between commands and files. Redirection and pipes allow you to combine simple commands into powerful workflows, making automation, troubleshooting, and data processing much more efficient.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 2: Linux Command Line Essentials → Lesson 9

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 35 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Linux Command Line Essentials

Lesson: 9 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Standard Input, Output, and Error
  • Redirect command output to files
  • Append output to existing files
  • Redirect errors
  • Combine commands using pipes
  • Use the tee command
  • Build powerful Linux command pipelines

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 Lessons 1–8

docs.title: Why Learn Redirection?
docs.text:
Imagine you run a command that produces thousands of lines.

Instead of displaying everything on the screen, you can:

  • Save it to a file
  • Send it to another command
  • Filter the results
  • Ignore errors
  • Build automation workflows

Almost every shell script and DevOps pipeline uses redirection.

docs.title: Standard Streams
docs.text:
Every Linux process has three standard data streams.

Stream Number Purpose Standard Input 0 Receives input Standard Output 1 Displays normal output Standard Error 2 Displays error messages

Visual representation:

          Keyboard
             │
             ▼
         Standard Input (0)
             │
             ▼
         Linux Command
          │         │
          ▼         ▼
 Standard Output   Standard Error
      (1)               (2)

docs.title: Standard Output (stdout)
docs.text:
Example:

echo "Hello Linux"

Output:

Hello Linux

Normally, output is displayed on the terminal.

docs.title: Redirect Output (>)
docs.text:
Save output to a file.

echo "Linux" > notes.txt

Check:

cat notes.txt

Output:

Linux

Important

If the file already exists:

echo "Docker" > notes.txt

The existing contents are overwritten.

docs.title: Append Output (>>)
docs.text:
Append instead of overwrite.

echo "Kubernetes" >> notes.txt

Now:

cat notes.txt

Output:

Linux
Kubernetes

docs.title: Standard Error (stderr)
docs.text:
Example:

ls file-does-not-exist

Output:

ls: cannot access 'file-does-not-exist'

This message is sent to Standard Error (2).

docs.title: Redirect Errors
docs.text:
Save only errors.

ls missing.txt 2> errors.log

View:

cat errors.log

Append errors.

ls missing.txt 2>> errors.log

docs.title: Redirect Output and Errors Together
docs.text:
command > output.log 2>&1

Example:

ls existing.txt missing.txt > result.log 2>&1

Both normal output and errors go into one file.

docs.title: Discard Output
docs.text:
Linux provides a special device:

/dev/null

Anything sent here disappears.

Ignore output.

ls > /dev/null

Ignore errors.

ls missing.txt 2> /dev/null

Ignore everything.

command > /dev/null 2>&1

docs.title: Standard Input (stdin)
docs.text:
Many commands accept input.

Example:

sort < names.txt

Instead of typing manually, the file becomes the command's input.

docs.title: Pipes (|)
docs.text:
A pipe sends the output of one command directly into another command.

Syntax:

command1 | command2

Visual representation:

Command 1

↓

Output

↓

Pipe

↓

Command 2

docs.title: Pipe Example
docs.text:
Display only the first five files.

ls | head -5

Count files.

ls | wc -l

Search for a process.

ps -ef | grep ssh

Sort output.

cat users.txt | sort

Count matching lines.

cat users.txt | grep admin | wc -l

docs.title: The tee Command
docs.text:
Normally:

echo "Hello"

displays output.

Using:

echo "Hello" | tee output.txt

Result:

  • Displays output
  • Saves output

Append:

echo "Docker" | tee -a output.txt

docs.title: Combining Multiple Pipes
docs.text:
Linux allows multiple pipes.

Example:

cat access.log | grep ERROR | sort | uniq | wc -l

Workflow:

Read Log

↓

Filter ERROR

↓

Sort

↓

Remove Duplicates

↓

Count

This is one of Linux's greatest strengths.

docs.title: Input and Output Flow
docs.text:
stdin (0)

↓

Command

↓

stdout (1)

↓

Pipe or File

↓

Another Command

↓

Result

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Display running Docker containers.

docker ps | grep nginx

Count Kubernetes Pods.

kubectl get pods | wc -l

Find failed services.

systemctl --failed | less

Search logs.

cat /var/log/syslog | grep ERROR

Save process list.

ps -ef > processes.txt

Monitor logs while saving.

tail -f app.log | tee app-output.log

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Every DevOps engineer uses pipes and redirection.

Examples:

Terraform

terraform plan > plan.txt

Kubernetes

kubectl get pods | grep Running

Docker

docker logs container | less

Git

git log | head

System Administration

journalctl | grep ssh

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Redirect output.

echo "Linux" > linux.txt

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Append.

echo "Docker" >> linux.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Display.

cat linux.txt

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Redirect error.

ls missing.txt 2> error.log

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
View errors.

cat error.log

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Count files.

ls | wc -l

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Display first five entries.

ls | head -5

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Use tee.

date | tee today.txt

docs.title: Task 9
docs.text:
Search.

history | grep docker

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Symbol / Command Purpose Example > Overwrite output ls > files.txt >> Append output date >> log.txt 2> Redirect errors ls missing 2> error.log 2>> Append errors ls missing 2>> error.log 2>&1 Combine stdout and stderr command > all.log 2>&1 < Redirect input sort < names.txt \| Pipe output ps -ef \| grep ssh tee Display and save output date \| tee log.txt

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

An application has stopped working.

Tasks:

  1. Save running processes to a file.
  2. Search for the application process.
  3. Count running services.
  4. Save error logs.
  5. Monitor logs while writing them to another file.

Solutions:

ps -ef > processes.txt

ps -ef | grep nginx

systemctl list-units | wc -l

journalctl -p err > errors.log

tail -f app.log | tee monitor.log

docs.title: Mini Challenge
docs.text:
Create a file named:

employees.txt

Add:

Alice

Bob

Charlie

David

Alice

Perform the following:

  • Sort the file.
  • Remove duplicate entries.
  • Count the number of unique names.
  • Save the sorted output to a new file.
  • Display the output while saving it.

Hints:

sort

uniq

wc

tee

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use >> when preserving existing data.
  • Redirect errors to separate log files during troubleshooting.
  • Use pipes instead of creating temporary files whenever possible.
  • Use tee to monitor output while saving it.
  • Understand standard streams before writing shell scripts.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Accidentally overwriting files.

✅ Use:

>

Always verify before using.

❌ Ignoring error messages.

✅ Redirect errors to a file for analysis.

❌ Creating unnecessary temporary files.

✅ Use pipes instead.

❌ Forgetting that 2> redirects only errors.

✅ Use:

> file 2>&1

to capture everything.

docs.title: Beginner
docs.text:
1. What are stdin, stdout, and stderr?
  2. What does > do?
  3. Difference between > and >>?
  4. What is a pipe?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Explain 2> and 2>&1.
  2. What is /dev/null?
  3. What does the tee command do?
  4. Why are pipes preferred over temporary files?

docs.title: Architect Level
docs.text:
1. How do pipes improve Linux automation?
  2. How would you capture logs and errors separately in production?
  3. Why is understanding standard streams essential for shell scripting?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Standard Input
  • Standard Output
  • Standard Error
  • Output redirection
  • Error redirection
  • Pipes
  • tee
  • Linux command pipelines

These concepts are fundamental to Linux automation and shell scripting. Almost every Bash script, CI/CD pipeline, and production troubleshooting workflow relies on redirection and pipes.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Linux uses three standard streams: stdin (0), stdout (1), and stderr (2).
  • > overwrites a file, while >> appends to it.
  • 2> redirects error messages.
  • | connects the output of one command to another.
  • tee displays output while simultaneously saving it.
  • Combining simple commands with pipes creates powerful automation workflows.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
Pipes (|) in Linux

In the final lesson of Module 2, you'll learn:

  • What a pipe is
  • How pipes work internally
  • Connecting multiple Linux commands
  • Filtering and processing command output
  • Building powerful command pipelines
  • Using pipes in real-world administration and DevOps tasks

docs.title: Repository Management — Managing Software Sources in Linux
Repository Management — Managing Software Sources in Linux
docs.text: A repository is a centralized location that stores software packages and their metadata. Package managers such as APT, DNF, and YUM retrieve software from repositories, ensuring applications are downloaded from trusted sources with verified integrity. Proper repository management is essential for maintaining secure, reliable, and up-to-date Linux systems.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 7: Package Management → Lesson 7

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 65 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Package Management

Lesson: 7 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand software repositories
  • Configure repositories
  • Add and remove repositories
  • Verify package authenticity
  • Manage GPG keys
  • Enable and disable repositories
  • Understand repository priorities
  • Apply repository management in production

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 – File Management and Permissions
  • Module 5 – Users and Groups
  • Module 6 – Process Management
  • Module 7 Lessons 1–6

docs.title: Why Learn Repository Management?
docs.text:
Imagine you need to install:

  • Docker
  • Kubernetes
  • Google Cloud SDK
  • Visual Studio Code
  • PostgreSQL

These packages may not exist in your operating system's default repository.

Instead of downloading software manually,

you add a trusted repository.

Then your package manager installs and updates software automatically.

docs.title: What is a Repository?
docs.text:
A repository is a server that stores:

  • Software packages
  • Package metadata
  • Package versions
  • Dependency information
  • Digital signatures

Package managers communicate with repositories to install and update software.

docs.title: Repository Workflow
docs.text:
Package Manager
      │
      ▼
Repository
      │
      ▼
Download Metadata
      │
      ▼
Verify Signature
      │
      ▼
Download Package
      │
      ▼
Install Software

docs.title: Types of Repositories
docs.text:
Common repository types include:

  • Official operating system repositories
  • Vendor repositories
  • Third-party repositories
  • Internal enterprise repositories
  • Local repositories

docs.title: Why Use Official Repositories?
docs.text:
Official repositories provide:

  • Tested software
  • Security updates
  • Verified packages
  • Automatic dependency resolution
  • Long-term support

They are the safest choice for production systems.

docs.title: Repository Configuration (APT)
docs.text:
Repository definitions are stored in:

/etc/apt/sources.list

and

/etc/apt/sources.list.d/

View configured repositories.

cat /etc/apt/sources.list

docs.title: Add an APT Repository
docs.text:
Example:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:graphics-drivers/ppa

Refresh package metadata.

sudo apt update

docs.title: Repository Configuration (DNF/YUM)
docs.text:
Repository files are stored in:

/etc/yum.repos.d/

Example:

docker.repo

epel.repo

google-cloud.repo

List repository files.

ls /etc/yum.repos.d/

docs.title: List Repositories
docs.text:
APT:

grep "^deb" /etc/apt/sources.list

DNF:

dnf repolist

YUM:

yum repolist

docs.title: Enable a Repository
docs.text:
DNF:

sudo dnf config-manager --set-enabled epel

YUM:

sudo yum-config-manager --enable epel

docs.title: Disable a Repository
docs.text:
DNF:

sudo dnf config-manager --set-disabled epel

YUM:

sudo yum-config-manager --disable epel

docs.title: What is a GPG Key?
docs.text:
Repositories digitally sign packages.

The package manager verifies the signature using a GPG (GNU Privacy Guard) key.

This ensures:

  • Package authenticity
  • Integrity
  • Protection against tampering

docs.title: Import a GPG Key
docs.text:
RPM-based systems:

sudo rpm --import https://example.com/RPM-GPG-KEY

APT repositories often install signing keys as part of the repository setup process using keyring files.

docs.title: Verify Imported Keys
docs.text:
RPM:

rpm -qa gpg-pubkey*

APT:

apt-key list

Note: apt-key is deprecated on modern Debian and Ubuntu systems. Current best practice is to use keyring files (for example, under /etc/apt/keyrings/) and reference them with the signed-by= option in repository definitions.

docs.title: Remove a Repository
docs.text:
APT:

Remove the repository file from:

/etc/apt/sources.list.d/

Then update:

sudo apt update

DNF/YUM:

Delete the .repo file.

sudo rm /etc/yum.repos.d/example.repo

Refresh metadata.

sudo dnf makecache

docs.title: Repository Priorities
docs.text:
Enterprise environments often configure repository priorities.

Example:

Priority 1

Official Repository

Priority 10

Third-Party Repository

Higher-priority repositories are preferred when multiple repositories provide the same package.

docs.title: Local Repository
docs.text:
Organizations often maintain internal repositories.

Benefits:

  • Faster installations
  • Internet-independent deployments
  • Approved software only
  • Better security
  • Consistent package versions

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
APT update.

sudo apt update

List DNF repositories.

dnf repolist

List YUM repositories.

yum repolist

Import GPG key.

sudo rpm --import KEY

List repository files.

ls /etc/yum.repos.d/

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Add Docker repository.

sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo \
https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/docker-ce.repo

Refresh metadata.

sudo dnf makecache

Install Docker.

sudo dnf install docker-ce

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Repository management is critical for:

  • Enterprise Linux servers
  • Kubernetes clusters
  • Cloud virtual machines
  • CI/CD environments
  • Air-gapped environments
  • Security compliance
  • Patch management

Poor repository management can expose systems to outdated or malicious software.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
List configured repositories.

APT:

grep "^deb" /etc/apt/sources.list

DNF:

dnf repolist

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
List repository configuration files.

ls /etc/yum.repos.d/

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
View a repository file.

cat /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Refresh package metadata.

APT:

sudo apt update

DNF:

sudo dnf makecache

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
List imported GPG keys.

rpm -qa gpg-pubkey*

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Check repository status.

dnf repolist

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Search for a package.

dnf search nginx

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Identify which repository provides an installed package.

dnf info nginx

Observe the Repository field.

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example apt update Refresh package metadata Ubuntu maintenance dnf repolist List repositories Repository verification yum repolist List repositories Legacy administration rpm --import Import GPG key Secure repository setup dnf makecache Refresh cache Performance optimization dnf config-manager Manage repositories Enterprise repository administration

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A system administrator attempts to install Kubernetes tools.

sudo dnf install kubectl

Error:

No match for argument: kubectl

Investigation:

dnf repolist

The Kubernetes repository has not been added.

Solution:

  • Add the official Kubernetes repository.
  • Import its GPG key.
  • Refresh the repository metadata.
sudo dnf makecache

sudo dnf install kubectl

The package installs successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:

✅ Avoid this mistake: installing software from untrusted repositories.

✅ Always review GPG signature verification.

✅ Do not leave obsolete repositories enabled.

✅ Avoid mixing incompatible repositories from different operating system versions.

docs.title: Restore — Recovering Data in Linux
docs.text: Restore is the process of recovering files, directories, applications, or entire systems from backups after data loss, corruption, hardware failure, accidental deletion, or disaster. A backup is only valuable if it can be successfully restored. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) must know how to restore data quickly and accurately to minimize downtime and ensure business continuity.

docs.title: Why Learn Restore?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • A production server accidentally deletes important files.
  • A storage device fails unexpectedly.
  • A ransomware attack encrypts application data.
  • A configuration mistake corrupts the operating system.
  • A cloud virtual machine becomes unusable.

Without restore procedures:

Failure

↓

Long Downtime

↓

Business Impact

With proper restore procedures:

Failure

↓

Restore Backup

↓

Business Continues

docs.title: What is Restore?
docs.text:
Restore is the process of recovering previously backed-up data.

Example:

Backup

↓

Restore

↓

Original Files Recovered

A restore can recover:

  • Individual files
  • Directories
  • Applications
  • Databases
  • Entire servers

docs.title: Types of Restore
docs.text:
Common restore operations include:

  • File restore
  • Directory restore
  • Application restore
  • Database restore
  • Full system restore

docs.title: Restore Using cp
docs.text:
Restore copied files.

cp backup/file.txt .

docs.title: Restore tar Archives
docs.text:
Extract an archive.

tar -xzf backup.tar.gz

Restore to another directory.

tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /restore

docs.title: Restore Using rsync
docs.text:
Restore files.

rsync -av backup/ /home/user/

Only changed files are copied.

docs.title: Restore Disk Images
docs.text:
Restore a disk image.

sudo dd if=disk.img of=/dev/sdb bs=4M

Warning

This overwrites the destination disk. Verify the target device before running the command.

docs.title: Verify Restored Files
docs.text:
Compare checksums.

Generate checksum.

sha256sum original.txt

sha256sum restored.txt

Matching values indicate that the files are identical.

docs.title: Verify File Permissions
docs.text:
Check restored permissions.

ls -l

Restore ownership if necessary.

sudo chown user:user file.txt

docs.title: Verify File Integrity
docs.text:
Check archive contents.

tar -tzf backup.tar.gz

Confirm that all required files are present.

docs.title: Recovery Validation
docs.text:
After restoring:

  • Verify files
  • Verify permissions
  • Verify ownership
  • Verify application configuration
  • Test application functionality

docs.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
docs.text:
RTO defines:

Maximum Acceptable Downtime

Example:

Failure

↓

Restore

↓

Application Online

30 Minutes

docs.title: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
docs.text:
RPO defines:

Maximum Acceptable Data Loss

Example:

Hourly Backups

↓

Maximum Data Loss

1 Hour

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Restore archive.

tar -xzf backup.tar.gz

Restore directory.

rsync -av backup/ /data/

Restore copied files.

cp backup/file.txt .

Restore disk.

dd if=disk.img of=/dev/sdb

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Restore website files.

rsync -av backup/web/ /var/www/html/

Restore configuration.

tar -xzf etc-backup.tar.gz -C /

Restore database storage.

docs.text:

  • Enterprise servers
  • Cloud virtual machines
  • Kubernetes clusters
  • Databases
  • File servers
  • Disaster recovery
  • Business continuity
  • Regulatory compliance

Organizations should regularly test restore procedures to ensure backups are usable.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create a sample backup.

mkdir ~/restore-demo

echo "Linux Mastery" > ~/restore-demo/file.txt

tar -czf demo-backup.tar.gz ~/restore-demo

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Delete the original directory.

rm -rf ~/restore-demo

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Restore the archive.

tar -xzf demo-backup.tar.gz

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Verify restored files.

ls ~/restore-demo

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Restore using rsync.

rsync -av backup/ restore/

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Compare checksums.

sha256sum original.txt restored.txt

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Verify permissions.

ls -l ~/restore-demo

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text: Confirm application or file functionality after restoration.

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example cp Restore copied files Small recoveries tar -xzf Restore compressed archive System restore rsync Restore synchronized data Incremental recovery dd Restore disk image Disaster recovery sha256sum Verify integrity Restore validation ls -l Verify permissions Post-restore validation

docs.title: Common Restore Errors
docs.text: Error Possible Cause File not found Incorrect backup location Permission denied Insufficient privileges Checksum mismatch Corrupted backup Device busy Target disk is in use Incomplete restore Missing backup files

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A production application fails after accidental deletion of configuration files.

Recovery steps:

Restore configuration.

tar -xzf config-backup.tar.gz -C /

Restore application data.

rsync -av backup/app/ /opt/app/

Restart the application.

sudo systemctl restart myapp

Verify:

  • Service status
  • Application logs
  • User access

The application is successfully restored with minimal downtime.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Test restore procedures regularly.
  • Verify backup integrity before restoration.
  • Validate restored applications after recovery.
  • Document restoration steps.
  • Monitor recovery time against RTO targets.
  • Keep multiple backup versions.
  • Practice disaster recovery drills.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Never testing restores.

✅ Always testing restores.

❌ Restoring to the wrong location.

✅ Avoid this mistake: restoring to the wrong location.

❌ Forgetting to verify permissions and ownership.

✅ Remember to to verify permissions and ownership.

❌ Assuming every backup is valid.

✅ Verify every backup is valid instead of assuming it.

❌ Restoring directly to production without validation.

✅ Avoid this mistake: restoring directly to production without validation.

Restoration is the final and most critical phase of any backup strategy. Successful recovery depends not only on having backups, but also on regularly testing restoration procedures and verifying that recovered data and applications function correctly.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A backup is valuable only if it can be restored.
  • Restore procedures should be tested regularly.
  • Verify permissions, ownership, and checksums after restoration.
  • Understand RTO and RPO when planning disaster recovery.

docs.title: Routing — How Linux Sends Network Traffic
Routing — How Linux Sends Network Traffic
docs.text: Routing is the process of determining the best path for network packets to travel from a source to a destination. Every Linux server, cloud instance, Kubernetes node, and network device relies on routing tables to decide where packets should be sent. Understanding routing is essential for Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, Network Engineers, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs).

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 70 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Networking

Lesson: 4 of 13

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand routing
  • Learn how routing tables work
  • Understand default gateways
  • Configure static routes
  • View routing information
  • Troubleshoot routing issues
  • Apply routing concepts in production

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 – File Management
  • Module 5 – Users and Groups
  • Module 6 – Process Management
  • Module 7 – Package Management
  • Module 8 Lessons 1–3

docs.title: Why Learn Routing?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • A Linux server cannot reach another network.
  • A Kubernetes node cannot communicate with another node.
  • SSH works locally but fails across subnets.
  • A cloud VM has Internet access but cannot reach a private network.

In many cases, the cause is an incorrect routing configuration.

docs.title: What is Routing?
docs.text:
Routing is the process of forwarding network packets from one network to another.

A router or a Linux system examines the destination IP address and determines the next hop based on its routing table.

docs.title: How Routing Works
docs.text:
Application
      │
      ▼
Destination IP
      │
      ▼
Routing Table Lookup
      │
      ▼
Next Hop Selected
      │
      ▼
Packet Sent

docs.title: What is a Routing Table?
docs.text:
A routing table is a list of routes that tells the operating system how to reach different networks.

Each route typically contains:

  • Destination network
  • Gateway (next hop)
  • Network interface
  • Metric (priority)

docs.title: View the Routing Table
docs.text:
Display all routes.

ip route

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1 dev ens160

192.168.1.0/24 dev ens160 proto kernel

docs.title: Understanding a Route
docs.text:
Example:

192.168.10.0/24 via 192.168.1.1 dev ens160

Meaning:

  • Destination network:
192.168.10.0/24
  • Next hop:
192.168.1.1
  • Interface:
ens160

docs.title: Default Route
docs.text:
The default route is used when no more specific route matches the destination.

Example:

default via 192.168.1.1

Without a default route, a system typically cannot communicate with external networks such as the Internet.

docs.title: Routing Decision Process
docs.text:
Linux searches the routing table using the longest prefix match.

Example:

Destination

↓

192.168.1.50

↓

Matches

192.168.1.0/24

↓

Forward Packet

The most specific matching route is selected.

docs.title: Add a Temporary Route
docs.text:
Add a route to another network.

sudo ip route add 10.10.0.0/16 via 192.168.1.1

Verify:

ip route

This route is temporary and will not survive a reboot.

docs.title: Delete a Route
docs.text: sudo ip route del 10.10.0.0/16

docs.title: Replace the Default Route
docs.text: sudo ip route replace default via 192.168.1.254

docs.title: Persistent Routes
docs.text:
Routes added with the ip command are temporary.

Persistent routes are configured using the operating system's networking tools.

Examples:

  • Ubuntu: Netplan
  • RHEL / Rocky / AlmaLinux: NetworkManager (nmcli) or network configuration files

docs.title: Route Lookup
docs.text:
Check which route Linux will use.

ip route get 8.8.8.8

Example:

8.8.8.8 via 192.168.1.1 dev ens160

This command is extremely useful when troubleshooting routing decisions.

docs.title: Enable IP Forwarding
docs.text:
Linux can act as a router by forwarding packets.

Temporarily enable IP forwarding.

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

Verify:

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

For permanent configuration, update the appropriate sysctl configuration file.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Display routing table.

ip route

View a specific route.

ip route get 8.8.8.8

Add route.

sudo ip route add 10.10.0.0/16 via 192.168.1.1

Delete route.

sudo ip route del 10.10.0.0/16

Enable IP forwarding.

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Verify default gateway.

ip route

Check Internet route.

ip route get 8.8.8.8

Add a route to a private subnet.

sudo ip route add 172.16.0.0/16 via 192.168.1.1

Enable packet forwarding on a gateway server.

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Routing is essential for:

  • Cloud virtual machines
  • Kubernetes clusters
  • VPN gateways
  • Firewalls
  • Load balancers
  • Multi-subnet environments
  • Hybrid cloud networks
  • Enterprise data centers

Incorrect routing is one of the most common causes of network connectivity problems.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Display the routing table.

ip route

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Identify the default route.

ip route

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Determine the route to Google's DNS server.

ip route get 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Add a temporary static route.

sudo ip route add 10.10.0.0/16 via 192.168.1.1

Replace the gateway with one appropriate for your network.

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Verify the new route.

ip route

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Delete the temporary route.

sudo ip route del 10.10.0.0/16

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Check whether IP forwarding is enabled.

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Enable IP forwarding temporarily.

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example ip route Display routing table Verify routes ip route get Show route to a destination Troubleshooting ip route add Add static route Multi-network connectivity ip route del Delete route Cleanup ip route replace Replace default route Gateway updates sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward Check IP forwarding Router verification

docs.title: Static vs Dynamic Routing
docs.text:
Feature Static Routing Dynamic Routing Configuration Manual Automatic Scalability Small networks Large networks Maintenance Higher Lower Complexity Simple More complex Common Use Small LANs, cloud VMs Enterprise networks

Dynamic routing commonly uses protocols such as:

  • OSPF
  • BGP
  • RIP
  • EIGRP (Cisco)

Linux servers typically use static routes unless participating in a routing infrastructure.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A Linux application server cannot communicate with a database located in another subnet.

Investigation:

Check the routing table.

ip route

Verify the route.

ip route get 10.20.30.40

Output:

Network unreachable

Add the required route.

sudo ip route add 10.20.30.0/24 via 192.168.1.1

Verify:

ip route get 10.20.30.40

The route now exists, and the application can communicate with the database.

A permanent route is then configured using the operating system's network management tools.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use the ip command instead of the deprecated route command.
  • Verify the routing table before troubleshooting applications.
  • Configure persistent routes through supported network management tools.
  • Use static routes only when necessary.
  • Document custom routes in production environments.
  • Verify routing after network configuration changes.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting that routes added with ip route add are temporary.

✅ Remember to that routes added with ip route add are temporary.

❌ Configuring an incorrect default gateway.

✅ Avoid this mistake: configuring an incorrect default gateway.

❌ Adding overlapping or conflicting routes.

✅ Avoid this mistake: adding overlapping or conflicting routes.

❌ Ignoring routing when troubleshooting connectivity issues.

✅ Always review routing when troubleshooting connectivity issues.

docs.text:

  • Routing fundamentals

  • Default gateways

  • Route troubleshooting

Routing determines how Linux systems send packets across networks. A solid understanding of routing tables, gateways, and static routes enables administrators to build reliable, scalable, and well-connected infrastructure.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Routing determines the path packets take to reach their destination.
  • The routing table contains information about reachable networks.
  • The default gateway handles traffic for unknown networks.
  • Use ip route to view and manage routes.
  • Use ip route get to understand routing decisions.
  • Routes added with the ip command are temporary unless configured persistently.

docs.title: RPM (Red Hat Package Manager) — Managing RPM Packages in Linux
RPM (Red Hat Package Manager) — Managing RPM Packages in Linux
docs.text: RPM (Red Hat Package Manager) is the low-level package management system used by Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Fedora, Oracle Linux, and other RPM-based distributions. While DNF and YUM manage software from repositories, RPM works directly with local .rpm package files. Linux administrators use RPM to install, verify, query, and inspect software packages.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 60 Minutes

Course Progress

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand RPM
  • Install local RPM packages
  • Upgrade packages
  • Remove packages
  • Query installed software
  • Verify package integrity
  • Inspect package contents
  • Understand the relationship between RPM, YUM, and DNF

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 – File Management and Permissions
  • Module 5 – Users and Groups

docs.title: Why Learn RPM?
docs.text:
Imagine you receive:

docker-ce-28.0.0.rpm

or

custom-agent.rpm

from your company.

The package isn't available in any repository.

How do you install it?

The answer is:

rpm

docs.title: What is RPM?
docs.text:
RPM stands for:

Red Hat Package Manager

It is the package management system used by RPM-based Linux distributions.

RPM works directly with package files.

Example:

nginx-1.24.0-1.el9.x86_64.rpm

docs.title: RPM vs DNF/YUM
docs.text:
RPM

↓

Local Package File

↓

Install Package

Whereas:

DNF / YUM

↓

Repository

↓

Download Package

↓

Install Package

DNF and YUM use RPM internally to install packages.

docs.title: RPM Package Structure
docs.text:
An RPM package typically contains:

  • Executable files
  • Libraries
  • Configuration files
  • Documentation
  • Metadata
  • Package scripts

docs.title: Install an RPM Package
docs.text:
sudo rpm -ivh package.rpm

Example:

sudo rpm -ivh nginx.rpm

Options:

Option Meaning -i Install -v Verbose output -h Display progress bar

docs.title: Upgrade an RPM Package
docs.text:
sudo rpm -Uvh package.rpm

Example:

sudo rpm -Uvh nginx.rpm

If the package already exists:

  • Upgrade

Otherwise:

  • Install

docs.title: Fresh Install Only
docs.text:
Prevent upgrades.

sudo rpm -ivh package.rpm

Fails if the package is already installed.

docs.title: Remove a Package
docs.text:
sudo rpm -e package-name

Example:

sudo rpm -e nginx

Use the package name—not the .rpm filename.

docs.title: Query Installed Packages
docs.text:
List all installed packages.

rpm -qa

Example:

bash

git

nginx

vim

docs.title: Search Installed Packages
docs.text: rpm -qa | grep nginx

docs.title: Display Package Information
docs.text:
rpm -qi nginx

Displays:

  • Version
  • Release
  • Architecture
  • Install date
  • Vendor
  • Description

docs.title: List Files Installed by a Package
docs.text:
rpm -ql nginx

Example:

/etc/nginx

/usr/sbin/nginx

/usr/share/doc

docs.title: Find Which Package Owns a File
docs.text:
rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash

Output:

bash

Useful when troubleshooting system files.

docs.title: Verify an Installed Package
docs.text:
rpm -V nginx

RPM compares installed files against package metadata.

If nothing is displayed,

the package matches the expected state.

docs.title: Query an RPM File
docs.text:
Without installing:

rpm -qpi package.rpm

Display package contents.

rpm -qpl package.rpm

docs.title: Verify Package Signature
docs.text:
rpm -K package.rpm

This checks package integrity and signature information.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Install package.

sudo rpm -ivh package.rpm

Upgrade package.

sudo rpm -Uvh package.rpm

Remove package.

sudo rpm -e package-name

List packages.

rpm -qa

Package information.

rpm -qi package-name

List package files.

rpm -ql package-name

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Install a monitoring agent.

sudo rpm -ivh monitoring-agent.rpm

Upgrade Kubernetes tools.

sudo rpm -Uvh kubectl.rpm

Verify Docker installation.

rpm -qi docker

Identify the package that owns a binary.

rpm -qf /usr/bin/ssh

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
RPM is commonly used for:

  • Installing vendor-provided software
  • Offline package installation
  • Enterprise software deployment
  • Custom internal packages
  • Troubleshooting package ownership
  • Package verification
  • Security auditing

Although DNF is preferred for repository-based installations, RPM is essential when working with standalone package files.

docs.title: rsync — Efficient File Synchronization and Backups in Linux
rsync — Efficient File Synchronization and Backups in Linux
docs.text: rsync (Remote Sync) is one of the most powerful Linux utilities for synchronizing files and directories between systems. Unlike SCP, rsync transfers only the changed portions of files, making it faster, more bandwidth-efficient, and ideal for backups, deployments, and data synchronization. Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) use rsync extensively in production environments.

docs.title: Why Learn rsync?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • Backing up production servers every night.
  • Deploying application files to multiple servers.
  • Synchronizing website content.
  • Copying only changed log files.
  • Migrating data between cloud servers.

rsync performs these tasks efficiently by transferring only the differences.

docs.title: What is rsync?
docs.text:
rsync stands for:

Remote Sync

It synchronizes files and directories between:

  • Local → Local
  • Local → Remote
  • Remote → Local
  • Remote → Remote (through SSH)

docs.title: How rsync Works
docs.text:
Source Directory
        │
Compare Files
        │
Transfer Only Changes
        │
        ▼
Destination Directory

Unlike traditional copy commands, rsync minimizes data transfer.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
rsync [options] source destination

Example:

rsync file.txt backup/

docs.title: Archive Mode
docs.text:
The most commonly used option is:

rsync -a source/ destination/

Archive mode preserves:

  • Permissions
  • Ownership
  • Symbolic links
  • Timestamps
  • Recursive directory structure

docs.title: Verbose Output
docs.text:
rsync -av source/ destination/

Options:

Option Meaning -a Archive mode -v Verbose output

docs.title: Synchronize Directories
docs.text:
rsync -av project/ backup/

Only modified files are copied.

docs.title: Transfer Files Over SSH
docs.text:
rsync -av \
project/ \
admin@server:/opt/project/

SSH is used automatically for secure communication.

docs.title: Specify SSH Port
docs.text:
rsync -av \
-e "ssh -p 2222" \
project/ \
admin@server:/opt/project/

docs.title: Delete Removed Files
docs.text:
Synchronize destination exactly with source.

rsync -av --delete \
source/ \
destination/

Warning: --delete permanently removes files from the destination that no longer exist in the source.

docs.title: Compress During Transfer
docs.text:
rsync -avz \
source/ \
admin@server:/backup/

Option:

-z

Compresses data during transmission.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
Preview changes without copying files.

rsync -av --dry-run \
source/ \
destination/

Highly recommended before using --delete.

docs.title: Exclude Files
docs.text:
Ignore log files.

rsync -av \
--exclude="*.log" \
project/ backup/

docs.title: Show Progress
docs.text:
rsync -av --progress \
largefile.iso \
admin@server:/backup/

Displays transfer progress and speed.

docs.title: Synchronize Using SSH Keys
docs.text:
rsync -av \
-e "ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519" \
project/ \
admin@server:/opt/project/

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:

rsync -av source/ destination/

Remote synchronization.

rsync -av source/ admin@server:/backup/

Compress transfer.

rsync -avz source/ destination/

Dry run.

rsync -av --dry-run source/ destination/

Delete obsolete files.

rsync -av --delete source/ destination/

admin@web01:/var/www/html/

backup:/configs/

rsync -av app/ \
admin@app01:/opt/app/

backup:/logs/

  • Nightly backups
  • Disaster recovery
