It is one of the most important Linux tools for efficient file management.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A nightly backup job is taking several hours.

Current command:

scp -r /data backup@server:/backup/

Improved solution:

rsync -avz --delete \
/data/ \
backup@server:/backup/

Result:

  • Only changed files are transferred.
  • Compression reduces bandwidth usage.
  • Backup time decreases significantly.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use archive mode (-a) for backups.
  • Always perform a --dry-run before using --delete.
  • Use SSH key authentication for automation.
  • Compress transfers (-z) over slower networks.
  • Verify synchronized files after completion.
  • Schedule recurring synchronization with cron or systemd timers.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting the trailing / on source directories.

✅ Example:

rsync -av source/ destination/

copies the contents of source.

rsync -av source destination/

copies the source directory itself.

❌ Using --delete without first running --dry-run.

✅ Avoid using --delete without first running --dry-run when a safer approach exists.

❌ Using SCP instead of rsync for recurring synchronization.

✅ Prefer rsync for recurring synchronization rather than using SCP.

❌ Ignoring file permissions after synchronization.

✅ Always review file permissions after synchronization.

docs.title: Scheduling with cron, at, and Timers
Scheduling with cron, at, and Timers
Overview
docs.text:
Servers run tasks while people sleep: backups, certificate checks, report scripts, and disk cleanup. cron, at, and systemd timers are the usual ways to schedule that work.

Plain problem: A backup “ran every night” but nobody checked logs. Disk filled up because the cleanup job silently failed for weeks. Scheduling is not “set and forget” — you must see output and prove the job ran.

Linux offers three common schedulers:

  1. cron — recurring calendar jobs (every minute, daily at 2 am, …)
  2. at — one-shot jobs (“run this once at 3 pm”)
  3. systemd timers — modern unit-based schedules integrated with journalctl

This is Tutorial 11 in Module 11: Scheduling & Automation of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 practice VM with sudo
  • Package Management completed (you can install packages)
  • Basic understanding of shell commands and redirection

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain cron, at, and systemd timers in plain language
  • Write a user crontab entry and verify it ran
  • Schedule a one-shot job with at
  • Create a simple systemd timer and read logs with journalctl
  • Diagnose a broken schedule (wrong path, missing env, silent failure)
  • Answer fresher interview questions on Linux scheduling

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: A scheduler wakes up at the right time and runs a command or unit. cron reads per-user crontab files and system files under /etc/cron.*. at queues one job in a spool. systemd pairs a .service unit (what to run) with a .timer unit (when to run).

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
Your team’s SSL certificate expired. The renewal script exists — it “should run weekly”. It did not. Root cause: cron used a relative path; the job ran as a user with a different PATH than your SSH session; output went nowhere.

Scheduling failures are quiet. You learn to log to a file and check journal or mail.

docs.title: What is cron? (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: cron is a wall calendar with alarms. Each line says “at this minute/hour/day, run this command”. The crontab is your personal calendar file; root and /etc/cron.d/ hold system calendars.

Five time fields + command:

* * * * * command
│ │ │ │ │
│ │ │ │ └── day of week (0–7, Sun=0)
│ │ │ └──── month (1–12)
│ │ └────── day of month (1–31)
│ └──────── hour (0–23)
└────────── minute (0–59)

Example — every 5 minutes, append a timestamp:

Terminal
# Edit with: crontab -e
*/5 * * * * date >> /tmp/cron-demo.log 2>&1

Interview line: “Cron jobs inherit a minimal environment — I use absolute paths and redirect stdout/stderr to a log file.”

docs.title: at — one-shot scheduling
docs.text:
Analogy: at is a single alarm clock. “Run this script once at 15:00 today.”

Terminal
echo "echo hello-at >> ~/at-demo.log" | at 15:00
atq    # list pending jobs

Install on Ubuntu if missing: sudo apt install -y at (and enable atd).

docs.title: systemd timers
docs.text:
Analogy: If cron is a paper calendar, a systemd timer is a calendar synced with your building’s maintenance system — same logs (journalctl), same dependency model as services.

A timer unit triggers a service unit. Prefer timers on modern Ubuntu when you already use systemd for services — easier observability.

Tool Best for Logs cron Simple recurring user scripts File you redirect to, or mail at Delayed one-shot /var/spool/at/ / mail systemd timer Service-integrated schedules journalctl -u

docs.title: Cron environment trap
docs.text:
Interactive SSH gives you full PATH, HOME, maybe AWS_* vars. Cron does not. Scripts that work in your shell fail in cron because python3 or kubectl is “not found”.

Fix: Absolute paths in scripts; set env in crontab (PATH=... line) or source a small env file at the top of the script.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting 2>&1 — errors hidden
  • Using % in cron lines without escaping (cron treats % specially)
  • Running heavy jobs every minute on production
  • No log rotation on cron output files

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Create a user cron job, schedule an at job, deploy a systemd timer, break the cron job on purpose, fix it, and prove all three under ~/rebash-linux/lab17.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM systemd-based sudo For timer install under /etc/systemd/system/ Packages cron, at (usually preinstalled)

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab17/logs
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab17
systemctl is-active cron || sudo systemctl enable --now cron

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Ticket: “Prove the nightly disk-report script runs and leaves evidence. Also schedule a one-time cleanup tomorrow. Platform team wants a systemd timer for the same report on reboot.” You implement all three and document proof.

docs.title: Task 1 – User crontab with logging
docs.text:
Create disk-report.sh:

disk-report.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
LOG="$HOME/rebash-linux/lab17/logs/disk-report.log"
{
  echo "=== $(date -Is) ==="
  df -h /
} >> "$LOG"
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab17
chmod +x disk-report.sh
./disk-report.sh
test -s logs/disk-report.log
crontab -l 2>/dev/null | tee crontab-before.txt || true

Add a crontab line (run every minute for lab speed):

Terminal
( crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo '* * * * * /home/$USER/rebash-linux/lab17/disk-report.sh' ) | crontab -
crontab -l | tee crontab-after.txt
sleep 65
tail -3 logs/disk-report.log | tee cron-proof.txt
grep -q '=== ' cron-proof.txt

Expected output

After ~65 seconds, cron-proof.txt shows a new timestamp line from the scheduled run.

docs.title: Task 2 – Break, fix, and prove (wrong path)
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab17
( crontab -l 2>/dev/null | sed 's|disk-report.sh|disk-report-BROKEN.sh|'; ) | crontab -
sleep 65
wc -l logs/disk-report.log | tee lines-before-fix.txt
( crontab -l 2>/dev/null | sed 's|disk-report-BROKEN.sh|disk-report.sh|'; ) | crontab -
sleep 65
tail -1 logs/disk-report.log | tee cron-after-fix.txt
grep -q '===' cron-after-fix.txt

Expected output

During the broken window, log line count stops growing. After fix, new timestamp appears in cron-after-fix.txt.

docs.title: Task 3 – at job and systemd timer
docs.text:
Create rebash-disk-report.service:

rebash-disk-report.service
[Unit]
Description=REBASH lab17 disk report (oneshot)

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/home/USER_PLACEHOLDER/rebash-linux/lab17/disk-report.sh

Create rebash-disk-report.timer:

rebash-disk-report.timer
[Unit]
Description=REBASH lab17 disk report timer

[Timer]
OnBootSec=2min
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

Replace USER_PLACEHOLDER with your username in the service file, then:

Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab17
sed "s/USER_PLACEHOLDER/$USER/" rebash-disk-report.service | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/rebash-disk-report.service >/dev/null
sudo cp rebash-disk-report.timer /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now rebash-disk-report.timer
systemctl list-timers --all | grep rebash | tee timer-list.txt
echo "echo at-ok >> $HOME/rebash-linux/lab17/logs/at.log" | at now + 1 minute 2>&1 | tee at-schedule.txt
sleep 70
test -s logs/at.log && echo "at ran OK" | tee at-proof.txt
echo "lab17 scheduling OK" | tee evidence.txt

Expected output

timer-list.txt shows rebash-disk-report.timer. at-proof.txt confirms the one-shot job ran.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• Cron job ran and appended to logs/disk-report.log
  • You broke cron with a bad path and fixed it
  • systemd timer is listed in systemctl list-timers
  • at job created logs/at.log

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Cron never runs cron service stopped sudo systemctl enable --now cron Script works manually, not in cron Relative path or missing PATH Absolute paths; log stderr at: command not found Package not installed sudo apt install -y at; start atd Timer inactive Not enabled sudo systemctl enable --now unit.timer

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text: Add a crontab comment line documenting RPO-style “max staleness 24h” for your disk report, and verify with crontab -l.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• You scheduled recurring, one-shot, and systemd-timer jobs
  • You diagnosed a silent cron failure
  • You can explain scheduling trade-offs in interviews

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
crontab -r 2>/dev/null || true
sudo systemctl disable --now rebash-disk-report.timer 2>/dev/null || true
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/rebash-disk-report.{service,timer}
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
atrm $(atq | awk '{print $1}') 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Lab evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab17
  • Can draw cron vs timer vs at on a whiteboard
  • Ready for logging tutorial next

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. */5 * * * * — every 5 minutes; use sparingly in production.
  2. Absolute script path in crontab — avoids PATH surprises.
  3. Type=oneshot service — runs once per timer trigger; good for reports.
  4. OnBootSec=2min — timer fires after boot; Persistent=true catches missed runs.
  5. Break/fix task — mirrors real on-call: job stopped updating log → wrong path in crontab.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Cron runs as the user who owns the crontab — protect script permissions (chmod 750, no world-writable dirs).
  • Do not store secrets in crontab; use restricted env files with 0600 permissions.
  • Review /etc/cron.d/ and root crontab on shared servers.
  • Limit who can use at (/etc/at.deny, /etc/at.allow).
  • systemd unit ExecStart must not invoke untrusted writable scripts.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ No logging from cron jobs.

✅ Always redirect stdout and stderr. Silent failure is the default failure mode.

❌ Editing system cron as root casually.

✅ A typo in /etc/cron.d/ affects the whole host. Test as user crontab first.

❌ Every-minute jobs in production.

✅ Wastes CPU and fills logs. Choose intervals that match business need.

docs.title: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) — Secure File Transfer Between Linux Systems
SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) — Secure File Transfer Between Linux Systems
docs.text: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) is a command-line utility used to securely transfer files and directories between Linux systems over an SSH (Secure Shell) connection. Since SCP uses SSH for authentication and encryption, all transferred data is protected during transmission. Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, Platform Engineers, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) use SCP to copy configuration files, application packages, backups, logs, and scripts between servers.

docs.text:
Imagine:

  • Copying application packages to a production server.
  • Uploading Kubernetes configuration files.
  • Downloading log files for troubleshooting.
  • Backing up configuration files.
  • Deploying scripts to multiple Linux servers.

SCP provides a simple and secure method for transferring files.

docs.title: What is SCP?
docs.text:
SCP stands for:

Secure Copy Protocol

It securely copies files between systems using SSH.

Advantages:

  • Encrypted communication
  • Simple syntax
  • SSH authentication
  • Cross-platform support
  • Secure file transfers

docs.title: How SCP Works
docs.text:
Source System
      │
Encrypted SSH Connection
      │
      ▼
Destination System

All transferred data is encrypted using SSH.

docs.title: Basic SCP Syntax
docs.text:
scp source destination

Example:

scp file.txt admin@192.168.1.100:/home/admin/

This copies file.txt to the remote server.

docs.title: Copy File to a Remote Server
docs.text: scp report.pdf admin@server:/home/admin/

docs.title: Copy File from a Remote Server
docs.text:
scp admin@server:/home/admin/report.pdf .

The file is copied to the current local directory.

docs.title: Copy an Entire Directory
docs.text:
Use the recursive option:

scp -r project/ admin@server:/home/admin/

docs.title: Copy Using a Different SSH Port
docs.text:
If SSH runs on port 2222:

scp -P 2222 file.txt admin@server:/tmp/

Note: SCP uses an uppercase -P for the port option.

docs.title: Use an SSH Private Key
docs.text:
scp -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 \
file.txt admin@server:/tmp/

docs.title: Preserve File Attributes
docs.text:
Preserve:

  • Permissions
  • Timestamps
  • Modification times
scp -p file.txt admin@server:/tmp/

docs.title: Enable Compression
docs.text:
Compress data during transfer.

scp -C largefile.iso admin@server:/backup/

Useful for slower network connections.

docs.title: Copy Between Two Remote Servers
docs.text:
scp admin@server1:/tmp/file.txt \
admin@server2:/tmp/

The local machine coordinates the transfer between the two remote systems.

docs.title: Display Transfer Progress
docs.text:
SCP displays progress by default.

Example:

file.txt

100%

5 MB

2.5 MB/s

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Upload file.

scp file.txt admin@server:/tmp/

Download file.

scp admin@server:/tmp/file.txt .

Copy directory.

scp -r website/ admin@server:/var/www/

Use SSH key.

scp -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 file.txt admin@server:/tmp/

Use compression.

scp -C backup.tar.gz admin@server:/backup/

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Deploy an application.

scp app.jar admin@web01:/opt/apps/

Upload Kubernetes configuration.

scp kubeconfig admin@master:/home/admin/.kube/config

Download log files.

scp admin@server:/var/log/nginx/error.log .

Backup configuration.

scp /etc/nginx/nginx.conf \
admin@backup:/configs/

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
SCP is commonly used for:

  • Application deployments
  • Configuration backups
  • Log collection
  • Cloud server administration
  • Kubernetes configuration
  • Infrastructure automation
  • Disaster recovery

Although SCP is simple and secure, rsync is often preferred for large or repeated transfers because it transfers only changed data.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create a test file.

echo "Linux Mastery" > test.txt

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Upload the file.

scp test.txt username@server:/tmp/

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Download the file.

scp username@server:/tmp/test.txt .

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Copy a directory.

scp -r project/ username@server:/tmp/

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Transfer using an SSH key.

scp -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 test.txt \
username@server:/tmp/

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Transfer using compression.

scp -C backup.tar.gz \
username@server:/backup/

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Transfer using a custom SSH port.

scp -P 2222 test.txt \
username@server:/tmp/

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Verify the copied file.

ssh username@server

ls -l /tmp/

docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example scp file user@host:path Upload file Application deployment scp user@host:file . Download file Log collection scp -r Copy directory Website deployment scp -P Use custom SSH port Hardened servers scp -i Use SSH private key Secure authentication scp -p Preserve timestamps and permissions Configuration backup scp -C Compress transfer Large file transfer

docs.title: Common SCP Errors
docs.text: Error Possible Cause Permission denied Incorrect credentials or file permissions Connection refused SSH service unavailable No such file or directory Incorrect source or destination path Host key verification failed SSH host key mismatch Connection timed out Firewall or network issue

docs.title: SCP vs FTP vs SFTP
docs.text: Feature SCP SFTP FTP Encryption ✅ ✅ ❌ Uses SSH ✅ ✅ ❌ Interactive File Management ❌ ✅ ✅ Secure ✅ ✅ ❌ Production Ready ✅ ✅ ❌

docs.title: SCP vs rsync
docs.text: Feature SCP rsync Simple File Copy ✅ ✅ Incremental Transfer ❌ ✅ Synchronization ❌ ✅ Compression ✅ ✅ Resume Interrupted Transfers Limited ✅ Best For One-time transfers Repeated synchronization

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A DevOps engineer attempts to deploy an application.

scp app.jar admin@server:/opt/apps/

Error:

Permission denied

Investigation:

Verify SSH access.

ssh admin@server

Check destination permissions.

ls -ld /opt/apps

The deployment directory is owned by another user.

Correct the ownership or permissions.

sudo chown admin:admin /opt/apps

Retry:

scp app.jar admin@server:/opt/apps/

The deployment completes successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use SSH key-based authentication.
  • Verify destination paths before transferring files.
  • Use compression (-C) for large transfers over slow networks.
  • Preserve file attributes when copying configuration files.
  • Use SCP for one-time transfers and rsync for recurring synchronization tasks.
  • Verify transferred files after completion.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting to use uppercase -P for the SSH port.

✅ Remember to to use uppercase -P for the SSH port.

❌ Using password authentication instead of SSH keys.

✅ Prefer SSH keys rather than using password authentication.

❌ Copying files to incorrect directories.

✅ Avoid this mistake: copying files to incorrect directories.

❌ Assuming SCP can synchronize changed files like rsync.

✅ Verify SCP can synchronize changed files like rsync instead of assuming it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • SCP fundamentals
  • Secure file transfers
  • Directory transfers
  • SSH key authentication
  • Compression
  • File preservation
  • Production deployment techniques

SCP provides a secure and straightforward method for transferring files between Linux systems using SSH encryption. It is ideal for one-time file transfers, application deployments, backups, and administrative tasks across production environments.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SCP securely transfers files using SSH.
  • Use scp -r to copy directories.
  • Use -P for custom SSH ports.
  • Use -i for SSH key authentication.
  • Use -C to compress large transfers.
  • Use SCP for simple transfers and rsync for efficient synchronization.

By the end of the lesson, you'll understand why rsync is one of the most powerful tools for backups, deployments, and synchronizing data across Linux systems.

docs.title: Searching Files and Directories
docs.text: Linux provides powerful tools to search for files, directories, commands, and executables. Whether you're locating configuration files, troubleshooting applications, or managing production servers, mastering file search commands is an essential Linux skill.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 2: Linux Command Line Essentials → Lesson 6

Difficulty: Beginner

Reading Time: 30 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Linux Command Line Essentials

Lesson: 6 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Search files and directories
  • Search by name
  • Search by type
  • Search by size
  • Search by owner
  • Search by permissions
  • Search by modification time
  • Locate executables
  • Search efficiently in production systems

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 Lessons 1–5

docs.title: Why Learn File Searching?
docs.text:
Imagine you're working on a production server.

You need to find:

  • NGINX configuration
  • Docker Compose file
  • Kubernetes manifests
  • SSH configuration
  • Log files
  • Recently modified files

Instead of manually browsing thousands of directories, Linux provides commands that can find them in seconds.

docs.title: Linux Search Commands
docs.text:
Linux offers several search utilities.

Command Purpose find Search files and directories locate Fast filename search which Find executable in PATH whereis Locate binary, source and man pages type Identify command type

Each command solves a different problem.

docs.title: The find Command
docs.text:
find is the most powerful file search command.

Syntax

find <path> <expression>

Search from current directory:

find .

Search entire filesystem:

find /

docs.title: Search by File Name
docs.text:
Find a file named:

find . -name "notes.txt"

Example output:

./Documents/notes.txt

docs.title: Case-Insensitive Search
docs.text:
find . -iname "notes.txt"

Matches:

Notes.txt

NOTES.TXT

notes.txt

docs.title: Search Directories
docs.text:
find . -type d

Output:

.

./projects

./logs

./backup

docs.title: Search Regular Files
docs.text: find . -type f

docs.title: Search Hidden Files
docs.text: find . -name ".*"

docs.title: Search Using Wildcards
docs.text:
Find all text files.

find . -name "*.txt"

Find all YAML files.

find . -name "*.yaml"

Find shell scripts.

find . -name "*.sh"

docs.title: Search by Size
docs.text:
Files larger than 100 MB

find . -size +100M

Files smaller than 10 KB

find . -size -10k

Exactly 50 MB

find . -size 50M

docs.title: Search by Owner
docs.text: find /home -user basha

docs.title: Search by Group
docs.text: find /home -group developers

docs.title: Search by Permissions
docs.text:
Example:

find . -perm 644

Find executable files.

find . -perm /111

docs.title: Search by Modification Time
docs.text:
Modified today

find . -mtime 0

Modified within last 7 days

find . -mtime -7

Older than 30 days

find . -mtime +30

docs.title: Search Empty Files
docs.text: find . -empty

docs.title: Execute Commands on Search Results
docs.text:
Delete log files.

find . -name "*.log" -delete

Display file details.

find . -name "*.txt" -exec ls -l {} \;

Warning

Always verify search results before using -delete.

docs.title: The locate Command
docs.text:
locate searches a pre-built database.

Example:

locate sshd_config

Much faster than find.

docs.title: Update locate Database
docs.text:
Ubuntu

sudo updatedb

Now:

locate nginx.conf

docs.title: which
docs.text:
Find executable location.

which python3

Example

/usr/bin/python3

Useful for verifying installed commands.

docs.title: whereis
docs.text:
Displays:

  • Binary
  • Source
  • Manual page

Example:

whereis ssh

Output

ssh:
/usr/bin/ssh
/usr/share/man/man1/ssh.1.gz

docs.title: type
docs.text:
Identify command type.

type ls

Output

ls is /usr/bin/ls

Example

type cd

Output

cd is a shell builtin

docs.title: Command Comparison
docs.text: Command Best For find Powerful searches locate Fast filename search which Executables whereis Binary + Man Page type Built-in vs External

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Find NGINX configuration.

find /etc -name nginx.conf

Find Docker Compose files.

find /opt -name docker-compose.yml

Find Kubernetes YAML.

find . -name "*.yaml"

Find large log files.

find /var/log -size +500M

Find recently modified files.

find /etc -mtime -1

Find executable shell scripts.

find . -name "*.sh" -perm /111

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
System administrators frequently search for:

  • Configuration files
  • Log files
  • Core dumps
  • Backup archives
  • SSL certificates
  • Shell scripts
  • Kubernetes manifests
  • Docker files

Knowing how to search efficiently can significantly reduce troubleshooting time.

docs.text:

cd search-lab

touch config.yaml

Search YAML.

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Search shell scripts.

find . -name "*.sh"

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Search files only.

find . -type f

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Search directories.

find . -type d

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Locate Python.

which python3

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Find SSH.

whereis ssh

docs.title: Task 9
docs.text:
Identify command type.

type cd

type ls

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Common Options Production Example find Search filesystem -name, -type, -size, -mtime Find configs and logs locate Fast filename search -i Locate SSH configs which Find executable Default Verify installed tools whereis Binary + docs Default Find binaries type Command type -a Check shell built-ins

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A web application has stopped working after a configuration change.

Your tasks:

  1. Find the NGINX configuration file.
  2. Locate all backup configuration files.
  3. Identify recently modified configuration files.
  4. Find log files larger than 100 MB.
  5. Verify where the nginx executable is installed.

Example commands:

find /etc -name "nginx.conf"

find /etc -name "*.bak"

find /etc -mtime -1

find /var/log -size +100M

which nginx

docs.title: Mini Challenge
docs.text:
Create the following structure.

project/

├── app.py

├── config/

│   ├── app.yaml

│   ├── db.yaml

│   └── nginx.conf

├── logs/

│   ├── access.log

│   └── error.log

└── scripts/

    ├── deploy.sh

    └── backup.sh

Complete these tasks:

  • Find all .yaml files.
  • Find all shell scripts.
  • Find all log files.
  • Display only directories.
  • Find all files modified today.
  • Locate the bash executable.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use find for comprehensive searches.
  • Use locate when speed is important.
  • Limit searches to specific directories instead of searching the entire filesystem.
  • Verify results before deleting files.
  • Combine search criteria for more precise results.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Searching the entire filesystem unnecessarily.

✅ Use:

find /

This can be slow.

Instead:

find /etc

❌ Using rm immediately after find.

✅ Always inspect results first.

❌ Forgetting quotes around wildcards.

✅ Correct:

find . -name "*.log"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Searching files and directories
  • Searching by name, type, size, owner, permissions, and modification time
  • Using find, locate, which, whereis, and type
  • Real-world search techniques used in production environments

Mastering these commands will make troubleshooting, automation, and system administration significantly faster and more efficient.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• find is the most powerful Linux search command.
  • locate provides fast filename searches using an indexed database.
  • which finds executables in your PATH.
  • whereis locates binaries, source files, and manual pages.
  • type identifies whether a command is built-in or external.
  • Always verify search results before performing destructive actions.

docs.title: Secrets Management — Protecting Sensitive Information in Linux
Secrets Management — Protecting Sensitive Information in Linux
docs.text: Secrets Management is the practice of securely storing, accessing, rotating, and protecting sensitive information such as passwords, API keys, SSH keys, database credentials, encryption keys, and certificates. Poor secrets management is one of the most common causes of security breaches. Hardcoding secrets into scripts, configuration files, or source code can expose critical infrastructure to attackers. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand how to manage secrets securely in production environments.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 11: Linux Security → Lesson 9

Difficulty: Beginner → Advanced

Reading Time: 95 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Linux Security

Lesson: 9 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand secrets management
  • Identify different types of secrets
  • Avoid common security mistakes
  • Secure secrets in Linux
  • Use environment variables safely
  • Learn enterprise secret management solutions
  • Rotate secrets securely
  • Apply production best practices

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Modules 1–10
  • Module 11 Lessons 1–8

docs.title: Why Learn Secrets Management?
docs.text:
Imagine a deployment script.

Poor practice:

PASSWORD="MyPassword123"

Anyone who can read the script now has the password.

Secure approach:

Secret Store

↓

Application Requests Secret

↓

Temporary Access

↓

Credential Never Stored in Code

Secrets remain protected throughout their lifecycle.

docs.title: What is a Secret?
docs.text:
A secret is any sensitive information used for authentication, authorization, or encryption.

Examples include:

  • Passwords
  • API keys
  • SSH private keys
  • Database credentials
  • Cloud access keys
  • OAuth tokens
  • TLS certificates
  • Encryption keys

docs.title: Why Secrets Must Be Protected
docs.text:
If secrets are exposed, attackers may gain:

  • Server access
  • Database access
  • Cloud account access
  • Application control
  • Sensitive customer data
  • Internal infrastructure access

docs.title: Common Secrets
docs.text: Secret Example Password Linux login API Key Cloud API SSH Key Remote access Token GitHub Personal Access Token Certificate TLS/SSL Database Password PostgreSQL login

docs.title: Common Security Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid:

Hardcoding passwords.

PASSWORD="admin123"

Storing secrets in:

  • Git repositories
  • Source code
  • Public cloud storage
  • Shared documents
  • Chat messages

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
A safer alternative for many applications.

Example:

export DB_PASSWORD="StrongPassword"

Read:

echo "$DB_PASSWORD"

Applications can access the variable without embedding it directly in source code.

Note

Environment variables are more secure than hardcoding credentials, but they are not a complete secrets management solution because privileged users or processes may still be able to access them.

docs.title: Using a .env File
docs.text:
Example:

DB_USER=admin

DB_PASSWORD=StrongPassword

Load:

source .env

Best practice:

.gitignore

↓

.env

Never commit .env files containing secrets to version control.

docs.title: File Permissions for Secrets
docs.text:
Restrict access.

Example:

chmod 600 .env

Owner only.

docs.title: SSH Private Keys
docs.text:
Secure permissions.

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Directory:

chmod 700 ~/.ssh

docs.title: Secret Rotation
docs.text:
Secrets should be changed regularly.

Example:

Old API Key

↓

Generate New Key

↓

Update Applications

↓

Remove Old Key

Benefits:

  • Limits exposure
  • Reduces long-term risk
  • Supports compliance

docs.title: Enterprise Secret Managers
docs.text:
Common solutions:

  • HashiCorp Vault
  • AWS Secrets Manager
  • Azure Key Vault
  • Google Secret Manager
  • Kubernetes Secrets (when combined with encryption and RBAC)

These systems provide:

  • Encryption
  • Access control
  • Auditing
  • Automatic rotation
  • Centralized management

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
Apply the principle of least privilege.

Only authorized users and applications should access secrets.

Example:

Application A

↓

Database Password

✓ Allowed

Application B

↓

Database Password

✗ Denied

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Secrets should be encrypted:

  • At rest
  • In transit

Use:

  • TLS
  • Disk encryption
  • Secret management platforms
  • Encrypted backups

docs.title: Auditing Secret Access
docs.text:
Monitor:

  • Who accessed a secret
  • When it was accessed
  • Which application requested it
  • Failed access attempts

Audit logs help detect misuse and support compliance.

docs.title: Kubernetes Secrets
docs.text:
Kubernetes provides:

Secret

resource objects.

Example:

kubectl get secrets

Remember:

  • Base64 encoding is not encryption.
  • Enable encryption at rest.
  • Use RBAC to restrict access.
  • Consider integrating with an external secrets manager for production workloads.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Create environment variable.

export API_KEY="value"

Display variable.

echo "$API_KEY"

Secure file.

chmod 600 .env

List secrets.

kubectl get secrets

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Secure SSH key.

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Secure configuration.

chmod 600 .env

Read environment variable.

echo "$DB_PASSWORD"

List Kubernetes secrets.

kubectl get secrets

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Secrets management is critical for:

  • Cloud platforms
  • Kubernetes
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Databases
  • Linux servers
  • Web applications
  • Enterprise infrastructure
  • DevOps automation

Poor secrets management is one of the leading causes of cloud security incidents.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create an environment variable.

export APP_TOKEN="example-token"

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Display the variable.

echo "$APP_TOKEN"

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Create a .env file.

API_KEY=example-key

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Protect the file.

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Load the file.

source .env

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Check SSH key permissions.

ls -l ~/.ssh

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
List Kubernetes secrets.

kubectl get secrets

(Requires access to a Kubernetes cluster.)

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text: Review your scripts and ensure that no passwords or API keys are hardcoded.

docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example export Create environment variable Application configuration source Load environment variables Deployment scripts chmod 600 Protect secret files Configuration security kubectl get secrets List Kubernetes secrets Cluster administration ls -l ~/.ssh Verify SSH key permissions SSH security printenv View environment variables Troubleshooting

docs.title: Common Secrets Management Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Solution Hardcoding passwords Use a secrets manager or secure configuration Committing secrets to Git Use .gitignore and secret scanning Weak file permissions Restrict access with chmod 600 Never rotating secrets Rotate credentials regularly Sharing secrets through email or chat Use secure secret-sharing methods

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A developer accidentally commits AWS credentials to a Git repository.

Result:

Git Repository

↓

Credentials Exposed

↓

Unauthorized Cloud Access

Correct response:

  1. Revoke the exposed credentials immediately.
  2. Generate new credentials.
  3. Update applications with the new secrets.
  4. Remove the secret from the repository history if appropriate.
  5. Enable secret scanning and review audit logs.
  6. Move the credentials to a dedicated secrets management solution.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Never hardcode secrets in scripts or source code.
  • Use dedicated secrets management platforms for production.
  • Encrypt secrets at rest and in transit.
  • Rotate credentials regularly.
  • Apply the principle of least privilege.
  • Audit access to sensitive credentials.
  • Protect secret files with restrictive permissions.
  • Enable secret scanning in CI/CD pipelines and version control workflows.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Hardcoding passwords in scripts.

✅ Avoid this mistake: hardcoding passwords in scripts.

❌ Uploading secrets to Git repositories.

✅ Avoid this mistake: uploading secrets to Git repositories.

❌ Sharing credentials through insecure communication channels.

✅ Avoid this mistake: sharing credentials through insecure communication channels.

❌ Never rotating API keys or passwords.

✅ Always rotating API keys or passwords.

❌ Granting unnecessary access to sensitive credentials.

✅ Avoid this mistake: granting unnecessary access to sensitive credentials.

docs.title: SELinux, AppArmor, Fail2Ban, Auditd, and PAM
SELinux, AppArmor, Fail2Ban, Auditd, and PAM
Overview
docs.text:
File permissions (chmod) feel like the whole security story — until something still fails with “Permission denied” and the mode bits look correct. Linux often has extra layers beyond owner/group/other: SELinux or AppArmor, PAM, Fail2Ban, and auditd.

Plain problem: A web server cannot write to a directory you chmod 777’d (bad practice anyway). Logs show AppArmor or SELinux denials. Someone suggests “disable security” — that is almost never the right first move.

This tutorial explains, in simple words first:

  1. Mandatory Access Control (MAC) — AppArmor (Ubuntu) and SELinux (RHEL family)
  2. Fail2Ban — ban IPs after repeated SSH failures
  3. auditd — security audit trail
  4. Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) — how login and sudo really authenticate

This is Tutorial 13b in Module 13: Linux Security of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ubuntu practice VM (AppArmor enabled by default)
  • SSH Hardening and Firewalls
  • sudo for installing Fail2Ban and reading audit logs

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain DAC vs MAC with a simple analogy
  • Check AppArmor status on Ubuntu without disabling it
  • Describe SELinux modes and where you meet SELinux at work
  • Install Fail2Ban, trigger a lab ban, and verify unban
  • Query auditd / journal for denial-style events
  • Name what PAM controls (login, sudo, password policy)
  • Answer fresher interview questions on these tools

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) is classic Unix permissions. MAC adds policy labels enforced by the kernel regardless of chmod. PAM stacks authentication modules for login paths. Fail2Ban watches logs and updates firewall. auditd records auditable events.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text: You deploy nginx to a new path. Config test passes. Service fails. journalctl shows AppArmor DENIED. Beginners often blame “Linux is broken”. The fix is read the denial, adjust policy or path — not turn off MAC globally.

docs.title: DAC vs MAC (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: DAC is a sticky note on your desk — “only Alice may open this drawer” (the owner decides). MAC is building security — even if Alice owns the drawer, fire policy says “no flammable liquids in this wing”.

Layer Who decides Example DAC File owner chmod 640 file MAC System policy AppArmor profile, SELinux context

AppArmor (Ubuntu): profiles per program (/etc/apparmor.d/). SELinux (RHEL/Rocky): labels on processes and files (contexts).

Interview line: “If permissions look correct but access fails, I check MAC denials and audit logs before chmod 777.”

docs.title: AppArmor on Ubuntu
docs.text:
Terminal
sudo aa-status
sudo journalctl -k | grep -i apparmor | tail -5

Profiles can be enforce or complain mode. Use complain while debugging new apps.

docs.title: SELinux (you will meet on RHEL/AWS)
docs.text:
Even on Ubuntu labs, interviews ask SELinux basics:

Mode Behaviour Enforcing Blocks policy violations Permissive Logs but allows Disabled Off (avoid without reason) Terminal
# On RHEL-family hosts:
getenforce
sestatus
ausearch -m avc -ts recent

Fix paths: correct context (restorecon), booleans, or tailored policy — not permanent disable.

docs.title: Fail2Ban
docs.text:
Analogy: A door sensor — after five bad key attempts, block that IP at the firewall for ten minutes.

Watches logs (often /var/log/auth.log or journal), updates iptables/nftables via actions.

docs.title: auditd
docs.text:
auditd writes structured security events — who changed what, MAC denials (AVC), syscall access. Compliance teams rely on it.

Terminal
sudo systemctl status auditd
sudo ausearch -m USER_LOGIN --start recent 2>/dev/null | head

docs.title: PAM
docs.text:
PAM is the stack of modules for authentication: local password, LDAP, MFA, sudo rules, session limits. Files under /etc/pam.d/ (e.g. sshd, sudo).

Interview line: “SSH auth goes through PAM; a typo in /etc/pam.d/sshd can lock login even when keys are fine.”

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• setenforce 0 / disabling AppArmor on first error
  • Fail2Ban jailing yourself during lab brute-force tests (use localhost carefully)
  • Editing PAM without a console backup
  • Confusing Fail2Ban with MAC — different layers

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Collect AppArmor status, configure a minimal Fail2Ban jail for SSH, simulate failed logins to trigger a ban, fix by unbanning, and save evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab21 — without disabling MAC.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM AppArmor active sudo Fail2Ban install Lab-only Do not aim brute force at production IPs

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab21 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab21
sudo aa-status 2>&1 | tee apparmor-status.txt | head -20

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Security review: “Prove AppArmor is enforcing, Fail2Ban protects SSH, and you can read a denial or ban event from logs — without turning off AppArmor.”

docs.title: Task 1 – AppArmor and audit evidence
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab21
sudo aa-status | tee apparmor-full.txt
grep -c 'enforce' apparmor-full.txt | tee apparmor-enforce-count.txt
sudo systemctl is-active auditd 2>/dev/null | tee auditd-state.txt || echo "inactive" | tee auditd-state.txt
sudo journalctl -k --no-pager | grep -i 'apparmor\|denied' | tail -10 | tee kernel-denial-sample.txt || echo "no recent denials" | tee kernel-denial-sample.txt
test -s apparmor-full.txt

Expected output

apparmor-full.txt lists profiles; many show enforce mode on Ubuntu desktop/server images.

docs.title: Task 2 – Fail2Ban install and jail
docs.text:
Create jail.local:

jail.local
[sshd]
enabled = true
port = ssh
filter = sshd
logpath = /var/log/auth.log
maxretry = 3
bantime = 300
findtime = 60
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab21
sudo apt install -y fail2ban
sudo cp jail.local /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/rebash-lab21.local
sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd | tee fail2ban-sshd-before.txt

Expected output

Fail2Ban active; fail2ban-sshd-before.txt shows sshd jail.

docs.title: Task 3 – Break (trigger ban), fix (unban), prove
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab21
for i in 1 2 3 4; do
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ConnectTimeout=2 baduser@127.0.0.1 2>/dev/null || true
done
sleep 3
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd | tee fail2ban-after-failures.txt
grep -q 'Banned IP list' fail2ban-after-failures.txt
sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 127.0.0.1 2>/dev/null || sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip ::1 2>/dev/null || true
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd | tee fail2ban-after-unban.txt
echo "lab21 security layers OK" | tee evidence.txt

Expected output

After deliberate failed SSH attempts, banned IP list may include 127.0.0.1. After unban, list clears or SSH succeeds again.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:

  • Fail2Ban sshd jail active
  • Ban/unban cycle demonstrated with logs
  • You can explain DAC vs MAC verbally

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Fail2Ban no ban Wrong logpath Ubuntu uses /var/log/auth.log; check journal backend Locked out (real IP) Testing on production IP Use lab VM; unban via console aa-status empty AppArmor not installed Rare on Ubuntu server — apt install apparmor-utils auditd inactive Minimal image Note in evidence; use journal for denials

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. aa-status — quick AppArmor health check on Ubuntu.
  2. Fail2Ban jail.local — small override; do not edit entire jail.conf.
  3. Deliberate failed SSH — lab-only; triggers filter on auth.log lines.
  4. fail2ban-client unbanip — recovery without disabling Fail2Ban.
  5. journal AppArmor lines — real denial signals when profiles block paths.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Never disable MAC fleet-wide to “fix” one app — tune profile or path.
  • Fail2Ban can block legitimate IPs behind NAT — tune thresholds.
  • PAM edits can brick login — test on console-backed VM only.
  • auditd logs may contain sensitive data — protect /var/log/audit/.
  • Document break-glass accounts and MFA outside PAM experiments.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ chmod 777 instead of reading MAC denial.

✅ Fix policy or file location; world-writable dirs are worse than the original problem.

❌ Permanently disabling SELinux.

✅ Enterprises expect Enforcing. Learn audit2allow / vendor guides instead.

❌ Fail2Ban on wrong log path.

✅ Journal-only systems may need backend=systemd in jail — read distro docs.

docs.title: SELinux Overview — Mandatory Access Control in Linux
SELinux Overview — Mandatory Access Control in Linux
docs.text: SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) is a Linux security framework that provides Mandatory Access Control (MAC). Unlike traditional Linux permissions, which rely on file ownership and user permissions, SELinux applies security policies that determine what processes are allowed to access specific files, directories, ports, and system resources. Even if a process is running as the root user, SELinux can still restrict its actions according to the defined security policy. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should understand SELinux to secure enterprise Linux systems.

docs.text:
Imagine a web server running as the root user.

Without SELinux:

Web Server

↓

Compromised

↓

Access Entire System

With SELinux:

Web Server

↓

Compromised

↓

Restricted by SELinux Policy

↓

Limited Damage

SELinux reduces the impact of successful attacks.

docs.title: What is SELinux?
docs.text:
SELinux stands for:

Security-Enhanced Linux

It is a security framework that enforces Mandatory Access Control (MAC).

Instead of relying only on:

  • User ownership
  • File permissions

SELinux also evaluates:

  • Security contexts
  • Security policies
  • Process permissions

docs.title: DAC vs MAC
docs.text:
Linux normally uses:

DAC

↓

Discretionary Access Control

Users control access through:

  • Owner
  • Group
  • Permissions

SELinux introduces:

MAC

↓

Mandatory Access Control

System policies decide whether access is allowed.

Even the root user must follow SELinux policies.

docs.title: How SELinux Works
docs.text:
Every object has a security context.

Example:

Process

↓

SELinux Policy

↓

File

↓

Allow or Deny

Both traditional Linux permissions and SELinux policies must allow access.

docs.title: SELinux Modes
docs.text:
SELinux has three operating modes.

Mode Description Enforcing Policies are enforced Permissive Violations are logged but not blocked Disabled SELinux is disabled

docs.title: Check SELinux Status
docs.text:
getenforce

Example:

Enforcing

Detailed information:

sestatus

Example output:

SELinux status: enabled

Current mode: enforcing

docs.title: Change SELinux Mode
docs.text:
Temporarily switch to permissive mode.

sudo setenforce 0

Return to enforcing mode.

sudo setenforce 1

These changes are temporary and last until the next reboot.

docs.title: Persistent Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration file:

/etc/selinux/config

Example:

SELINUX=enforcing

Possible values:

enforcing

permissive

disabled

Reboot the system after changing the configuration file.

docs.title: Security Contexts
docs.text:
Display SELinux contexts.

ls -Z

Example:

-rw-r--r-- root root system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 index.html

docs.title: Understanding Security Context
docs.text:
Example:

system_u

object_r

httpd_sys_content_t

s0

Components:

Component Description User SELinux user Role SELinux role Type Security type Level Security level

The type is the most commonly used component in policy enforcement.

docs.title: View Process Contexts
docs.text:
ps -eZ

Example:

system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0

docs.title: Common SELinux Commands
docs.text:

getenforce

Restore the default SELinux context.

restorecon -Rv /var/www/html

Useful after moving or copying files.

docs.title: Change File Context
docs.text:
Assign a new context.

sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t index.html

Note

chcon changes are temporary and may be lost after a relabel. For permanent changes, use semanage fcontext followed by restorecon.

docs.title: Managing Ports
docs.text:

semanage port -l

Example:

http_port_t

Enable a boolean permanently.

sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on

docs.title: Common SELinux Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Solution Disabling SELinux permanently Keep it enabled whenever possible Ignoring SELinux logs Review audit logs to identify denials Using chcon for permanent changes Use semanage fcontext and restorecon Switching to permissive mode permanently Use only for troubleshooting Changing file permissions instead of fixing SELinux contexts Restore or assign the correct context

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A web server cannot access newly copied website files.

Linux permissions:

Correct

Application still fails.

Investigation:

ls -Z /var/www/html

The files have incorrect SELinux contexts.

Solution:

sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html

The correct SELinux labels are restored, and the web server can access the files without changing Linux file permissions.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Keep SELinux in Enforcing mode in production.
  • Use Permissive mode only for troubleshooting.
  • Never disable SELinux unless absolutely necessary.
  • Restore correct file contexts after moving files.
  • Review SELinux denials using audit logs.
  • Use semanage for permanent policy changes.
  • Test policy changes in a non-production environment.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Disabling SELinux to bypass configuration issues.

✅ Avoid disabling SELinux to bypass configuration issues; fix the configuration instead.

❌ Ignoring SELinux denial messages.

✅ Always review SELinux denial messages.

❌ Using chmod 777 instead of fixing SELinux contexts.

✅ Prefer fixing SELinux contexts rather than using chmod 777.

❌ Forgetting to restore file contexts after copying application files.

✅ Remember to to restore file contexts after copying application files.

❌ Leaving systems in permissive mode permanently.

✅ Do not leave systems in permissive mode permanently.

By configuring your shell, you can improve productivity, automate repetitive tasks, personalize your environment, and create a consistent development experience. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, and SRE customizes their shell to work more efficiently.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Aliases create shortcuts for frequently used commands.

Syntax:

alias name='command'

Example:

alias ll='ls -lah'

Now simply run:

ll

instead of:

ls -lah

docs.title: Useful Aliases
docs.text:
alias ll='ls -lah'

backup() {

backup report.txt

report.txt.bak

PS1

Linux Profiles — Configuring User Login Environments
docs.text: Every time a user logs into a Linux system, the shell automatically loads a series of configuration files that define the user's working environment. These files, known as profile files, configure environment variables, aliases, shell settings, startup commands, and application behavior. Understanding Linux profiles is essential for system administrators, DevOps engineers, and developers who want to customize or standardize Linux environments.

docs.title: Why Learn Profiles?
docs.text:
Imagine you configure:

export JAVA_HOME=/opt/java

Everything works perfectly.

You log out.

Log back in.

The variable is gone.

Why?

Because it wasn't saved in a profile file.

docs.title: What is a Profile?
docs.text:
A profile is a configuration file that Linux reads automatically when a shell starts.

Profiles are used to configure:

  • Environment variables
  • PATH
  • Aliases
  • Startup commands
  • Default editors
  • Application settings

docs.title: Login Shell
docs.text:
Started when:

  • Logging in through SSH
  • Logging in at the console
  • Starting a login terminal

Reads login profile files.

docs.title: Non-login Shell
docs.text:
Started when:

  • Opening another terminal window
  • Running Bash inside Bash

Reads shell configuration files instead.

docs.title: Linux Startup Sequence
docs.text:
A typical Bash login shell loads files in this order:

System Profile
      │
      ▼
/etc/profile
      │
      ▼
~/.bash_profile
      │
      ▼
~/.bash_login
      │
      ▼
~/.profile
      │
      ▼
~/.bashrc

Note

Bash reads the first existing file among .bash_profile, .bash_login, and .profile.

docs.title: System-wide Profile
docs.text:
/etc/profile

Applies to:

All Users

Typical uses:

  • Global PATH
  • Corporate environment variables
  • Company-wide shell settings

View:

cat /etc/profile

docs.title: User Profile
docs.text:
~/.profile

Applies only to:

Current User

Example:

export JAVA_HOME=/opt/java

export PATH=$PATH:$JAVA_HOME/bin

docs.title: Bash Login Profile
docs.text:
~/.bash_profile

Common contents:

if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then
    . ~/.bashrc
fi

This loads .bashrc automatically for login shells.

docs.title: Shell Configuration
docs.text:
~/.bashrc

Loaded for:

  • Interactive non-login shells

Typically contains:

  • Aliases
  • Functions
  • Prompt (PS1)
  • Shell options

We'll explore .bashrc in detail in the next lesson.

docs.title: System Environment File
docs.text:
/etc/environment

Stores system-wide environment variables.

Example:

JAVA_HOME=/opt/java
EDITOR=vim

Unlike shell profile files, this file typically contains simple variable assignments without shell scripting syntax.

docs.title: Viewing Profile Files
docs.text:
ls -la ~

cat ~/.profile

cat ~/.bash_profile

cat ~/.bashrc

docs.title: Adding a Variable Permanently
docs.text:
Edit:

nano ~/.profile

Add:

export PROJECT=REBASH

Save the file.

docs.title: Reload a Profile
docs.text:
Without logging out:

source ~/.profile

or

. ~/.profile

Verify:

echo $PROJECT

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A developer configures:

export JAVA_HOME=/opt/java

The application works.

After logging in again:

echo $JAVA_HOME

Output:

The variable was set only for the current session.

Solution:

Add it to:

~/.profile

or

~/.bash_profile

Reload:

source ~/.profile

The variable is now available in future login sessions.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Store permanent environment variables in profile files.
  • Keep user-specific settings in your home directory.
  • Use /etc/profile only for system-wide settings.
  • Reload profile files after making changes.
  • Document custom environment variables for team members.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:

✅ They disappear after logout.

❌ Editing system-wide profile files when only one user needs the change.

✅ Edit system-wide profile files when only one user needs the change only when appropriate and with a backup.

❌ Forgetting to reload the profile after editing it.

✅ Remember to to reload the profile after editing it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
“Write a small script” sounds scary until you see it is mostly saved commands with safety rails. Good Bash habits surface errors early instead of hiding them on production hosts.

Plain problem: A midnight cron script fails silently — no set -e, errors swallowed, exit code always 0. Monitoring thinks all is well. Good scripts fail loudly and leave evidence.

This page teaches the operations minimum: shebang, set -euo pipefail, arguments, exit codes, and readable output. Full Bash curriculum lives in the Shell Scripting track.

This is a Command Line tutorial in the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ubuntu practice VM or WSL2
  • Essential Linux Commands
  • Text editor (nano, vim, or VS Code)

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain what a shell script is in plain language
  • Write a script with shebang and safe mode flags
  • Use positional arguments ($1, $#) and exit codes
  • Build a small host-check script that fails clearly
  • Break a script on purpose and fix it
  • Answer fresher interview questions on Bash scripting basics

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: You write a text file → mark executable → shell reads lines top to bottom → each command returns an exit code → caller (cron/systemd/human) sees success or failure.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
Team script:

grep ERROR /var/log/app.log
echo "check done"

Log missing → grep fails → without set -e script continues → “check done” anyway → false green status.

docs.title: What is a shell script? (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: A recipe card for the shell — step 1, step 2, same every time. Bash is the cook reading the card.

First line shebang picks the interpreter:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

Interview line: “I start ops scripts with set -euo pipefail so failures stop the script and unset variables error.”

docs.title: Safe mode — set -euo pipefail
docs.text: Flag Meaning -e Exit on first command failure -u Error on unset variables -o pipefail Pipeline fails if any command fails

docs.title: Arguments and exit codes
docs.text:
Terminal
echo "First arg: ${1:-none}"
exit 0   # success
exit 1   # generic failure

$? holds last exit code. Cron and systemd use it for success/failure.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• No shebang → wrong shell on cron
  • Unquoted variables breaking on spaces
  • Parsing ls output (use find or globs)
  • Missing chmod +x

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Build host-check.sh with safe modes, arguments, intentional break, fix, and evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab-shell.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM bash Lab only Script checks local disk

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab-shell && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-shell

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Mentor: “Give me a script I can run from cron that checks root disk usage and exits non-zero if above a threshold — must not hide errors.”

docs.title: Task 1 – host-check.sh (working version)
docs.text:
Create host-check.sh:

host-check.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

THRESH="${1:-90}"
LOG="${HOME}/rebash-linux/lab-shell/host-check.log"
MOUNT="/"

usage="$(df -P "$MOUNT" | awk 'NR==2 {print $5}' | tr -d '%')"
{
  echo "=== $(date -Is) ==="
  echo "mount=$MOUNT usage_percent=$usage threshold=$THRESH"
} >> "$LOG"

if [[ "$usage" -ge "$THRESH" ]]; then
  echo "FAIL: disk usage ${usage}% >= ${THRESH}%" >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: disk usage ${usage}%"
exit 0
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-shell
chmod +x host-check.sh
./host-check.sh 90 | tee run-ok.txt
grep -q '^OK:' run-ok.txt
tail -3 host-check.log | tee log-ok-tail.txt
echo $? | tee exit-code-ok.txt

Expected output

OK: disk usage … printed; exit code 0; log appended.

docs.title: Task 2 – Break (disable -e), observe silent failure
docs.text:
Create host-check-broken.sh:

host-check-broken.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# intentionally missing set -e for lab break demo
THRESH="${1:-90}"
false
echo "This line should not run if -e were enabled"
exit 0
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-shell
chmod +x host-check-broken.sh
./host-check-broken.sh; echo "exit=$?" | tee broken-exit.txt
grep -q 'exit=0' broken-exit.txt
echo "break: script reported success after false command" | tee break-notes.txt

Expected output

Broken script prints misleading success line; exit=0 despite false — demonstrates why -e matters.

docs.title: Task 3 – Fix threshold test and prove non-zero exit
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab-shell
./host-check.sh 0; echo "exit=$?" | tee fail-threshold-exit.txt || true
grep -q 'exit=2' fail-threshold-exit.txt
./host-check.sh 90 | tee run-after-fix.txt
echo "lab-shell OK" | tee evidence.txt

Expected output

Threshold 0 forces FAIL exit code 2 (disk always >= 0%). Normal threshold returns OK again.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• host-check.sh uses shebang and set -euo pipefail
  • Broken script demonstrates silent failure without -e
  • Exit codes 0 vs 2 verified
  • Log file receives timestamped entries

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Permission denied Not executable chmod +x script.sh bad interpreter Windows CRLF line endings dos2unix script.sh Unbound variable -u and missing arg ${1:-default} Pipeline wrong status Missing pipefail set -o pipefail

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text: Add a second check: fail if loadavg first field > 10 (use uptime or /proc/loadavg) — keep script under 40 lines.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• You wrote a production-shaped mini script
  • You saw why safe modes matter
  • You can discuss exit codes in interviews

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
# Keep scripts and logs for revision

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab-shell
  • Can explain set -euo pipefail in one sentence each
  • Ready for environment variables tutorial next

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. #!/usr/bin/env bash — portable shebang finding bash on PATH.
  2. ${1:-90} — default threshold if no argument — avoids unset with -u.
  3. df -P + awk — predictable parsing; avoid bare df locale surprises.
  4. exit 2 — distinct code for disk threshold vs generic 1.
  5. Broken script without -e — intentional anti-pattern for learning.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Quote variables: "$LOG" prevents word splitting/injection.
  • Do not run curl|bash; review scripts before cron as root.
  • Restrict script write permissions — attackers replace your script.
  • Avoid secrets in scripts; use env files with tight permissions.
  • Validate arguments ([[ "$THRESH" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]) before use.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ No set -e on ops scripts.

✅ Failures cascade silently — always use safe modes unless you handle each error.

❌ Unquoted $variables.

✅ Filenames with spaces break scripts; quoting is mandatory.

❌ Ignoring exit codes in cron.

✅ Cron only emails on failure if exit non-zero — return meaningful codes.

docs.title: Snap — Universal Package Management for Linux
Snap — Universal Package Management for Linux
docs.text: Snap is a universal package management system developed by Canonical that allows applications to be packaged once and installed across multiple Linux distributions. Snap packages include their required dependencies, provide automatic updates, and run in isolated environments for improved security and portability.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 7: Package Management → Lesson 5

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 55 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Package Management

Lesson: 5 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Snap packages
  • Install and remove Snap applications
  • Search the Snap Store
  • Manage Snap updates
  • Work with Snap channels
  • Understand Snap confinement
  • Compare Snap with traditional package managers
  • Apply Snap in real-world environments

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals

docs.title: Why Learn Snap?
docs.text:
Imagine you want to install:

  • Visual Studio Code
  • Postman
  • Spotify
  • Docker
  • Node.js
  • Slack

Different Linux distributions use different package managers.

Wouldn't it be easier if one package worked everywhere?

That's exactly what Snap provides.

docs.title: What is Snap?
docs.text:
Snap is a universal package format that works across multiple Linux distributions.

A Snap package contains:

  • Application
  • Required libraries
  • Dependencies
  • Metadata
  • Runtime information

Everything required to run the application is bundled together.

docs.title: How Snap Works
docs.text:

      │

Run in Sandboxed Environment

docs.title: What is snapd?
docs.text:
snapd is the background service that manages Snap packages.

It handles:

  • Installation
  • Updates
  • Security
  • Snap services
  • Communication with the Snap Store

Verify the service:

systemctl status snapd

docs.title: Install Snap (Ubuntu)
docs.text:
Snap is pre-installed on most Ubuntu systems.

Check:

Example:

snap    2.xx

snapd   2.xx

docs.title: Install Snap (RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux)
docs.text:
Install snapd.

sudo dnf install snapd

Enable the service.

sudo systemctl enable --now snapd

Create the symbolic link.

sudo ln -s /var/lib/snapd/snap /snap

docs.title: Search for Applications
docs.text:
snap find vscode

Example:

code

code-insiders

docs.title: Install a Snap Package
docs.text:
Example:

sudo snap install code --classic

Install VLC.

sudo snap install vlc

Install Postman.

sudo snap install postman

docs.title: List Installed Snaps

Name

Version

docs.title: Remove a Snap Package

docs.title: Refresh Installed Packages
docs.text:
Update all installed Snap packages.

sudo snap refresh

Update a specific package.

sudo snap refresh code

docs.title: Check for Updates

Displays available Snap updates.

docs.title: Snap Channels
docs.text:
Each Snap package may provide different release channels.

Common channels:

Channel Description stable Production-ready releases candidate Pre-release candidate beta Testing releases edge Latest development builds

Install from a specific channel.

sudo snap install node --channel=edge

docs.title: Switch Channels
docs.text: sudo snap refresh node --channel=stable

docs.title: Revert to Previous Version
docs.text:
sudo snap revert code

Useful if an update introduces unexpected issues.

docs.title: View Package Information
docs.text:
snap info code

Displays:

  • Version
  • Channels
  • Publisher
  • Description

docs.title: Snap Services
docs.text:
Some Snap packages include services.

View services.

snap services

Start a service.

sudo snap start <service>

Stop a service.

sudo snap stop <service>

Restart a service.

sudo snap restart <service>

docs.title: Security and Sandboxing
docs.text:
Snap applications run inside isolated environments.

Benefits:

  • Better security
  • Reduced impact of vulnerabilities
  • Controlled access to system resources

Permissions are managed through interfaces.

View connected interfaces.

snap connections

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Search package.

snap find nginx

Install package.

sudo snap install nginx

List packages.

snap list

Update packages.

sudo snap refresh

Remove package.

sudo snap remove nginx

View information.

sudo snap install node

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Snap is commonly used for:

  • Developer workstations
  • Desktop Linux systems
  • Cross-distribution software deployment
  • IoT devices
  • Rapid application delivery
  • Applications requiring automatic updates

Traditional package managers are still preferred for most core operating system packages on enterprise Linux servers.

docs.title: Snap vs Traditional Package Managers
docs.text: Feature Snap APT/DNF/YUM Package Format .snap .deb / .rpm Cross-Distribution ✅ ❌ Automatic Updates ✅ Manual or scheduled Bundled Dependencies ✅ Shared system libraries Sandboxed Applications ✅ Usually no Ideal For Desktop & portable apps Core operating system software

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A developer installs Visual Studio Code.

sudo snap install code

The application cannot access a removable USB drive.

Investigation:

snap connections code

The required interface is not connected.

After granting the necessary permission, the application can access the device successfully.

This demonstrates how Snap improves security through application isolation and controlled permissions.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use the stable channel for production environments.
  • Keep Snap packages updated.
  • Review application permissions using snap connections.
  • Prefer traditional package managers for core operating system packages.
  • Use Snap for cross-distribution desktop and developer applications.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Installing development (edge) builds on production systems.

✅ Avoid this mistake: installing development (edge) builds on production systems.

❌ Ignoring Snap application permissions when troubleshooting access issues.

✅ Always review Snap application permissions when troubleshooting access issues.

❌ Assuming Snap packages behave exactly like traditional packages.

✅ They run in isolated environments and may have different filesystem access.

❌ Using Snap as the primary package manager for core operating system components.

✅ Avoid using Snap as the primary package manager for core operating system components when a safer approach exists.

docs.title: Symbolic (Soft) Links in Linux — Creating Flexible File References
Symbolic (Soft) Links in Linux — Creating Flexible File References
docs.text: A Symbolic Link (Soft Link or Symlink) is a special type of file that points to another file or directory by its pathname. Unlike a hard link, a symbolic link has its own inode and acts like a shortcut. Symbolic links are widely used in Linux for application deployments, version management, configuration sharing, and storage management.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 40 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Lesson: 3 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand symbolic links
  • Create soft links
  • Understand relative and absolute symlinks
  • Identify broken symbolic links
  • Compare hard links and symbolic links
  • Manage symlinks in production
  • Troubleshoot common symlink issues

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 Lessons 1–2

docs.title: Why Learn Symbolic Links?
docs.text:
Suppose your application is deployed here:

/opt/myapp/releases/v1.0/

Later you deploy:

/opt/myapp/releases/v2.0/

Instead of changing every script, update a single symbolic link:

/opt/myapp/current

Now every service automatically uses the latest version.

This is exactly how many production deployments work.

docs.title: What is a Symbolic Link?
docs.text:
A symbolic link is a special file that stores the path to another file or directory.

It behaves like a shortcut.

Syntax:

ln -s TARGET LINK_NAME

docs.title: Linux View
docs.text:
latest
   │
   ▼
notes.txt
   │
   ▼
Actual File Data

Unlike a hard link, the symbolic link points to the pathname, not the inode.

docs.title: Create a Symbolic Link
docs.text:
Create a file.

echo "Linux Mastery" > notes.txt

Create a symbolic link.

ln -s notes.txt latest.txt

Display:

ls -l

Output:

lrwxrwxrwx 1 basha users 9 Jan 10 latest.txt -> notes.txt

Notice:

  • Starts with l
  • Shows the target using ->

docs.title: Read Using the Link
docs.text:
cat latest.txt

Output:

Linux Mastery

The symbolic link behaves like the original file.

docs.title: Modify Through the Link
docs.text:
Append data.

echo "Docker" >> latest.txt

Display original.

cat notes.txt

Output:

Linux Mastery

Docker

docs.title: View Link Details
docs.text:
ls -l latest.txt

Output:

latest.txt -> notes.txt

Display inode information.

ls -li

Example:

524288 notes.txt

524450 latest.txt

Notice:

  • Different inode numbers
  • Different file types
  • The symbolic link stores only the target path

docs.title: Delete the Original File
docs.text:
rm notes.txt

Now:

cat latest.txt

Output:

cat: latest.txt: No such file or directory

The symbolic link still exists, but its target is gone.

This is called a broken symbolic link.

docs.title: Broken Symbolic Link
docs.text:
View:

ls -l

Output:

latest.txt -> notes.txt

Although the link exists, it no longer points to a valid file.

Find broken symbolic links.

find . -xtype l

docs.title: Remove a Symbolic Link
docs.text:
Delete the link.

rm latest.txt

or

unlink latest.txt

Only the link is removed.

The original file (if it exists) is unaffected.

docs.title: Symbolic Links to Directories
docs.text:
Create:

mkdir projects

Create a symbolic link.

ln -s projects workspace

Display.

ls -l

Output:

workspace -> projects

Navigate:

cd workspace

This works exactly like entering the original directory.

docs.title: Absolute Path
docs.text:
ln -s /home/basha/docs/report.txt report-link

Stores:

/home/basha/docs/report.txt

docs.title: Relative Path
docs.text:
ln -s ../docs/report.txt report-link

Stores:

../docs/report.txt

docs.title: Which One Should You Use?
docs.text:
Type Best For Absolute Fixed system paths Relative Portable projects and repositories

Many software projects prefer relative symbolic links because they continue working if the project directory is moved.

docs.title: Hard Link vs Symbolic Link
docs.text: Hard Link Symbolic Link Same inode Different inode Points to file data Points to pathname Cannot span filesystems Can span filesystems Usually cannot link directories Can link directories Continues working if original filename is removed Becomes broken if target is removed

docs.title: View Link Target
docs.text:
readlink latest.txt

Output:

notes.txt

Display the absolute target.

readlink -f latest.txt

docs.title: Find All Symbolic Links
docs.text:
find . -type l

Find broken symbolic links.

find . -xtype l

readlink target

docs.text:
Symbolic links are heavily used in:

  • Kubernetes deployments
  • NGINX configuration

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

An application suddenly fails after a deployment.

Investigation:

  1. Verify the current symbolic link.
  2. Check if the target directory exists.
  3. Confirm the application points to the correct release.
  4. Update the symbolic link if necessary.

Commands:

ls -l /opt/myapp/current

readlink /opt/myapp/current

find /opt/myapp -xtype l

A broken symbolic link is discovered after the old release directory was accidentally removed.

The fix:

ln -sfn /opt/myapp/releases/v2.0 /opt/myapp/current

The -n and -f options replace the existing link without affecting the target directory.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Prefer symbolic links when linking directories.
  • Use relative symbolic links inside projects for portability.
  • Verify links after deployments.
  • Remove broken symbolic links during maintenance.
  • Use meaningful link names such as current, latest, or active.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Deleting the target instead of the symbolic link.

✅ Always verify with:

ls -l

before deleting files.

❌ Assuming a symbolic link stores the file itself.

✅ It stores only the target path.

❌ Using absolute symbolic links in portable projects.

✅ Relative links are often more resilient when moving directories.

docs.title: ss (Socket Statistics) — Viewing Network Connections in Linux
ss (Socket Statistics) — Viewing Network Connections in Linux
docs.text: The ss (Socket Statistics) command is the modern Linux utility for displaying network sockets, active connections, listening ports, and protocol statistics. It is significantly faster and more powerful than the legacy netstat command and is the preferred tool for network diagnostics on modern Linux systems. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Network Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) should be proficient with ss.

Feature ss netstat Performance Faster Slower Default on Modern Linux ✅ ❌ Displays Socket Statistics ✅ Limited Shows Listening Ports ✅ ✅ Shows Active Connections ✅ ✅ Shows Processes ✅ ✅ (with options)

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users report they cannot access a web application.

Investigation:

Check whether NGINX is listening.

sudo ss -tulpn | grep :80

No output.

Check the service.

systemctl status nginx

NGINX is stopped.

Start the service.

sudo systemctl start nginx

Verify again.

sudo ss -tulpn | grep :80

Output:

LISTEN

*:80

The application is now reachable.

docs.text:

docs.title: Common Mistakes

❌ Ignoring connection states such as TIME-WAIT and CLOSE-WAIT.

✅ Always review connection states such as TIME-WAIT and CLOSE-WAIT.

❌ Using netstat on systems where ss is available.

✅ Avoid using netstat on systems where ss is available when a safer approach exists.

docs.title: SSH (Secure Shell) — Secure Remote Access to Linux Systems
SSH (Secure Shell) — Secure Remote Access to Linux Systems
docs.text: SSH (Secure Shell) is the standard protocol for securely accessing and managing remote Linux systems over a network. It encrypts all communication between the client and the server, making it the preferred method for remote administration, file transfers, automation, and infrastructure management. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Security Engineer, and Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) uses SSH daily.

docs.text:
SSH stands for:

Secure Shell

It is a cryptographic network protocol that provides secure remote access to systems over untrusted networks.

SSH encrypts:

  • Passwords
  • Commands
  • File transfers

docs.text:
SSH Client
      │
Encrypted Connection
      │
      ▼
SSH Server (sshd)
      │
      ▼
Remote Linux System

All communication is encrypted before it travels across the network.

TCP Port 22

sudo ss -tulpn | grep :22

docs.text:
Connect to a remote server.

ssh username@192.168.1.100

Example:

ssh admin@192.168.1.100

On the first connection, SSH displays the server's fingerprint.

Example:

Are you sure you want to continue connecting?

Type:

yes

The server's public key is then stored in:

~/.ssh/known_hosts

docs.text:
SSH supports:

  • Password authentication
  • Public key authentication

Public key authentication is recommended for production systems.

docs.title: Generate an SSH Key Pair
docs.text:
Generate an Ed25519 key pair (recommended):

ssh-keygen -t ed25519

Or generate an RSA key pair:

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096

Default location:

~/.ssh/

Generated files:

id_ed25519

id_ed25519.pub

or

id_rsa

id_rsa.pub
