docs.title: sed Command — Stream Editor for Text Processing and Automation
sed Command — Stream Editor for Text Processing and Automation
docs.text: The sed (Stream Editor) command is one of the most powerful text-processing tools in Linux. It allows you to search, replace, insert, delete, transform, and manipulate text without opening a text editor. sed is heavily used in Linux administration, DevOps, CI/CD pipelines, automation scripts, and production environments.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 3: Text Processing → Lesson 16

Difficulty: Intermediate → Advanced

Reading Time: 60 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Text Processing

Lesson: 16 of 18

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand how sed works
  • Print specific lines
  • Search and replace text
  • Replace globally
  • Edit files in-place
  • Delete lines
  • Insert and append lines
  • Replace using regular expressions
  • Process configuration files
  • Automate text transformations
  • Use sed in production DevOps workflows

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1
  • Module 2
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–15

docs.title: Why Learn sed?
docs.text:
Imagine you have a configuration file containing 10,000 lines.

You need to replace:

dev.example.com

with

prod.example.com

Opening the file manually isn't practical.

Instead:

sed 's/dev.example.com/prod.example.com/' config.txt

Done instantly.

docs.title: What is sed?
docs.text:
sed stands for:

Stream Editor

Unlike editors such as vim or nano, sed processes text line by line.

It can:

  • Search
  • Replace
  • Delete
  • Insert
  • Append
  • Print
  • Transform

without modifying the original file unless requested.

docs.title: Command Syntax
docs.text: sed [OPTIONS] 'COMMAND' FILE

docs.title: Sample File
docs.text:
Create:

cat > employees.txt

Contents:

Alice Engineering

Bob HR

Charlie Finance

David DevOps

Eve Engineering

docs.title: Display File
docs.text:
sed '' employees.txt

Equivalent to:

cat employees.txt

docs.title: Print Specific Line
docs.text:
Display line 3.

sed -n '3p' employees.txt

Output:

Charlie Finance

Display lines 2–4.

sed -n '2,4p' employees.txt

docs.title: Search and Replace
docs.text:
Replace first occurrence.

sed 's/Engineering/Cloud/' employees.txt

Output:

Alice Cloud

Bob HR

Charlie Finance

David DevOps

Eve Engineering

Only the first occurrence per line is replaced.

docs.title: Global Replacement
docs.text:
Replace every occurrence.

sed 's/Linux/Ubuntu/g'

The g flag means:

Global

docs.title: Replace Only Line 2
docs.text: sed '2 s/HR/Human-Resources/' employees.txt

docs.title: Replace Between Lines
docs.text: sed '2,4 s/DevOps/SRE/'

docs.title: Ignore Case
docs.text: sed 's/linux/ubuntu/i'

docs.title: Edit File In-Place
docs.text:
Normally:

sed 's/HR/Human Resources/' employees.txt

does not change the file.

Modify the file permanently.

sed -i 's/HR/Human Resources/' employees.txt

docs.title: Create Backup Before Editing
docs.text:
Highly recommended.

sed -i.bak 's/HR/Human Resources/' employees.txt

Creates:

employees.txt

employees.txt.bak

docs.title: Delete Line
docs.text:
Delete line 3.

sed '3d' employees.txt

Delete lines 2–4.

sed '2,4d' employees.txt

Delete blank lines.

sed '/^$/d' file.txt

docs.title: Insert Line
docs.text:
Insert before line 2.

sed '2i\
Department List
' employees.txt

docs.title: Append Line
docs.text:
Append after line 2.

sed '2a\
Cloud Team
' employees.txt

docs.title: Replace Entire Line
docs.text:
sed '3c\
Charlie Security
' employees.txt

docs.title: Print Matching Lines
docs.text: sed -n '/Engineering/p' employees.txt

docs.title: Delete Matching Lines
docs.text: sed '/HR/d' employees.txt

docs.title: Using Regular Expressions
docs.text:
Replace all digits.

sed 's/[0-9]/X/g'

Remove extra spaces.

sed 's/  */ /g'

Replace multiple spaces with one.

docs.title: Replace Tabs
docs.text: sed 's/\t/ /g'

docs.title: Remove Trailing Spaces
docs.text: sed 's/[[:space:]]*$//'

docs.title: Number Lines
docs.text: sed = employees.txt

docs.title: Using Multiple Commands
docs.text:
sed -e 's/Linux/Ubuntu/' \
    -e 's/Docker/Podman/'

docs.title: Common sed Options
docs.text: Option Description -n Suppress automatic printing -i Edit file in place -e Multiple expressions -f Read commands from file

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Replace image tag.

sed -i 's/v1.2.0/v1.3.0/' deployment.yaml

Update namespace.

sed -i 's/dev/prod/' deployment.yaml

Replace environment.

sed -i 's/ENV=dev/ENV=prod/'

Update Terraform variables.

sed -i 's/us-central1/us-east1/'

Modify NGINX config.

sed -i 's/listen 80/listen 8080/'

docs.title: Kubernetes Example
docs.text:
Update image.

sed -i 's/nginx:1.24/nginx:1.27/' deployment.yaml

docs.title: Docker Example
docs.text:
Replace base image.

sed -i 's/python:3.10/python:3.12/'

docs.title: CI/CD Example
docs.text:
GitLab pipeline.

sed -i "s/IMAGE_TAG/$CI_COMMIT_SHA/"

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Every DevOps engineer uses sed.

Typical use cases:

  • CI/CD
  • Configuration management
  • YAML editing
  • Log cleanup
  • Kubernetes manifests
  • Terraform variables
  • Helm templates
  • Automation scripts

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Replace Engineering.

sed 's/Engineering/Cloud/' employees.txt

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Replace globally.

sed 's/e/E/g'

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Delete line 2.

sed '2d' employees.txt

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Print line 4.

sed -n '4p' employees.txt

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Insert header.

sed '1i\
Employee Report
'

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Append footer.

sed '$a\
End of Report
'

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Edit file.

sed -i 's/HR/Human Resources/'

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Create backup.

sed -i.bak 's/DevOps/SRE/'

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A company has 500 Kubernetes Deployment YAML files that still reference an old container image:

image: nginx:1.24

The new approved version is:

image: nginx:1.27

Update all deployment files safely while keeping backups.

find . -name "*.yaml" -print0 | \
xargs -0 sed -i.bak 's/nginx:1.24/nginx:1.27/g'

docs.title: Performance Tip
docs.text:
Use sed for stream processing.

It processes files line by line without loading the entire file into memory, making it suitable for very large log files and configuration files.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always test before using -i.
  • Create backups with -i.bak.
  • Use regular expressions carefully.
  • Validate YAML/JSON after modifications.
  • Combine sed with grep, find, and xargs.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Editing production files without backups.

✅ Always use:

sed -i.bak

❌ Forgetting the g flag.

✅ Use:

sed 's/a/b/'

Only replaces the first match on each line.

❌ Confusing sed with tr.

✅ - tr → Character replacement - sed → Pattern and line-based editing

docs.title: Beginner
docs.text:
1. What does sed stand for?
  2. How do you replace text?
  3. What does -i do?
  4. What does the g flag mean?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Explain sed -n.
  2. Difference between sed and tr.
  3. How do you delete blank lines?
  4. How do you create backups before editing?

docs.title: Architect Level
docs.text:
1. How would you update thousands of Kubernetes manifests automatically?
  2. Why is sed preferred over manual editing in CI/CD pipelines?
  3. How would you safely update configuration files across hundreds of servers?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Search and replace
  • Global replacement
  • In-place editing
  • Line deletion
  • Line insertion
  • Appending text
  • Regular expressions
  • Production automation

sed is one of the most important Linux commands for automation and configuration management. It is used extensively in DevOps, cloud engineering, CI/CD, and system administration.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• sed is a Stream Editor.
  • It edits text without opening a text editor.
  • Use -i for in-place editing.
  • Use -i.bak to create backups.
  • g performs global replacement.
  • sed is indispensable for DevOps and automation.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
awk Command — The Ultimate Linux Text Processing Language

In the next lesson, you'll master field-based processing, calculations, reporting, filtering, and advanced text manipulation using awk.

docs.title: sort Command — Sorting Text in Linux
sort Command — Sorting Text in Linux
docs.text: The sort command is used to arrange lines of text in alphabetical, numerical, or custom order. It is one of the most commonly used Linux text-processing utilities and is frequently combined with commands like grep, cut, uniq, and awk to analyze logs, reports, and structured data.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 3: Text Processing → Lesson 4

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 30 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Text Processing

Lesson: 4 of 18

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the sort command
  • Sort text alphabetically
  • Sort numbers
  • Sort in reverse order
  • Sort using specific columns
  • Remove duplicate entries
  • Perform case-insensitive sorting
  • Analyze real-world log and report files

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–3

docs.title: Why Learn sort?
docs.text:
Imagine you receive a report with thousands of employee records.

Charlie

Alice

David

Bob

Instead of manually rearranging the data:

sort employees.txt

Output:

Alice

Bob

Charlie

David

Sorting data is a common task in Linux administration, DevOps, and data analysis.

docs.title: What is sort?
docs.text:
The sort command reads lines from one or more files and arranges them in a specified order.

Syntax:

sort [OPTIONS] FILE

docs.title: Sample File
docs.text:
Create a sample file.

cat > employees.txt

Contents:

Charlie

Alice

David

Bob

Press:

Ctrl + D

docs.title: Alphabetical Sorting
docs.text:
sort employees.txt

Output:

Alice

Bob

Charlie

David

docs.title: Reverse Sorting
docs.text:
Use the -r option.

sort -r employees.txt

Output:

David

Charlie

Bob

Alice

docs.title: Numeric Sorting
docs.text:
Create:

cat > numbers.txt

Contents:

25

8

100

50

10

Default sort:

sort numbers.txt

Output:

10

100

25

50

8

Numeric sort:

sort -n numbers.txt

Output:

8

10

25

50

100

docs.title: Sort Unique Values
docs.text:
Remove duplicate entries.

Create:

Alice

Bob

Alice

David

Bob

Command:

sort -u employees.txt

Output:

Alice

Bob

David

docs.title: Ignore Case
docs.text:
Create:

apple

Banana

APPLE

banana

Command:

sort -f fruits.txt

The -f option ignores case while sorting.

docs.title: Sort by Month
docs.text:
Useful for log files.

Create:

Jan

Mar

Feb

Dec

Command:

sort -M months.txt

Output:

Jan

Feb

Mar

Dec

docs.title: Sort Human-Readable Sizes
docs.text:
Create:

5K

100M

2G

500K

Command:

sort -h sizes.txt

Output:

5K

500K

100M

2G

docs.title: Sort CSV Files by Column
docs.text:
Create:

cat > employees.csv

Contents:

Alice,85000

Bob,60000

Charlie,90000

David,75000

Sort by salary.

sort -t "," -k2 -n employees.csv

Output:

Bob,60000

David,75000

Alice,85000

Charlie,90000

Explanation:

  • -t "," → Delimiter
  • -k2 → Second column
  • -n → Numeric sort

docs.title: Remove Duplicates with uniq
docs.text:
sort employees.txt | uniq

Count duplicates.

sort employees.txt | uniq -c

docs.title: Sort Command Output
docs.text:
Sort users.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | sort

Sort processes.

ps -ef | sort

Sort mounted filesystems.

mount | sort

docs.title: Combining with Pipes
docs.text:
Count unique departments.

cut -d "," -f2 employees.csv | sort | uniq | wc -l

Sort running processes.

ps -ef | grep nginx | sort

Sort log entries.

grep ERROR application.log | sort

docs.title: Common sort Options
docs.text: Option Description -r Reverse order -n Numeric sort -u Unique values -f Ignore case -M Month names -h Human-readable sizes -t Field delimiter -k Sort by column

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Sort system users.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | sort

Sort log entries.

grep ERROR app.log | sort

Sort Docker images.

docker images | sort

Sort Kubernetes namespaces.

kubectl get namespaces | sort

Sort disk usage.

du -sh * | sort -h

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
The sort command is commonly used to:

  • Organize reports
  • Sort log entries
  • Process CSV files
  • Prepare data for uniq
  • Analyze command output
  • Generate readable reports

Nearly every Linux engineer uses sort as part of daily workflows.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create:

cat > students.txt

Contents:

Rahul

Anita

Vijay

Deepa

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Sort alphabetically.

sort students.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Reverse sort.

sort -r students.txt

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Create numbers.

cat > marks.txt

Contents:

95

80

100

70

85

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Sort numerically.

sort -n marks.txt

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Remove duplicates.

sort -u students.txt

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Sort usernames.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | sort

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Sort salaries.

sort -t "," -k2 -n employees.csv

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example sort file Alphabetical sort Reports sort -n Numeric sort CPU usage sort -r Reverse sort Latest entries sort -u Unique values User lists sort -k2 Sort by column CSV reports sort -h Human-readable sizes Disk usage

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

You receive a report showing disk usage across multiple servers.

server01 500M

server02 2G

server03 250M

server04 1G

Tasks:

  1. Sort servers by disk usage.
  2. Display the largest server.
  3. Remove duplicate entries.
  4. Generate a sorted report.

Solutions:

sort -k2 -h servers.txt

sort -k2 -h servers.txt | tail -1

sort -u servers.txt

sort servers.txt > sorted-report.txt

docs.title: Mini Challenge
docs.text:
Create:

employees.csv

Alice,85000

Bob,60000

Charlie,90000

David,75000

Bob,60000

Perform the following:

  • Sort alphabetically.
  • Sort by salary.
  • Sort in reverse order.
  • Remove duplicate entries.
  • Count unique employees.
  • Display the employee with the highest salary.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use sort -n for numbers instead of default sorting.
  • Use sort -h for file sizes.
  • Always sort before using uniq.
  • Use field-based sorting for CSV files.
  • Combine sort with grep, cut, and awk for powerful text processing.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Sorting numbers without -n.

✅ Incorrect:

sort numbers.txt

Correct:

sort -n numbers.txt

❌ Using uniq on unsorted data.

✅ Incorrect:

uniq file.txt

Correct:

sort file.txt | uniq

❌ Forgetting the delimiter when sorting CSV files.

✅ Correct:

sort -t "," -k2 employees.csv

docs.text:
1. What does the sort command do?
  2. What is the purpose of -n?
  3. What does -r do?
  4. How do you remove duplicate entries?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Why should data be sorted before using uniq?
  2. Explain sort -k.
  3. What does sort -h do?
  4. How do you sort CSV data by a specific column?

docs.text:
1. How would you sort a report containing millions of records efficiently?
  2. Why is sort commonly used before uniq in shell pipelines?
  3. How can sort improve automation and reporting in DevOps workflows?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Alphabetical sorting
  • Numeric sorting
  • Reverse sorting
  • Field-based sorting
  • Case-insensitive sorting
  • Human-readable size sorting
  • Removing duplicates
  • Real-world production use cases

The sort command is one of the most essential Linux text-processing tools. It is frequently combined with cut, grep, uniq, awk, and sed to organize and analyze data efficiently.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• sort arranges text in ascending order by default.
  • Use -n for numeric values.
  • Use -r for reverse order.
  • Use -u to remove duplicates.
  • Use -k and -t to sort by specific columns.
  • Always sort data before using uniq.

docs.title: split Command — Splitting Large Files in Linux
split Command — Splitting Large Files in Linux
docs.text: The split command divides a large file into smaller, more manageable pieces. It is commonly used when handling huge log files, database exports, backups, large CSV files, and files that need to be transferred over networks with size limitations.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 3: Text Processing → Lesson 10

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 30 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Text Processing

Lesson: 10 of 18

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the split command
  • Split files by number of lines
  • Split files by size
  • Create custom file prefixes
  • Create numeric suffixes
  • Reassemble split files
  • Process large production files

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–9

docs.title: Why Learn split?
docs.text:
Imagine you have a:

  • 20 GB log file
  • 10 GB database export
  • 5 GB CSV report

You cannot easily:

  • Email it
  • Upload it
  • Analyze it
  • Transfer it

Instead:

split

breaks the file into smaller pieces.

docs.title: What is split?
docs.text:
The split command divides a large file into multiple smaller files.

Syntax:

split [OPTIONS] FILE [PREFIX]

docs.title: Sample File
docs.text:
Create a sample file.

seq 1 20 > numbers.txt

Display:

cat numbers.txt

Output:

1
2
3
...
20

docs.title: Split by Number of Lines
docs.text:
Split every five lines.

split -l 5 numbers.txt

Files created:

xaa

xab

xac

xad

View:

cat xaa

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

docs.title: Custom Prefix
docs.text:
Instead of:

xaa

xab

Use:

split -l 5 numbers.txt part-

Files:

part-aa

part-ab

part-ac

part-ad

docs.title: Numeric Suffixes
docs.text:
Instead of alphabetic suffixes.

split -d -l 5 numbers.txt chunk-

Files:

chunk-00

chunk-01

chunk-02

chunk-03

docs.title: Specify Suffix Length
docs.text:
split -d -a 3 -l 5 numbers.txt piece-

Files:

piece-000

piece-001

piece-002

docs.title: Split by File Size
docs.text:
Split into 1 KB files.

split -b 1K logfile.log

Split into 10 MB files.

split -b 10M backup.tar

Split into 1 GB files.

split -b 1G database.sql

docs.title: Human-Readable Sizes
docs.text:
Supported units:

Unit Meaning K Kilobytes M Megabytes G Gigabytes

Example:

split -b 100M archive.tar

docs.title: Split by Number of Files
docs.text:
Suppose you want exactly four output files.

split -n 4 numbers.txt

The file is divided into four approximately equal parts.

docs.title: Display Created Files
docs.text: ls part-*

docs.title: Reassemble Files
docs.text:
Suppose:

part-aa

part-ab

part-ac

Merge:

cat part-* > complete.txt

Verify:

diff numbers.txt complete.txt

No output means the files are identical.

docs.title: Verify Integrity
docs.text:
Compare original and reconstructed files.

cmp numbers.txt complete.txt

or

sha256sum numbers.txt complete.txt

Matching checksums confirm the files are identical.

docs.title: Common split Options
docs.text: Option Description -l Split by lines -b Split by bytes/size -d Numeric suffixes -a Suffix length -n Split into N files --verbose Show created files

docs.title: Combining with Other Commands
docs.text:
Compress after splitting.

split -b 500M backup.tar backup-

gzip backup-*

Split compressed logs.

gzip -dc access.log.gz | split -l 100000 - access-

Merge again.

cat backup-* > backup.tar

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Split a database export.

split -b 2G database.sql db-

Split an application log.

split -l 500000 application.log log-

Split a Kubernetes audit log.

split -b 500M audit.log audit-

Split a CSV report.

split -l 100000 employees.csv emp-

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
The split command is commonly used for:

  • Database backups
  • Large log analysis
  • Data migration
  • Cloud uploads
  • Secure file transfer
  • Batch processing

Many enterprise environments split files before uploading them to cloud storage or transferring them across networks.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create a sample file.

seq 1 100 > numbers.txt

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Split into 20-line files.

split -l 20 numbers.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Use a custom prefix.

split -l 20 numbers.txt batch-

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Use numeric suffixes.

split -d -l 20 numbers.txt part-

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Split by size.

split -b 1K numbers.txt size-

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Merge files.

cat part-* > merged.txt

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Verify.

diff numbers.txt merged.txt

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Display generated files.

ls part-*

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example split -l 1000 Split by lines CSV reports split -b 100M Split by size Log archives split -d Numeric suffixes Automation split -a 3 Three-digit suffix Large datasets split -n 5 Equal parts Parallel processing

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A DevOps engineer needs to upload a 12 GB backup to cloud storage, but the storage service only accepts files up to 2 GB.

Tasks:

  1. Split the backup into 2 GB chunks.
  2. Verify the generated files.
  3. Reassemble the backup after download.
  4. Confirm that the reconstructed file matches the original.

Solutions:

split -b 2G backup.tar backup-

ls backup-*

cat backup-* > backup.tar

sha256sum backup.tar

docs.title: Mini Challenge
docs.text:
Create:

seq 1 500 > records.txt

Perform the following:

  • Split into files containing 100 lines each.
  • Create numeric suffixes.
  • Use the prefix records-.
  • Merge all files.
  • Verify the merged file.
  • Count the number of generated files.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use meaningful file prefixes.
  • Verify reconstructed files using sha256sum or cmp.
  • Split large backups before transferring them over the network.
  • Prefer numeric suffixes (-d) in automation scripts.
  • Remove temporary split files after successful verification.

docs.title: Performance Tip
docs.text:
For very large files:

split -b 1G huge-backup.tar backup-

Choose a chunk size appropriate for your storage or network limitations.

When transferring files over unreliable networks, smaller chunks are often easier to retry than a single massive file.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting to verify the reconstructed file.

✅ Always compare:

sha256sum original.file merged.file

❌ Using alphabetic suffixes when scripts expect numeric ordering.

✅ Prefer:

split -d

❌ Choosing chunk sizes that exceed upload limits.

✅ Verify platform restrictions before splitting.

docs.text:

  2. How do you split a file every 100 lines?
  3. How do you split a file by size?
  4. What does -d do?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Explain split -n.
  2. How do you reassemble split files?
  3. Why should you verify reconstructed files?
  4. What is the purpose of -a?

docs.title: Architect Level
docs.text:
1. How would you split and transfer a 100 GB database backup?
  2. Why is split useful in cloud migrations?
  3. How would you automate backup splitting, transfer, and verification in a shell script?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Splitting files by lines
  • Splitting files by size
  • Creating custom prefixes
  • Using numeric suffixes
  • Reassembling files
  • Verifying file integrity
  • Production backup workflows

The split command is an essential tool for handling large files in Linux. It simplifies storage, transfer, and processing while making large datasets easier to manage.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• split divides large files into smaller parts.
  • Use -l to split by lines.
  • Use -b to split by size.
  • Use -d for numeric suffixes.
  • Reassemble files using cat.
  • Always verify reconstructed files using diff, cmp, or sha256sum.

docs.title: strings Command — Extracting Printable Text from Binary Files
strings Command — Extracting Printable Text from Binary Files
docs.text: The strings command extracts printable text from binary files. It is widely used in Linux system administration, malware analysis, reverse engineering, digital forensics, incident response, software debugging, and cybersecurity to inspect executables, libraries, firmware, memory dumps, and other binary files.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 3: Text Processing → Lesson 13

Difficulty: Intermediate

Reading Time: 35 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Text Processing

Lesson: 13 of 18

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the strings command
  • Extract printable text from binary files
  • Analyze executable files
  • Inspect shared libraries
  • Investigate suspicious binaries
  • Use strings in malware analysis
  • Combine strings with other Linux commands

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–12

docs.title: Why Learn strings?
docs.text:
Imagine someone sends you an executable file.

backup_tool

You don't have its source code.

You want to know:

  • Does it contain URLs?
  • Does it reference passwords?
  • Which libraries does it use?
  • Does it connect to external servers?
  • Is it suspicious?

Instead of opening it in a hex editor:

strings backup_tool

You immediately see readable text embedded inside the binary.

docs.title: What is strings?
docs.text:
The strings command scans binary files and displays sequences of printable characters.

Syntax:

strings [OPTIONS] FILE

It does not execute the file. It only extracts readable text.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Display printable strings from the ls command.

strings /bin/ls

Sample output:

Usage:

--help

--version

invalid option

coreutils

GNU

docs.title: Extract Longer Strings
docs.text:
By default, strings displays printable sequences of 4 or more characters.

Display only strings with 8 or more characters.

strings -n 8 /bin/ls

or

strings --bytes=8 /bin/ls

docs.title: Display File Offsets
docs.text:
strings -t x /bin/ls

Output:

0000340 GNU

00005ac Usage

00008f2 invalid option

Options:

  • x → Hexadecimal
  • d → Decimal
  • o → Octal

docs.title: Analyze Shared Libraries
docs.text:
Example:

strings /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6

You may see:

malloc

free

printf

GNU C Library

docs.title: Search for URLs
docs.text:
strings application.bin | grep "http"

Example:

https://api.example.com

docs.title: Search for IP Addresses
docs.text: strings malware.bin | grep -E "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+"

docs.title: Search for Email Addresses
docs.text: strings file.bin | grep "@"

docs.title: Search for API Keys
docs.text: strings app.bin | grep -i "apikey"

docs.title: Search for Passwords
docs.text: strings application.bin | grep -i password

docs.title: Analyze Shell Scripts Inside Binaries
docs.text:
Some compiled applications embed shell commands.

strings application.bin | grep "/bin"

Example:

/bin/bash

/bin/sh

docs.title: Search for Configuration Files
docs.text:
strings application.bin | grep ".conf"

Example:

config.yaml

application.conf

docs.title: Analyze Environment Variables
docs.text: strings application.bin | grep PATH

docs.title: Search for SQL Queries
docs.text: strings database-tool | grep SELECT

docs.title: Search for Error Messages
docs.text: strings application.bin | grep ERROR

docs.title: Search for Certificates
docs.text:
strings application.bin | grep BEGIN

Example:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----

docs.title: Common strings Options
docs.text: Option Description -n N Minimum string length -t x Display hexadecimal offsets -t d Display decimal offsets -a Scan the entire file -e Specify character encoding

docs.title: Combining with Other Commands
docs.text:
Search for URLs.

strings app.bin | grep http

Sort unique strings.

strings app.bin | sort | uniq

Count extracted strings.

strings app.bin | wc -l

Search for AWS references.

strings app.bin | grep AWS

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Inspect an executable.

strings myapp

Inspect a Docker binary.

strings /usr/bin/docker

Inspect Kubernetes components.

strings /usr/local/bin/kubectl

Inspect OpenSSL.

strings /usr/bin/openssl

Inspect firmware.

strings firmware.bin

docs.title: Cybersecurity Use Cases
docs.text:
strings is commonly used by:

  • Malware Analysts
  • Incident Responders
  • Security Researchers
  • Reverse Engineers
  • Digital Forensics Teams
  • SOC Analysts

Typical investigations include:

  • Hidden URLs
  • Hardcoded passwords
  • API endpoints
  • Encryption keys
  • Command execution paths
  • Suspicious domains

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
Although developers and administrators use strings for debugging, it is especially valuable in:

  • Security audits
  • Binary inspection
  • Software verification
  • Incident response
  • Malware triage
  • Firmware analysis

It provides a quick first look at a binary without executing it.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Inspect the ls executable.

strings /bin/ls

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Display only strings longer than 10 characters.

strings -n 10 /bin/ls

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Search for "GNU".

strings /bin/ls | grep GNU

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Display hexadecimal offsets.

strings -t x /bin/ls

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Count extracted strings.

strings /bin/ls | wc -l

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Search for URLs.

strings /usr/bin/curl | grep http

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Search for configuration files.

strings application.bin | grep ".conf"

(Replace application.bin with a sample binary if available.)

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Sort unique strings.

strings /bin/ls | sort | uniq

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example strings file Extract printable text Binary inspection strings -n 8 Longer strings Malware analysis strings -t x Show offsets Reverse engineering strings \| grep Search extracted text Incident response

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A security engineer receives an unknown executable from a compromised server.

Tasks:

  1. Extract readable strings.
  2. Search for URLs.
  3. Search for IP addresses.
  4. Search for embedded shell commands.
  5. Count extracted strings.

Solutions:

strings suspicious.bin

strings suspicious.bin | grep http

strings suspicious.bin | grep -E "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+"

strings suspicious.bin | grep "/bin"

strings suspicious.bin | wc -l

Note

strings provides clues but does not prove malicious behavior. Further analysis with tools like file, readelf, objdump, or a sandbox may be required.

docs.title: Mini Challenge
docs.text:
Analyze:

/bin/ls

Perform the following:

  • Display all printable strings.
  • Display only strings longer than 12 characters.
  • Search for "GNU".
  • Search for "help".
  • Count extracted strings.
  • Display hexadecimal offsets.
  • Display unique strings.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use strings as a first step when analyzing unknown binaries.
  • Combine with grep to locate specific indicators.
  • Avoid executing unknown files during initial analysis.
  • Verify findings using additional tools such as file, readelf, or objdump.
  • Document interesting findings during investigations.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming every extracted string is meaningful.

✅ Some strings may be unrelated data or compiler-generated content.

❌ Treating strings output as proof of malicious behavior.

✅ The presence of a URL or command does not necessarily indicate malicious activity.

❌ Ignoring string length.

✅ Using -n can reduce noise and highlight more useful information.

docs.title: Beginner
docs.text:
1. What does the strings command do?
  2. Does strings execute a binary?
  3. What does the -n option specify?
  4. How do you search extracted strings for URLs?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. Why is strings useful in malware analysis?
  2. Explain the purpose of -t x.
  3. How would you identify hardcoded configuration values?
  4. What are the limitations of strings?

docs.title: Architect Level
docs.text:
1. How would you perform an initial investigation of an unknown executable?
  2. Why should strings be combined with tools like file, readelf, and objdump?
  3. How would you automate binary inspection across hundreds of servers?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Extracting printable text from binaries
  • Filtering strings by length
  • Displaying offsets
  • Searching for URLs, IPs, passwords, and configuration files
  • Using strings in security investigations
  • Combining strings with other Linux commands

The strings command is a simple yet powerful utility for examining binary files without executing them. It plays an important role in Linux administration, software debugging, and cybersecurity investigations.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• strings extracts printable text from binary files.
  • It does not execute the target file.
  • Use -n to control the minimum string length.
  • Use -t to display offsets.
  • Combine strings with grep, sort, and wc for efficient analysis.
  • strings is a valuable first step in binary inspection and malware triage.

tee Command — Writing Output to Both Screen and File

  • Saving command output while displaying it
  • Appending to files
  • Logging automation output

docs.title: tee Command — Writing Output to Both Screen and File
tee Command — Writing Output to Both Screen and File
docs.text: The tee command reads data from standard input and writes it simultaneously to the terminal and one or more files. It is an essential Linux utility for logging command output, debugging shell scripts, monitoring automation, and building CI/CD pipelines.

After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the tee command
  • Save command output while displaying it
  • Append output to files
  • Write to multiple files
  • Use tee in shell pipelines
  • Log automation output
  • Apply tee in DevOps and CI/CD workflows

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–13

docs.title: Why Learn tee?
docs.text:
Normally:

ls > files.txt

Output goes to the file.

Nothing appears on the screen.

Or:

ls

Output appears on the screen.

Nothing is saved.

What if you need both?

ls | tee files.txt

Now you can:

  • View the output
  • Save it to a file

At the same time.

docs.title: What is tee?
docs.text:
The tee command copies its input to:

  • Standard Output (Terminal)
  • One or more files

Syntax:

tee [OPTIONS] FILE...

Think of it as a T-junction in a pipe.

Command
   │
   ▼
  tee
 ┌──┴──┐
 ▼     ▼
Screen File

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
echo "Welcome to REBASH Academy" | tee output.txt

Output on screen:

Welcome to REBASH Academy

File:

cat output.txt

Output:

Welcome to REBASH Academy

docs.title: Save Command Output
docs.text:
ls -l | tee files.txt

You will see the directory listing while also saving it.

docs.title: Append Instead of Overwrite
docs.text:
Normally:

tee output.txt

overwrites the file.

Append instead:

echo "Docker" | tee -a output.txt

View:

cat output.txt

Output:

Linux

Docker

docs.title: Write to Multiple Files
docs.text:
echo "Cloud Computing" | tee file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt

All files receive the same output.

docs.title: Use with grep
docs.text:
Save matching lines.

grep ERROR application.log | tee errors.log

Display:

ERROR Database Connection Failed

The same output is saved to errors.log.

docs.title: Use with sort
docs.text: sort employees.txt | tee sorted.txt

docs.title: Use with wc
docs.text:
cat access.log | tee backup.log | wc -l

Workflow:

access.log
      │
      ▼
     tee
   ↙     ↘
backup.log  wc -l

docs.title: Use with find
docs.text: find . -name "*.sh" | tee scripts.txt

docs.title: Logging Script Output
docs.text:
./backup.sh | tee backup.log

You can monitor progress in real time while keeping a log for later review.

docs.title: Capture Both Standard Output and Errors
docs.text:
Normally, tee captures only standard output.

To capture both:

command 2>&1 | tee output.log

Example:

ls /existing /missing 2>&1 | tee result.log

Output on screen:

/existing

ls: cannot access '/missing': No such file or directory

The same content is saved to result.log.

docs.title: Ignore Interrupt Signals
docs.text:
Useful for long-running processes.

tee -i output.log

The -i option ignores interrupt signals (Ctrl+C) sent to tee.

docs.title: Common tee Options
docs.text: Option Description -a Append instead of overwrite -i Ignore interrupt signals

docs.title: Combining with Other Commands
docs.text:
Monitor disk usage.

df -h | tee disk-report.txt

Save running processes.

ps -ef | tee processes.txt

Save Kubernetes Pods.

kubectl get pods | tee pods.txt

Save Docker containers.

docker ps | tee containers.txt

Save environment variables.

printenv | tee env.txt

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Save deployment logs.

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml | tee deployment.log

Save Terraform output.

terraform apply | tee terraform.log

Save Ansible execution.

ansible-playbook site.yml | tee ansible.log

Save Helm installation.

helm install myapp chart/ | tee helm.log

Save Docker build logs.

docker build -t app . | tee build.log

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
The tee command is one of the most frequently used utilities in:

  • CI/CD pipelines
  • DevOps automation
  • System administration
  • Deployment scripts
  • Infrastructure provisioning
  • Production troubleshooting

It allows engineers to monitor commands while simultaneously creating logs for auditing and debugging.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Display and save text.

echo "Linux" | tee linux.txt

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Append another line.

echo "Docker" | tee -a linux.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Display the file.

cat linux.txt

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Save directory listing.

ls -l | tee files.txt

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Save process list.

ps -ef | tee processes.txt

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Write to multiple files.

echo "REBASH Academy" | tee file1.txt file2.txt

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Capture both output and errors.

ls /tmp /invalid 2>&1 | tee errors.log

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Count files while saving the list.

ls | tee listing.txt | wc -l

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example tee file Save output Reports tee -a Append logs Automation tee file1 file2 Multiple outputs Backups 2>&1 \| tee Capture stdout + stderr Troubleshooting

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A DevOps engineer is deploying an application to Kubernetes.

Tasks:

  1. Watch deployment progress live.
  2. Save deployment logs.
  3. Capture errors.
  4. Share the log with the support team.

Solution:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml 2>&1 | tee deployment.log

Benefits:

  • Live monitoring
  • Permanent log file
  • Easier troubleshooting
  • Audit trail

docs.title: Mini Challenge
docs.text:
Perform the following:

  • Save the output of df -h while displaying it.
  • Save the output of ps -ef.
  • Append a custom message to an existing log.
  • Capture errors from an invalid command.
  • Save the list of shell scripts in the current directory.
  • Write the same output to two different files.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use tee in deployment and automation scripts.
  • Use -a for log files that should be preserved.
  • Capture both stdout and stderr using 2>&1.
  • Use descriptive log file names.
  • Rotate or archive large log files regularly.

docs.title: Performance Tip
docs.text:
For long-running commands that produce continuous output:

tail -f application.log | tee live-monitor.log

This allows real-time monitoring while creating a persistent copy for later analysis.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting -a.

✅ Without -a, the file is overwritten.

Incorrect:

echo "New Entry" | tee log.txt

Correct:

echo "New Entry" | tee -a log.txt

❌ Assuming tee captures error output automatically.

✅ Incorrect:

command | tee output.log

Correct:

command 2>&1 | tee output.log

❌ Using tee without considering log file growth.

✅ Regularly rotate or clean up logs in long-running systems.

  • Appending to log files

The tee command is a simple yet powerful utility that bridges the gap between visibility and logging. It is widely used in Linux administration, automation, CI/CD, and production troubleshooting.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• tee writes output to both the terminal and files.
  • Use -a to append instead of overwrite.
  • Use 2>&1 | tee to capture both standard output and errors.
  • tee integrates naturally with pipelines.
  • It is a standard tool for logging deployments, builds, and automation tasks.

docs.title: tr Command — Translating and Transforming Text in Linux
tr Command — Translating and Transforming Text in Linux
docs.text: The tr (translate) command is used to transform, replace, delete, and compress characters from standard input. It is one of the most useful Linux text-processing utilities for formatting data, cleaning text, converting letter cases, and preparing data for scripts and automation.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 3: Text Processing → Lesson 6

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 30 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Text Processing

Lesson: 6 of 18

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the tr command
  • Replace characters
  • Convert lowercase to uppercase
  • Convert uppercase to lowercase
  • Delete characters
  • Remove repeated characters
  • Process command output
  • Use tr in shell pipelines

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–5

docs.title: Why Learn tr?
docs.text:
Imagine you receive inconsistent user input.

linux
Linux
LINUX
LiNuX

You want everything in uppercase.

Instead of editing manually:

echo "linux" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

Output:

LINUX

This is a common task in automation and shell scripting.

docs.title: What is tr?
docs.text:
tr stands for:

Translate

It reads text from Standard Input (stdin) and transforms it.

Unlike commands such as cat or grep, tr does not read files directly.

Syntax:

tr [OPTIONS] SET1 [SET2]

Most commonly used with pipes:

cat file.txt | tr ...

or

echo "text" | tr ...

docs.title: Character Translation
docs.text:
Replace one character with another.

echo "Linux" | tr 'L' 'W'

Output:

Winux

Replace spaces with underscores.

echo "REBASH Academy" | tr ' ' '_'

Output:

REBASH_Academy

docs.title: Convert Lowercase to Uppercase
docs.text:
echo "linux" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

Output:

LINUX

Another example:

echo "docker kubernetes" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

Output:

DOCKER KUBERNETES

docs.title: Convert Uppercase to Lowercase
docs.text:
echo "LINUX" | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z'

Output:

linux

docs.title: Using POSIX Character Classes
docs.text:
Instead of ranges:

tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

Use:

tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'

Convert to lowercase:

tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'

POSIX character classes are more portable across different locales.

docs.title: Delete Characters
docs.text:
Remove vowels.

echo "Linux Administration" | tr -d 'aeiouAEIOU'

Output:

Lnx dmnstrtn

Remove spaces.

echo "Hello World" | tr -d ' '

Output:

HelloWorld

Remove digits.

echo "Server123" | tr -d '0-9'

Output:

Server

docs.title: Squeeze Repeated Characters
docs.text:
Suppose:

Linux     Docker      Kubernetes

Compress repeated spaces.

echo "Linux     Docker      Kubernetes" | tr -s ' '

Output:

Linux Docker Kubernetes

Compress repeated blank lines.

cat file.txt | tr -s '\n'

docs.title: Replace Tabs
docs.text:
Convert tabs to spaces.

cat file.txt | tr '\t' ' '

docs.title: Replace Colons
docs.text:
Example:

basha:x:1000:1000

Command:

echo "basha:x:1000:1000" | tr ':' ','

Output:

basha,x,1000,1000

docs.title: One Character Per Line
docs.text:
Display every character on its own line.

echo "Linux" | tr '' '\n'

A more common approach is:

echo "Linux" | fold -w1

docs.title: Combining with Pipes
docs.text:
Convert usernames to uppercase.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

Remove spaces.

cat names.txt | tr -d ' '

Count words.

cat file.txt | tr ' ' '\n' | wc -l

Convert log entries.

grep ERROR app.log | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'

docs.title: Common tr Options
docs.text: Option Description -d Delete characters -s Squeeze repeated characters -c Complement character set -t Truncate SET1 to match SET2

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Convert usernames.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'

Remove spaces from configuration values.

cat config.txt | tr -d ' '

Normalize CSV delimiters.

cat data.csv | tr ';' ','

Clean log output.

journalctl | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'

Prepare environment variables.

echo "production" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
The tr command is commonly used for:

  • Data cleanup
  • Case conversion
  • Formatting reports
  • Removing unwanted characters
  • Normalizing input
  • Preparing text for shell scripts

It is lightweight, fast, and works exceptionally well in command pipelines.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Convert to uppercase.

echo "linux" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Convert to lowercase.

echo "LINUX" | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z'

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Replace spaces.

echo "REBASH Academy" | tr ' ' '_'

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Delete vowels.

echo "Cloud Computing" | tr -d 'aeiouAEIOU'

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Remove digits.

echo "Server2026" | tr -d '0-9'

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Compress spaces.

echo "Linux     Docker     Kubernetes" | tr -s ' '

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Convert usernames.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Replace commas.

echo "A,B,C,D" | tr ',' ';'

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' Uppercase conversion Normalize input tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' Lowercase conversion Standardize logs tr -d Delete characters Remove spaces or digits tr -s Compress repeats Clean formatted reports tr ':' ',' Replace delimiters Convert data formats

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

An operations team receives a user report with inconsistent formatting.

alice

BOB

Charlie

david

Tasks:

  1. Convert all names to uppercase.
  2. Remove blank spaces.
  3. Replace commas with semicolons.
  4. Compress multiple spaces into one.
  5. Remove numeric characters from usernames.

Solutions:

cat users.txt | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'

cat users.txt | tr -d ' '

cat users.txt | tr ',' ';'

cat users.txt | tr -s ' '

cat users.txt | tr -d '0-9'

docs.title: Mini Challenge
docs.text:
Create:

users.txt

Contents:

alice

BOB

Charlie

David123

Dev Ops Team

Perform the following:

  • Convert all text to uppercase.
  • Convert all text to lowercase.
  • Remove digits.
  • Replace spaces with underscores.
  • Remove repeated spaces.
  • Replace underscores back with spaces.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Remember that tr reads from standard input, not directly from files.
  • Prefer POSIX character classes ([:upper:], [:lower:]) for portability.
  • Use tr -s to clean repeated delimiters.
  • Combine tr with cut, grep, sort, and awk for efficient text processing.
  • Test transformations on sample data before using them in production scripts.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Trying to use tr directly on a file.

✅ Incorrect:

tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' file.txt

Correct:

cat file.txt | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

or

tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < file.txt

❌ Expecting tr to replace words.

✅ tr works on individual characters, not words.

Use sed for word replacement.

❌ Forgetting that tr preserves line structure.

✅ It transforms characters but does not rearrange lines.

docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Character translation
  • Case conversion
  • Character deletion
  • Character replacement
  • Squeezing repeated characters
  • Using tr in command pipelines
  • Production text transformation techniques

The tr command is a fast and efficient tool for character-level transformations. It is widely used in Linux administration, automation, and shell scripting to clean and normalize text.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• tr performs character-by-character transformations.
  • It reads input from stdin.
  • Use -d to delete characters.
  • Use -s to squeeze repeated characters.
  • Prefer POSIX character classes for portability.
  • Use sed when you need to replace words or patterns instead of individual characters.

docs.title: uniq Command — Removing Duplicate Lines in Linux
uniq Command — Removing Duplicate Lines in Linux
docs.text: The uniq command is used to identify, remove, and count duplicate lines in text files. It is commonly used after the sort command to clean data, generate reports, analyze logs, and process large datasets. Every Linux Administrator, DevOps Engineer, and Cloud Engineer should know how to use uniq effectively.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 3: Text Processing → Lesson 5

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 25 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Text Processing

Lesson: 5 of 18

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the uniq command
  • Remove duplicate lines
  • Count duplicate entries
  • Display only duplicate lines
  • Display only unique lines
  • Combine uniq with sort
  • Analyze production logs and reports

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–4

docs.title: Why Learn uniq?
docs.text:
Imagine you have a log file containing repeated error messages.

ERROR

ERROR

WARNING

INFO

INFO

INFO

Instead of manually identifying duplicates:

sort logfile.txt | uniq

Output:

ERROR

INFO

WARNING

This is one of the most common Linux data-cleaning operations.

docs.title: What is uniq?
docs.text:
The uniq command filters or reports repeated lines in a text file.

Important: uniq only works on adjacent duplicate lines.

For reliable results, always sort the file first.

Syntax:

uniq [OPTIONS] FILE

docs.title: Sample File
docs.text:
Create a file.

cat > fruits.txt

Contents:

Apple

Apple

Banana

Banana

Banana

Orange

Orange

Mango

Press:

Ctrl + D

docs.title: Remove Duplicate Lines
docs.text:
uniq fruits.txt

Output:

Apple

Banana

Orange

Mango

docs.title: Why sort is Important
docs.text:
Consider:

Apple

Banana

Apple

Orange

Command:

uniq fruits.txt

Output:

Apple

Banana

Apple

Orange

The duplicate Apple is not removed because the duplicate lines are not adjacent.

Correct approach:

sort fruits.txt | uniq

Output:

Apple

Banana

Orange

docs.title: Count Duplicate Lines
docs.text:
sort fruits.txt | uniq -c

Output:

2 Apple

3 Banana

1 Mango

2 Orange

The -c option prefixes each line with the number of occurrences.

docs.title: Display Only Duplicate Lines
docs.text:
sort fruits.txt | uniq -d

Output:

Apple

Banana

Orange

Only repeated values are displayed.

docs.title: Display Only Unique Lines
docs.text:
sort fruits.txt | uniq -u

Output:

Mango

Only lines that appear once are displayed.

docs.title: Ignore Case
docs.text:
Create:

Apple

APPLE

apple

Banana

Command:

sort -f fruits.txt | uniq -i

Treats uppercase and lowercase letters as identical.

docs.title: Skip Characters
docs.text:
Suppose:

001 Alice

002 Alice

003 Bob

Ignore the first four characters.

uniq -s 4 users.txt

Useful for fixed-width reports.

docs.title: Skip Fields
docs.text:
Example:

1 Alice

2 Alice

3 Bob

Command:

uniq -f 1 users.txt

Ignores the first field while comparing lines.

docs.title: Combining with Pipes
docs.text:
Remove duplicate users.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq

Count duplicate IP addresses.

cat access.log | cut -d " " -f1 | sort | uniq -c

Display unique departments.

cut -d "," -f2 employees.csv | sort | uniq

docs.title: Common uniq Options
docs.text: Option Description -c Count duplicate lines -d Display only duplicates -u Display only unique lines -i Ignore case -f Skip fields -s Skip characters

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Count failed login attempts.

grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | sort | uniq -c

Find duplicate IP addresses.

cat access.log | cut -d " " -f1 | sort | uniq -c

Display unique Docker images.

docker images | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq

Count Kubernetes namespaces.

kubectl get namespaces | sort | uniq

Generate unique usernames.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
The uniq command is commonly used for:

  • Cleaning reports
  • Removing duplicate records
  • Counting repeated log entries
  • Security log analysis
  • Audit reporting
  • Data preprocessing before scripting

It is almost always used together with sort.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create:

cat > servers.txt

Contents:

server01

server02

server01

server03

server02

server04

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Sort the file.

sort servers.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Remove duplicates.

sort servers.txt | uniq

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Count duplicates.

sort servers.txt | uniq -c

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Display duplicates only.

sort servers.txt | uniq -d

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Display unique entries only.

sort servers.txt | uniq -u

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Count unique usernames.

cut -d ":" -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq | wc -l

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Count duplicate shells.

cut -d ":" -f7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -c

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example uniq Remove adjacent duplicates Reports uniq -c Count duplicates Log analysis uniq -d Show duplicates Security audits uniq -u Show unique values Data validation uniq -i Ignore case User reports uniq -f Skip fields Fixed-format reports

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A web server's access log contains repeated client IP addresses.

Tasks:

  1. Display unique client IPs.
  2. Count how many requests came from each IP.
  3. Display only duplicate IP addresses.
  4. Identify IPs that appear only once.

Solutions:

cut -d " " -f1 access.log | sort | uniq

cut -d " " -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c

cut -d " " -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -d

cut -d " " -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -u

docs.title: Mini Challenge

Bob

Alice

Charlie

David

Charlie

Alice

Eve

Perform the following:

  • Sort the file.
  • Remove duplicate names.
  • Count each name.
  • Display duplicate names only.
  • Display names that appear only once.
  • Count the total number of unique employees.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always sort data before using uniq.
  • Use uniq -c to generate quick frequency reports.
  • Combine uniq with cut and grep for advanced analysis.
  • Use uniq -u to identify unique records.
  • Use uniq -d to detect duplicate entries.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using uniq on unsorted data.

✅ Incorrect:

uniq file.txt

Correct:

sort file.txt | uniq

❌ Assuming uniq removes all duplicates automatically.

✅ It only removes adjacent duplicate lines.

❌ Forgetting to sort before counting duplicates.

✅ Always use:

sort file.txt | uniq -c

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Removing duplicate lines
  • Counting duplicate entries
  • Displaying only duplicate or unique lines
  • Combining uniq with sort
  • Production log analysis

The uniq command is a simple but powerful utility for cleaning and summarizing data. When combined with sort, it becomes an essential tool for Linux administration and text processing.

  • uniq -d displays only duplicate lines.
  • uniq -u displays only unique lines.
  • uniq is commonly used for log analysis, reporting, and data cleanup.

docs.title: xargs Command — Building Powerful Command Pipelines in Linux
xargs Command — Building Powerful Command Pipelines in Linux
docs.text: The xargs command reads input from standard input (stdin) and converts it into command-line arguments for another command. It is one of the most powerful Linux utilities for automation, batch processing, file management, and DevOps workflows. Almost every Linux administrator eventually uses xargs to build efficient command pipelines.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:

Difficulty: Intermediate → Advanced

Reading Time: 40 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Text Processing

Lesson: 15 of 18

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the xargs command
  • Convert stdin into command arguments
  • Process multiple files efficiently
  • Combine find with xargs
  • Execute commands in parallel
  • Handle filenames containing spaces
  • Use xargs in production automation

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 Lessons 1–14

docs.title: Why Learn xargs?
docs.text:
Suppose you have hundreds of log files.

log1.log

log2.log

log3.log

...

log500.log

You want to delete all of them.

Without xargs, this becomes difficult.

With xargs:

find . -name "*.log" | xargs rm

Done.

This is one of the most common automation patterns in Linux.

docs.title: What is xargs?
docs.text:
xargs reads items from standard input and builds command-line arguments for another command.

Think of it like this:

Input
 │
 ▼
xargs
 │
 ▼
Command Arguments

Syntax:

xargs [OPTIONS] COMMAND

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Input:

echo "Linux Docker Kubernetes"

Pipe to xargs:

echo "Linux Docker Kubernetes" | xargs echo

Output:

Linux Docker Kubernetes

Not very exciting—but it shows how xargs converts stdin into arguments.

docs.title: Passing Arguments
docs.text:
Create files.

echo "file1 file2 file3" | xargs touch

Result:

file1

file2

file3

docs.title: Remove Multiple Files
docs.text: echo "file1 file2 file3" | xargs rm

docs.title: Count Lines in Multiple Files
docs.text: find . -name "*.txt" | xargs wc -l

docs.title: Display File Information
docs.text: find . -name "*.sh" | xargs ls -l

docs.title: Using Placeholder (-I)
docs.text:
Suppose:

Alice

Bob

Charlie

Command:

cat users.txt | xargs -I {} echo "Welcome {}"

Output:

Welcome Alice

Welcome Bob

Welcome Charlie

{} is replaced by each input item.

docs.title: Execute Multiple Commands
docs.text:
cat users.txt | xargs -I {} sh -c 'echo "Creating {}"; touch {}'

Output:

Creating Alice

Creating Bob

Creating Charlie

docs.title: Working with find
docs.text:
Create test files.

touch a.log b.log c.log

Find:

find . -name "*.log"

Delete:

find . -name "*.log" | xargs rm

docs.title: Safe File Handling
docs.text:
Problem:

A filename contains spaces.

My File.txt

Incorrect:

find . -name "*.txt" | xargs rm

This breaks because spaces split arguments.

Correct:

find . -name "*.txt" -print0 | xargs -0 rm

This is the recommended approach.

docs.title: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
Suppose you have multiple files to compress.

find . -name "*.log" | xargs -P 4 gzip

Explanation:

  • -P 4 → Run four commands in parallel.

Useful for multicore systems.

docs.title: Limit Number of Arguments
docs.text:
Execute two files at a time.

echo "1 2 3 4 5 6" | xargs -n 2 echo

Output:

1 2

3 4

5 6

docs.title: Limit Number of Processes
docs.text:
Run one command per file.

find . -name "*.txt" | xargs -n 1 wc -l

docs.title: Prompt Before Execution
docs.text:
echo "file1 file2" | xargs -p rm

Output:

rm file1 file2 ?...

The user is prompted before the command runs.

docs.title: Replace Existing Files
docs.text:
Create backups.

find . -name "*.conf" | xargs -I {} cp {} {}.bak

docs.title: Common xargs Options
docs.text: Option Description -0 Read null-separated input -I {} Placeholder replacement -n Number of arguments per command -P Parallel execution -p Prompt before execution -t Display command before running

docs.title: Combining with Other Commands
docs.text:
Count shell scripts.

find . -name "*.sh" | xargs wc -l

Search configuration files.

find /etc -name "*.conf" | xargs grep "port"

Calculate disk usage.

find . -name "*.log" | xargs du -sh

Display file types.

find . -type f | xargs file

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Delete old logs.

find /var/log -name "*.gz" | xargs rm

Backup configuration files.

find /etc -name "*.conf" | xargs -I {} cp {} backup/

Check permissions.

find /var/www -type f | xargs ls -l

Compress log files.

find logs/ -name "*.log" | xargs gzip

Generate checksums.

find . -type f | xargs sha256sum

docs.text:
The xargs command is heavily used in:

  • DevOps automation
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Kubernetes administration
  • Backup automation
  • Security auditing
  • Log management

It enables efficient processing of large numbers of files and command outputs.

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Run in parallel.

find . -name "*.txt" | xargs -P 2 wc -l

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Safely delete files.

find . -name "*.bak" -print0 | xargs -0 rm

docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example xargs rm Delete files Log cleanup xargs wc -l Count lines Reports xargs ls -l Display details Audits xargs -I {} Placeholder Backups xargs -0 Safe filenames Production scripts xargs -P Parallel execution Large datasets

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A DevOps engineer needs to clean up old log files across hundreds of directories.

Tasks:

  1. Find all .log files.
  2. Compress them.
  3. Generate SHA256 checksums.
  4. Remove compressed files older than 30 days.

Solutions:

find /var/log -name "*.log" | xargs gzip

find /var/log -name "*.gz" | xargs sha256sum

find /var/log -name "*.gz" -mtime +30 -print0 | xargs -0 rm

docs.text:

  • Delete backup files safely.
  • Run commands in parallel.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Always use -print0 with find and -0 with xargs when filenames may contain spaces.
  • Test commands with echo or xargs -t before performing destructive operations.
  • Use -P to improve performance on multicore systems.
  • Combine xargs with find, grep, and sha256sum for automation.
  • Avoid using xargs rm without verifying the input.

docs.title: Performance Tip
docs.text:
For CPU-intensive operations:

find . -name "*.log" | xargs -P 8 gzip

This processes multiple files simultaneously, reducing execution time on systems with multiple CPU cores.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Ignoring filenames with spaces.

✅ Incorrect:

find . -name "*.txt" | xargs rm

Correct:

find . -name "*.txt" -print0 | xargs -0 rm

❌ Running destructive commands without verification.

✅ Safer:

find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs -t rm

or

find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs -p rm

❌ Assuming xargs is always required.

✅ Many modern commands support find -exec ... +, which can be a suitable alternative.

docs.title: The top Command — Real-Time Process Monitoring in Linux
The top Command — Real-Time Process Monitoring in Linux
docs.text: The top command is one of the most powerful Linux monitoring tools. Unlike the ps command, which displays a snapshot of running processes, top provides a real-time, continuously updating view of system activity. It allows administrators to monitor CPU usage, memory consumption, load averages, running processes, and system performance from a single interactive interface.

Course Progress

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the top command
  • Monitor system performance in real time
  • Interpret CPU and memory usage
  • Analyze running processes
  • Sort processes interactively
  • Identify resource-intensive applications
  • Manage processes from top
  • Troubleshoot production performance issues

docs.text:

docs.title: Why Learn top?
docs.text:
Imagine users report:

  • The server is slow.
  • Applications are hanging.
  • CPU usage is very high.
  • Memory is almost full.

The first command many Linux administrators execute is:

top

It immediately shows which processes are consuming system resources.

docs.title: What is top?
docs.text:
top is a real-time system monitoring utility.

It continuously displays:

  • Running processes
  • CPU usage
  • Memory usage
  • Load averages
  • Process states
  • System uptime

The display refreshes automatically every few seconds.

docs.title: Starting top
docs.text:
Run:

top

Example:

top - 10:45:12

Tasks: 245 total

Cpu(s): 12.5% us

Mem: 16 GB

PID USER %CPU %MEM COMMAND

Exit by pressing:

q

docs.title: Understanding the Header
docs.text:
The top section provides an overview of system health.

Example:

top - 10:45:12 up 5 days, 3 users

Tasks: 215 total

%Cpu(s): 12 us, 3 sy, 85 id

MiB Mem : 16000 total

MiB Swap: 4096 total

docs.title: Load Average
docs.text:
Example:

load average:

0.42

0.50

0.61

These values represent the average system load over:

  • Last 1 minute
  • Last 5 minutes
  • Last 15 minutes

Generally:

  • A value close to the number of CPU cores indicates normal utilization.
  • Values significantly higher than the available CPU cores may indicate CPU contention.

docs.title: CPU Usage
docs.text:
Example:

%Cpu(s)

us

sy

ni

id

wa

hi

si

st

Meaning:

Field Description us User processes sy Kernel (system) processes ni Nice processes id Idle CPU time wa Waiting for I/O hi Hardware interrupts si Software interrupts st Stolen CPU time (virtualized environments)

docs.title: Memory Usage
docs.text:
Example:

MiB Mem :

16000 total

4200 used

9800 free

2000 buff/cache

Key fields:

Field Description Total Installed memory Used Memory currently in use Free Unused memory Buff/Cache Memory used for buffers and filesystem cache

Linux intentionally uses available RAM for caching to improve performance.

docs.title: Swap Usage
docs.text:
Example:

Swap

4096 total

120 used

3976 free

Heavy swap usage may indicate memory pressure.

docs.title: Process Table
docs.text:
Typical columns:

Column Description PID Process ID USER Process owner PR Priority NI Nice value VIRT Virtual memory RES Physical memory used SHR Shared memory S Process state %CPU CPU usage %MEM Memory usage TIME+ CPU time COMMAND Executable

docs.title: Interactive Commands
docs.text:
While top is running:

Key Action q Quit P Sort by CPU usage M Sort by memory usage T Sort by CPU time k Kill a process r Change process priority (renice) h Display help 1 Show CPU usage per core

docs.text:

L

Enter:

nginx

or

java

1

CPU0

CPU1

CPU2

top

  • CPU utilization is above 95%.
  • One Java process is consuming most of the CPU.
  • Memory usage is normal.
  • Load average is significantly higher than the number of CPU cores.

Next steps:

  • Identify the application.
  • Review application logs.
  • Investigate the workload.
  • Optimize or restart the application if appropriate.

The top command quickly identifies the source of the performance issue.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use top as the first step in performance troubleshooting.
  • Monitor CPU, memory, and load average together.
  • Sort by CPU or memory to identify resource-intensive processes.
  • Verify process ownership before terminating processes.
  • Use batch mode for automation and reporting.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming high memory usage always indicates a problem.

✅ Linux uses free memory for filesystem caching, which is generally beneficial.

❌ Confusing CPU utilization with load average.

✅ Load average includes processes waiting for CPU time or uninterruptible resources such as disk I/O.

❌ Terminating high CPU processes without understanding their purpose.

✅ Always investigate the root cause first.

docs.text:

  3. How would you use top during a production incident involving performance degradation?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Real-time process monitoring
  • CPU utilization
  • Memory usage
  • Load averages
  • Interactive process management
  • Process sorting
  • Production troubleshooting

The top command is one of the most valuable Linux administration tools. It provides a live view of system performance, making it indispensable for diagnosing resource bottlenecks, identifying runaway processes, and monitoring production systems.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• top provides a real-time view of system performance.
  • Monitor CPU, memory, swap, and load average together.
  • Use P to sort by CPU usage.
  • Use M to sort by memory usage.
  • Use top -p to monitor a specific process.

docs.title: traceroute — Discovering the Network Path to a Destination
traceroute — Discovering the Network Path to a Destination
docs.text: traceroute is a Linux networking tool that identifies the path packets take from a source system to a destination. It displays every intermediate router (hop) along the route, helping administrators locate network delays, routing problems, and connectivity failures. It is one of the most valuable tools for Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, Network Engineers, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs).

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 8: Networking → Lesson 6

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 60 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Networking

Lesson: 6 of 13

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand how traceroute works
  • Discover network paths
  • Identify routing issues
  • Measure network latency
  • Interpret traceroute output
  • Use common traceroute options
  • Troubleshoot production network problems

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 – File Management
  • Module 5 – Users and Groups
  • Module 6 – Process Management
  • Module 7 – Package Management
  • Module 8 Lessons 1–5

docs.title: Why Learn traceroute?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • A website loads slowly.
  • SSH connections time out.
  • Cloud servers cannot communicate.
  • A Kubernetes cluster has network latency.

ping only tells you whether a host is reachable.

traceroute tells you:

Where the packets are traveling and where they stop or slow down.

docs.title: What is traceroute?
docs.text:
traceroute is a diagnostic tool that displays every network device (hop) between your computer and the destination.

It helps answer:

  • Which routers are involved?
  • Where is the delay?
  • Which hop is unreachable?

docs.title: How traceroute Works
docs.text:
traceroute sends packets with gradually increasing TTL (Time To Live) values.

Example:

TTL = 1

↓

Router 1 replies

TTL = 2

↓

Router 2 replies

TTL = 3

↓

Router 3 replies

This continues until the destination is reached.

docs.title: What is TTL?
docs.text:
TTL stands for:

Time To Live

It limits how many routers (hops) a packet can pass through.

Each router decreases the TTL by 1.

When TTL reaches 0:

  • The router discards the packet.
  • It sends an ICMP "Time Exceeded" message back.

traceroute uses these replies to identify each hop.

docs.title: Basic traceroute Command
docs.text:
Trace the route to Google.

traceroute google.com

Example output:

1 192.168.1.1

2 10.20.0.1

3 203.0.113.1

4 google.com

Each numbered line represents one network hop.

docs.title: Understanding the Output
docs.text:
Example:

3 203.0.113.1 15.4 ms 16.2 ms 15.8 ms

Meaning:

Field Description 3 Hop number 203.0.113.1 Router IP address 15.4 ms First response time 16.2 ms Second response time 15.8 ms Third response time

Multiple response times help identify latency variations.

docs.title: Install traceroute
docs.text:
Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt install traceroute

RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux:

sudo dnf install traceroute

docs.title: Trace Using an IP Address
docs.text: traceroute 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Numeric Output Only
docs.text:
Avoid DNS lookups.

traceroute -n google.com

This is faster because hostnames are not resolved.

docs.title: Limit Maximum Hops
docs.text:
traceroute -m 10 google.com

Stops tracing after 10 hops.

docs.title: Set Probe Count
docs.text:
Send two probes per hop.

traceroute -q 2 google.com

Default:

3 probes

docs.title: Use ICMP Instead of UDP
docs.text:
Some firewalls block UDP-based traceroute.

Use ICMP:

traceroute -I google.com

docs.title: Use TCP Probes
docs.text:
Useful when ICMP or UDP traffic is filtered.

sudo traceroute -T google.com

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Basic trace.

traceroute google.com

Numeric output.

traceroute -n google.com

Limit hops.

traceroute -m 15 google.com

Use ICMP.

traceroute -I google.com

Use TCP.

sudo traceroute -T google.com

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Trace a Kubernetes API server.

traceroute api.example.com

Trace a cloud server.

traceroute 34.120.x.x

Trace a database server.

traceroute db.example.com

Trace Google DNS.

traceroute 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
traceroute is widely used for:

  • Network troubleshooting
  • Cloud networking
  • Kubernetes clusters
  • VPN diagnostics
  • WAN connectivity
  • Internet routing
  • ISP troubleshooting
  • Performance analysis

It helps identify the location of routing failures or excessive latency.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Trace the route to Google.

traceroute google.com

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Trace to Google's DNS server.

traceroute 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Disable DNS resolution.

traceroute -n google.com

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Limit the trace to 10 hops.

traceroute -m 10 google.com

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Use ICMP probes.

traceroute -I google.com

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Use TCP probes.

sudo traceroute -T google.com

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Compare routes to two different websites.

traceroute google.com

traceroute cloudflare.com

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Observe:

  • Number of hops
  • Latency at each hop
  • Final destination

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example traceroute host Display network path Connectivity troubleshooting traceroute -n Skip DNS resolution Faster diagnostics traceroute -m Limit maximum hops Controlled tracing traceroute -q Set probes per hop Latency analysis traceroute -I Use ICMP Firewall testing traceroute -T Use TCP probes Production troubleshooting

docs.title: Common traceroute Symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning * No response received ms Response time in milliseconds Hop Number Router sequence in the path

Example:

5 * * *

This may indicate:

  • Firewall filtering
  • Router not responding to traceroute probes
  • Network congestion

It does not necessarily mean traffic cannot pass through that router.

docs.title: traceroute vs ping
docs.text: Feature ping traceroute Tests Connectivity ✅ ✅ Measures Latency ✅ ✅ Shows Network Path ❌ ✅ Displays Each Hop ❌ ✅ Detects Routing Problems Limited Excellent

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users report that a web application hosted in the cloud is slow.

Investigation:

Verify connectivity.

ping app.example.com

Connectivity is successful.

Trace the network path.

traceroute app.example.com

Output:

Hop 8

250 ms

All previous hops show latency below 20 ms.

This indicates a significant delay beginning at hop 8.

The network team investigates the corresponding router and resolves the issue, restoring normal application performance.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use ping first to verify basic connectivity.
  • Use traceroute to locate routing or latency problems.
  • Use -n for faster troubleshooting.
  • Compare traces from multiple locations when diagnosing distributed systems.
  • Remember that some routers intentionally ignore traceroute probes.
  • Combine traceroute with tools such as ping, ss, and curl for comprehensive diagnostics.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming * always means the network is broken.

✅ Verify * always means the network is broken instead of assuming it.

❌ Confusing latency at an intermediate hop with the destination's performance.

✅ Distinguish clearly between latency at an intermediate hop with the destination's performance.

❌ Ignoring firewall policies that block traceroute traffic.

✅ Always review firewall policies that block traceroute traffic.

❌ Using only one network diagnostic tool.

✅ Avoid using only one network diagnostic tool when a safer approach exists.

docs.title: Beginner
docs.text:
1. What is the purpose of traceroute?
  2. What does TTL stand for?
  3. What does each hop represent?
  4. Which command traces the path to a destination?

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
1. How does traceroute discover each router?
  2. What does * * * indicate?
  3. Why would you use traceroute -n?
  4. What is the difference between ping and traceroute?

docs.title: Architect Level
docs.text:
1. How would you troubleshoot intermittent latency between two cloud regions?
  2. Why might traceroute show high latency at one hop while the destination remains fast?
  3. How would you diagnose routing issues in a hybrid cloud environment?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • How traceroute works
  • TTL and hop discovery
  • Reading traceroute output
  • Measuring latency
  • Identifying routing issues
  • Common traceroute options
  • Production troubleshooting

traceroute is an essential networking tool that reveals the path packets take across networks. By identifying each hop and measuring response times, it helps administrators diagnose routing problems, locate network bottlenecks, and troubleshoot connectivity issues in production environments.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• traceroute displays the path packets take to reach a destination.
  • It works by sending packets with increasing TTL values.
  • Each router along the path is displayed as a hop.
  • Use -n to skip DNS lookups and speed up troubleshooting.
  • * responses do not always indicate a failure.
  • Combine traceroute with other networking tools for effective diagnostics.
