The ss command is the modern and preferred tool for inspecting network sockets and active connections on Linux.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Panic looks like random command typing. Good troubleshooting looks like detective work: symptom → facts → one hypothesis → one change → proof. This tutorial builds that method on a real break-and-fix lab.

Plain problem: “The API is down.” Is it the app, the service unit, disk full, out of memory, or a bad deploy? Without order, you restart everything and hope — extending the outage.

This tutorial teaches a repeatable loop and a lab where you break a systemd unit, diagnose with logs and status commands, fix it, and prove recovery.

This is Tutorial 15 in Module 15: Troubleshooting of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ubuntu VM with systemd
  • systemd Services and journalctl or equivalent comfort
  • sudo for unit files under /etc/systemd/system/

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • State a troubleshooting method in plain language
  • Gather first facts: time, change, disk, memory, failed units, logs
  • Diagnose a failed systemd unit with systemctl and journalctl
  • Break and fix a misconfigured unit on purpose
  • Write a short incident evidence pack
  • Answer fresher interview questions on Linux troubleshooting

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Incidents flow from user-visible symptom down through service state, resources, and logs. Your job is narrowing which layer failed before changing production.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text: 3 am page: “Site unreachable.” Junior restarts nginx three times. Disk was 100% full from logs — nginx was innocent. Gather facts first would have shown df -h at 0 bytes free in thirty seconds.

docs.title: The method (simple words)
docs.text:
Analogy: Doctor visit — symptoms, vitals, one test, one treatment, follow-up. Not random medicine.

Step Action 1. Symptom What fails, for whom, since when? 2. Timeline Deploys, cron, config changes? 3. Scope One host or many? One service? 4. Facts uptime, df -h, free -h, failed units, logs 5. Hypothesis One likely cause 6. Change One fix at a time 7. Proof Metric/log showing recovery 8. Document What broke, why, how you fixed

Interview line: “I never restart without checking systemctl status, journalctl -u, disk, and recent changes.”

docs.title: First-fact commands
docs.text:
Terminal
uptime
df -h
free -h
systemctl --failed
journalctl -p err -b --no-pager | tail -30
ss -tlnp

docs.title: systemd failure patterns
docs.text: Signal Tool Unit failed systemctl status app.service Why exit code journalctl -u app.service -b Config syntax systemd-analyze verify unit.file Dependency order systemctl list-dependencies

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Restarting before reading logs (loses evidence)
  • Multiple changes at once (cannot tell what worked)
  • Ignoring disk/memory until late
  • No written timeline for post-incident review

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Deploy a small systemd app unit, break it with a bad ExecStart, diagnose and fix, prove recovery — evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab23.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu VM systemd sudo Install unit to /etc/systemd/system/

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab23/bin && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab23

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Ticket: “rebash-report.service failed after deploy.” You have no prior context — only SSH. Follow the method and attach an evidence pack.

docs.title: Task 1 – Working unit and baseline
docs.text:
Create report.sh:

report.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
echo "$(date -Is) report OK" >> /tmp/rebash-report.log

Create rebash-report.service:

rebash-report.service
[Unit]
Description=REBASH lab23 report oneshot

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/home/USER_PLACEHOLDER/rebash-linux/lab23/bin/report.sh

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab23
mkdir -p bin
cp report.sh bin/
chmod +x bin/report.sh
sed "s/USER_PLACEHOLDER/$USER/" rebash-report.service | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/rebash-report.service >/dev/null
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now rebash-report.service
systemctl status rebash-report.service --no-pager | tee status-ok.txt
test -f /tmp/rebash-report.log
tail -1 /tmp/rebash-report.log | tee log-ok.txt

Expected output

Unit active/exited successfully; log line with timestamp in log-ok.txt.

docs.title: Task 2 – Break (bad ExecStart), diagnose
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab23
sudo sed -i 's|report.sh|report-MISSING.sh|' /etc/systemd/system/rebash-report.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start rebash-report.service 2>&1 | tee start-broken.txt || true
systemctl status rebash-report.service --no-pager | tee status-broken.txt
journalctl -u rebash-report.service -b --no-pager | tail -15 | tee journal-broken.txt
grep -i 'failed\|error\|not found' journal-broken.txt status-broken.txt | tee diagnosis.txt

Expected output

Status shows failed state; journal mentions missing script or exit code failure.

docs.title: Task 3 – Fix and prove recovery
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab23
sudo sed -i 's|report-MISSING.sh|report.sh|' /etc/systemd/system/rebash-report.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start rebash-report.service
systemctl status rebash-report.service --no-pager | tee status-fixed.txt
journalctl -u rebash-report.service -b --no-pager | tail -5 | tee journal-fixed.txt
grep -q 'report OK' /tmp/rebash-report.log
echo "lab23 troubleshoot OK" | tee evidence.txt

Create incident-summary.md:

incident-summary.md
# Incident summary — lab23

- Symptom: rebash-report.service failed after change
- Cause: ExecStart pointed to missing script path
- Fix: restored correct path, daemon-reload, start
- Proof: status-fixed.txt and new log line in /tmp/rebash-report.log

Expected output

Service succeeds again; incident summary documents break→fix→prove.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• Baseline success captured before break
  • Diagnosis used systemctl + journalctl (not blind restart)
  • Fix restored service with evidence files
  • incident-summary.md completed

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix Unit not found Not daemon-reload sudo systemctl daemon-reload Permission denied in script Path or perms chmod +x; absolute paths Empty journal Wrong unit name Match -u to unit file Fix does not apply Forgot reload Always reload after unit edit

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text: Add systemctl --failed output before and after fix to failed-units.txt.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• You followed a structured troubleshoot loop
  • You broke and fixed a real systemd unit
  • You produced interview-ready incident notes

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
sudo systemctl disable --now rebash-report.service 2>/dev/null || true
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/rebash-report.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
rm -f /tmp/rebash-report.log

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab23
  • Can recite first-fact commands from memory
  • Ready for production hardening next

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Type=oneshot — runs script once per start; good for report/cron-style tasks.
  2. Break via ExecStart typo — mirrors real deploy typo incidents.
  3. journalctl -u -b — this boot’s unit story only.
  4. One change fix — restore path, reload, start — scientific method.
  5. incident-summary.md — habit hiring managers like in postmortems.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Preserve logs before restart during real incidents (audit trail).
  • Do not paste production secrets into ticket evidence.
  • Verify you are on the correct host (hostname, ip) before fixes.
  • Use sudo deliberately; document privileged changes.
  • Blameless postmortems focus on process, not individuals.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Restart without logs.

✅ Read journalctl first — restarting may clear transient clues (still check after too).

❌ Many changes at once.

✅ One hypothesis, one change — otherwise you cannot explain what fixed it.

❌ Skipping disk and memory.

✅ df -h and free -h belong in the first two minutes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Methodology — Solving Linux Production Problems Systematically
Troubleshooting Methodology — Solving Linux Production Problems Systematically
docs.text: Troubleshooting Methodology is a structured approach to identifying, analyzing, isolating, resolving, and validating problems in Linux systems. Rather than relying on guesswork, experienced Linux administrators follow repeatable troubleshooting processes that reduce downtime, minimize risk, and improve operational reliability. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Operations Engineer should master systematic troubleshooting techniques.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 14: Production Linux Administration → Lesson 9

Difficulty: Beginner → Advanced

Reading Time: 120 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Production Linux Administration

Lesson: 9 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand structured troubleshooting
  • Identify production problems
  • Collect evidence effectively
  • Isolate root causes
  • Resolve Linux issues safely
  • Validate system recovery
  • Document troubleshooting activities
  • Apply production troubleshooting best practices

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Modules 1–13
  • Module 14 Lessons 1–8

docs.title: Why Follow a Methodology?
docs.text:
Imagine a production application suddenly becomes unavailable.

Without methodology:

Problem

↓

Random Changes

↓

More Problems

↓

Long Downtime

With methodology:

Problem

↓

Collect Evidence

↓

Analyze

↓

Find Root Cause

↓

Resolve

↓

Validate

↓

Document

A structured approach reduces recovery time and prevents unnecessary changes.

docs.title: What is Troubleshooting?
docs.text:
Troubleshooting is the process of:

  • Identifying problems
  • Collecting information
  • Analyzing symptoms
  • Isolating root causes
  • Implementing solutions
  • Validating recovery
  • Preventing recurrence

The objective is not only to fix issues but also to understand why they occurred.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Problem

↓

Collect Evidence

↓

Analyze

↓

Develop Hypothesis

↓

Test Hypothesis

↓

Resolve

↓

Validate

↓

Document

Always work methodically.

docs.title: Step 1 — Identify the Problem
docs.text:
Determine:

  • What is failing?
  • When did it begin?
  • Which systems are affected?
  • Is the issue intermittent or continuous?
  • Has anything changed recently?

Avoid making assumptions.

docs.title: Step 2 — Collect Evidence
docs.text:
Gather information before making changes.

Check:

Operating system

hostnamectl

System uptime

uptime

Processes

ps aux

Memory

free -h

Disk

df -h

Logs

journalctl

Network

ip addr

ss -tuln

docs.title: Step 3 — Analyze Symptoms
docs.text:
Look for patterns.

Examples:

  • High CPU usage
  • Memory exhaustion
  • Disk full
  • Service failures
  • Network connectivity issues
  • Authentication failures
  • Kernel errors

Analyze multiple data sources before reaching conclusions.

docs.title: Step 4 — Develop a Hypothesis
docs.text:
Example:

Application Slow

↓

High Disk I/O

↓

Log Files Growing

↓

Disk Bottleneck

Create one or more possible explanations based on evidence.

docs.title: Step 5 — Test the Hypothesis
docs.text:
Example:

Check disk usage.

df -h

Check large directories.

du -sh /var/*

Review application logs.

journalctl -u application

Confirm the hypothesis before applying changes.

docs.title: Step 6 — Implement the Solution
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Restart service
  • Expand storage
  • Apply configuration changes
  • Roll back deployment
  • Restore backup
  • Patch software
  • Replace failed hardware

Implement the smallest safe change first.

docs.title: Step 7 — Validate the Fix
docs.text:
Verify:

  • Service is running
  • Users can access applications
  • Monitoring reports healthy status
  • Logs contain no new errors
  • Performance has returned to normal

Commands:

systemctl status

curl

journalctl

top

docs.title: Step 8 — Document Everything
docs.text:
Record:

  • Problem description
  • Timeline
  • Investigation
  • Commands executed
  • Root cause
  • Resolution
  • Preventive recommendations

Documentation accelerates future troubleshooting.

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
Monitor:

top

htop

mpstat

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Review:

free -h

vmstat

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Review:

df -h

du -sh

lsblk

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Verify:

ip addr

ip route

ping

ss -tuln

curl

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Review:

systemctl status

systemctl --failed

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
System logs.

journalctl

Recent errors.

journalctl -p err

Application logs.

/var/log/

Logs are often the most valuable source of troubleshooting information.

docs.title: Root Cause Analysis
docs.text:
Avoid stopping at the first symptom.

Example:

Application Down

↓

Database Offline

↓

Disk Full

↓

Log Rotation Failed

↓

Root Cause

Always identify the underlying cause rather than only treating symptoms.

docs.title: Change Verification
docs.text:
After implementing a solution:

Verify:

  • Service availability
  • System health
  • Performance
  • Monitoring
  • User experience

Successful troubleshooting always includes validation.

docs.title: Escalation
docs.text:
Escalate when:

  • Additional expertise is required
  • Business impact increases
  • Security incidents are suspected
  • Vendor support is needed
  • Recovery exceeds acceptable timelines

Timely escalation helps reduce prolonged outages.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
Automation can assist with:

  • Log collection
  • Health checks
  • Diagnostic scripts
  • Alerting
  • Service recovery
  • Infrastructure validation

Automation complements, but does not replace, systematic troubleshooting.

docs.title: Common Linux Commands
docs.text:
System information.

hostnamectl

Processes.

ps aux

Memory.

Disk.

Services.

Logs.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

Users report that a production application is responding very slowly.

Investigation:

Check system load.

uptime

Load is normal.

Review memory.

free -h

Memory usage is healthy.

Review storage.

df -h

Filesystem is 100% full.

Review disk usage.

du -sh /var/log/*

Application logs have grown unexpectedly because log rotation stopped working.

Actions performed:

  • Archive old logs.
  • Restore free disk space.
  • Fix log rotation configuration.
  • Verify application response.

Application performance returns to normal.

Root cause:

Disk Full Due to Log Rotation Failure

docs.title: umask Command — Controlling Default File and Directory Permissions
umask Command — Controlling Default File and Directory Permissions
docs.text: The umask (User File Creation Mask) command determines the default permissions assigned to newly created files and directories. Instead of adding permissions, umask removes permissions from the system defaults. Understanding umask is essential for Linux security, DevOps automation, cloud infrastructure, and production system administration.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 4: File Management and Permissions → Lesson 6

Difficulty: Intermediate

Reading Time: 45 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: File Management and Permissions

Lesson: 6 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the purpose of umask
  • View the current umask value
  • Calculate default permissions
  • Change the umask temporarily
  • Configure permanent umask values
  • Apply security best practices
  • Troubleshoot permission-related issues

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1
  • Module 2
  • Module 3

docs.title: Why Learn umask?
docs.text:
Imagine you're deploying an application.

A configuration file is created automatically.

Instead of:

rw-------

it becomes:

rw-rw-rw-

Now every user on the system can modify it.

This is a serious security risk.

The default permissions are controlled by umask.

docs.title: What is umask?
docs.text:
umask stands for:

User File Creation Mask

It defines which permissions should NOT be assigned when creating new files and directories.

Important:

umask removes permissions—it does not grant permissions.

docs.title: How Default Permissions Work
docs.text: Linux starts with these defaults:

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
666

rw-rw-rw-

Why not 777?

Regular files are not executable by default for security reasons.

docs.title: Directories
docs.text:
777

rwxrwxrwx

Directories require execute permission for traversal.

docs.title: The Permission Formula
docs.text:
Default Permission

        -

     umask

----------------

Final Permission

docs.title: Example: umask 022
docs.text:
Current mask:

umask

Output:

0022

For files:

666

-022

----

644

Result:

rw-r--r--

For directories:

777

-022

----

755

Result:

rwxr-xr-x

docs.title: Example: umask 027
docs.text:
Files:

666

-027

----

640

Directories:

777

-027

----

750

docs.title: Example: umask 077
docs.text:
Files:

666

-077

----

600

Directories:

777

-077

----

700

This is commonly used for sensitive environments.

docs.title: Viewing Current umask
docs.text:
umask

Example:

0022

Display symbolic format:

umask -S

Output:

u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx

docs.title: Changing umask Temporarily
docs.text:

Verify:

umask

Create a file:

touch test.txt

Check:

ls -l test.txt

docs.title: Changing umask Permanently
docs.text:
User-specific:

~/.bashrc

~/.profile

~/.bash_profile

Example:

Reload:

source ~/.bashrc

System-wide:

Depending on the Linux distribution:

/etc/profile

/etc/bash.bashrc

/etc/login.defs

Note

Always verify your distribution's documentation before changing system-wide defaults.

docs.title: Common umask Values
docs.text: umask Files Directories Typical Use 000 666 777 Testing only 002 664 775 Team collaboration 022 644 755 Default on many Linux systems 027 640 750 Shared production environments 077 600 700 High-security systems

docs.title: Demonstration
docs.text:
Current:

umask 022

Create:

touch file1

mkdir dir1

Check:

ls -ld file1 dir1

Output:

-rw-r--r--

drwxr-xr-x

Change:

umask 077

Create:

touch secret.txt

mkdir secrets

Output:

-rw-------

drwx------

docs.title: Understanding the Calculation
docs.text:
Example:

Default File

666

umask

022

Final

644

Notice:

6 = rw-

2 removes write permission

Result:

r--

Think of umask as blocking permissions, not assigning them.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A DevOps engineer discovers that newly created configuration files are world-readable.

Investigation:

umask

touch app.conf

ls -l app.conf

Output:

-rw-r--r--

The application stores sensitive credentials.

Solution:

umask 077

touch app.conf

New permissions:

-rw-------

Sensitive configuration files are now accessible only to the owner.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use 022 for general-purpose Linux systems.
  • Use 027 for production application servers.
  • Use 077 for sensitive environments and secrets.
  • Verify file permissions after changing the umask.
  • Configure permanent umask values through appropriate shell initialization files when required.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Thinking umask adds permissions.

✅ It removes permissions from the default values.

❌ Expecting umask to change existing files.

✅ umask affects only newly created files and directories.

❌ Setting 000 on production servers.

✅ This can make newly created files writable by everyone, creating a significant security risk.

docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • What umask is
  • How default permissions are calculated
  • Viewing and modifying the umask
  • Temporary vs permanent configuration
  • Secure umask values
  • Production security practices

umask is one of Linux's most important preventive security mechanisms. By controlling the default permissions of newly created files and directories, it helps protect sensitive data and supports secure system administration.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• umask removes permissions from default values.
  • Default file permissions start at 666.
  • Default directory permissions start at 777.
  • umask 022 results in 644 for files and 755 for directories.
  • umask 077 is recommended for sensitive files and private environments.
  • umask affects only newly created files and directories.

docs.title: Understanding the Shell
docs.text: The shell is the primary interface between you and the Linux operating system. Every command you type is interpreted by the shell before being executed. Understanding how the shell works is the first step toward becoming a confident Linux administrator or DevOps engineer.

Reading Time: 20 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Linux Command Line Essentials

Lesson: 1 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand what the Linux Shell is
  • Differentiate the Shell, Terminal, and Kernel
  • Learn how the shell executes commands
  • Explore different shell types
  • Identify your current shell
  • Change shells
  • Understand why the shell is important in Cloud and DevOps

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, you should complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals

docs.title: Why Learn the Shell?
docs.text:
Every interaction with Linux happens through the shell.

When you:

  • Create files
  • Start services
  • Deploy applications
  • Configure Kubernetes
  • Manage cloud servers

you're communicating with Linux through a shell.

The shell is one of the most important tools for every Linux professional.

docs.title: What is a Shell?
docs.text:
A Shell is a command interpreter.

It reads commands entered by the user, interprets them, and asks the Linux Kernel to execute them.

Simply put:

The shell acts as a translator between the user and the operating system.

docs.title: How the Shell Works
docs.text:
User

↓

Shell

↓

Kernel

↓

Hardware

↓

Kernel

↓

Shell

↓

User

Example:

mkdir projects

Execution flow:

User

↓

Types:

mkdir projects

↓

Shell interprets command

↓

Kernel creates directory

↓

Result returned

↓

Shell displays prompt

The shell itself doesn't create the directory—it requests the kernel to do so.

docs.title: Shell vs Terminal
docs.text:
Many beginners confuse these terms.

Terminal Shell Application Command Interpreter Provides a window Executes commands GNOME Terminal, Konsole Bash, Zsh, Fish User Interface Program

Example:

GNOME Terminal

↓

Bash Shell

↓

Linux Kernel

docs.title: Shell vs Kernel
docs.text: Shell Kernel Accepts commands Controls hardware Runs in User Space Runs in Kernel Space Can be changed Core of Linux Multiple shells available Only one running kernel

docs.title: Popular Linux Shells
docs.text:
Linux supports multiple shells.

Shell Description Bash Default on most Linux distributions Zsh Powerful and customizable Fish Beginner-friendly shell Korn Shell (ksh) Enterprise UNIX environments C Shell (csh) BSD systems

Among these, Bash is the most widely used and is the shell you'll use throughout this course.

docs.title: Bash (Bourne Again SHell)
docs.text:
Bash is the default shell on most Linux distributions.

Features include:

  • Command history
  • Auto-completion
  • Variables
  • Aliases
  • Loops
  • Conditions
  • Functions
  • Shell scripting

Most DevOps tools and automation scripts assume Bash is available.

docs.title: Check Your Current Shell
docs.text:
Display your current shell:

echo $SHELL

Example output:

/bin/bash

or

docs.text:

Example:

/bin/bash
/bin/sh

docs.text:

Example:

PID TTY      TIME CMD

docs.title: Changing Your Default Shell
docs.text:
Display your current shell:

echo $SHELL

Change your default shell:

chsh -s /bin/bash

or

chsh -s /bin/zsh

Log out and log back in for the change to take effect.

docs.title: How the Shell Executes Commands
docs.text:
When you type:

ls

the shell follows these steps:

Read Command

↓

Parse Command

↓

Find Executable

↓

Execute Program

↓

Wait for Completion

↓

Display Output

↓

Show Prompt

This entire process happens in milliseconds.

docs.title: Built-in Commands vs External Commands
docs.text:
Some commands are built into the shell.

Examples:

cd

pwd

history

alias

export

Others are external programs.

Examples:

ls

cp

mv

grep

find

Check command type:

type cd

type ls

Example output:

cd is a shell builtin

ls is /usr/bin/ls

docs.title: Shell Prompt
docs.text:
Example:

basha@rebash:~$

Meaning:

Component Description basha Username rebash Hostname ~ Current Directory $ Normal User

Root prompt:

root@server:~#

The # symbol indicates the root user.

docs.text:
Cloud engineers spend most of their day working inside a shell.

Examples:

kubectl get pods

Every DevOps tool is controlled through a shell.

Learning the shell is essential for automation and infrastructure management.

docs.text:

  • Understand the difference between built-in and external commands.
  • Practice using the terminal every day.
  • Avoid running commands as the root user unless necessary.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Thinking the terminal and shell are the same.

✅ The terminal is the interface; the shell interprets commands.

❌ Assuming Linux has only one shell.

✅ Linux supports multiple shells such as Bash, Zsh, Fish, and Korn Shell.

❌ Believing the shell executes hardware operations.

✅ The shell requests the Linux Kernel to perform system operations.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every Linux server asks three questions on every login:

  1. Who are you? → user (account with a user ID, or UID)
  2. Which teams do you belong to? → groups (group ID, or GID)
  3. May you run admin commands? → sudo (“superuser do”)

When you SSH to a cloud VM, you log in as a user — not as “Linux itself”. File permissions, services, containers, and deploy scripts all depend on this identity layer. Wrong users or groups cause Permission denied, failed CI jobs, or accounts with far more power than they should have.

Plain problem: Many people stay logged in as root (full admin) because it “just works”. In production, one compromised script then owns the entire server. Good teams use normal users + small sudo rules.

This is Tutorial 6 in Module 4: Users & Permissions of the REBASH Academy Linux for Cloud & DevOps Engineers series — practical Linux for Cloud and DevOps work.

Lab safety

Create and delete lab users only on a practice VM. Do not run user-management tasks on a shared production server.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Disk Usage and File Attributes
  • A practice Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VM where you already have sudo
  • Willingness to create temporary lab users (rebash-alice, rebash-svc, …)

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Explain users, groups, and sudo using /etc/passwd, /etc/group, and /etc/sudoers.d/
  • Create a login user and a system (service) account with the correct shell
  • Add a user to a group with usermod -aG without removing other groups
  • Create a limited sudoers file with visudo and prove it with sudo -l
  • Demonstrate both allow and deny for sudo — then clean up lab accounts

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Linux identity sits between people (or automation) and the kernel. Account files store UID/GID. sudo decides which privileged commands are allowed. Files and processes then run as those identities.

docs.title: The problem (before any jargon)
docs.text:
Imagine three people on a small team:

  • Alice needs to restart one application service
  • Bob owns files for a background app — but must not log in interactively
  • You need to prove Alice cannot become full root

If everyone shares one root password, one stolen laptop key opens everything. Linux separates identities and gives small permission lists — the same idea as AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), but on the server itself.

docs.title: Users and groups — simple words
docs.text:
Analogy: A user is an employee badge. A group is a department badge shared by many employees. The UID/GID are the numeric IDs on the badge — storage systems care about numbers, not names.

Term Plain meaning Where stored User Account with UID, home folder, login shell /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow Group Named team with GID and member list /etc/group Primary group Default group for new files the user creates Field in /etc/passwd Secondary groups Extra teams (for example deploy, docker) /etc/group membership System user Low UID, often nologin shell — for apps, not people /etc/passwd root UID 0 — full admin Special account

What you can say in an interview: “Humans get login shells and limited sudo. Services get system accounts with nologin so nobody SSHs in as the app user.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
id
getent passwd "$USER"
getent group sudo

docs.title: What is sudo?
docs.text:
sudo lets an allowed user run specific commands as another user (usually root), based on rules in /etc/sudoers and files under /etc/sudoers.d/.

Analogy: sudo is borrowing a master key for one named door — not keeping the building master key on your lanyard all day.

Pattern Plain meaning Risk sudo command Run one command as root (if allowed) Safe if allow-list is narrow sudo -l List what you may run Always check before assuming NOPASSWD:ALL No password + any command Very dangerous on shared servers visudo Safe editor that checks syntax Always use this — never raw vim on sudoers

What you can say in an interview: “I grant exact command paths in /etc/sudoers.d/, run visudo -c, prove with sudo -l, and show one command that must fail.”

Tiny example:

Terminal
sudo -l
sudo systemctl status ssh

docs.title: How identity work flows
docs.text:
1. Check — id, getent passwd name, getent group name, sudo -l
  2. Create — useradd / groupadd (use --system for service accounts)
  3. Add to group — usermod -aG group user (-a means add; without it you can replace the whole secondary group list)
  4. Edit sudo rules — only with visudo or visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/file
  5. Prove — allow test + deny test + evidence files

docs.title: Key comparisons
docs.text: Object Important fields Files User UID, home, shell, primary GID /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow Group GID, members /etc/group sudo rule Who, as whom, which commands /etc/sudoers, /etc/sudoers.d/* Account type Shell Use for Login user /bin/bash People System user /usr/sbin/nologin Apps, daemons root /bin/bash or restricted Break-glass admin only

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Using usermod -G without -a — removes other groups silently
  • Editing /etc/sudoers with nano/vim — one typo locks everyone out of sudo
  • Giving NOPASSWD:ALL “for CI convenience” on a shared jump server
  • Same username, different UID on two servers sharing Network File System (NFS) — ownership breaks
  • Assuming cloud “admin” group means least privilege — check sudo -l on every new image

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: On a practice Ubuntu VM, create a team group, one human lab user, one system service account, and a limited sudoers file. Prove group membership, sudo allow, and sudo deny — then pack evidence under ~/rebash-linux/lab06.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Notes Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 Admin user with sudo VM snapshot Recommended before creating users Packages sudo, passwd (default on Ubuntu)

docs.title: Lab environment
docs.text:
Terminal
mkdir -p ~/rebash-linux/lab06 && cd ~/rebash-linux/lab06
set -euo pipefail
whoami | tee admin-user.txt
id | tee admin-id.txt
sudo -n true 2>/dev/null || sudo -v

Expected output

admin-user.txt and admin-id.txt exist; sudo works (you may enter your password once).

docs.title: Real-world scenario
docs.text: Security ticket: set up a practice VM with (1) a shared deploy group, (2) a non-login service account for app files, and (3) a human engineer who may restart only rebash-lab.service with sudo — not full root. Attach proof to the change ticket.

docs.title: Task 1 – Create group, human user, and service account
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab06
set -euo pipefail

sudo groupadd rebash-lab || true

if ! id rebash-alice >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G rebash-lab rebash-alice
fi

if ! id rebash-svc >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sudo useradd --system --home /opt/rebash-lab-svc --shell /usr/sbin/nologin \
    --gid rebash-lab rebash-svc
fi

sudo usermod -aG rebash-lab rebash-alice

id rebash-alice | tee id-alice.txt
id rebash-svc | tee id-svc.txt
getent group rebash-lab | tee group-rebash-lab.txt
grep -E 'rebash-alice|rebash-svc' /etc/passwd | tee passwd-snippet.txt

Expected output

id-alice.txt shows group rebash-lab. id-svc.txt shows nologin shell. group-rebash-lab.txt lists members.

docs.title: Task 2 – Limited sudoers file (file fence + visudo)
docs.text:
Create the sudoers drop-in as a file first:

99-rebash-lab-alice
# REBASH lab — limited sudo for rebash-alice
Defaults:rebash-alice !requiretty
rebash-alice ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl status rebash-lab.service, /bin/systemctl restart rebash-lab.service
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab06
set -euo pipefail

# Save the sudoers file-fence above as ~/rebash-linux/lab06/99-rebash-lab-alice first
test -f 99-rebash-lab-alice
sudo visudo -c -f 99-rebash-lab-alice
sudo install -m 0440 99-rebash-lab-alice /etc/sudoers.d/99-rebash-lab-alice
sudo visudo -c

sudo -u rebash-alice sudo -l | tee sudo-l-alice.txt
grep -F 'systemctl' sudo-l-alice.txt
ls -l /etc/sudoers.d/99-rebash-lab-alice | tee sudoers-mode.txt

Expected output

visudo -c reports syntax OK. sudo-l-alice.txt lists the two systemctl paths — not ALL. File mode is -r--r----- (0440).

docs.title: Task 3 – Negative test and evidence pack
docs.text:
Prove alice is not full root.

Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab06
set -euo pipefail

if sudo -u rebash-alice sudo -n /bin/true 2>sudo-denied.txt; then
  echo "ERROR: unrestricted sudo — abort" >&2
  exit 1
fi
grep -Ei 'not allowed|sorry|denied|password' sudo-denied.txt || test -s sudo-denied.txt

tar -czf identity-evidence.tgz \
  admin-user.txt admin-id.txt \
  id-alice.txt id-svc.txt group-rebash-lab.txt passwd-snippet.txt \
  sudo-l-alice.txt sudo-denied.txt sudoers-mode.txt 99-rebash-lab-alice
ls -l identity-evidence.tgz | tee evidence-ls.txt
test -s identity-evidence.tgz

Expected output

/bin/true with sudo is denied for alice. identity-evidence.tgz is not empty.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
• id rebash-alice shows group rebash-lab
  • id rebash-svc uses a non-login shell
  • /etc/sudoers.d/99-rebash-lab-alice mode is 0440
  • sudo -u rebash-alice sudo -l shows only intended systemctl commands
  • identity-evidence.tgz exists under ~/rebash-linux/lab06

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Error Cause Fix useradd: user already exists Lab re-run Script checks with id; continue visudo: parse error Wrong sudoers syntax Fix file; never install broken drop-in sudo: a password is required NOPASSWD rule missing Check drop-in path; visudo -c Locked out after bad sudoers Edited without visudo Root console / recovery; remove bad file

docs.title: Challenge exercise
docs.text:
Create user rebash-bob, add to rebash-lab, and add a second drop-in allowing only sudo -u rebash-svc /usr/bin/id:

99-rebash-lab-bob
rebash-bob ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/id -u rebash-svc
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab06
set -euo pipefail
if ! id rebash-bob >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash rebash-bob
fi
sudo usermod -aG rebash-lab rebash-bob
sudo visudo -c -f 99-rebash-lab-bob
sudo install -m 0440 99-rebash-lab-bob /etc/sudoers.d/99-rebash-lab-bob
sudo -u rebash-bob sudo -l | tee sudo-l-bob.txt

Expected output

sudo-l-bob.txt shows only the narrow id command for rebash-svc.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Created human and system accounts with correct shells
  • Used usermod -aG safely
  • Installed checked sudoers files; proved allow and deny
  • Saved identity proof suitable for a change ticket

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Terminal
cd ~/rebash-linux/lab06
set -euo pipefail

sudo rm -f /etc/sudoers.d/99-rebash-lab-alice /etc/sudoers.d/99-rebash-lab-bob
sudo visudo -c

sudo userdel -r rebash-alice 2>/dev/null || sudo userdel rebash-alice || true
sudo userdel -r rebash-bob 2>/dev/null || sudo userdel rebash-bob || true
sudo userdel rebash-svc 2>/dev/null || true
sudo groupdel rebash-lab 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Lab completed under ~/rebash-linux/lab06
  • Can explain UID, GID, and why usermod -aG matters
  • Can explain risk of server-wide NOPASSWD:ALL
  • Know when to use a system user with nologin

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. id and getent before change — know current state.
  2. Small files under /etc/sudoers.d/ — mode 0440; one file per role.
  3. visudo -c before and after — syntax check is non-negotiable.
  4. Prove allow and deny — sudo -l plus one command that must fail.
  5. Separate people from services — login shell vs nologin.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Treat sudo access as critical — review in change tickets
  • Never store passwords or API tokens in sudoers
  • Prefer SSH keys for people; disable password login on internet-facing servers (later modules)
  • Keep human accounts separate from service accounts
  • Log privileged use in /var/log/auth.log or journalctl

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using usermod -G without -a

✅ Secondary groups are replaced, not added. Fix: always usermod -aG group user, then id user.

❌ Editing sudoers with vim directly.

✅ One typo can remove sudo for everyone. Fix: use visudo only; keep root console open while testing.

❌ Giving NOPASSWD:ALL for convenience.

✅ Any process running as that user becomes root. Fix: allow only exact command paths.

❌ Deleting users without checking file ownership.

✅ Old files keep the old UID. Fix: find / -user name before userdel.

docs.title: Viewing File Contents
docs.text: Linux provides powerful commands to view, inspect, and monitor file contents. Whether you're reading configuration files, analyzing application logs, or debugging production issues, mastering these commands is essential for every Linux administrator, DevOps Engineer, and Cloud Engineer.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 2: Linux Command Line Essentials → Lesson 5

Difficulty: Beginner

Reading Time: 25 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Linux Command Line Essentials

Lesson: 5 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • View file contents efficiently
  • Read large log files
  • Display specific lines from files
  • Monitor files in real time
  • Compare different file viewing commands
  • Choose the right command for different scenarios

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 Lessons 1–4

docs.title: Why Learn File Viewing Commands?
docs.text:
Linux systems store everything in files.

Examples include:

  • Configuration files
  • Application logs
  • Shell scripts
  • Kubernetes YAML files
  • Docker Compose files
  • Service logs

As a Linux administrator, reading files is one of the most common daily tasks.

docs.title: Sample File
docs.text:
Throughout this lesson we'll use the following file.

Line 1: Linux
Line 2: Docker
Line 3: Kubernetes
Line 4: Terraform
Line 5: Ansible
Line 6: GitLab
Line 7: Jenkins
Line 8: Prometheus
Line 9: Grafana
Line 10: REBASH Academy

docs.title: cat
docs.text:
The cat command displays the complete contents of a file.

Syntax

cat filename

Example

cat notes.txt

Display multiple files

cat file1 file2

Display line numbers

cat -n notes.txt

Useful when viewing:

  • Configuration files
  • Small scripts
  • README files

docs.title: less
docs.text:
less is one of the most useful Linux commands.

Unlike cat, it lets you scroll through large files.

less logfile.log

Navigation

Key Action Space Next Page b Previous Page ↑ ↓ Scroll / Search n Next Match q Quit

Perfect for:

  • System logs
  • Large configuration files
  • Long text files

docs.title: more
docs.text:
Older pager command.

more notes.txt

Displays one screen at a time.

Although still available, most Linux administrators prefer less.

docs.title: head
docs.text:
Display the beginning of a file.

head notes.txt

Default:

First 10 lines

Display first five lines

head -5 notes.txt

Production example

head /var/log/syslog

docs.title: tail
docs.text:
Display the end of a file.

tail notes.txt

Display last five lines

tail -5 notes.txt

Production example

tail /var/log/syslog

docs.title: Real-Time Monitoring
docs.text:
One of the most useful Linux commands.

tail -f /var/log/syslog

Linux continuously displays new lines as they are written.

Widely used for:

  • Application logs
  • Kubernetes logs
  • Web server logs
  • Docker logs

Stop monitoring:

Ctrl + C

docs.title: tac
docs.text:
Reverse of cat.

tac notes.txt

Displays the file from bottom to top.

Useful when newest information is at the end of the file.

docs.title: nl
docs.text:
Display line numbers.

nl notes.txt

Output

1 Linux

2 Docker

3 Kubernetes

Useful when discussing specific lines in configuration files.

docs.title: file
docs.text:
Determine the file type.

file notes.txt

Example output

ASCII text

Check executable

file /bin/ls

docs.title: wc
docs.text:
Count lines, words and characters.

wc notes.txt

Example

10 10 90 notes.txt

Only count lines

wc -l notes.txt

Count words

wc -w notes.txt

docs.title: strings
docs.text:
Display printable text from binary files.

strings binaryfile

Useful when investigating executables.

docs.title: Command Comparison
docs.text: Command Best Used For cat Small files less Large files more Basic paging head Beginning of file tail End of file tail -f Live log monitoring tac Reverse output nl Line numbers file Identify file type wc Count lines and words

docs.title: Production Example
docs.text:
A web application is failing.

Check logs:

tail -50 /var/log/nginx/error.log

Monitor new errors:

tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log

View configuration:

less /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

Verify line numbers:

cat -n /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

This workflow is common during production troubleshooting.

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
These commands are used daily by engineers.

Examples

View Kubernetes YAML

cat deployment.yaml

Read Docker logs

less docker.log

Monitor application

tail -f application.log

Read configuration

less /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Count log entries

wc -l access.log

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Create a file.

cat > commands.txt

Add:

Linux
Docker
Kubernetes
Terraform
Ansible
Git

Press:

Ctrl + D

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Display file.

cat commands.txt

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Display first three lines.

head -3 commands.txt

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Display last two lines.

tail -2 commands.txt

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Display line numbers.

nl commands.txt

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Count lines.

wc -l commands.txt

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Open using less.

less commands.txt

Quit:

q

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Display reverse order.

tac commands.txt

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Common Options Production Example cat Display files -n View configuration less Scroll files Search / Read logs head Beginning -5 Verify headers tail End -10 View recent logs tail Live logs -f Monitor applications nl Line numbers Default Debug configs wc Count -l -w Count log entries file File type Default Verify downloads

docs.text:

Add at least 10 Linux commands.

  • Display the first 5 lines.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use less instead of cat for large files.
  • Use tail -f for monitoring logs.
  • Use head to inspect file headers.
  • Use wc to quickly summarize file contents.
  • Learn keyboard shortcuts in less.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using cat on huge log files.

✅ Use:

less logfile.log

or

tail logfile.log

❌ Opening multi-GB log files in editors.

✅ Use:

tail

head

less

❌ Forgetting to quit less.

✅ Use:

q

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Displaying file contents
  • Reading large files
  • Viewing file headers and footers
  • Monitoring logs in real time
  • Counting lines
  • Identifying file types
  • Choosing the right command for different situations

These commands form the foundation of Linux troubleshooting and system administration.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• cat is ideal for small files.
  • less is the preferred tool for large files.
  • head displays the beginning of a file.
  • tail displays the end of a file.
  • tail -f monitors log files in real time.
  • wc counts lines, words, and characters.

docs.title: wget — Downloading Files from the Command Line
wget — Downloading Files from the Command Line
docs.text: wget (Web Get) is a powerful command-line utility used to download files from web servers using HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP. It is designed for reliable, non-interactive downloading, making it ideal for automation, scripts, software installation, backups, and mirroring websites. Linux administrators, DevOps engineers, Cloud Architects, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) frequently use wget to retrieve files and automate downloads.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 8: Networking → Lesson 10

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 65 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Networking

Lesson: 10 of 13

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand the wget command
  • Download files from the Internet
  • Resume interrupted downloads
  • Download files in the background
  • Mirror websites
  • Authenticate downloads
  • Automate file downloads
  • Troubleshoot download issues

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 – Linux Command Line Essentials
  • Module 3 – Text Processing
  • Module 4 – File Management
  • Module 5 – Users and Groups
  • Module 6 – Process Management
  • Module 7 – Package Management
  • Module 8 Lessons 1–9

docs.title: Why Learn wget?
docs.text:
Imagine:

  • Downloading an ISO image.
  • Fetching application binaries.
  • Downloading backup files.
  • Mirroring a documentation website.
  • Automating software installation.

wget is the preferred tool for these tasks because it is reliable and script-friendly.

docs.title: What is wget?
docs.text:
wget stands for:

Web Get

It is a non-interactive download utility that supports:

  • HTTP
  • HTTPS
  • FTP

It is commonly used for:

  • Downloading files
  • Automation scripts
  • Software installation
  • Website mirroring
  • Scheduled downloads

docs.title: How wget Works
docs.text:
Client
   │
   ▼
HTTP Request
   │
   ▼
Web Server
   │
   ▼
File Download
   │
   ▼
Local System

docs.title: Basic Download
docs.text:
Download a file.

wget https://example.com/file.zip

The file is saved using its original filename.

docs.title: Save with a Different Name
docs.text:
wget -O backup.zip \
https://example.com/file.zip

docs.title: Resume an Interrupted Download
docs.text:
wget -c https://example.com/file.zip

The -c option resumes downloading from where it stopped.

docs.title: Download in the Background
docs.text:
wget -b https://example.com/file.zip

Check the log:

tail -f wget-log

docs.title: Limit Download Speed
docs.text:
wget --limit-rate=500k \
https://example.com/file.zip

Useful when sharing network bandwidth.

docs.title: Download Multiple Files
docs.text:
Create a file named urls.txt:

https://example.com/file1.zip
https://example.com/file2.zip
https://example.com/file3.zip

Download all files.

wget -i urls.txt

docs.title: Mirror a Website
docs.text:
wget --mirror \
https://example.com

Commonly used for:

  • Documentation
  • Static websites
  • Offline browsing

docs.title: Recursive Download
docs.text:
wget -r \
https://example.com/docs

Downloads linked content recursively.

docs.title: Download Without Parent Directories
docs.text:
wget -np -r \
https://example.com/docs

The -np option prevents ascending to parent directories.

docs.title: Download with Authentication
docs.text:
Basic Authentication:

wget \
--user=username \
--password=password \
https://example.com/file.zip

Avoid placing passwords directly on the command line in shared or production environments because they may be visible in process listings.

docs.title: Ignore Certificate Validation
docs.text:
wget --no-check-certificate \
https://example.com

Warning: Use this only for testing. It disables TLS certificate validation and should not be used in production.

docs.title: Continue Existing Downloads
docs.text:
If a file already exists:

wget -c \
https://example.com/file.iso

This prevents restarting large downloads from the beginning.

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Basic download.

wget https://example.com/file.zip

Resume download.

wget -c https://example.com/file.zip

Background download.

wget -b https://example.com/file.zip

Mirror website.

wget --mirror https://example.com

Download list of files.

wget -i urls.txt

docs.title: Real Production Examples
docs.text:
Download Kubernetes CLI.

wget https://dl.k8s.io/release/<version>/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl

Download Terraform.

Download an application backup.

wget https://backup.example.com/db.sql.gz

Mirror documentation.

wget --mirror https://docs.example.com

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
wget is commonly used for:

  • Software deployment
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Backup retrieval
  • Infrastructure automation
  • Cloud provisioning
  • Configuration downloads
  • Offline documentation
  • Scheduled maintenance

It is a reliable tool for unattended downloads in production environments.

https://example.com

Monitor progress.

tail -f wget-log

https://example.com/file1.zip
https://example.com/file2.zip

Download all files.

https://example.com/file.zip

https://example.com

https://example.com/docs

docs.title: Command Deep Dive
docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example wget URL Download file Software installation wget -O Save with custom filename Backup download wget -c Resume download Large ISO files wget -b Background download Automation wget -i Download file list Batch downloads wget --mirror Mirror website Documentation backup wget -r Recursive download Static website retrieval wget --limit-rate Limit bandwidth Shared networks

docs.title: wget vs curl
docs.text:
Feature wget curl Download Files ✅ Excellent ✅ Resume Downloads ✅ Excellent Basic Recursive Downloads ✅ ❌ Website Mirroring ✅ ❌ REST API Testing Limited ✅ Excellent Multiple HTTP Methods Limited ✅

Use:

  • wget for downloading files and websites.
  • curl for APIs, HTTP requests, and web service testing.

docs.title: Common wget Errors
docs.text: Error Possible Cause Unable to resolve host DNS problem Connection refused Service unavailable 404 Not Found File does not exist 403 Forbidden Access denied SSL certificate error Certificate validation failed Connection timed out Network or firewall issue

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A CI/CD pipeline fails while downloading a deployment package.

Command:

wget https://repo.example.com/app.tar.gz

Error:

Unable to resolve host

Investigation:

Verify DNS.

ping repo.example.com

Check DNS resolution.

getent hosts repo.example.com

After correcting the DNS configuration:

wget https://repo.example.com/app.tar.gz

The package downloads successfully, allowing the deployment to continue.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use -c when downloading large files.
  • Use -O to save files with meaningful names.
  • Use -b for long-running downloads.
  • Limit download speed when sharing bandwidth.
  • Verify downloaded files using checksums when available.
  • Avoid exposing credentials on the command line.
  • Use HTTPS whenever possible.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Restarting large downloads instead of resuming them.

✅ Prefer resuming them rather than restarting large downloads.

❌ Downloading files without verifying their integrity.

✅ Avoid this mistake: downloading files without verifying their integrity.

❌ Using --no-check-certificate in production.

✅ Avoid using --no-check-certificate in production when a safer approach exists.

❌ Storing passwords directly in scripts.

✅ Avoid this mistake: storing passwords directly in scripts.

In this lesson, you learned:

  • The wget command

  • Production download automation

wget is one of the most reliable tools for downloading files in Linux. Its ability to resume downloads, work in the background, and automate file retrieval makes it indispensable for system administration, DevOps workflows, and infrastructure automation.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:

  • Use -c to resume interrupted downloads.

docs.title: Wildcards and Globbing
docs.text: Wildcards and globbing allow you to work with multiple files using simple patterns instead of typing each filename individually. They are essential for Linux administration, shell scripting, DevOps automation, and production operations.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 2: Linux Command Line Essentials → Lesson 7

Difficulty: Beginner

Reading Time: 25 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Linux Command Line Essentials

Lesson: 7 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand what wildcards are
  • Learn how Bash performs globbing
  • Use *, ?, and []
  • Match files using character ranges
  • Use brace expansion
  • Combine wildcard patterns
  • Use wildcards safely in production

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting this lesson, complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals
  • Module 2 Lessons 1–6

docs.title: Why Learn Wildcards?
docs.text:
Imagine you have thousands of files.

Instead of typing:

rm app1.log

rm app2.log

rm app3.log

rm app4.log

You simply type:

rm *.log

One command.

Thousands of files.

This is the power of wildcards.

docs.title: What is Globbing?
docs.text:
Globbing is the process performed by the Bash shell to expand wildcard patterns into matching filenames.

Example:

You type:

ls *.txt

Bash converts it to:

ls notes.txt report.txt users.txt

before executing the command.

Notice:

The shell expands the pattern, not the ls command.

docs.title: Common Wildcards
docs.text: Wildcard Meaning * Zero or more characters ? Exactly one character [] Match one character from a set {} Brace expansion [a-z] Character range

docs.title: The * Wildcard
docs.text:
Matches zero or more characters.

Example files:

notes.txt

report.txt

linux.txt

config.yaml

backup.log

Display all text files:

ls *.txt

Output:

linux.txt

notes.txt

report.txt

Display all log files.

ls *.log

Display every file.

ls *

docs.title: The ? Wildcard
docs.text:
Matches exactly one character.

Example files:

a.txt

b.txt

ab.txt

abc.txt

Command:

ls ?.txt

Matches:

a.txt

b.txt

Does NOT match:

ab.txt

docs.title: Character Sets
docs.text:
Use square brackets.

Example:

app1.log

app2.log

app3.log

app4.log

Command:

ls app[12].log

Output:

app1.log

app2.log

docs.title: Character Ranges
docs.text:
Example:

ls file[1-5].txt

Matches:

file1.txt

file2.txt

file3.txt

file4.txt

file5.txt

Alphabet range:

ls [a-f]*

Matches:

apple.txt

config.txt

docker.txt

docs.title: Negation
docs.text:
Exclude characters.

ls [!0-9]*

Matches files not starting with numbers.

docs.title: Brace Expansion
docs.text:
Brace expansion is not globbing.

It generates multiple strings.

Example:

mkdir project{1,2,3}

Creates:

project1

project2

project3

Create files:

touch server{1..5}.log

Creates:

server1.log

server2.log

server3.log

server4.log

server5.log

Alphabet expansion:

touch file{A..E}.txt

Creates:

fileA.txt

fileB.txt

fileC.txt

fileD.txt

fileE.txt

docs.title: Combining Wildcards
docs.text:
Example:

ls project*.txt

Matches:

project1.txt

project_backup.txt

project-final.txt

Another example:

ls server?.log

Matches:

server1.log

server2.log

server3.log

Does NOT match:

server10.log

docs.title: Hidden Files
docs.text:
Remember:

*

does not match hidden files.

Hidden files begin with:

.

Display hidden files.

ls -a

Match hidden files.

ls .*

docs.title: Using Wildcards with Commands
docs.text:
Copy all YAML files.

cp *.yaml backup/

Delete all log files.

rm *.log

Move all shell scripts.

mv *.sh scripts/

Count all text files.

wc -l *.txt

docs.title: Preview Before Deleting
docs.text:
Never run:

rm *.log

without checking.

Preview first:

ls *.log

Then:

rm *.log

This simple habit prevents accidental deletions.

docs.title: Wildcards vs Regular Expressions
docs.text:
Many beginners confuse them.

Wildcards Regular Expressions Used by Shell Used by Programs Expand filenames Match text patterns *.txt .*\.txt Simple More Powerful

We'll cover Regular Expressions later in the course.

docs.title: Real Production Example
docs.text:
Backup Kubernetes YAML files.

cp *.yaml backup/

Delete old logs.

rm *.old

Archive reports.

tar -czf reports.tar.gz *.csv

Move certificates.

mv *.crt certificates/

docs.title: Production Perspective
docs.text:
DevOps engineers frequently use wildcards.

Examples:

Docker:

docker cp *.sql database:/

Git:

git add *.yaml

Terraform:

ls *.tf

Kubernetes:

kubectl apply -f *.yaml

Automation becomes much easier with wildcard patterns.

docs.text:

docs.text:

ls *.log

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Match single character.

ls server?.log

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Create multiple files.

touch backup{1..5}.sql

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
List SQL files.

ls *.sql

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Create alphabet files.

touch demo{A..D}.txt

docs.title: Task 9
docs.text:
Display only demo files.

ls demo*

docs.text:

config-old.yaml

  2. Display only application logs.
  3. Delete only backup files.
  4. Copy all YAML files to a backup directory.
  5. Display files beginning with "config".

docs.text:

server3.log

  • List all .txt files.
  • List all .log files.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Preview wildcard matches with ls before using destructive commands.
  • Use quotes when you want to prevent shell expansion.
  • Prefer specific patterns over broad ones.
  • Combine wildcards with other commands for automation.
  • Test wildcard commands in a lab before running them in production.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Running:

✅ Use:

rm *

without checking the current directory.

Always verify first:

pwd

ls

❌ Assuming * matches hidden files.

✅ It does not.

Use:

ls -a

ls .*

❌ Confusing brace expansion with globbing.

✅ Brace expansion creates filenames.

Globbing matches existing filenames.

  3. How do wildcards simplify DevOps automation?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson, you learned:

  • Wildcards
  • Globbing
  • *
  • ?
  • Character sets
  • Character ranges
  • Brace expansion
  • Production-safe wildcard usage

Wildcards are one of the most powerful features of the Linux shell. Mastering them will help you work faster, write cleaner scripts, and automate repetitive tasks with confidence.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Bash performs wildcard expansion before executing commands.
  • * matches zero or more characters.
  • ? matches exactly one character.
  • [] matches characters from a specified set or range.
  • Brace expansion generates multiple filenames.
  • Always preview wildcard matches before performing destructive operations.

docs.title: YUM (Yellowdog Updater Modified) — Package Management for Legacy RHEL Systems
YUM (Yellowdog Updater Modified) — Package Management for Legacy RHEL Systems
docs.text: YUM (Yellowdog Updater Modified) is the traditional package manager used by older versions of Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), CentOS, Oracle Linux, and other RPM-based Linux distributions. Although modern distributions use DNF as the default package manager, YUM remains important because many enterprise environments continue to run legacy Linux servers. Understanding YUM is essential for maintaining older production systems and supporting enterprise infrastructure.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Linux Mastery → Module 7: Package Management → Lesson 3

Difficulty: Beginner → Intermediate

Reading Time: 50 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Linux Mastery

Module: Package Management

Lesson: 3 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand YUM
  • Install and remove packages
  • Update software
  • Search package repositories
  • Manage repositories
  • View package history
  • Compare YUM and DNF
  • Maintain legacy Linux systems

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Module 1 – Linux Fundamentals

docs.title: Why Learn YUM?
docs.text:
Although DNF has replaced YUM on modern systems, many organizations still run:

  • RHEL 7
  • CentOS 7
  • Oracle Linux 7
  • Legacy enterprise servers

As a Linux administrator or DevOps engineer, you'll often encounter environments where YUM is still the standard package manager.

docs.title: What is YUM?
docs.text:
YUM stands for:

Yellowdog Updater Modified

It is a package manager for RPM-based Linux distributions.

YUM works with:

.rpm

packages and automatically:

  • Resolves dependencies
  • Downloads packages
  • Installs software
  • Removes packages
  • Updates software

docs.title: Package Management Workflow
docs.text:
YUM Command
      │
      ▼
Repository
      │
      ▼
Download Package
      │
      ▼
Resolve Dependencies
      │
      ▼
Install Package
      │
      ▼
Ready to Use

docs.title: Check for Available Updates
docs.text:
sudo yum check-update

This refreshes package metadata and displays available package updates.

docs.title: Install a Package
docs.text:
Install NGINX.

sudo yum install nginx

Install multiple packages.

sudo yum install git curl vim

YUM automatically installs required dependencies.

docs.title: Update Packages
docs.text:
Update all installed packages.

sudo yum update

Update a specific package.

sudo yum update nginx

docs.title: Remove a Package
docs.text:
sudo yum remove nginx

Unused dependencies may remain and should be reviewed separately.

docs.title: Search for Packages
docs.text:
yum search nginx

Example:

nginx

nginx-all-modules

nginx-filesystem

docs.title: View Package Information
docs.text:
yum info nginx

Displays:

  • Version
  • Repository
  • Description
  • Size
  • Architecture

docs.title: List Installed Packages
docs.text:
yum list installed

Find a package.

yum list installed | grep nginx

docs.title: List Enabled Repositories
docs.text:
yum repolist

Example:

base

extras

updates

docs.title: Clean Package Cache
docs.text:
Remove cached packages.

sudo yum clean packages

Remove all cached metadata and packages.

sudo yum clean all

Rebuild the cache.

sudo yum makecache

docs.title: View Package History
docs.text:
Display transaction history.

yum history

View a specific transaction.

yum history info <ID>

Undo a transaction.

sudo yum history undo <ID>

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
Install package.

sudo yum install nginx

Update packages.

sudo yum update

Remove package.

sudo yum remove nginx

Search package.

yum search nginx

Package information.

yum info nginx

List repositories.

yum repolist

docs.text:

sudo yum install git

sudo yum update

sudo yum install docker

docs.text:
YUM is commonly found on:

  • RHEL 7
  • CentOS 7
  • Oracle Linux 7
  • Older enterprise Linux servers
  • Legacy production environments

Although DNF is now the default package manager on newer releases, many enterprise systems continue to rely on YUM.

docs.text: Command Purpose Production Example yum install Install packages Software deployment yum update Update packages Security patching yum remove Remove packages Cleanup yum search Search packages Package discovery yum info Package details Verification yum repolist View repositories Repository management yum history View transactions Auditing yum clean all Clear cache Maintenance

docs.title: YUM vs DNF
docs.text: Feature YUM DNF Default On RHEL/CentOS 7 RHEL/Rocky/AlmaLinux 8+ and Fedora Package Format .rpm .rpm Dependency Resolution Good Improved Performance Good Faster and more efficient Transaction History ✅ ✅ Active Development Maintenance only Active development

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario

A system administrator attempts to install Docker.

sudo yum install docker

Error:

No package docker available.

Investigation:

yum repolist

The required repository is not enabled.

After enabling the correct repository:

sudo yum makecache

sudo yum install docker

The installation completes successfully.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Apply package updates regularly.
  • Use only trusted repositories.
  • Clean the package cache periodically.
  • Review package dependencies before installation.
  • Plan migrations from YUM-based systems to DNF-supported platforms where appropriate.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using outdated repositories.

✅ Avoid using outdated repositories when a safer approach exists.

❌ Ignoring security updates.

✅ Always review security updates.

❌ Installing packages from untrusted sources.

✅ Avoid this mistake: installing packages from untrusted sources.

❌ Assuming every RPM-based distribution uses DNF.

✅ Older enterprise systems may still rely on YUM.

In this lesson, you learned:

YUM remains an important tool for maintaining older RPM-based Linux systems. While DNF has become the standard package manager on modern Red Hat-based distributions, understanding YUM enables you to support legacy enterprise environments and smoothly transition to newer platforms.

docs.title: Capstone Project 5 — Automate User Provisioning with Bash
Capstone Project 5 — Automate User Provisioning with Bash
docs.text: Managing Linux users manually becomes inefficient and error-prone as organizations grow. System administrators often need to provision dozens or even hundreds of users while ensuring consistent usernames, groups, home directories, SSH access, passwords, and permissions. In this capstone project, you'll build a production-ready Bash automation script that provisions Linux users from a CSV file, applies security policies, generates reports, and logs every action. This project demonstrates real-world Linux automation using Bash scripting.

docs.title: Capstone Project 2 — Configure a Bastion Host
Capstone Project 2 — Configure a Bastion Host
docs.text: A Bastion Host (also called a Jump Server or Jump Box) is a hardened Linux server that acts as the single secure entry point for administrators to access private infrastructure. Instead of exposing every production server to the Internet, only the Bastion Host is publicly accessible, while all other servers remain inside a private network. In this capstone project, you'll build a production-ready Bastion Host with SSH hardening, firewall protection, user management, auditing, monitoring, and logging.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Build a secure Bastion Host that provides controlled administrative access to private Linux servers.

Capstone Project 3 — Deploy a Git Server
docs.text: Git is the industry-standard version control system used to manage source code, Infrastructure as Code (IaC), documentation, automation scripts, and configuration files. While cloud-hosted Git platforms such as GitHub and GitLab are widely used, many organizations deploy self-hosted Git servers for greater control, security, compliance, and integration with internal infrastructure. docs.title: Capstone Project 7 — Harden an Ubuntu Server
Capstone Project 7 — Harden an Ubuntu Server
docs.text: A default Ubuntu installation is designed to be functional, but it is not fully optimized for production security. Before deploying a server into production, organizations apply security hardening to reduce the attack surface, enforce strong authentication, secure network access, enable auditing, and implement continuous monitoring. In this capstone project, you'll transform a default Ubuntu Server into a production-ready hardened server by applying industry best practices inspired by CIS Benchmarks and enterprise security standards.

Capstone Project 6 — Build a Linux Server Baseline
docs.text: A Linux Server Baseline is a standardized operating system configuration that serves as the foundation for all production Linux servers. Instead of configuring every server manually, organizations create a baseline containing approved security settings, system packages, user accounts, logging, monitoring, networking, and operational standards. Every new server starts from this baseline, ensuring consistency, security, compliance, and easier maintenance. In this capstone project, you'll build a production-ready Linux Server Baseline suitable for enterprise environments.

docs.text: Welcome to the final capstone project of the Linux Mastery course. This challenge simulates a real production incident where multiple failures occur simultaneously. Your objective is not only to restore services but also to investigate the root cause, validate the recovery, document your findings, and implement preventive improvements. This project combines everything you've learned throughout the course and mirrors the responsibilities of Linux Administrators, DevOps Engineers, Platform Engineers, Cloud Architects, and Site Reliability Engineers (SREs).

docs.title: Phase 1 — Install Linux

Install Ubuntu Server.

Verify installation.

hostnamectl

ip addr

ip route

sudo adduser adminuser

Grant sudo.

Verify.

id adminuser

docs.title: Phase 4 — Secure SSH
docs.text:
Edit configuration.

sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Recommended settings:

PermitRootLogin no

PasswordAuthentication no

PubkeyAuthentication yes

X11Forwarding no

MaxAuthTries 3

Restart SSH.

sudo systemctl restart ssh

docs.title: Phase 5 — Configure Firewall
docs.text:
Install UFW.

sudo apt install ufw

Allow SSH.

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH

Allow HTTPS.

sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

Allow HTTP.

sudo ufw allow 80/tcp

Enable firewall.

sudo ufw enable

Verify.

sudo ufw status

docs.title: Phase 6 — Install Nginx

sudo apt install nginx

Start service.

sudo systemctl enable nginx

sudo systemctl start nginx

Verify.

systemctl status nginx

Test.

Linux Mastery

curl localhost

Verify.

curl https://your-domain

journalctl -u nginx

Access logs.

tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log

tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log

logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.conf

docs.title: Phase 10 — Configure Monitoring

CPU.

top

Memory.

free -h

Disk.

df -h

Processes.

ps aux

systemctl status nginx

sudo tar -czf nginx-backup.tar.gz /etc/nginx

Synchronize.

rsync -av /var/www /backup

Verify.

ls -lh

sudo apt install fail2ban

Start.

sudo systemctl enable fail2ban

Verify.

fail2ban-client status

Review listening ports.

ss -tuln

Remove unnecessary packages.

sudo apt autoremove

Apply updates.

sudo apt update

sudo apt upgrade

docs.title: Access Control Lists (ACLs) — Controlling Network Traffic
docs.text: An Access Control List (ACL) is a set of rules used by routers, switches, and firewalls to permit or deny network traffic based on defined criteria such as source IP address, destination IP address, protocol, and port number. ACLs are one of the most fundamental security mechanisms in networking and are used to enforce security policies, restrict unauthorised access, and control packet forwarding. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Network Engineer should understand ACLs.

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
Networking Mastery → Module 7: NAT & Firewalls → Lesson 5

Difficulty: Intermediate

Reading Time: 100 Minutes

Course Progress

Course: Networking Mastery

Module: NAT & Firewalls

Lesson: 5 of 10

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand Access Control Lists (ACLs)
  • Differentiate Standard and Extended ACLs
  • Understand packet filtering
  • Learn inbound and outbound ACLs
  • Understand ACL processing order
  • Apply ACLs in enterprise and cloud environments
  • Troubleshoot ACL-related connectivity issues

  • PAT

docs.title: Why Learn ACLs?
docs.text:
Imagine a company wants:

  • Employees to access the Internet
  • HR servers accessible only by HR staff
  • Database servers protected from public access

Without ACLs:

Everyone

Can Access

Everything

❌

With ACLs:

Only

Authorized Users

↓

Allowed

docs.title: What is an ACL?
docs.text:
An Access Control List is an ordered list of rules that determines whether network traffic is:

Permit

OR

Deny

Each packet is checked against the ACL before being forwarded.

docs.title: ACL Workflow
docs.text:
Packet Arrives

↓

Check ACL

↓

Rule Match?

↓

Permit

↓

Forward Packet

OR

Deny

↓

Drop Packet

docs.title: Why Use ACLs?
docs.text:
ACLs provide:

  • Network Security
  • Traffic Filtering
  • Access Control
  • Policy Enforcement
  • Reduced Attack Surface
  • Segmentation

docs.title: Types of ACLs
docs.text:
The two primary ACL types are:

  • Standard ACL
  • Extended ACL

docs.title: Standard ACL
docs.text:
A Standard ACL filters traffic based only on:

Source IP Address

Example:

Allow

192.168.10.0/24

It cannot filter based on:

  • Destination IP
  • Protocol
  • Port Number

docs.title: Extended ACL
docs.text:
An Extended ACL can filter using:

  • Source IP
  • Destination IP
  • Protocol
  • Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Port
  • User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Port
  • Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP)

Example:

Allow

HTTPS

To

Web Server

Extended ACLs provide much finer control.

docs.title: Permit and Deny
docs.text:
ACL rules are based on two actions:

Permit

Traffic is allowed.

or

Deny

Traffic is blocked.

docs.title: Implicit Deny
docs.text:
Every ACL ends with an invisible rule:

Deny All

If traffic does not match any permit rule:

Packet

Dropped

This is known as the implicit deny.

docs.title: ACL Processing Order
docs.text:
ACLs are evaluated:

Top

↓

Bottom

The first matching rule is applied.

Example:

Rule 1

Permit

↓

Rule 2

Deny

If Rule 1 matches, Rule 2 is never evaluated.

docs.title: Inbound ACL
docs.text:
Applied to:

Incoming Traffic

Workflow:

Packet Arrives

↓

ACL

↓

Routing Decision

If denied, the packet is discarded before routing.

docs.title: Outbound ACL
docs.text:
Applied to:

Outgoing Traffic

Workflow:

Routing Decision

↓

ACL

↓

Forward Packet

The packet is filtered after the routing decision but before leaving the interface.

docs.title: Example Standard ACL
docs.text:
Requirement:

Allow only:

192.168.10.0/24

All other sources:

Denied

docs.title: Example Extended ACL
docs.text:
Requirement:

Allow HTTPS:

TCP

443

to:

Web Server

Block everything else.

docs.title: Enterprise Example
docs.text:
Company:

Users

↓

Router

↓

ACL

↓

Database Server

Only:

Application Servers

↓

Database

Direct user access is denied.

docs.title: Branch Office Example
docs.text:
Branch Users:

Internet

↓

Allowed

Access to:

Head Office

Finance Server

↓

Denied

ACLs enforce organisational security policies.

docs.title: Cloud Perspective
docs.text:
Cloud providers implement ACL-like functionality through:

  • Network ACLs
  • Route-Based Filtering
  • Security Policies

ACLs can control traffic between:

  • Subnets
  • Virtual Networks
  • Internet Gateways

docs.title: Kubernetes Perspective
docs.text:
Kubernetes uses Network Policies to control communication between Pods.

Although implemented differently, Network Policies serve a similar purpose to ACLs by controlling which workloads can communicate.

docs.title: Linux Perspective
docs.text:
Linux uses firewall frameworks to implement packet filtering.

Display nftables rules.

sudo nft list ruleset

Display iptables rules.

sudo iptables -L -n -v

Allow SSH using iptables.

sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

Block ICMP using iptables.

sudo iptables -A INPUT -p icmp -j DROP

docs.title: ACL Packet Flow
docs.text:
Client

↓

Router

↓

ACL

↓

Permit?

↓

Yes

↓

Server

If denied:

Packet

docs.title: API Gateways — Managing and Securing APIs in Modern Microservices
docs.text: An API Gateway is a centralized entry point that receives, processes, secures, and routes API requests to backend services. Instead of clients communicating directly with multiple microservices, they communicate with a single API Gateway that handles authentication, authorization, routing, rate limiting, request transformation, logging, monitoring, caching, and API versioning. API Gateways are a core component of modern microservices, Kubernetes, cloud-native applications, and DevOps platforms. Every DevOps Engineer, Platform Engineer, SRE, Cloud Engineer, and Cloud Architect should understand API Gateway architecture and operation.

docs.title: APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) — Understanding Self-Assigned IP Addresses
docs.text: Have you ever noticed an IP address beginning with 169.254.x.x and wondered why it was assigned? This is known as APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing). APIPA is a feature built into modern operating systems that automatically assigns an IP address when a DHCP server is unavailable. While APIPA enables basic communication between nearby devices on the same network segment, it also serves as an important troubleshooting indicator. Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, Cloud Architect, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer (SRE), and Network Engineer should understand APIPA and its role in network diagnostics.

Course Progress

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
After completing this lesson, you'll be able to:

  • Understand what APIPA is
  • Identify APIPA addresses
  • Explain why APIPA is assigned
  • Understand DHCP failure scenarios

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete:

  • Binary Numbers
  • IPv4 Address Structure
  • IPv4 Classes
